decisions.reason: Keep Abacha as a reviewed but unallocated cassava-strip candidate. Nigerian studies distinguish the product from fufu and garri and describe dried strips rehydrated for Abacha Ncha. A French-facing Canadian retailer lists Abacha by that name, but it does not establish a Quebec-specific label or clarify the product state; other sources span wet slices, dried strips, rehydrated strips, and the prepared salad. Do not add an active row, aliases, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions until the exact product state and Quebec French display are resolved. Keep Abacha separate from cassava flour, tapioca, gari, lafun, Pupuru, attiéké, Placali, fufu, and the prepared Abacha Ncha dish.

Keep Abacha unallocated. The standards-title evidence narrows one product class to dried shredded cassava and provides the French wording manioc râpé séché (Abacha); Canadian listings also describe dried strips. The French-facing Canadian storefront listing remains state-unspecified and no Québec-specific product label or community terminology source was found. Retain the distinction among wet/dry strips, rehydrated strips, and Abacha Ncha; add no active row, alias, form, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

decisions.reason: The French display spelling allulose is supported by OQLF biochemical usage and a Québec retailer ingredient statement. Keep the active reference held because the reviewed sources do not determine Canadian status for the exact food-grade specification/process and intended use. The sweetener-list search is not an all-purpose authorization, prohibition, or novelty determination. No alias, form, density, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution is added.

Rechecked current Canadian public materials. The reviewed sweetener, completed novel-food, and non-novel lists contain no allulose/psicose match, but absence is not an approval, prohibition, or novelty determination. A Natural Health Products Database record lists D-allulose as a non-medicinal ingredient in a licensed NHP; it does not determine a conventional-food sweetening use. The candidate still lacks one selected product specification, manufacturing process, and intended food use/level. Keep it held and request a written product-specific Food Directorate determination only after that dossier is defined; no inquiry was sent. Add no active reference, alias, form, recipe link, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Hold barley meal as a research candidate. Canadian product/classification sources establish that barley meal exists, but no exact Québec French product display or precise boundary against active barley flour is supported. Do not add an English-only identity or infer gruau/semoule wording.

Keep barley meal unresolved. Canadian sources use the phrase for both ground whole barley and cross-cut whole-barley pieces. The French retailer wording farine d’orge is used for a finished-food ingredient and collides with the OQLF-supported barley-flour term; another Québec bread label uses orge finement concassée for cracked barley. No exact French display for a standalone barley-meal product is supported. Add no row, alias, form, recipe link, or numeric behavior.

The eCFR definition narrows a U.S. soluble-fiber health-claim use of barley meal and distinguishes it from sieved barley meal. It does not resolve consumer identity, particle-size or grind boundary, Québec French display, or overlap with the active whole-barley-flour identity. Keep this research candidate unresolved and add no active reference, alias, form, measure, or substitution.

R1083 confirms generic historical human culinary use of barley meal in two recipe contexts, but neither recipe defines a transferable milling class. The existing U.S. claim-specific definition also does not establish a general boundary against whole barley flour and barley grits, and no reviewed source supports a distinct Québec French display. Keep this candidate inactive; add no reference, alias, form, measurement, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Keep pastirma/basturma out of the active picker and retain only a ledger candidate for the narrower Québec-listed beef product. MAPAQ uses the spellings basterma and pastirma for salted-and-dried beef charcuterie; the Québec producer pairs basturma and pastirma for one beef product; the Turkish standard applies pastırma to cattle, water buffalo, and camel. The unqualified names therefore cannot safely route to a beef-only identity. A provisional candidate scope would be the producer’s named beef product with provisional French display pastirma de bœuf; do not imply that it covers all pastırma/basturma, and do not alias pastrami, charqui, cecina, jerky, biltong, bresaola, or tasajo. The producer’s approximately 50 g listing remains product-specific source evidence, not a reusable measure. No active row, alias, form, measure, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported.

It is a blend, not a standalone pure-bracken-starch package or Québec-origin label.

sources.title: Fun Foods Canada, About us and terms of service
sources.locator: Service-area and shipping statements, paragraphs 432 and 450–451.
sources.supports: The seller says it serves customers across Canada and ships orders from near Barrie, Ontario. This establishes distribution context, not Québec-origin labelling or Québec-preferred product terminology.

decisions.reason: Hold pure bracken-rhizome starch as a distinct ingredient candidate. MAFF and the primary Pteridium aquilinum study support the source-specific starch identity, while current Canadian warabi-ko listings are composite blends and the OQLF source supports plant terminology only. No standalone Canadian pure-starch package with a Québec French product name was established, and no bundled recipe line creates immediate demand. Keep warabi-ko, warabiko, bracken flour, and broad fern-starch wording off active names and aliases; keep the candidate separate from fiddleheads, lotus-root starch, kudzu starch, sweet-potato starch, and tapioca. Add no active reference, alias, form, measurement, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution until a current package identifies pure bracken starch and supports its product name.

decisions.reason: Keep the Cuban tasajo gap unallocated. A Cuban regional source and historical scholarship document Cuban food use, while Mexican dictionary and current Oaxaca sources document additional tasajo products. A Cuban-only active row would become the sole result for bare tasajo, and no Quebec tasajo-specific French product name was found. Do not add aliases to charqui, cecina, jerky, or another dried-meat identity; do not activate a regional identity, form, measure, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution until regional picker behavior and Quebec naming are resolved.

sources.supports: Bilingual Cultured/de culture, Unsalted/non salé, and Salted/salé labels and the cited conditions. Labelling conditions do not establish recipe equivalence.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Grade Compendium: Volume 4 — Dairy Products
sources.locator: Butter grade requirements; cultured-butter flavor description.
sources.supports: Grade Canada 1 cultured butter has a slightly acidulous typical/desirable flavor; this is quality guidance, not a universal acidity or taste measurement.

decisions.reason: Cultured butter is a distinct named product, but the bundled corpus has no ingredient demand and the reviewed sources do not establish one universal salt/fat formulation. Keep it inactive; do not alias to unsalted butter, ghee, or beurre doux.

sources.title: Tradin Organic, Watermelon Seeds
sources.locator: Current supplier portfolio; product details and available product states.
sources.supports: Separately lists whole kernels, milled watermelon seed flour, defatted protein powder, and seed butter; gives China as origin. This is supplier portfolio evidence, not a Canadian retail package, French label, grind specification, or proof of identical oil content across products.

sources.title: Mello et al., Mineral, Nutritional, and Phytochemical Composition and Baking Properties of Teff and Watermelon Seed Flours
sources.locator: Primary research, 2023; whole-seed flour and pomace/defatted flour definitions and food formulations.
sources.supports: Distinguishes whole watermelon-seed flour from pomace/defatted flour and tests study-specific food formulations. It does not establish a household measure, Québec label, or universal substitution.

sources.title: Płóciennik et al., Preliminary Data of the Nutritive, Antioxidative, and Functional Properties of Watermelon Flour and Seed Protein Concentrate
sources.locator: Molecules 30(1), 181; 2025; commercial flour and separately prepared defatted sample.
sources.supports: Discusses commercial seed flour and a laboratory defatted-flour preparation, supporting a research process boundary. The solvent treatment does not establish a standalone Canadian/Québec product or a catalog form.

decisions.reason: Research distinguishes defatted watermelon-seed pomace flour from the milled-seed base identity, but no reviewed Canadian/Québec standalone product establishes its market-facing name or catalog allocation.

sources.title: OQLF, gruau (Québec cooked dish) (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition of the Québec consumer meaning
sources.supports: Defines gruau as a cooked oatmeal dish; it does not establish a dry oat-meal milling product or its Québec French name.

sources.title: Arva Flour Mill, Scotch Oatmeal 650g
sources.locator: Product description
sources.supports: Defines this named product as whole oat groats ground into coarse meal and distinguishes it from steamed, flattened rolled oats; does not define generic oatmeal.

sources.title: Bob's Red Mill, Scottish Oatmeal
sources.locator: Product description
sources.supports: Describes the named Scottish product as stone-ground rather than steamed and rolled; product-specific process evidence only.

sources.title: Bob's Red Mill Canada, Gruau écossais
sources.locator: French product name and description
sources.supports: Uses gruau écossais for this named dry Scottish oatmeal product; local product wording does not make bare gruau a dry-oat term.

sources.title: Well.ca, Bob’s Red Mill Scottish oatmeal / gruau écossais
sources.locator: Product title and indexed description
sources.supports: Corroborates the Canadian retail name and described coarse meal; one listing uses inconsistent flocons wording, which is not adopted.

sources.title: Metro, Granola et céréales santé
sources.locator: Product listing
sources.supports: Lists Bob’s Red Mill Gruau écossais as a distinct cereal product; does not define generic oatmeal.

sources.title: OQLF, farine d’avoine (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalents
sources.supports: Defines farine d’avoine broadly as a milled oat product and lists oatmeal and oat flour as English equivalents; does not define a coarse Scottish meal.

sources.title: OQLF, gruau (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalents
sources.supports: Defines Québec gruau as a cooked oat-flake dish and lists oatmeal as an English equivalent; does not define the dry compound gruau écossais.

sources.title: OQLF, flocon d’avoine (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and recommended term
sources.supports: Defines an oat grain steamed and flattened as a flocon d’avoine; this supports keeping rolled flakes distinct from ground Scottish oatmeal.

sources.title: Health Canada, Summary of Assessment of a Health Claim about Oat Products and Blood Cholesterol Lowering
sources.locator: Rolled-oat and oatmeal terminology in the assessment
sources.supports: Uses oatmeal for rolled oats in a health-claim context, demonstrating that the English word is not limited to ground meal.

sources.title: CFIA, Bacterial Pathogens and Indicators in Oats, April 1, 2018 to March 31, 2020
sources.locator: Oat groat processing and product classes
sources.supports: Describes oat groats and further cutting, steaming, and rolling, with steel-cut, quick, rolled, and instant product classes; does not define Scottish oatmeal.

decisions.reason: Hold dry oat meal/oatmeal as a research candidate. The reviewed Québec gruau entry is a cooked oatmeal dish; it does not establish a dry milled oat-meal identity. Keep oat groats, flakes, and oat flour distinct.

Keep generic oat meal, oatmeal, and dry oatmeal unresolved because English oatmeal is used for rolled oats and flour, while Québec gruau names a cooked dish. The sources support a separate named Scottish/Scotch whole-groat meal identity only. Do not add a generic alias or merge the Scottish product with active oat flour, groats, steel-cut oats, rolled oats, quick oats, or instant oats.

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius Commission, Regional Standard for Edible Sago Flour (Asia), CXS 301R-2011
sources.locator: Sections 1, 2.1, and 7.1.
sources.supports: Defines edible sago flour from Metroxylon palm pith for direct human consumption, excludes cassava products sometimes called sago flour, and requires the product name Edible sago flour. It does not equate edible sago flour with edible sago starch.

sources.title: FAO Terminology Portal, edible sago flour, entry 172732
sources.locator: English and French entry terms and definition.
sources.supports: Pairs edible sago flour with farine de sagou comestible under the same Codex palm-pith definition; it is not independent evidence that starch is a synonym.

sources.title: Department of Standards Malaysia, MS 470:2012 Edible sago starch — Specification
sources.locator: Official standards preview, title and scope metadata.
sources.supports: Names an edible sago starch product for food applications derived from Metroxylon palm pith or soft core. The public preview does not provide enough specification detail for a product-level crosswalk to Codex edible sago flour.

sources.title: OQLF, fécule de sagou (Grand Dictionnaire terminologique; entry cites AFNOR 1979)
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalent.
sources.supports: Pairs fécule de sagou with sago starch; the definition includes Metroxylon species and, in smaller quantity, Cycas, so it is not a palm-only French crosswalk to the current edible sago-flour identity.

sources.title: TERMIUM Plus, sagou search result
sources.locator: Food Industries terminology result for sago starch.
sources.supports: Describes starch made from sago-palm pith and used in pudding; this terminology entry does not compare the Malaysian and Codex standards or provide a precise Québec French display.

sources.title: Department of Standards Malaysia, MS 468:2012 Industrial sago starch — Specification
sources.locator: Official standards preview, title and foreword.
sources.supports: Shows industrial sago starch has a separately named standard; the available preview is not used to infer a food product identity or equivalence.

sources.title: East India Pantry Canada, Sabudana Flour (Sago Flour), 400 g
sources.locator: Product title and product description.
sources.supports: Canadian retailer describes a flour milled from tapioca pearls as sago flour, documenting the cassava-derived phrase collision; this does not establish palm-sago flour or starch equivalence.

decisions.reason: Keep edible sago starch as a distinct held candidate. Malaysian MS 470:2012 and Codex CXS 301R-2011 identify food products processed from the same Metroxylon pith source, but the reviewed public specification does not establish whether their standardized products are equivalent. Do not alias sago starch to edible sago flour or create an active row until a product-level crosswalk is available.

Keep fécule de sagou unassigned because the OQLF-hosted AFNOR definition includes Cycas as well as Metroxylon; obtain a Québec French term scoped to the edible Metroxylon product before promoting the candidate.
Keep palm-sago pearls and cassava/tapioca products separate; do not map sago flour, sabudana, sagu, or sagú to the palm-sago flour identity without exact product scope.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Amorphophallus paeoniifolius
sources.locator: Accepted taxon, Kew Species Profile, Uses, and Common Names sections.
sources.supports: Accepts A. paeoniifolius in Araceae, documents edible tubers and the English common name elephant yam, and distinguishes it from Dioscorea yams and A. konjac. This does not establish a retail starch product.

sources.title: ICAR-Central Coastal Agricultural Research Institute, Elephant foot yam
sources.locator: Crop identity, local names, food use, and corm composition.
sources.supports: Identifies A. paeoniifolius and the local names Suran and Zamikand; says tubers are used as vegetables, starch-rich chips are made, and tubers contain 18.0% starch. The percentage is whole-tuber composition, not extracted-starch yield or a kitchen value.

sources.title: Karmakar et al., Optimization of starch extraction from Amorphophallus paeoniifolius corms using response surface methodology and artificial neural network
sources.versionOrDate: International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 237 (2023), article 124183
sources.locator: Abstract; extraction study and reported maximum starch yield.
sources.supports: Primary research isolates and characterizes A. paeoniifolius corm starch and reports a maximum extraction yield of 51.76 g per 100 g dry corm under its tested laboratory process. This is not a home-preparation yield, household measure, density, or conversion.

sources.title: Health Canada, Natural Health Products Ingredients Database, English listing
sources.locator: A. paeoniifolius ingredient row, common name, plant part, and preparation columns.
sources.supports: Lists A. paeoniifolius as Elephant yam, with root/tuber parts and fresh/dry preparations. NHP terminology is not a food-label standard and does not name extracted starch.

sources.title: Health Canada, Base de données des ingrédients des produits de santé naturels, fiche française
sources.locator: A. paeoniifolius ingredient row, common name, plant part, and preparation columns.
sources.supports: Lists A. paeoniifolius as Igname d'éléphant, with root/tuber parts and fresh/dry preparations. NHP terminology is not a food-label standard and does not name extracted starch.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, igname (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and Latin equivalent.
sources.supports: Defines igname as an edible tuber of Dioscorea. It does not establish igname as a Québec product name for A. paeoniifolius starch.

sources.title: Spice Divine, Suran congelé Vadilal 312 g
sources.locator: French-facing Canadian retail product title, description, and package state.
sources.supports: Lists frozen, pre-cut whole corm pieces as Suran congelé and igname pied d'éléphant. It is not an isolated-starch product and was out of stock when reviewed.

sources.title: Nagar et al., Development and characterization of elephant foot yam starch-hydrocolloids based edible packaging film
sources.versionOrDate: Journal of Food Science and Technology 57 (2020), 1331-1341
sources.locator: Methods, film preparation.
sources.supports: The packaging-film experiment disperses 4 g starch with hydrocolloids in 100 mL distilled water and adds glycerol. This film-specific formulation is not a kitchen measure or starch-powder density; finished-film properties do not describe the powder.

decisions.reason: Keep starch isolated from A. paeoniifolius corms as a held candidate, separate from Dioscorea yam starch, yam flour, konjac flour, corm flour, and whole corm. Research supports an extracted starch fraction, but the reviewed Canadian and Québec-facing names apply to the whole edible tuber or a frozen cut-corm product, not isolated starch. OQLF defines igname for Dioscorea, while activating elephant-foot-yam starch would make the generic yam starch picker query resolve only to this row. The bundled recipe corpus has no demand. Keep the candidate outside active references and forms; add no aliases, measures, density, mappings, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions. Revisit substitution research after the identity boundary is resolved.

sources.title: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius Commission, Regional Standard for Fermented Soybean Paste (Asia), CXS 298R-2009
sources.locator: Sections 2.1 and 8.1
sources.supports: Defines fermented soybean paste as a broad soy-based fermented paste class and uses a generic product name; it does not identify one Korean product. Current PDF notes amendments through 2025.

sources.title: FAO/WHO Codex GSFA, Fermented soybean paste (e.g. miso), category 12.9.1
sources.locator: Food category description
sources.supports: Groups dou jiang (China), doenjang (Republic of Korea), and miso (Japan) in a broad food category; it is not a product identity crosswalk.

decisions.reason: Keep generic fermented soybean/soy paste unresolved. Codex treats it as a broad category including distinct regional products such as dou jiang, doenjang, and miso; do not add it as an alias of any named paste.

sources.title: ICAR–Indian Institute of Millets Research, Latest Millet Production and Processing Technologies
sources.locator: Section 11, “Millets semolina (Rawa/Suji)”; the large PDF could not be opened directly, and the indexed section was available.
sources.supports: Includes finger millet among grains dry-milled into ready-to-cook semolina and describes coarse, medium, and fine particle-size variants. Reported process yields are grade- and millet-specific, not a household measure, cooking yield, Québec label, or universal SKU specification.

sources.title: TastyGrains, Millets & Millet Products
sources.locator: Current collection page, entry “Finger Millet Rava”; direct product page returned a cache miss.
sources.supports: Uses the exact heading “Finger Millet Rava,” names “Ragi Rava,” and describes a milled form of finger millet. The collection page gives no ingredient declaration, mesh size, or French name.

sources.title: TastyGrains, Contact
sources.locator: Store contact and address.
sources.supports: Gives a Kitchener, Ontario, Canada address, establishing Canadian retailer context for the product listing; it does not add product identity evidence.

sources.title: Organic Wisdom, Ragi Rava 400 g
sources.locator: Product title, description, ingredients field, and recipe page; page showed sold out when reviewed.
sources.supports: Identifies one SKU as “Ragi (Finger Millet) Rava,” lists Ragi Rava as its ingredient, describes it as stone-ground and a semolina substitute, and lists 400 g net weight. These are SKU-specific claims and provide no generic conversion or substitution ratio.

sources.title: CSIR–Central Food Technological Research Institute, Finger millet based multigrain semolina for upma, kesari bhat and alike products
sources.locator: Technology sheet.
sources.supports: Defines a separate ready-to-cook multigrain semolina/rava/soji product from mixed cereals, millets, legumes, and other inputs. Supports keeping blends distinct; it is not a formula or process specification for single-grain ragi rava.

sources.title: OQLF, millet
sources.locator: Preferred French terms, English translation, and generic-use note
sources.supports: Supports millet / millet as a bilingual broad food name and explicitly notes that the unqualified name may group several species or abbreviate a specific species.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: semoule
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalents; source attributed to Agence de coopération culturelle et technique, 1977.
sources.supports: Defines semoule in soft- and durum-wheat milling contexts and gives semolina and farina as English terms. This supports caution around the unqualified French term for a rice product; it does not decide whether semoule de riz is acceptable French wording.

decisions.reason: Keep finger millet rava / ragi rava as a ledger-only Section F candidate. Technical and current Canadian retailer evidence support a distinct processed finger-millet product, but the reviewed sources do not establish a Québec French display or a universal milling grade. Keep it separate from finger-millet grain and flour, rice idli rava, sorghum semolina, Sankhal, multigrain semolina, prepared mixes, and dishes. Add no active reference or alias, form, recipe link, measurement, density, conversion, yield, or substitution; the manufacturer’s “semolina substitute” claim supplies no tested ratio.

sources.title: OQLF, fonio blanc
sources.locator: Definition, preferred terms, English translations, and Latin name
sources.supports: Pairs fonio blanc with English white fonio and Digitaria exilis; lists fonio, acha, fundi, and findi as French terms and fonio, acha, and hungry rice among English terms.

sources.title: CBI, Entering the European market for fonio
sources.locator: Breakfast-cereal section.
sources.supports: Says flakes are a possible cereal format and notes fonio had not penetrated Europe’s breakfast segment. Market-development evidence, not a product standard or Canadian name.

sources.title: Africa Eats, Agromyx
sources.locator: Company profile and linked fonio-flakes product.
sources.supports: Identifies Agromyx as a Ghana processor of fonio cereal meals with added fruit/vegetables and links to its fonio flakes. Secondary company-profile source; not a present product label.

sources.title: Amazon, Nourimeal FONIO (FLAKES)
sources.locator: Product title, availability, and listed ingredients.
sources.supports: Product page names the flake item and lists whole-grain fonio, pineapple, and ginger; it was unavailable at review. Marketplace content is not a Canadian package or proof of current availability.

sources.title: Kedar Health, Fonio Flakes & Shake Powder | Nourimeal
sources.locator: 250 g Original and With Dates variants and separate shake powder listing.
sources.supports: Lists 250 g Original and With Dates flakes and describes their ingredients; variants were sold out. The same page also lists a separate shake powder product. Retailer data, not evidence of a plain-flake formula.

sources.title: Anaemene, Adifeseso, and Adesanya, Nutritional and Sensory Evaluation of Locally Produced Acha (Digitaria exilis) Flakes Fortified with Bambara Nut and Crayfish
sources.versionOrDate: European Journal of Nutrition & Food Safety 16(4), 2024; DOI 10.9734/ejnfs/2024/v16i41413
sources.locator: Study formulation and ingredients.
sources.supports: Describes a study formulation made from fonio flour, Bambara-nut flour, and crayfish powder. Supports a composite-flake sense only; batch percentages are not product measures.

sources.title: CIPO, SIMPLI — Canadian trademark application 1483767
sources.locator: Official English-language record; goods wording, proposed-use status, and withdrawal.
sources.supports: Supports the English goods wording “processed fonio flakes,” the 2010 filing, proposed-use status, and owner withdrawal in 2016. This PDF contains no French wording and is not evidence of actual retail use.

sources.title: CIPO, Canadian Trademarks Journal, Vol. 59, No. 3001, May 2, 2012, application 1,483,767 / SIMPLI
sources.locator: Official French-language issue; entry begins on printed p. 49 and continues onto p. 50; front matter on p. 1.
sources.supports: English is the first-listed, applicant-filed goods language in the entry. CIPO publishes “flocons de fonio transformés” as its French translation for convenience only; the front matter says later goods text is a convenience translation and registration is restricted to the first-listed filed language. This is not applicant-filed French wording, a package label, evidence of actual sale, current Québec usage, an OQLF term, or support for the shorter display “flocons de fonio.”

sources.title: Mako Foods Exotik, Fonio précuit (400 g)
sources.locator: Current Québec retailer/manufacturer product listing.
sources.supports: Shows a current Québec-facing French fonio product sold as précuit. It supports local use of the base noun and a separate precooked product, not the availability or name of puffed fonio or flakes.

decisions.reason: Keep fonio flakes as an unresolved ledger-only candidate. Product-format evidence exists, but reviewed Ghana-market examples use the name for fruit-containing ready-to-eat cereal and experimental “acha flakes” can be a distinct multi-ingredient baked product. CIPO’s French phrase is only a convenience translation in a historical proposed-use entry; no current Canadian or Québec product label establishes a plain flake identity or French display. Keep all active references, aliases, forms, numeric data, recipe links, and substitutions unchanged until a current Canadian/Québec product source settles the product boundary and French label.

sources.title: Latest Millet English Full Book (2020)
sources.locator: ICAR–Indian Institute of Millets Research, Latest Millet English Full Book (2020), pp. 83–84, “Millets semolina (Rawa/Suji)”.
sources.supports: Calls millet semolina ready-to-cook, includes foxtail among millet grains processed by dry milling, distinguishes coarse/medium/fine grades, and says output varies by millet. General processing evidence; it does not supply a universal foxtail SKU grade, household measure, or recipe conversion.

sources.title: Millets in Daily
sources.locator: ICAR–Indian Institute of Millets Research, Millets in Daily, “Foxtail Millet Porridge (Navane Payasa)”.
sources.supports: The recipe directs the cook to make coarse rava from foxtail millet. Its ¼ kg grain input and prepared-mixture water ratio belong only to that recipe; they are not a product density or reusable rava measure.

sources.title: OQLF, millet des oiseaux
sources.locator: Botanique > poacee; definition, note on bird feed, preferred French terms, and English translation
sources.supports: Identifies foxtail millet as Setaria italica, defines the plant as cultivated for its seeds, maps it to English foxtail millet, and lists millet d'Italie among preferred French terms. Notes that millet des oiseaux is also used for bird feed.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: semoule
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalents; source attributed to Agence de coopération culturelle et technique, 1977.
sources.supports: Defines semoule in soft- and durum-wheat milling contexts and gives semolina and farina as English terms. This supports caution around the unqualified French term for a rice product; it does not decide whether semoule de riz is acceptable French wording.

sources.title: Foxtail Millet Rava 1 Kg
sources.locator: FreshOnTheGo Grocery, Foxtail Millet Rava 1 Kg, Scarborough, Ontario.
sources.supports: Exact English product title and package descriptor. The product page shows a stale expiry-date field; use as product-name evidence only, not a claim of current stock or a generally valid package weight.

sources.title: TastyGrains, Millets & Millet Products
sources.locator: Current collection page: Foxtail Millet Rava and Red Sorghum (Jowar) listings and descriptions.
sources.supports: The Kitchener retailer’s current catalog lists Foxtail Millet Rava with Thinai Rava and describes a finely broken foxtail product; it also lists a Red Sorghum (Jowar) grain product and describes it as red sorghum. This supports the seller’s product wording for those scoped items, not independent grade standards, a French name, cultivar identity, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Keep foxtail millet rava / thinai rava as an unresolved, unallocated Section F candidate. ICAR–IIMR processing evidence and Ontario retailer listings establish a distinct processed-grain candidate, but no Québec French product display was verified. Keep it separate from intact foxtail millet, foxtail flour, finger-millet rava, rice rava, sorghum semolina, and Sankhal. Package weights and external recipe quantities are not reusable measures or conversions; add no active reference, alias, form, density, mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, haricot
sources.locator: Definition, terminology note, and English terms for common bean.
sources.supports: The edible common-bean pod is eaten whole before maturity, while the term haricot can also name its seeds; Québec colloquial fève is broader and usage varies.

sources.title: OQLF, gourgane
sources.locator: Definition identifies edible-seed plant Vicia faba and Québec term gourgane.
sources.supports: Supports gourgane / broad bean as a species-specific product, not a synonym for every fresh shell bean.

sources.title: CFIA, Organic OGD codes for fresh fruits and vegetables
sources.locator: Fresh-produce classifications list green peas, cowpeas, lima beans, wax beans, green beans, and fababeans separately.
sources.supports: Shows that the broad shell-bean bucket contains distinct species/products; it does not establish one global culinary identity or Québec alias.

decisions.reason: Do not create a global fresh shell beans identity. The phrase spans species, and the edible part may be a young whole pod or mature seeds removed from the pod; Québec haricot/fève wording is also ambiguous. Keep future references species- and product-specific, such as fresh green beans or gourganes, and add no generic aliases, forms, recipe links, measures, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Processed bean products
sources.locator: Characteristics and types; production methods.
sources.supports: Separates tofu from yuba, describes yuba as a soy-milk surface film, and distinguishes aburaage, atsuage, and ganmodoki as different fried products. Japanese process taxonomy does not resolve every regional retail name.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File: Tofu, fried (food code 6577)
sources.locator: Bilingual food name.
sources.supports: Uses the bilingual CNF name Tofu, fried / Tofu, frit. The entry does not resolve whether recipe wording is a retail product or preparation instruction.

decisions.reason: Keep fried tofu / tofu frit unresolved. Health Canada uses a bilingual food class, while MAFF distinguishes several fried products (aburaage, atsuage, and ganmodoki); without an exact ingredient line, the phrase may identify a purchased product or a preparation step. Do not create an active reference or alias it to a named product.

sources.title: OQLF, chutney
sources.locator: French usage and definition
sources.supports: Confirms integrated French usage and a broad cooked sweet-sour condiment; does not define a single variety.

decisions.reason: Hold a generic chutney identity and links. OQLF supports the broad term, but sweet mango chutney remains a specific product and no exact generic recipe line appears.

sources.title: China State Administration for Market Regulation, Soy product production-license review rules
sources.locator: Fermented soybean product categories
sources.supports: Separately classifies douchi and fermented bean curd among fermented soybean products; does not establish Canadian display wording.

sources.title: Wei-Chuan, White Fermented Bean Curd in Seasoning Sauce
sources.locator: Manufacturer product title and product series
sources.supports: Names the standalone white fermented-curd product class; does not define a universal formula.

sources.title: Zheng Sheng Food, Red Fermented Bean Curd
sources.locator: Product page and manufacturer product menu
sources.supports: Manufacturer names a red fermented-bean-curd product; its ingredients and processing are product-specific.

sources.title: Lee Kum Kee Hong Kong, Sauce Pack for Braised Meat in Local Style
sources.locator: Ingredient list
sources.supports: Prepared sauce pack lists white fermented bean curd and red fermented bean curd separately; supports their boundary.

decisions.reason: Keep unqualified fermented bean curd / fermented tofu unresolved. Available product evidence distinguishes white and red products but does not support mapping the unqualified phrase to either one.

sources.title: Briess Malt & Ingredients, Malted Flours
sources.locator: MRF L100 listing under Diastatic Malt Flours at 100 degrees Lintner; adjacent product grades.
sources.supports: Names malted rye flour as a cereal-specific product and identifies MRF L100 as a diastatic malt flour at 100 degrees Lintner. The product page also describes malt flour as a dough conditioner. This is product-specific functional evidence, not a general replacement ratio or Québec French display.

sources.title: Government of Canada Translation Bureau, TERMIUM Plus, malt flour
sources.locator: Milling and Cereal Industries, record 1 (2011-02-18), English and French term and definition sections
sources.supports: Lists malt flour and malted cereal flour as correct English terms and farine maltée as the correct French term; defines the product as ground malted wheat or barley.

sources.title: IREKS, The IREKS Compendium of Baking Technology, Definition and composition of malt flour and malt extract
sources.locator: Malt section, paragraphs on grain types, kiln-drying, enzyme activity and malt extract
sources.supports: Describes malt flour from barley, wheat, rye, or spelt; says processing controls enzyme activity and distinguishes malt extract as a further processed product.

sources.title: Molino Merano, General Product Catalogue (2024)
sources.locator: Pages 23 and 47, rye-bread ingredient list and complimentary-product entries
sources.supports: Lists MALT FLOUR and BARLEY MALT FLOUR separately; corroborates that the generic product name is not a cereal-specific malted-flour name.

decisions.reason: Hold generic malt flour and broad diastatic/non-diastatic qualifiers. The reviewed manufacturer names cereal-specific malted-flour products; the broad picker phrase already overlaps roasted wheat malt flour. Do not make a universal generic alias or add grades.

Resolve the broad malt-flour candidate into ingredient-ref-malt-flour after the source-backed identity follow-up. Keep the earlier cereal-specific product source as historical boundary evidence; TERMIUM and current technical/product sources now support the generic bilingual identity. No measurement, form, mapping, recipe link, or substitution is inferred.

sources.title: OQLF, marinades
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalent
sources.supports: Gives Québec/Canadian French marinades for pickles and names cucumbers and onions; does not make preserved products interchangeable.

sources.title: OQLF, cornichon
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalents
sources.supports: Defines a small immature cucumber used as a vinegar condiment; does not identify every pickle style as a cornichon.

sources.title: Brine&Co., Québec product catalogue

decisions.reason: Hold idli rava / rice rava as an unallocated Section F candidate. Sources support a dry, coarse rice-granule product used for idli, while current Canadian listings vary in whether they specify parboiled rice; the available evidence does not establish whether parboiling is required for the generic product class. Canadian French listings use semoule de riz and semoule de riz grossière inconsistently, while the OQLF semoule entries reviewed concern wheat milling and do not establish a preferred Québec French name for this rice product. Keep idli rava, idly rava, idli rawa, rice rava, rice semolina, rice sooji, semoule de riz, and related names off active references until the processing boundary and Québec French display are supported. Keep bare rava/rawa, wheat semolina, prepared rava/idli/dosa mixes, fermented batter, finished idlis, intact/parboiled rice, rice flour, and cream-of-rice hot cereal distinct. Add no active reference or alias, form, density, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Hold catalog integration for plain tubular Korean rice-cake sticks marketed for tteokbokki pending a Québec French terminology review. The local title Gâteau de riz pour tteobokki is not enough to set a canonical display: tteobokki is unresolved wording, the listing supplies no shape or composition, and OQLF uses unqualified gâteau de riz for rice pudding. Keep this candidate distinct from broader tteok, oval soup slices, niangao, sweet or filled cakes, wheat-based products, and seasoned meal kits. Add no active reference, aliases, forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

Resolve the held candidate into ingredient-ref-korean-tteokbokki-rice-cake-sticks after the Québec terminology follow-up. Canadian retail now attests bâtonnet(s) de gâteau de riz for the narrow stick product, and the paired Tokimi listing identifies it as Korean and intended for tteokbokki. Keep the fully qualified display and stick-format aliases; do not merge generic rice cakes, tteok, niangao, oval soup slices, wheat-based products, or prepared meals. Add no forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

decisions.reason: Keep human-food little millet (Panicum sumatrense) as a held candidate. The English identity is supported, but no distinct Québec French display has been verified and petit mil conflicts with OQLF names for foxtail and pearl millet. Keep rice wording out of aliases and add no active reference, forms, measures, yield, conversion, recipe link, or substitution.

Reconsider the held human-food little millet (Panicum sumatrense) grain name with new Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada French evidence for petit millet and current Canadian grain wording. Keep the grain unallocated because the current picker makes a petit mil query return only the proposed little-millet grain/flour pair, omitting the foxtail and pearl millet choices also named by OQLF. Keep the older generic spelling and rice-product boundaries, measurements, forms, recipe links, and substitutions unchanged until the picker can represent this distinction safely.

sources.title: Mannuramath, Yenagi, and Orsat, Quality evaluation of little millet (Panicum miliare) incorporated functional bread
sources.locator: Journal of Food Science and Technology 52(12) (2015), pp. 8357–8363; abstract, sensory results, and conclusion.
sources.supports: Reports wheat-flour replacement with little-millet flour at 10%, 30%, and 50%; the 10% and 30% samples had sensory scores not significantly different from control. This is a formula-specific bread trial, not a general replacement ratio or kitchen measure.

sources.title: Pradhan and Tripathy, Effect of little millet (Panicum miliare) on physical, rheological, nutritional and microstructural properties of bread
sources.locator: Journal of Food Processing and Preservation 46 (2022), e16782; abstract and practical applications.
sources.supports: Tests composite bread with 10%, 25%, and 40% little-millet flour; the tested 25% formulation was acceptable and flour incorporation affected dough and loaf properties. This is formula-specific, not a general substitution rule or kitchen measure.

substitutionFindings.context: Partial replacement of wheat flour with little-millet flour in the studied functional-bread formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study tested 10%, 30%, and 50% little-millet flour; the 10% and 30% breads had sensory scores not significantly different from the control. The study evaluates a particular bread system and does not establish transfer to other recipes.
limitations: Formula-specific bread results do not support replacement in arbitrary bread, roti, cakes, cookies, pastry, or thickening.
Do not infer a general replacement percentage, hydration change, or baking adjustment from the tested formula.

substitutionFindings.context: Partial replacement of refined-wheat flour with little-millet flour in the studied composite-bread formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study tested 10%, 25%, and 40% flour blends; the 25% formulation was acceptable, while the dough and loaf properties changed. This is a single tested composite-bread system.
limitations: The reported result does not establish a replacement percentage for arbitrary bread, roti, cakes, cookies, pastry, or thickening.
Do not transfer the study ratio, hydration, or process adjustments to another flour blend or recipe.

decisions.reason: Keep little-millet flour as an unallocated candidate paired with the held little-millet grain. Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada identifies Panicum sumatrense as petit millet, and Canadian retailers list plain little-millet flour, but the current picker makes a petit mil query show only the proposed little-millet grain/flour pair while OQLF uses petit mil broadly and for foxtail and pearl millet. Canadian package sizes are not kitchen measures. The two bread studies are formula-specific and do not support an active substitution rule.

decisions.reason: Keep malted buckwheat flour unresolved and unallocated. Québec sources establish a malted-buckwheat food product and general custom-milling capability, but not a standalone flour SKU, item-specific grind or product specification, or Québec French flour label. Research and external recipes use the English phrase but do not establish the local product boundary. Keep it distinct from plain buckwheat flour, sprouted buckwheat flour, whole malted buckwheat, and generic malt flour; add no active reference, alias, legacy identity, form, measure, density, mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Keep malted sorghum flour unresolved and unallocated. Tanzania’s compulsory standards list establishes a separately named product class, and one study distinguishes its experimental malting process from its fermented-flour process. The Canadian-facing bilingual wording found is from an unavailable third-party listing whose title says fermented while its package image says malted; Rwanda FDA separately records an Akanozo fermented sorghum flour, without proving the same SKU. A Canadian/Québec product boundary and Québec French display remain unverified. Keep it separate from plain sorghum flour, generic malt flour, and other cereal-specific malted flours. substitutionFindings.context: General recipe substitution for dried mealworms, mealworm powder, or mealworm flour.
substitutionFindings.basis: No source establishes a general replacement ratio or function for mealworm product states. Landish and Jimini’s guidance is product-specific, and there are no matching recipe lines.
limitations: Do not apply the Landish 2 tbsp (12.5 g) serving to another product or recipe.
Do not infer equivalence to flour, whey, plant protein, other insects, or a supplement.

decisions.reason: Keep the general active mealworm identity on hold. Jimini’s current human-food listing identifies a whole-dehydrated Tenebrio molitor powder, but no Canadian availability or Canadian package label was verified. Health Canada’s 2023 entry is specific to a named protein-rich flour, and the European ŸnMeal process summary is not the Canadian submission; it describes mechanical separation before drying, unlike Jimini’s whole-larva powder. TriCycle’s Québec human-food powder listing does not name species or process. This evidence does not establish the status of other products. Do not infer novelty, prohibition, or safety from an absent list entry. Add no active reference, aliases, forms, measures, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

substitutionFindings.context: General conversion or substitution involving unqualified palm sugar / sucre de palme.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed term spans multiple palm species and finished states. A Nypa-sugar study tests selected Thai formulas, and an Arenga report gives farm-scale sap yield; neither supports a shared household measure or arbitrary recipe replacement.
limitations: Do not map coconut sugar, Kampong Speu sugar, nipa/gula apong, Arenga gula aren, date-palm products, or cane jaggery to an unqualified palm-sugar identity.
No bundled recipe line supplies a product origin or preparation state.
Do not transfer source-specific process yields or recipe trials to other palm products.

decisions.reason: Keep generic palm sugar / sucre de palme out of the active catalog. Sources use these broad terms for sweeteners from multiple palm species and product states; some regional names conflict. Preserve coconut, Kampong Speu/Borassus, nipa/Nypa, Arenga, date-palm, and cane-sugar identities separately. No exact bundled recipe line requires an unqualified product, and no generic measure, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported.

decisions.reason: Hold isolated plantain starch as a separate research candidate, not an active reference. Primary studies establish isolated starch as distinct from plantain flour and distinguish plantain from dessert-banana starch, but current Canadian/Québec evidence does not establish a standalone product label or a validated Québec French display. Amidon de banane plantain is only a component-based description; do not adopt fécule compounds without product evidence. Keep plantain flour aliases scoped to flour and banana starch separate. Study-specific extraction yields and laboratory properties do not support a transferable measure or conversion; substitution research remains unreviewed. Add no active row, aliases, forms, recipe links, numeric values, conversions, yields, or substitutions until qualifying Canadian/Québec product and naming evidence is available.

decisions.reason: Retain plain puffed corn as an unallocated Section F candidate. Manufacturer and Canadian retailer evidence support a plain puffed-corn cereal product, and the Arrowhead 3/4 cup (14 g) serving is recorded only as that branded product label observation. A reviewed Québec French term is not established: OQLF assigns maïs soufflé and maïs éclaté to popcorn, Metro uses céréales de maïs soufflé for a different formulated cornmeal cereal, and grain de maïs soufflé lacks product detail. Reopen when product-specific Québec/Canadian bilingual naming distinguishes the plain product from popcorn and formulated cereals.

decisions.reason: Hold the manufacturer-named Roasted Mong Flour. Its description says very fine grain starch from mong beans but leaves species, flour versus extracted starch, and process sequence unresolved. Keep separate from mung-bean starch, mung-bean grain, chana sattu, and roasted mung grain; request species, composition, treatment order, and French product name.

Keep the manufacturer-named Roasted Mong Flour held. Current product wording does not resolve species, flour versus extracted starch, or whether roasting occurs before or after milling. Keep it separate from mung-bean starch, whole mung, chana sattu, and roasted urid; add no active row, alias, recipe link, form, or numeric behavior.

sources.title: Niru Enterprise Inc., Rice & Flour collection
sources.locator: Current product listings
sources.supports: Lists roasted mong flour, roasted red rice flour, urid flour, and roasted urid flour separately; does not list roasted white-rice flour.

sources.supports: Lists roasted white-rice flour and package SKUs as historical product-name evidence only.

decisions.reason: Hold roasted white rice flour because direct evidence is only an older product list and the current collection does not list it. Require a current product page or bilingual package; do not alter generic white-rice flour.

sources.title: OQLF, choucroute
sources.locator: Definition and English equivalent
sources.supports: Pairs choucroute with sauerkraut and defines fermented salted cabbage; terminology evidence is not recipe demand.

decisions.reason: Hold a generic sauerkraut identity and links until exact bundled demand appears; OQLF establishes the product and Québec French term, not recipe demand.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, concombre de mer
sources.locator: Grand dictionnaire terminologique, food/fishery-products domain; last updated 1983.
sources.supports: Lists concombre de mer, bêche-de-mer, bêche de mer, and biche-de-mer as preferred terms, translates the name as sea cucumber, and notes that several holothurian species carry this name. Terminology only.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, holothurie touffue
sources.locator: Grand dictionnaire terminologique, updated 2026; English and Latin terms.
sources.supports: Identifies Cucumaria frondosa and gives the Québec/Canada preferred term holothurie touffue, with concombre de mer du Nord also listed. Supports this species-specific name only, not a generic alias.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List lookup results
sources.locator: Dynamic search results for sea cucumber names and species, including Cucumaria frondosa and Parastichopus californicus.
sources.supports: The Fish List uses sea cucumber / concombre de mer for multiple species and also lists species-associated alternatives. This is a dynamic regulatory naming list; it does not identify a recipe-compatible product part or establish that species/product forms are interchangeable.

sources.title: Seafood from Canada, Sea Cucumber — Cucumaria frondosa
sources.locator: Canadian East Coast product description and Product Forms section.
sources.supports: Identifies the East Coast product as Cucumaria frondosa, describes fresh or dried culinary use, and lists frozen and dried forms. Industry product information, not a household measure or universal species definition.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Pacific Region Sea Cucumber Integrated Fisheries Management Plan Summary, 2025/2026
sources.locator: Economic profile: product processing and fishery landing basis.
sources.supports: Describes the managed Pacific fishery products as frozen muscle strips and dried skin; describes the commercial TAC in split pounds. Fishery-specific product and landing information, not a recipe measure.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Giant Red Sea Cucumber (Apostichopus californicus)
sources.locator: Species overview, fishery history, and processing sections; updated 2026-06-12.
sources.supports: Names the British Columbia species Apostichopus californicus, reports 47 sea-cucumber species in BC, and describes split landings and processing into frozen muscle strips and dried skin. The profile is species/fishery scoped and does not establish product interchangeability.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, holothurie touffue
sources.locator: Grand dictionnaire terminologique, updated 2026; English and Latin terms
sources.supports: Maps Cucumaria frondosa to the Québec/Canada-preferred French term holothurie touffue and lists concombre de mer du Nord; English terms include orange-footed, Atlantic, northern, and North Atlantic sea cucumber. Species terminology, not a generic product name.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List lookup results
sources.locator: Dynamic results for Cucumaria frondosa and other sea-cucumber species
sources.supports: Uses Sea Cucumber / Concombre De Mer for Cucumaria frondosa and other species, so the bare common name is not species-specific.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Évaluation du potentiel de la pêche au concombre de mer (Cucumaria frondosa) en Minganie
sources.locator: 2013 technical report, section 1.1
sources.supports: Identifies Cucumaria frondosa, describes the body wall and muscles as edible parts, and documents dried/frozen market products. It does not establish recipe quantities or interchangeability among products.

sources.title: Couillard, Maltais, and Belley, Morphometrics and processing yield of Cucumaria frondosa from the St. Lawrence Estuary, Canada
sources.locator: 2021 abstract and Québec commercial-processing study
sources.supports: Reports that Cucumaria frondosa is usually sold as dried gutted body wall and describes commercial processing. Stock-specific recovery rates are not culinary conversions.

sources.title: Exploramer / Fourchette bleue, Concombre de mer
sources.locator: Current species and culinary page
sources.supports: Identifies Cucumaria frondosa, gives local French names, and says the product is sold dried or frozen. The page does not identify the tissue in each product.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Concombre de mer séché
sources.locator: Current Québec product listing
sources.supports: Confirms local use of the French dried-product name for a Québec seafood product family; the listing does not state its species or edible part.

sources.title: Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Pêcheries et de l’Alimentation du Québec, Les entreprises maritimes du Québec exportatrices de produits de la mer
sources.locator: 2026 directory, Poissonnerie de Cloridorme product list and nomenclature
sources.supports: Lists sea cucumber as chair avec peau (séché) for a Québec processor; its nomenclature maps concombre de mer (holothuride) to Cucumaria frondosa. It does not put all species and part details on one consumer-facing SKU.

decisions.reason: Keep generic sea cucumber / concombre de mer reviewed but unallocated because OQLF and CFIA apply the common name across multiple species. A follow-up verifies a separate Cucumaria frondosa identity and dried, gutted body-wall form; this does not resolve the generic candidate or activate generic aliases. Keep muscles, frozen or whole products, and other species distinct. Add no recipe link, quantity, conversion, density, package behavior, drying or rehydration yield, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, oursin vert
sources.locator: Preferred term, species, and commercial-label note
sources.supports: Normalizes oursin vert for Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis and excludes châtaigne de mer from Québec commercial fish labeling to avoid consumer confusion. It names a species-specific animal, not extracted gonads or all uni products.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Sea Urchin by dive — Pacific Region Integrated Fisheries Management Plan summary 2025–26
sources.locator: Foreword, fishery overview, and economic profile of red and green urchins
sources.supports: Distinguishes Pacific red and green sea urchin species; describes extracted red-urchin roe treated and packaged for sale as Uni, while West Coast green sea urchins are sold whole and live. This is Pacific fishery evidence, not a universal species or product standard; the summary is not legally binding.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, 2024 Economic Profile of the Red Sea Urchin Fishery
sources.locator: Commercial fishery profile; red urchin reproductive organs
sources.supports: States that red sea urchins are harvested for reproductive organs (gonad) or “roe”. The profile is limited to British Columbia’s red-urchin fishery and does not set a universal product name or species for uni.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Labelling requirements for fish and fish products
sources.locator: Common name requirements for fish products
sources.supports: Provides a general common-name rule for fish products when no prescribed standardized name applies. It does not designate a specific English or French name for uni.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Sea Urchin and Periwinkle Exploitation in Quebec
sources.locator: Historical survey summary of Québec sea-urchin fisheries and markets
sources.supports: Reports historical fresh gonads and salted/frozen, baked, or boiled gonad preserves for further processing, and distinguishes whole-urchin and extracted-gonad markets. It is historical market-survey material, not a current product or preparation standard.

sources.title: Capone Gourmet, Unis d’oursins du Québec — gonades fraîches ou surgelées, 200 g
sources.locator: Product description, edible portion, and listed fresh/frozen formats
sources.supports: Québec retailer calls the edible portion gonades (Uni), offers fresh or frozen products in 200 g packs, and does not state a particular sea-urchin species. This is one retailer’s product information, not a terminology authority or universal package/state rule.

sources.title: Poissonnerie La Mer, Urchin Roe (QC) — 100 g
sources.locator: English product heading, French product image wording, and description
sources.supports: Montréal retailer pairs Urchin Roe (QC) with Gonades d’oursins (QC) wording and describes fresh, opened product in 100 g platters. This is one source-specific retail item, not a species definition or generic measure.

decisions.reason: Keep extracted sea-urchin gonads/uni off the active catalog until a bundled recipe or confirmed import creates demand. The product is a distinct edible-gonad scope; do not merge it with whole/live sea urchin, species-qualified oursin vert, fish roe, salmon roe/ikura, tobiko, masago, caviar, or preserved fish roe. The contingent names sea urchin roe (uni) and gonades d’oursin (uni) are source-supported wording candidates only, not approved picker names. The reviewed Quebec 100 g and 200 g packs are source-specific retail amounts and do not support a generic package yield or recipe conversion. No density, measure mapping, form, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution is activated. The current 114-recipe/1,123-row corpus has no matching demand.

sources.title: Shanghai Municipal Government Information Office, Sticky rice dishes are traditional festival fare
sources.locator: Regional description of thin oval Shanghai niangao slices used in stir-fries and soups.
sources.supports: Distinguishes Shanghai’s thin oval, less-sticky slices made with non-glutinous rice from many glutinous-rice-flour festival cakes also called niangao. It does not provide Québec French product terminology.

sources.title: Lordford, Montréal frozen-food listings
sources.locator: Current Tastie Frozen ShangHai Rice Cake slice case listing and separate Korean rice-cake sticks listing.
sources.supports: Supports local wholesale English wording and distinction from tubular Korean sticks. The listing does not provide a French product name or ingredient panel.

sources.title: Walmart Canada, Tastie Shanghai Rice Cake
sources.locator: Retail listing for a frozen Shanghai-style Chinese product and supplier-provided ingredient statement.
sources.supports: Supports one retail SKU labelled Shanghai-style rice cake with rice and water listed. Product data is supplier-provided and SKU-specific; it does not establish a Québec French ingredient name.

sources.title: Sangji, Montréal menu
sources.locator: French prepared-dish wording “Galettes de riz au bouillon de poisson” with an English description.
sources.supports: Shows Québec French wording for a prepared rice-cake soup, not a product label for plain Shanghai-style slices.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, gâteau de riz (GDT)
sources.locator: Unqualified French expression and English equivalent.
sources.supports: Uses gâteau de riz for rice pudding, warning against using the unqualified expression as the display for Shanghai-style slices. It does not define the Chinese ingredient.

decisions.reason: Hold active integration of plain Shanghai-style rice-cake slices pending Québec French naming evidence for the packaged ingredient. The regional source distinguishes the non-glutinous thin oval Shanghai product from other niangao, and Montréal listings support the English product wording, but local French wording found names prepared dishes and OQLF uses unqualified gâteau de riz for rice pudding. Keep separate from Korean tteok sticks, generic or glutinous rice cakes, rice-paper wrappers, mochi, crackers, and puffed rice. Add no active reference, aliases, forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: OQLF, couscous (céréale traitée)

sources.supports: Defines the food ingredient as agglomerated durum-wheat semolina grains that are steamed and dried; gives couscous in French and English and notes it also names a prepared dish.

sources.title: OQLF, couscous (mets)
sources.locator: Alimentation > mets; definition and preferred term
sources.supports: Documents the separate North African prepared-dish sense of couscous, supporting product-versus-dish scope for the ingredient reference.

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Couscous CXS 202-1995
sources.locator: Section 2, product scope and description
sources.supports: Defines couscous as a product made from durum-wheat semolina that is physically treated, including cooking and drying; corroborates the food-product scope without adding catalog measurements or forms.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: sorgho
sources.locator: Preferred term, English equivalent, and Latin name.
sources.supports: Lists sorgho as the preferred French term and pairs it with sorghum and Sorghum bicolor. Supports the base noun, not an official ruling on the semolina compound.
