sources.locator: Page 164, whole-grain guide and food suggestions
sources.supports: Québec educational guide lists couscous made from whole-wheat semolina, bulgur, millet, quinoa, or sorghum. This is food-suggestion wording only, not a product specification, terminology ruling, or current package label.

sources.title: ICRISAT, Sidibe, Diarra, and Scheuring, “Sorghum Couscous: Quality Considerations,” Proceedings of the International Symposium on Sorghum Grain Quality
sources.locator: 1982 proceedings, pp. 109–113
sources.supports: Describes Sahelian sorghum couscous as steamed cereal-flour granules and details agglomeration, sieving, steaming, optional drying, and reconstitution. Regional processing evidence does not establish one current retail formula or household measure.

sources.title: Extent of decortication and quality of flour, couscous and porridge made from different sorghum cultivars, International Journal of Food Science & Technology 41(6)
sources.locator: 2006 study of four cultivars and 10–40% decortication
sources.supports: Primary study describes flour/water agglomeration, steaming, drying, and sizing for sorghum couscous. Process results vary by cultivar and decortication; they are not household-measure evidence or one universal retail formula.

sources.title: North African Journal of Food and Nutrition Research, Influence of Grain Size on the Agglomeration and Quality of Fine Couscous Derived from Decorticated White Sorghum bicolor L.
sources.locator: 2025 primary study
sources.supports: Study makes sorghum semolina from decorticated white sorghum and agglomerates it into couscous. Grain size and decortication affect yield and product quality; the paper does not establish Québec consumer naming or a household measure.

sources.title: Réseau National des Chambres d’Agriculture du Niger, Typologie des produits locaux transformés avec des céréales, note 1
sources.locator: Pages 4–5, local product typology and couscous naming
sources.supports: Explains that some products labelled couscous are precooked but unrolled broken grain and lists “couscous de sorgho aux légumes” as an example. Regional nomenclature evidence cautions against assuming one stable rolled, single-ingredient identity.

sources.title: Mako Foods Exotik, Sorgho (400 g)
sources.locator: Current Longueuil whole-grain sorghum product page
sources.supports: Québec retailer lists whole sorghum grain and suggests “couscous revisité” as a use. It does not sell or name a processed sorghum couscous product.

sources.title: Coop Marketplace, Couscous de Sorgho blanc
sources.locator: Current indexed product title and composition statement; direct page unavailable during review
sources.supports: Indexed listing says the product contains white sorghum grits and white sorghum flour. It provides no proportions, process specification, household measure, or Québec market evidence.

sources.title: Laya et al., Effect of different processing methods on maize, sorghum and millet flours on nutritional couscous quality consumed in the Far North region of Cameroon, Journal of Agriculture and Food Research 9 (2022)
sources.locator: 2022 primary study
sources.supports: Evaluates cereal-specific processing variants and reports density and absorption properties for experimental samples. These properties do not establish a general household conversion, universal product form, or Québec product name.

sources.title: The Green Souk, Artisanal Gluten-Free Sorghum Couscous – 500 g.
sources.locator: Current English product page: title, model name, product description, and listing details.
sources.supports: Lists an artisanal gluten-free sorghum-couscous product and gives the model name “Couscous Artisanal au Sorgho Sans Gluten – 500 g.” The product text says it is made from selected organic sorghum and describes natural ingredients without additives or preservatives, but provides no full ingredient panel or defined processing and packaged state. The Moroccan listing does not establish Québec availability.

sources.title: The Green Souk, Farines & Couscous Bio, French retail category listing.
sources.locator: Current French category listing for “Couscous Artisanal au Sorgho Sans Gluten – 500 g.”
sources.supports: Provides French retail wording for the listed sorghum-couscous product. This category listing does not provide a full ingredient panel or define the product’s processing and packaged state, and it does not establish Québec availability.

sources.title: International Center for Biosaline Agriculture, “Making couscous from sorghum in Togo.”
sources.locator: Article text and process photographs; published 2024-04-01.
sources.supports: Documents a Togo training and household process in which sorghum flour is sprinkled with water, hand-rolled into granules, sieved, and steamed. This establishes one regional preparation method, not the composition or packaged state of the Moroccan retail product.

decisions.reason: Keep sorghum couscous out of active references while `couscous de sorgho` has an unstable product scope: research sources describe rolled flour/semolina granules, while a regional report applies the same label to unrolled precooked broken grain and a vegetable-enriched product. A Québec guide lists sorghum couscous as a food suggestion, but the current Québec retailer found sells whole sorghum used in a couscous-style dish rather than a processed product. Reopen after a Québec bilingual producer or retail source identifies a single-ingredient rolled/agglomerated product and its state. Add no active row, alias, form, measure, recipe link, or substitution.

2026-10-18 product-boundary recheck: a current Moroccan bilingual retail listing establishes that a sorghum-couscous product is sold, but its description does not provide a full ingredient panel or define the product’s processing and packaged state. The listing does not meet the plan’s Québec bilingual product-label criterion. Keep the candidate ledger-only until a Québec-facing source resolves the product boundary; add no active reference, alias, form, measurement, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, sorgho (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred French base term and English/Latin equivalents; updated in 2010.
sources.supports: Supports sorgho / sorghum for the plant and grain, not a flaked-product name.

sources.title: Statistics Canada, Enquête mensuelle auprès des minotiers, 2024
sources.locator: Question 8, céréales et cultures non céréalières moulues.
sources.supports: Lists sorgho among products of milling for human consumption and uses farine de sorgho for flour; it does not identify consumer flakes.

sources.title: Well.ca, GoGo Quinoa Organic Instant Sorghum Flakes
sources.locator: Product description, ingredients, serving, and cooking directions; listing marked unavailable when reviewed.
sources.supports: Describes a one-ingredient instant sorghum-flake product and a product-specific 1/3 cup (40 g) serving; the page does not identify a flaking process or provide a paired French label.

sources.title: OM Foods, Organic Sorghum Crisps, flakes
sources.locator: Current product title, description, listed ingredients, package variants, and ready-to-eat uses; page rechecked 2026-10-16.
sources.supports: Currently calls the product Organic Sorghum Crisps, flakes, lists sorghum as its ingredient, and describes ready-to-eat cereal/snack/topping uses. The page currently offers 454 g, 2.27 kg, and 11.34 kg packages. It does not specify a rolling, puffing, or expansion process; package amounts are not measures.

sources.title: CerealVeneta, Flocons de sorgho blanc
sources.locator: Product heading and process description.
sources.supports: Names a European semi-finished product flocons de sorgho blanc and describes cleaned grain being flaked/rolled and dried; does not establish Québec usage or equivalence to instant/crisp products.

sources.title: Puratos Canada, Softgrain Treize
sources.locator: Ingredient statement for the formulated grain mix.
sources.supports: Lists cracked sorghum as one component of a formulated bakery grain mix; it is not a standalone flake product.

sources.title: S & V Millets, White Sorghum Flakes (Poha)
sources.locator: Product title, overview, process description, and product category; direct page fetch timed out, so current indexed product text was reviewed.
sources.supports: Identifies a white-sorghum flakes/poha product and describes soaking, cooking, flattening, and drying. This supports one process-defined product candidate, not a generic sorghum-flakes class or Québec French product name. The listed package amount is product-specific and is not a reusable measure.

sources.title: Indian Grocery Store Canada, S&V White Sorghum Flakes
sources.locator: Product title, 2 lb variant, SKU, stock status, and retailer address.
sources.supports: Lists an S&V white-sorghum-flakes product as a 2 lb item and showed it in stock at review at the retailer’s Burlington, Ontario address. Supports Canadian market presence and product wording only; it does not specify processing or composition.

sources.title: Boulangerie Cannelle, Le sorgho : la céréale qu'on mange depuis 5 000 ans et qu'on redécouvre
sources.locator: French-language article, introductory sorghum description.
sources.supports: Says sorghum may be used as flour, whole grain, or flakes. This supports general Canadian French culinary wording, not an exact Québec retail product title or the S&V product identity.

sources.title: BuyNearby / Desi Indian Market Calgary, S&V Millets White Sorghum Flakes
sources.locator: Current indexed product listing, seller and product-use text.
sources.supports: Identifies an S&V white-sorghum-flakes listing from a Calgary seller and suggests poha-style uses including upma, breakfast cereal, chivda, and porridge. The listing showed out-of-stock status; it gives no French product name, processing specification, or reusable measure.

decisions.reason: Keep sorghum flakes unallocated. Canadian product examples include instant flakes and ready-to-eat crisp flakes without a shared process specification, while flocons de sorgho blanc is supported only by a European semi-finished product source and is not established as a Québec display. Keep grain sorghum, sorghum flour, cracked sorghum, and puffed sorghum separate. No recipe demand or reusable measure, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported; add no active reference, alias, form, or recipe link.

R226 rechecked sorghum flakes against current Canadian listings. S&V identifies a narrower White Sorghum Flakes (Poha) product made by soaking, cooking, flattening, and drying; an Ontario retailer lists the 2 lb product, and a Calgary seller describes poha-like uses. This distinguishes one process-defined candidate from the previously reviewed instant GoGo Quinoa flakes and ready-to-eat OM Foods crisps, but does not resolve the broader sorghum-flakes family or establish a product-matched Québec French display. The Canadian French-language culinary page supports only general sorghum-in-flakes wording. Keep the candidate unallocated; a single row would make the broad query sorghum flakes return only this narrower product, and adding poha would change an existing broad flattened-rice query. Package sizes remain SKU-specific. No recipe demand, reusable measure, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported; add no active reference, alias, form, recipe link, or numeric behavior.

sources.title: Nu Life Market, Sorghum Meal
sources.locator: Product overview, meal variants, grind profiles, and applications
sources.supports: Current manufacturer page distinguishes sorghum meal from flour, lists white whole and pearled products, and offers coarse, medium, and fine grinds. Supports a human-food product family but not one generic grind or consumer specification.

sources.title: Nu Life Market, White Whole Sorghum Meal
sources.locator: Product description and bulk package options
sources.supports: Identifies one coarse meal made from the entire white sorghum grain. This is a manufacturer-specific product; its bulk package sizes are not household measures or a generic specification.

sources.title: Dempsey Food, Product Lines — Canada
sources.locator: Canada section, Nu Life Market listing
sources.supports: The Canadian distributor lists Nu Life sorghum meal, flour, and whole grains in its product range. This supports Canadian distribution context, not a current consumer SKU, stock status, package label, or Québec French display.

sources.title: Statistics Canada, Customs Tariff 2025, Section II: Vegetable Products
sources.locator: Chapter 11, cereal table and note 3 for heading 11.03
sources.supports: Includes grain sorghum in the cereal table and defines groats and meal under heading 11.03 as fragmented cereal products meeting a sieve criterion. This is customs classification, not a consumer milling specification or Québec French label.

sources.title: Les Aliments Kabeya International, Nos produits — Québec
sources.locator: Entries Farine de sorgho and Grain de Sorgho
sources.supports: A Québec-facing product list describes farine de sorgho as powdery dried, ground seed and separately describes dry sorghum grain as lightly ground for porridge. It does not name sorghum meal or establish a meal-specific French display.

decisions.reason: Keep sorghum meal as an unresolved ledger-only candidate. Current milling-company and Canadian distributor sources establish a human-food meal product family, but the manufacturer offers distinct whole and pearled products and several grind profiles, while no Québec French product name is established. Preserve the existing farine de sorgho, gruau de sorgho, and semoule de sorgho owners. Add no active identity, alias, form, legacy entry, recipe link, measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: South African Department of Basic Education, 2024 NSNP Food Specification Guidelines
sources.locator: Section 4.6 and table 4.6.3.
sources.supports: Presents amasi/maas as named cultured-milk classes. Numeric composition, packaging, and other regulatory details are not transferred.

sources.title: South African Government Gazette, Agricultural Product Standards Act regulations
sources.locator: Government Notice R.1510 (2019), cultured-milk and buttermilk sections.
sources.supports: Permits amasi as an alternate cultured-milk designation and separately defines/classes buttermilk and cultured buttermilk. This supports a product-class boundary but not consistent market usage.

sources.title: South African Dairy Standard Agency, Code of Practice, Chapter 3: Processing of Dairy Products
sources.locator: Section 3.4, “Cultured milk and cultured buttermilk.”
sources.supports: Says South African cultured buttermilk is equivalent to maas and gives “Amasi/maas or cultured buttermilk” as an example product name. This overlap does not authorize Quebec-wide equivalence.

decisions.reason: Keep amasi/maas out of active references and buttermilk aliases. South African standards and industry guidance show overlapping cultured-milk and cultured-buttermilk descriptions; require product- and market-specific evidence before choosing a separate identity or qualified relation.

sources.locator: 2025 definition, shape list, use notes, and English equivalents.
sources.supports: Defines generic extruded, dehydrated textured vegetable protein and lists commercial forms flocons, petits morceaux, languettes, and boulettes. Also states that both rehydrated and dry uses occur; no universal shape measure or hydration ratio is supplied.

sources.title: OQLF, protéine de soya texturée (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and terms.
sources.supports: Defines textured soy protein / PST as the soy-based subtype of TVP; supports keeping PST outside generic TVP form aliases.

sources.title: Butler Foods, Soy Curls
sources.locator: Product title, description, ingredient identity, and product use.
sources.supports: Manufacturer uses Soy Curls as a branded product for protein strips made from whole soybeans; product scope does not establish generic soy-curl identity or alias.

sources.title: Butler Foods, Frequently Asked Questions
sources.locator: Soy Curls production and preparation description.

sources.title: Les Brutes, PVT Lanières de soya
sources.locator: French product title, ingredient declaration, and shape description.
sources.supports: Québec manufacturer product is titled PVT Lanières de soya and lists defatted soy flour; it supports a local strip presentation only, not a generic soy-curl alias.

sources.title: Les Brutes, TVP Soy Curls
sources.locator: English product title and product description.
sources.supports: Paired English page names one Québec producer product TVP Soy Curls. The wording is product-specific and is not activated as a generic soy-curl alias.

decisions.reason: Keep generic soy curls unresolved: the phrase is brand/product-specific in current sources, and Québec TVP strip product labels use it for a product with a different ingredient/process description. Do not activate a generic alias or identity without matching recipe demand and broader product-boundary evidence.

sources.title: Anita’s Organic Mill / Nature’s Path, 60/40 Baker’s Blend Flour

sources.supports: Names Organic Sprouted Rye Flour as one component of a 60/40 flour blend and says Anita’s grains are milled, sprouted, blended, and packaged at its Chilliwack mill. sources.title: Everspring Farms, Sprouted Rye Flour

sources.supports: Indexed manufacturer text lists sprouted rye flour, organic and regenerative variants, and dark and medium products; medium flour may have some bran sifted out. Use only the indexed wording; it does not establish current stock or a universal grade or process.

sources.title: Hartley & Berg, Anita’s 60/40 Baker’s Blend package sheet
sources.locator: Pages 1–2; bilingual ingredient declaration and Nutrition Facts basis.
sources.supports: Names “Sprouted rye flour” / “Farine de seigle germé” as ingredients in a blend. The 1/4 cup (30 g) Nutrition Facts basis belongs to the composite blend only and is not a flour measure or transferable density.

sources.title: Walmart Canada, Stonemill 12-grain sprouted rye bread
sources.locator: French ingredient statement.
sources.supports: The French-Canadian listing uses “Farine de seigle germé” for a bread component. Retailer details are supplied by manufacturers, suppliers, or sellers and are not independently verified; this corroborates Canadian retail wording only.

sources.title: OQLF, farine de seigle
sources.locator: Preferred Québec French term, English equivalent, and note on rye flour classes.
sources.supports: Prefers farine de seigle and lists rye flour as its English equivalent. Describes rye flour and notes light and dark flour differences; only the general bilingual identity is adopted here. It does not attest the sprouted compound.

sources.title: Ferme La Défriche / Marché Outaouais, producer profile and current product listing
sources.locator: Farm profile and linked listing title “Seigle Germé bio Qué-Vrai”.
sources.supports: The farm profile describes a living-food producer and rye among its germinated cereals; its live listing shows “Seigle Germé bio” in 200 g and 1 kg formats. The product-specific page returned a cache miss, so processing and storage could not be confirmed. Do not treat the package formats as measures or the product as dried rye.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Culture des pousses et germinations
sources.locator: See proposal source register for the cited term, food, product, or data table.
sources.supports: Distinguishes water-grown germinations from pousses/micropousses grown in soil or fabric and lists species for each technique. Cultivation guidance does not by itself make every listed plant a catalog identity.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Consommation des pousses et germinations
sources.locator: Updated 2026-07-06; consumption, refrigeration, and post-harvest timing guidance.
sources.supports: Says germinated seeds are consumed whole, kept refrigerated, and consumed within a week of harvest or purchase. This supports the fresh-germination boundary only and does not establish that the same conditions apply to manufacturer-dried shelf-stable grain.

decisions.reason: Keep sprouted rye flour unallocated pending independent Québec review of the provisional display and its picker effect. The source-attested phrase “farine de seigle germé” makes a bare “seigle germé” query select the flour, while Québec-facing evidence also uses “Seigle Germé” for fresh living germinations; no disambiguating search behavior is available. Record no active reference, alias, form, measure, density, conversion, package yield, recipe link, or substitution.

sources.title: Puratos Canada, Softgrain Treize, French product page
sources.locator: Product description, ingredient statement, and specifications

It does not attest a French name or separate triticale product.

sources.title: Canadian Grain Commission, Triticale: Grading factors
sources.locator: French factor Grains germés (SPTD)
sources.supports: Defines visibly germinated triticale kernels as a grading factor. This is grain-quality language, not an intentional sprouted-food product name or specification.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, triticale (GDT)

sources.title: Usito, triticale

sources.supports: Defines the base French term triticale as a wheat–rye cereal and uses it for its grains and flour; it does not name a sprouted product.

decisions.reason: Keep sprouted triticale grains as a ledger-only candidate. A current Canadian manufacturer names the component in a ready-to-use 13-grain blend, but the source does not establish a standalone ingredient, component quantity, or reusable product state. The French product page leaves the exact component name in English; grading terminology and a Québec label for cracked triticale do not establish a French name for sprouted triticale. Add no active reference, alias, form, measure, density, mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Keep unqualified surimi unresolved. Québec terminology sources distinguish surimi paste, raw surimi, and added-ingredient surimi paste, while Canadian labeling guidance and retailer listings also use surimi in names for finished imitation products. No recipe line clarifies the intended ingredient. Do not add a general surimi reference, alias, fish-ball form, recipe link, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution until a specific product or recipe defines the paste/product boundary.

decisions.reason: Keep a separate extracted-starch candidate from taro root and whole-corm taro flour, but do not activate until a Québec/Canadian French product name is supported. OQLF gives general starch and plant terms, not a taro-starch entry; fécule de taro remains a linguistic inference, and amidon de taro appears only in non-Québec commercial classification evidence. No exact recipe demand, kitchen measure, generic conversion, form, or substitution is supported.

Keep candidate-taro-corm-starch at needs_clarification. This exact Québec/Canadian French product-name follow-up found no retail listing for isolated Colocasia esculenta corm starch. OQLF supports the general plant and starch terms, while farine de taro names a separate flour product; fécule de taro remains a linguistic construction and amidon de taro is only found in non-Canadian classification evidence. Do not activate a display or alias, add a form or numeric data, or infer a recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Keep extracted Colocasia esculenta corm starch on hold. This bounded Québec/Canadian French product-name search found no current local label or terminology entry for the isolated starch; general amidon/fécule wording and non-Canadian amidon de taro do not attest a local product name. Keep whole-corm taro flour and taro leaves separate; add no active identity, alias, form, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution until a local source names the extracted product and confirms the botanical source.

Keep unqualified toasted rye flour unresolved. The Québec retailer wording found is specifically farine de seigle malté toasté in a finished bun; the exact farine de seigle toasté wording is from a French-market catalogue, and manufacturer products do not settle whether the candidate is malted or whether grain or flour is heated. Keep ordinary rye flour, whole rye flour, malted rye flour, and rye meal separate; add no active row, alias, form, recipe link, or behavior data.

sources.supports: Pairs Ochro/Okra and Chadon Beni/Culantro; lists pimento pepper separately from Scotch Bonnet.

decisions.reason: Keep Trinidadian pimento pepper as a distinct but unresolved identity candidate. Sources distinguish it from Scotch Bonnet and allspice but give only Capsicum sp.; a precise product boundary and Québec French display remain unreviewed. Do not merge with allspice or activate an alias.

sources.title: Marché ShengTai, Pure Water Chestnut Flour / 纯正马蹄粉, 250 g
sources.locator: Product title, product code GPWCF, package size, availability label, and temporary-closure notice.
sources.supports: Current Montréal retailer listing uses the English/Chinese title Pure Water Chestnut Flour / 纯正马蹄粉 for a 250 g product, code GPWCF, and marks the product in stock while also showing a temporary-closure notice. It gives no French product name, botanical source, ingredient declaration, or processing method; no purchase-availability claim is inferred.

decisions.reason: Keep the unqualified retail phrase unresolved because it may refer to whole Eleocharis dulcis corm flour, extracted E. dulcis corm starch, or flour from dried Trapa fruit. No reviewed Québec product name safely distinguishes the products. Do not alias it to the active water-chestnut vegetable, tree-chestnut flour, or generic starch.

Do not add the literal branded/current product wording as an alias on the active Chinese water-chestnut-starch row. The Montréal title does not resolve whole-corm flour versus extracted starch, supplies no product-matched French name, and contains the generic query water chestnut flour. Because the picker falls back to substring matching, that alias would make the generic query select the starch row alone. Keep the product wording proposal-local and the generic candidate unresolved.

sources.title: Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Indicator 2.1d
sources.locator: Commercial native-food product entries for quandong and wattle
sources.supports: Identifies quandong as a commercial native food and associates it with Santalum acuminatum; wattle seed is described at broader Acacia scope.

sources.title: Tourism Australia, Native Australian ingredients
sources.locator: Wattleseed entry
sources.supports: Describes wattleseed flour in damper and powdered wattleseed in baking and desserts.

sources.title: Mayi Harvests, Recipes
sources.locator: Quandong recipe list
sources.supports: Indigenous-owned Australian native-food recipe publisher names quandong products in desserts and preserves and wattleseed baking uses.

sources.title: Australian Native Food and Botanicals, Native food names (2005 proposed list)
sources.locator: Wattleseed names and species notes
sources.supports: Historical industry proposal covers five Acacia species and recommends identifying species on seed products; it is not a current regulatory or consumer naming standard.

sources.title: Wide Bay Hospital and Health Service, NAIDOC Week 2025 recipe collection
sources.locator: Native-ingredient glossary
sources.supports: Describes roasted Acacia seed as a seasoning and baking ingredient but does not establish which species the generic market term covers.

decisions.reason: Held as a candidate. The baking review documents a stable commercial culinary name and use, while the pantry review finds the source family spans multiple Acacia species and an older industry proposal recommends species identification on seed products. Do not create a species-free seed identity or generic acacia aliases until the product and species boundary is resolved.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List lookup
sources.locator: Dynamic exact scientific-name lookups for Buccinum undatum, Busycon, Colus stimpsoni, Neptunea lyrata decemcostata, Nucella lapillus, Littorina, Lobatus gigas, and Haliotis.
sources.supports: The Fish List uses bare Whelk for both Buccinum undatum and Busycon, compound whelk names for several other gastropods, and Buccin for more than one taxon. It separately lists periwinkle, conch, and abalone names. This is a common-name list, not a species assignment for an unqualified recipe term.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, buccin
sources.locator: Grand dictionnaire terminologique, food/fishery-product entry; updated 2012.
sources.supports: Gives normalized buccin as a Québec food/fishery term and English equivalents including whelk, waved whelk, and common whelk; notes Buccinum undatum and Neptunea despecta tornata in catches. Says bourgot and escargot de mer were not retained for Québec fish-product marketing. It does not prove that each common-name use denotes one species.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Integrated Fisheries Management Plan for Whelk (Buccinum undatum), Areas 1–15
sources.locator: Québec commercial fishery identity and species scope.
sources.supports: Says the Québec commercial fishery focuses on waved whelk, Buccinum undatum, while other Buccinum species are present in the Estuary and Gulf. Fishery context does not resolve all market uses of bare whelk.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Plan de gestion intégrée de la pêche du Buccin (Buccinum undatum), zones 1–15
sources.locator: French Québec commercial fishery plan and species name.
sources.supports: Uses buccin commun for Buccinum undatum and notes bourgot as a local Québec name. This supports a species-scoped future candidate, not a name for every whelk product.

sources.title: Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Pêcheries et de l’Alimentation du Québec, Les mollusques du Québec
sources.locator: Page 2, buccin product entry.
sources.supports: Documents buccin as a Québec edible seafood product and presents the scientific heading at Buccinidae family level with English Whelk. It does not establish one species or a household recipe amount.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Labelling requirements for fish and fish products
sources.locator: Labelling of seafood mix products.
sources.supports: Includes whelks among examples of invertebrates in products that may be labelled fruits de mer; this is a broad seafood-mix category, not an individual whelk name or synonym.

decisions.reason: Keep generic whelk / buccin as a reviewed but unallocated candidate. Canadian and Québec sources support food use, a normalized Québec food term, and a Québec fishery focused on Buccinum undatum; however, CFIA assigns bare Whelk to multiple taxa and OQLF buccin spans more than one species in Québec catches. No bundled recipe or supplied product identifies a species. Retain waved whelk / buccin commun only as a future candidate when a source explicitly identifies Buccinum undatum. Add no active reference, aliases, forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe link, or substitution; keep periwinkle, conch, abalone, other gastropods, and generic shellfish distinct.

sources.title: Nutritional, Chemical, and Functional Properties of Wholegrain Einkorn Pasta Through Cooking and Digestion: A Comparative Study with Wholegrain Durum Wheat Pasta
sources.locator: Section 2.2, Sample Description; wholegrain einkorn pasta sample input
sources.supports: Reports that the study’s wholegrain einkorn pasta sample was made using stone-ground wholegrain einkorn semolina. This is a sample-specific culinary use of the phrase, not a generic milling specification or transferable composition, cooking, measure, or yield claim.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, Grand dictionnaire terminologique, semoule
sources.locator: Definition, English equivalent, and notes on semolina grades and uses
sources.supports: Defines Québec French semoule as a broken durum-wheat kernel and gives semolina as its English equivalent. It does not name einkorn semolina or establish that the same French display transfers to einkorn.

decisions.reason: Keep wholegrain einkorn semolina as a source-bounded research candidate. One study reports this ingredient phrase for its pasta sample, but it does not establish a generally transferable milling class, grind or wholegrain boundary, or identity distinct from einkorn flour. The OQLF semoule definition is scoped to durum wheat, and the existing TERMIUM source establishes only the species names, not a milling-product name. Do not assign a Québec French display, active reference, alias, form, measure, or substitution until general milling and Québec terminology evidence resolves these boundaries.

sources.supports: Lists separate species-linked common names for Atlantic, pink, keta/chum, coho, sockeye, and chinook/quinnat salmon; the fish-list entries do not identify the taxon in recipe 077.

sources.title: OQLF GDT, saumon de l’Atlantique
sources.locator: Preferred Québec fish-product term, English translation, and Latin name
sources.supports: Pairs saumon de l’Atlantique with Atlantic salmon and Salmo salar; the name is species-specific and does not identify the bundle’s unqualified salmon fillets.

sources.title: OQLF GDT, saumon coho
sources.locator: Preferred Québec fish-product term, English translation, and Latin name
sources.supports: Pairs saumon coho with coho salmon and Oncorhynchus kisutch as a separate species-specific fish identity.

sources.title: OQLF GDT, saumon rouge
sources.locator: Preferred Québec fish-product terms, English translations, and Latin name
sources.supports: Pairs saumon rouge / saumon sockeye with sockeye salmon and Oncorhynchus nerka; the bundle does not name this species.

sources.title: CFIA, Labelling requirements for fish and fish products
sources.locator: CFIA Fish List and Labelling of Pacific salmon sections
sources.supports: States that Pacific salmon is not an acceptable common name replacing a species name because its species have different market values; labeling guidance only.

decisions.reason: Do not map ingredient-ref-salmon-fillets-without-skin or recipe 077 row 10 to Salmo salar or any Oncorhynchus species. The recipe says only salmon fillets without skin; named Canadian/Québec terms distinguish multiple salmon taxa and no source or label in the bundled recipe selects one. This unresolved candidate tracks only the species of that unqualified recipe line. It does not block separately sourced species identities such as ingredient-ref-chum-salmon. Keep the recipe line and broad reference unchanged and add no species alias, form, or recipe link.

sources.title: CFIA, Guidance on determining the common names for fish sold or processed in Canada
sources.locator: Section 4, CFIA Fish List
sources.supports: The Fish List supplies English/French fish common names and taxonomic serial numbers for species-specific Canadian labeling; it is not a recipe-species inference rule.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List, tuna query
sources.locator: Rows returned for the Tuna search: multiple Thunnus taxa and their English/French names.
sources.supports: Lists `Tuna` / `Thon` for multiple Thunnus species, alongside species-specific names. It does not identify the species in recipe 111.

sources.title: OQLF GDT, thon rouge
sources.locator: Preferred Québec fish-product term, English translation, Latin name, and note on unqualified thon
sources.supports: Pairs thon rouge with bluefin tuna and Thunnus thynnus; says bare thon was not retained for Québec fish-product marketing to avoid species confusion.

decisions.reason: Do not add a tuna-species reference or map the existing generic tuna row to a Thunnus species. Recipe 111 row 1 says only `1 tuna steak`; the CFIA Fish List assigns Tuna/Thon to multiple species and the recipe gives no species label. Preserve the existing Anova one-steak interval solely as its recorded source observation; it does not identify a species or establish the bundled recipe’s steak mass. Keep the current generic reference, measurement observation, and recipe link unchanged.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, malanga (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred terms, Latin equivalent, definition, and context note for macabo.
sources.supports: Provides plant terminology for Xanthosoma sagittifolium but no extracted-starch product name; macabo is qualified in a context note for a neighboring species in Cameroon.

sources.title: Espinosa-Solis et al., Physicochemical Characterization of Resistant Starch Type-III (RS3) Obtained by Autoclaving Malanga (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) Flour and Corn Starch
sources.locator: Molecules 26(13) (2021), article 4006, abstract and introduction.
sources.supports: Distinguishes malanga flour from corn starch but does not establish a Québec name for extracted Xanthosoma starch.

sources.title: Karmakar, Chakraborty, and Roy, Assessment of yield and characterization of starch extracted using different methods from the corms of some aroids in North Bengal region of India
sources.locator: Discover Food 5 (2025), article 290; Table 1 and starch-extraction methods.
sources.supports: Reports starch extracted from an Xanthosoma sp. sample; the sampled species is not identified as Xanthosoma sagittifolium. Extraction yield and laboratory characteristics do not establish a culinary measure, Québec product term, or substitution ratio.

decisions.reason: Keep extracted Xanthosoma corm starch as a genus-level held candidate. The reviewed extraction study identifies its sample only as Xanthosoma sp.; it does not establish a species-specific malanga-starch identity or a Québec French product name. Add no active reference, alias, form, density, unit mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, igname (GDT)
sources.locator: Updated 1991; preferred term, definition, and Latin equivalent.
sources.supports: Uses Québec French igname for yam and identifies the genus Dioscorea, distinguishing it from sweet potato. Names the plant/root, not a starch product.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, amidon (GDT)
sources.locator: Updated 2026; preferred term and usage note for fécule.
sources.supports: Prefers amidon generally and says fécule is more specific for starch contained in tubers or other underground organs. Does not approve either fécule d’igname or amidon d’igname as a product name.

sources.title: Alves, Grossmann, and Silva, Chemical and Functional Characterization of Products Obtained from Yam Tubers
sources.locator: Starch/Stärke 54(10) (2002), pp. 476–481; product preparation and characterization.
sources.supports: Primary study distinguishes flour made by drying and milling peeled Dioscorea alata tubers from starch extracted from mashed yam. Laboratory samples do not establish household measures or a Québec product term.

sources.title: Lu et al., Structure and Functional Properties of Purple Yam (Dioscorea alata L.) Starch from China
sources.locator: Starch/Stärke 74(5–6) (2022); abstract and comparative characterization.
sources.supports: Primary study reports source-specific structural and functional properties for purple-yam starch and comparisons with other yam varieties. It does not establish a universal yam-starch product, retail grade, or kitchen measure.

sources.title: Sinochem Nanjing, Yam Starch product page
sources.locator: Product title, source statement, and product-description table; no publication date shown.
sources.supports: Commercial supplier page uses the product name Yam Starch and says its source is yam tubers, but does not identify a species or provide a Canadian/Québec label. Vendor bulk-density and package statements are not imported as culinary measures.

sources.title: A.P.E.T.T.I.T., L’igname sous toutes ses formes, volume 1
sources.locator: Third edition, pp. 67–69; sections Fécule d’igname and extraction flow.
sources.supports: New Caledonian guide uses fécule d’igname, distinguishes extracted starch from flour, and describes extraction and method-specific yields. It is not Québec terminology authority and does not establish arrow-root equivalence.

decisions.reason: Keep isolated edible Dioscorea-tuber starch as a held candidate. The English phrase yam starch is attested and the sources distinguish extracted starch from whole-tuber flour, but the exact Québec French product name and the scope of unqualified market products remain unresolved. Keep fécule d’igname as a reviewer proposal only; do not alias arrow-root de Guyane or add an active row, measurement, form, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

sources.title: Metro Canada, Marmite Yeast Extract 125 g, product 667803001506
sources.locator: English product display and ingredient panel.
sources.supports: Current Canadian retailer display uses Yeast Extract for this Marmite SKU and lists yeast extract with salt, dehydrated carrots, spice extracts, and dehydrated onions. Retailer wording is product-specific and does not establish a generic class name.

sources.title: Metro Canada, Extrait de levure Marmite 125 g, product 667803001506

sources.title: Marmite UK, Frequently Asked Questions, What is Marmite and how is it made?
sources.locator: FAQ answer describing the product and its principal ingredient.
sources.supports: The manufacturer describes Marmite as a dark, thick yeast-extract spread made from concentrated yeast extract. This is product-specific evidence, not a Canadian generic food name.

sources.title: Canadian Intellectual Property Office, MARMITE trademark record
sources.locator: Product identification and goods description.
sources.supports: The Canadian trademark record identifies yeast-extract products with vegetable extract and spices. Supports treating Marmite as a brand example rather than a generic alias; not a terminology authority.

sources.title: Bega, VEGEMITE product page and brand history
sources.locator: Current product description and linked 1923/1946 history pages.
sources.supports: The manufacturer describes VEGEMITE as a spread developed from brewer's yeast, documents its label wording change to Concentrated Yeast Extract, and identifies VEGEMITE as a trademark. These brand statements do not set a Canadian generic name.

sources.title: OQLF, tartinade (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition, Québec/Canada usage label, and English equivalent.
sources.supports: Supports tartinade as a Québec/Canada term for a culinary preparation for spreading and as the equivalent of spread; it does not attest the full phrase tartinade à l’extrait de levure.

sources.title: OQLF, levure alimentaire (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred term, English equivalent, definition, and food-use notes.
sources.supports: Defines nutritional yeast / levure alimentaire as inactive yeast sold as flakes or yellowish powder, commonly sprinkled on food, with no leavening property. Supports keeping it distinct from a yeast-extract spread and baker’s yeast.

sources.title: Asahi Group Foods, What is yeast extract?
sources.locator: Manufacturer description of available formats and uses.
sources.supports: Describes generic yeast extract as available in powder, paste, or liquid form and used as seasoning. Supports keeping broad yeast extract separate from a prepared savory spread; does not establish Canadian home-cooking usage or a French name.

sources.title: OQLF, extrait de malt (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred French term, English equivalent, and definition.
sources.supports: Defines malt extract as a malt-wort concentrate obtained before fermentation; supports keeping malt extract separate from yeast-extract spreads. The existing WP02 review defers an active malt-extract row.

decisions.reason: Recognize savory yeast-extract spreads represented by Marmite and Vegemite as a candidate product class, but defer an active reference until an exact generic Québec French display is reviewed. The Canadian bilingual retailer listing uses brand-specific Extrait de levure while manufacturer sources describe a spread; OQLF supports tartinade only as the general headword. Keep brand names and unqualified yeast extract off active aliases, and keep nutritional yeast, baker’s yeast, and malt extract distinct. No recipe demand, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are established.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether a Pacific-cod fillet has a supported directed recipe substitution with another cod cut or fish.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed product sources establish the form and individual SKU properties but no tested replacement amount, recipe role, method, or adjustment. The bundled recipe corpus has no matching cod-fillet demand.
limitations: Do not infer equivalence with Atlantic cod, Pacific cod loin, haddock, or another fish from shared fillet wording.
Do not treat SKU weights, packs, freezing, thawing, additives, or boneless state as a substitution ratio or form-level property.
No matching bundled recipe supports a contextual rule or recipe-line link.

decisions.reason: Add one species-qualified fillet-cut form beneath the existing Pacific-cod identity. Metro’s matched bilingual product 229353 identifies the species and Québec French name; High Liner product 8894 independently corroborates Pacific-cod fillets. Keep the English and French form labels plural, with only the species-qualified singular French match phrase. No reusable fillet measure, yield, conversion, or recipe substitution is supported; keep product states and pack properties SKU-specific.

decisions.reason: Add one whole-goat-milk-powder form under ingredient-ref-goat-milk, displayed as whole goat milk powder / lait de chèvre entier en poudre. The Canadian producer and French-language Canadian listing attest the qualified whole product; federal rules separately name skimmed and partly skimmed goat milk powder, so leave unqualified powder wording without an exact form term. Keep the parent fluid-goat-milk identity and other animal milk powders separate. Published reconstitution instructions are product-specific; the tablespoon amounts differ between the producer’s English and French pages, so record them in source notes only and add no general measure, conversion, or density. The bundled corpus contains no matching recipe demand. Add no recipe link, yield, or active substitution.

sources.title: He et al., Effect on bread properties of partial substitution of wheat flour with oat flour and flour from oat grain germinated in the light or dark
sources.versionOrDate: International Journal of Food Science and Technology 58(4), 2023, 1979–1986; DOI 10.1111/ijfs.16352
sources.locator: Abstract and methods; wheat-bread formulation and 10% (w/w) oat-flour replacement results.
sources.supports: The study tests a 10% (w/w) oat-flour addition/replacement in one bread formulation and reports lower specific volume, darker crust and crumb, and increased hardness and chewiness. The authors call for further formulation optimization. These results apply to the tested formula and flours and do not establish a reusable household substitution amount.

sources.title: OQLF, farine d’avoine (GDT)

sources.supports: Defines the broader preferred term farine d’avoine for flour ground from whole or non-whole oat grains. It does not rule on the qualified whole-grain grade display, which is supported here by product evidence.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether sprouted whole-grain oat flour can generally replace wheat flour or another ingredient in home recipes.
substitutionFindings.basis: One Degree makes broad qualitative oat-flour replacement claims but gives no sprouted-form replacement amount or tested exchange. Its form-specific recipes show use in particular formulas, not equivalence to another ingredient. The R287 bread study is formula-specific and does not identify this retail product.
limitations: Do not activate a global or contextual substitution rule or infer a mass- or volume-based exchange.
Do not transfer the R287 10% bread-study result or generic oat-flour findings to this form.
Do not combine the separate 190 g and 1½-cup recipe amounts into a conversion.

decisions.reason: Add sprouted oat flour / farine d'avoine germée as a sprouted form under the existing whole-grain oat-flour identity. Keep the generic oat-flour row and sprouted oat-grain identities separate; add no aliases, measurements, density, mappings, conversions, yield, recipe link, or active substitution.

decisions.reason: Add açaí fruit / açaï as one FRUIT identity. Activate English assai as an OQLF-listed term; keep the unaccented French spelling out of aliases because accent-fold search already covers it. Keep the common-name identity unassigned to one palm species, and keep pulp, frozen/lyophilized products, beverages, palm heart, sweetened preparations, forms, measurements, conversions, substitutions, and recipe links outside this row.

Botanical scope remains source-specific: the OQLF entry lists Euterpe edulis and Euterpe oleracea, while Embrapa also documents Euterpe precatoria. No species-level mapping is inferred; review regional and market naming if species-specific references become necessary.

sources.supports: acerola/cerise des Antilles and uncertainty between two species. Identity and Québec terminology evidence only; no measurement, yield, or substitution data.

decisions.reason: Accept acerola / cerise des Antilles as a distinct identity-only FRUIT reference using the OQLF-supported Québec term and English equivalent. Keep documented near-neighbour and product boundaries separate. No forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are established.

sources.title: Prendre Racine, Farine de chênes
sources.locator: Current indexed Québec producer listing; title, product description, and recipe suggestions. The page was marked out of stock and direct retrieval returned HTTP 403.
sources.supports: Current indexed text describes a 120 g human-food product from Québec oak fruit, cold-water soaking to remove tannins, and milling; it gives culinary uses and source-attested French product wording. The listing was out of stock and direct text retrieval failed, so current availability and preparation details remain unverified.

decisions.reason: Accept acorn flour / farine de glands de chêne as human-food flour made from edible oak fruits/acorn kernels, in FLOUR_AND_STARCH. The Québec producer product listing and local reporting support the French display; retain only source-attested product wording as French aliases. Keep the identity distinct from extracted acorn starch, acorn meal, acorn squash, and animal feed. Add no forms, recipe links, yields, active measures, conversions, or substitutions.

Keep the USDA SR28 full-fat NDB 12060 value only as its source-specific 1 oz = 28.35 g portion. The reviewed sources do not provide an applicable general cup or spoon measure for the catalog identity; do not activate density or unit mappings, and do not attach the value to recipe lines. Keep measurement research blocked pending applicable evidence.

The reviewed product guidance and bread studies are source- or formula-specific and do not establish a reusable acorn-flour substitution ratio or context rule. No global or contextual substitution rule is supported; keep acorn flour separate from acorn starch, acorn meal, and wheat flour for substitution purposes.

substitutionFindings.context: One publication’s baking note for replacing agave syrup with honey or maple syrup.
substitutionFindings.basis: The publication gives a 1/2 cup agave to 1/2 cup honey-or-maple option, but does not tie it to a particular recipe, role, product, or controlled test.

substitutionFindings.context: All-purpose flour replaced with bread flour in King Arthur’s named Classic Sandwich Bread formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: Same amount only in the tested formula; source does not provide a reusable mass/volume basis or universal adjustment.
adjustments: Add water or flour only as needed to match dough feel in that formula.
expectedEffects: Similar rise and shape; tighter crumb and stiffer dough from greater absorption.
limitations: Formula- and source-brand-specific; do not generalize to other breads.

substitutionFindings.context: All-purpose flour replaced with bread flour in tested chocolate-chip cookies.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur recommends 1:1 in the tested context, but the article does not identify whether this is mass or volume.
adjustments: If dough seems dry, source suggests adding 1–2 tsp liquid per cup of flour.
expectedEffects: Cookies become chewier and bendier.
limitations: Do not generalize to other cookie styles or brands; no automatic reverse rule.

substitutionFindings.context: Generic all-purpose flour replaced with cake flour in AP-developed cakes, bars, or cookies; bounded review found no general supported replacement (a named Angel Food Cake recipe is a formula-specific exception).
limitations: Source warns cake flour can sink in AP-developed cakes/bars and make cookies too delicate or prone to falling apart. This is not a universal impossibility claim; the named Angel Food Cake exception does not establish other uses.

substitutionFindings.context: All-purpose flour replaced with self-rising flour only when the recipe’s leavening and salt can be adjusted as the source directs.
substitutionFindings.basis: Conditional recipe modification; no stand-alone flour ratio is supported.
adjustments: Check baking powder and salt already in the recipe and omit or adjust them as the source specifies.
Recipes relying on baking soda alone remain unresolved.
expectedEffects: In the tested cookie context, cookies spread more and faster.
limitations: Compound change to flour, leavener, and salt; do not activate as a direct flour conversion.

substitutionFindings.context: Generic all-purpose flour ↔ generic whole-wheat flour in the reviewed cookie/bar/brownie, cake, and yeast-bread contexts.
limitations: Reviewed positive guidance is for King Arthur Golden Wheat, a named white whole-wheat product not established as equivalent to the catalog’s generic whole-wheat identity. The sources describe texture, hydration, and rest effects; they do not support a general rule for this catalog identity.

rejectedCandidates.candidate: King Arthur Golden Wheat white whole-wheat flour
rejectedCandidates.reason: Product-specific recipe tests cannot be assigned to generic whole-wheat flour without evidence that the products are equivalent.

substitutionFindings.context: Sauce or gravy thickening only, when all-purpose flour is the thickener and the source-supported fixed-liquid comparison applies.
substitutionFindings.basis: Illinois Extension compares 2 Tbsp all-purpose flour per 1 cup liquid with 1 Tbsp cornstarch per 1 cup liquid. USU separately gives 1 Tbsp flour used as thickener → 1/2 Tbsp cornstarch. Fixed-liquid volume evidence, not a standalone mass ratio or formula-wide replacement.
expectedEffects: Flour-thickened sauce is cloudy and opaque; cornstarch-thickened sauce is transparent and glossy.
limitations: Evidence is limited to sauce/gravy thickening; do not transfer it to pudding, pastry cream, pie or fruit filling, coatings, baked goods, or other custards.
Flour works best in sauces prepared with fat, such as a roux; the sources do not give a recipe-specific slurry amount, method change, or adjustment to other liquids and fats.
The active resolver cannot enforce thickener role, sauce/gravy context, cooking method, or the fixed-liquid volume basis; do not activate as an automatic rule.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether all-purpose flour can be partly replaced by almond flour under a source-neutral, non-yeasted-baking contextual catalog rule.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur and Bob's Red Mill Canada both describe replacing about 25% of flour in baking, making a non-yeasted-baking rule a plausible candidate. King Arthur defines the denominator as total recipe flour for non-yeasted treats and says its guidance works by either weight or volume; Bob's statement instead names all-purpose flour and does not identify the amount basis or resolve recipes that contain multiple flours. Robin Hood recommends adding up to 25% almond flour to existing wheat-flour recipes without adjustment, not replacing that share, and King Arthur separately recommends adding almond flour to yeast dough. The catalog's almond-flour reference is unqualified and has no form that limits it to the finely ground blanched products represented by the converging guidance. It also cannot distinguish other grind, skin, or defatted variants. This overlap is therefore recorded as a lead, not an active reusable rule; current evidence does not define a consistent denominator, amount method, and product scope that the picker/resolver can enforce. The two bundled almond-flour lines request mass and contain no replacement instruction.
limitations: Do not encode the King Arthur 25% non-yeasted-treatment guidance or its yeast-dough addition as a global rule.
Do not treat Bob's Red Mill Canada's percentage as a weight/volume conversion or as an unambiguous denominator for recipes with multiple flours.
Do not treat Robin Hood's product-specific add-in guidance as a wheat-flour replacement.
A future contextual rule would need an enforceable non-yeasted-baking scope, a defined denominator and amount basis, and product/form scope consistent with the supported source products.
This bounded review does not establish substitutions for almond meal, defatted almond flour, other nut flours, or non-baking roles.

sources.title: Tamang et al., “Microorganisms and Nutritional value of Ethnic fermented foods and alcoholic beverages of North East India”
sources.locator: Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 11(1) (2012), 7–25; Table 2, p. 9.
sources.supports: Review table names Antramthu as a mustard-leaf preserve described as dried and acidic, used as a pickle, and associated with Hmar and Biate communities. It lists Antramthu separately from Inziang-sang and Inziang-dui. This is a regional secondary classification, not a universal preparation or specification.

sources.title: Chakrabarty, Sharma, and Tamang, “Traditional technology and product characterization of some lesser-known ethnic fermented foods and beverages of North Cachar Hills District of Assam”
sources.locator: Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 13(4) (2014), 706–715; Table 1, p. 709; abstract and characterized-sample list.
sources.supports: Primary field inventory lists two Antramthu entries made with mustard/Brassica leaves and differing pickle-with-rice and dried-curry uses. The analyzed sample set contains five other foods, not Antramthu; the inventory supports the named food and variable reported uses, not a standardized recipe or characterized sample.

sources.title: Tamang et al., “Ethnic fermented foods and beverages of India”
sources.locator: Ethnic Fermented Foods and Alcoholic Beverages of Asia (2016), pp. 17–72; table entry citing Chakrabarty et al. (2014).
sources.supports: Secondary table restates a mustard-leaf, dried/semi-liquid, pickle-with-rice description for Antramthu. It is not independent field confirmation or a universal form.

sources.title: Tamang et al., “Ethno-microbiology of ethnic Indian fermented foods and alcoholic beverages”
sources.locator: Journal of Applied Microbiology (2022), review of ethnic fermented foods.
sources.supports: Review lists Antramthu among fermented vegetable foods. General preservation descriptions are not assigned to every named food.

sources.title: Keishing et al., “Nutrient Content, Antioxidant and Antidiabetic Activities of Fermented Mustard Sauce of the tribal Community of Manipur, India”
sources.locator: Journal of Applied Bioanalysis 11(10s) (2025), 85–91; two vendor samples and naming discussion.
sources.supports: Primary study reports a Manipur fermented mustard sauce with close spellings and source-specific equivalences. These do not establish that the 2025 sauce is the same as the exact Antramthu spelling in the 2012 and 2014 preserve entries; sample and sauce claims remain source-scoped.

sources.title: OQLF, feuilles de moutarde (GDT)
sources.locator: Terme privilégié, traduction anglaise, and note on edible leaves consumed raw or cooked.
sources.supports: Supports feuilles de moutarde / mustard greens as edible leaves of various mustard types. It does not equate leafy mustard with mustard seeds, prepared mustard, gai choy, or other Brassica greens.

substitutionFindings.context: General replacement review for the named Hmar/Biate mustard-leaf preserve, including reported pickle-with-rice and dried-curry uses; no exact recipe line or dish method is specified.
substitutionFindings.basis: A bounded exact-name online search found no credible replacement direction. The 2012 review and 2014 field inventory describe Antramthu and nearby fermented leafy foods separately and report overlapping uses, but neither recommends one in place of another or gives a tested quantity. The 2025 close-spelling mustard sauce study is a distinct source-scoped preparation and gives no replacement advice.
limitations: Do not recommend generic pickled mustard greens, gundruk, inziangsang, inziang-dui, or takana-zuke as an equal or universal substitute.
No source establishes a matching dish type, ingredient role, cooking method, texture or moisture state, quantity basis, ratio, or adjustment.
Keep Anthramthu/Ankamthu/ziangsang-dui wording and sauce observations scoped to the 2025 study; do not convert them into aliases, forms, or substitution evidence.

rejectedCandidates.reason: The review reports a similar dried, sour fermented-leaf class and overlapping soup/pickle uses, but distinguishes gundruk from Antramthu by name and community; it supplies no replacement direction or ratio.
The review reports mustard leaves and dried soup/curry use for Inziang-sang but lists it separately from Antramthu; shared substrate and partial use overlap do not establish a contextual replacement.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic antramthu as a named regional mustard-leaf preserve. Keep it distinct from raw mustard greens, generic pickled mustard greens, inziangsang, gundruk, takana-zuke, and the separately named inziang-dui. The French display is provisionally borrowed. Preserve all existing entries and source-scoped observations; do not infer a universal form, process, measurement, or recipe use.

Keep substitution research blocked. Similar substrates and overlapping uses do not establish a dish-specific, method-specific, or quantity-based replacement; the reported close-spelling sauce evidence remains separate.

decisions.reason: Add an identity-only LEGUME_AND_PULSE reference for the food seed of Vigna subterranea, displayed as Bambara beans / pois bambara. CFIA lists that bilingual pair and separately codes Vigna aconitifolia moth bean. Retain only source-attested Bambara-specific English and French aliases; keep immature fresh seed, mature dry seed, pods, flour, milk, and fermented products distinct. Add no forms, measures, density, mappings, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution. An independent terminology recheck also found the Translation Bureau’s Voandzeia subterranea record listing pois bambara. The existing French display is corroborated by federal and Translation Bureau usage, but this is not an OQLF crop-specific ruling and no Québec retail preferred-name claim is made.

decisions.reason: Add fresh-market banana pepper / piment banane as one heat-unspecified market identity. Do not add a reusable measure, density, unit mapping, per-pepper mass, package yield, conversion, or general substitution from retail package sizes, survey sample masses, cultivar dimensions, or Scoville claims. The bundle has no matching ingredient demand.

decisions.reason: Add a PROTEIN identity only for human-food powder made from whole Gryllodes sigillatus crickets, displayed as banded cricket powder / poudre de grillon domestique des tropiques. The French display combines the official French species term with the product state and remains open to independent Québec terminology review. Keep house cricket, other insect species, flour, whole roasted crickets, extracts/concentrates, animal-feed products, and generic insect/cricket aliases distinct. Preserve Entomo Farms’ approximate 1 level tbsp / 10 g only as a product-specific ledger observation; activate no density, unit mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

Revise the French display to poudre de grillon à bandes. Combine Health Canada/manufacturer-supported poudre de grillon product wording for Gryllodes sigillatus with the Québec edible-insect sector’s preferred species name grillon à bandes. This is a Québec-oriented editorial combination, not a phrase quoted whole from a source or an OQLF ruling. Keep generic cricket powder / poudre de grillon searches shared across the two species and retain empty aliases.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only barley bran / son d’orge as a dry-milled barley fraction. Keep it separate from barley grain, extracted barley beta-glucan, and bran from other cereals. Preserve the French display as Canadian terminology pending independent Québec review. Add no health claim or numeric behavior.

Reviewed no supported household measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, form, or cooking yield for barley bran. Do not infer numeric values from the accepted-fibre list or its physiological classification.
No reviewed source supports a tested recipe substitution for barley bran against wheat, oat, rice, or corn bran. Add no global or contextual rule.

Retain the existing French display son d'orge as the current source-supported Québec-facing term. No exact OQLF barley-bran entry or standalone Québec barley-bran label was found, so do not call son d'orge an OQLF-preferred term. Keep the reference unchanged and add no aliases, forms, numeric values, recipe links, conversions, yields, health claims, or substitutions. decisions.reason: Accept barley flour / farine d'orge as a distinct A4 milling identity, separate from hulled and pearl barley grains. sources.title: Babarinde et al., Nutritional composition of gluten-free flour from blend of fonio (Digitaria iburua) and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and its suitability for breakfast food

sources.title: Malomo, Bosrosti, and Fabiyi, Studies On Microbiological Contents, Nutrient Composition and Functional Properties of Flour Produced from Fermented Acha (Digitaria exilis) And Iburu (Digitaria iburua)
sources.locator: Abstract; §2.2 flour preparation; §2.5.3 bulk-density method; Table 2; §3.5 discussion. Full text in publisher PDF: https://ijt.oauife.edu.ng/index.php/ijt/article/download/223/161/886.
sources.supports: Identifies fermented Iburu (Digitaria iburua) flour and describes 3-day and 5-day samples. Table 2 and §3.5 report bulk densities of 0.80 ± 0.03 and 0.83 ± 0.05 g/mL; the abstract gives a combined range of 0.83–0.94 g/mL, which conflicts with the I3 table value. The source does not define the ± statistic. Values are specific to fermented research samples, not retail flour or a household measure.

decisions.reason: Add black fonio flour / farine de fonio noir as an identity-only FLOUR_AND_STARCH reference for culinary flour made from Digitaria iburua, separate from black-fonio grain and the existing white-fonio flour identity. The French display is a transparent construction from the Government of Canada's standardized species term; it is not a Québec retail label, so independent Québec wording review remains open. Add no aliases, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

Record the available black-fonio substitution evidence as a blocked, source-scoped finding. The reviewed studies document fermented flour described broadly as a wheat alternative for snacks and fonio/pigeon-pea breakfast blends, but neither provides a recipe-specific replacement amount or a transferable rule. Keep the separate white-fonio findings, measurement research, and active substitution behavior unchanged.

Record Malomo et al.’s Table 2 and §3.5 bulk-density values for 3-day and 5-day fermented Iburu flour as separate source-scoped observations. The table and discussion report 0.80 ± 0.03 and 0.83 ± 0.05 g/mL but do not define the ± statistic; the abstract’s 0.83–0.94 g/mL range conflicts with the I3 value. Retain both details in the evidence record. These laboratory results do not establish retail flour default density or a household measure. Keep defaultDensity null and unitMappings empty.

substitutionFindings.context: Using culinary flour made from black fonio (Digitaria iburua) to replace wheat flour or another recipe flour.
substitutionFindings.basis: Malomo et al. (2024) state that fermented Acha and Iburu flours may provide an alternative to wheat flour in snack production, but report no snack formula or replacement amount. Babarinde et al. (2020) test black-fonio/pigeon-pea blend ratios and develop the 100:0 and 80:20 fonio:pigeon-pea blends into breakfast food; this composite formulation does not replace a named recipe flour.
limitations: The 2024 wheat-alternative statement is not paired with a tested snack recipe, a replacement percentage, an identified base flour, or adjustment instructions.
The 2020 article studies fonio and pigeon-pea blend proportions; it does not test substituting black-fonio flour for wheat in an existing formula.

The 2024 study uses fermented flour and reports some property ranges for Acha and Iburu together; do not transfer those findings to unfermented flour or treat them as species-specific replacement evidence.
Do not transfer the separate white-fonio (Digitaria exilis) sugar-cookie study to this Digitaria iburua reference.
No matching bundled recipe line supplies a role, amount, or method for a recipe-specific replacement.

sources.locator: Sections 2.1–2.2 (materials and bread formula), 3.2 (bread results), and 4 (conclusions).
sources.supports: Primary study uses whole white, red, and black royal quinoa flours in a controlled bread formula. The researchers grind ANAPQUI organic royal quinoa seeds with a commercial blender and use commercial wheat flour from a local Carrefour supermarket. Methods specify 25 g quinoa flour per 100 g flour, while the results and conclusion characterize the bread as a 25% replacement of wheat flour. The study does not identify a catalog-grade wheat flour, match the Naturquinoa product, or establish a reusable recipe rule.

decisions.reason: Accepted black quinoa flour as a distinct color-qualified milling identity. The French wording farine de quinoa noir is supported by a Canadian certification annex and masculine agreement; this is narrower than consumer-package evidence. Add no aliases or numeric behavior.

Record Naturquinoa's declared 60 g nutrition portion as product-specific evidence on the existing black-quinoa-flour row. No volume or method supports a reusable measure, density, mapping, or conversion; keep substitution research unreviewed and active catalog data unchanged.

Complete the deferred black-quinoa-flour substitution review by retaining the 25% bread-trial result as formula-specific evidence. The source does not identify a catalog wheat-flour counterpart or establish a tested match to the Naturquinoa product, so reusable substitution research remains blocked and no active substitution behavior is added.

substitutionFindings.context: One controlled bread study incorporating whole black royal quinoa flour at 25 g per 100 g flour; the authors describe the bread as replacing 25% of wheat flour.
substitutionFindings.basis: The formula combines the study's black quinoa flour with its supermarket Carrefour commercial wheat flour, yeast, salt, water, and breadmaking process. limitations: The study's source flour is ungraded supermarket wheat flour. Do not assign the result to all-purpose flour, whole-wheat flour, or any other active wheat-flour reference without a source match.
The researchers grind ANAPQUI organic black royal quinoa seeds with a commercial blender; no tested match to Naturquinoa's described milling process or flour batch is established.

sources.title: Allzone Trading, Non-GMO Blue Corn

sources.supports: A current Canadian B2B supply page lists a food-use blue-corn grain product and a whole-kernel grade, separately from masa/nixtamal and milling lots. Origin, grade, packaging, availability, and specifications remain quotation-dependent; this is not a consumer-retail or fixed-lot claim.

sources.title: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension, Food-grade Corn for New Mexico, Guide H-260
sources.locator: Pages 1–2, food-grade corn colour classes and blue corn food uses.
sources.supports: States that food-grade corn can be blue and that USDA colour classes are yellow, white, and mixed, with no USDA colour standard for blue corn. Supports a market colour class rather than one cultivar or universal kernel specification.

sources.title: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension, Blue Corn Production and Marketing in New Mexico, Guide H-226
sources.locator: Kernel Characteristics, Harvesting, and Blue Corn Products sections.
sources.supports: Describes blue corn as dried and stored as grain, shelled, and ground as needed, and notes that kernel traits vary by variety. This supports a dry whole-grain product boundary; it does not establish one cultivar, universal process, household measure, or substitution.

sources.title: Usito, maïs, subentry maïs bleu
sources.locator: Lexical subentry `maïs bleu`.
sources.supports: Defines maïs bleu as an older variety with blue-violet kernels used in Latin American cooking. Supports the Québec French base term; the full display `grains de maïs bleu` is a transparent product construction, not a direct package title or OQLF ruling.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only `blue corn kernels / grains de maïs bleu` for dry, food-grade whole blue-corn kernels for human food use. Keep it separate from sweet corn, generic corn kernels, Chulpe, popcorn, hominy, milled corn products, and prepared blue-corn foods. The French display is a construction from Usito’s Québec term `maïs bleu` plus the whole-kernel qualifier. Add no aliases, forms, measures, density, mappings, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions; the manifest contains no matching demand.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only blue crab / crabe bleu for Callinectes sapidus, using OQLF's direct Québec English/French/scientific-name pairing and corroborating CFIA and DFO naming evidence. Keep aliases empty and distinguish blue swimming crab / étrille bleue (Portunus pelagicus). Broad crab/crabe picker searches remain multiple-choice alongside generic crab meat and Dungeness crab. The Super C frozen-crab SKU does not disclose a species and its 454 g package amount remains SKU-specific. Add no form, measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

Accept the one historical published edible-portion count observation for raw blue crab in CNF 2015 Food Code 3096 only. Preserve the page’s separately reported total refuse 86% without calculation or reconciliation with the parenthetical 150 g and 23.1 g values. CNF 2026 row-level contents remain unverified; do not infer a form, yield, or reusable count conversion.

sources.locator: Abstract; volume 85, issue 2, pages 540–545.
sources.supports: Reports about 21 Caranx crysos specimens caught by commercial fishermen at two sites off southern Newfoundland in August–September 2013. This is historical capture evidence, not current retail supply or a kitchen-use measure.

sources.title: Préfecture de la région Guadeloupe / DEAL, Arrêté DM pêche de loisir du 20 août 2019
sources.locator: Annex 1, table of venomous fish, Carangue jaune / Yellow jack / Caranx bartholomaei.
sources.supports: A Guadeloupe regulatory table pairs Yellow jack and Carangue jaune with Caranx bartholomaei, supporting exclusion of Yellow Jack as a universal alias for Caranx crysos. This cross-jurisdiction naming context does not override OQLF’s Québec product term.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only blue runner / carangue jaune for Caranx crysos. CFIA pairs Blue Runner with the taxon; OQLF independently pairs the English and Latin terms and selects carangue jaune for Québec fish-product terminology. Keep aliases empty, including carangue coubali, yellow jack, hard tail, generic jack/carangue, and the scientific binomial. The Canadian supplier page and dated Newfoundland catches do not establish current Québec supply. Add no form, measure, density, unit mapping, yield, conversion, recipe link, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Keep the verified Portunus pelagicus identity as a candidate, but do not activate ingredient-ref-blue-swimming-crab while phrase-first search would make the broader CFIA name swimming crab (for Portunus spp.) and the shorter French query étrille (also used in étrille commune for Necora puber) resolve to this one species. Do not promote the SKU-specific crabe batailleur wording or Ocean’s crabes bleus wording to aliases; the latter conflicts with OQLF’s species-scoped crabe bleu. No active row, form, numeric value, recipe link, conversion, or substitution is added until picker behavior can preserve the broader naming boundaries.

decisions.reason: Add the brand-specific Bob's Red Mill 7 Grain Hot Cereal identity separately from other named hot-cereal blends and component grains. decisions.reason: Add identity-only bocaccio / bocaccio for Sebastes paucispinis, with no aliases. Keep sébaste bocace, bocaccio rockfish, and the shared Pacific red snapper/snapper/rock-salmon names outside the picker. The reviewed sources and bundled recipes establish no reusable measures, forms, yields, conversions, or recipe links; no substitution research is claimed.

decisions.reason: Add source-named Brazilian polvilho azedo as a distinct identity-only cassava-starch product.
