substitutionFindings.context: Only the polvilho biscuit ('biscoito de polvilho azedo' / peta-style biscuit) formulation reported in the 2016 UFC conference abstract.
substitutionFindings.basis: The abstract reports 30%, 40%, and 50% replacement of polvilho azedo by polvilho doce. Given the formula's 100-part polvilho azedo line, those percentages most naturally refer to that ingredient portion, not total dough (inference). The abstract does not say whether the parts or percentages are by mass, volume, or another basis. It reports decreasing dough acidity and no significant variation in measured specific volumes at the authors' stated p=0.05 criterion through 50% replacement in the tested formulations; it provides no per-formulation values, exact p-values, or full statistical method.
expectedEffects: Lower measured dough acidity as the polvilho-doce share increases in the tested formulation.
No statistically significant specific-volume change was reported for the tested 30%, 40%, and 50% replacement levels in this experiment.
limitations: The source is a conference-proceedings abstract, not a full methods/results report. Brands and processing details are not identified; the denominator reading is inferred from the 100-part azedo formula line, and the mass/volume/other basis of the parts and percentages is unstated; per-formulation measurements, exact p-values, and full statistical method are absent.
Evidence applies only to this biscuit formulation and its tested partial replacement levels; do not infer full replacement, another direction, or transfer to pão de queijo or other recipes.
The source reports expansion and acidity, not sensory acceptance, flavor, texture, handling, shelf life, or general baking performance.
Do not create an active global or contextual rule, a recipe-line link, a density, a measurement conversion, or a reusable amount from this finding.

decisions.reason: Add source-named Brazilian polvilho doce as a distinct identity-only cassava-starch product. MAPA guidance and Brazilian technical/manufacturer sources distinguish the named product from non-fermented fécula and polvilho azedo; MAPA also cautions that a repeatable/reproducible method to distinguish these products and mixtures is unavailable. Keep polvilho doce visible in the French display pending Québec terminology review. Use only the manufacturer-attested English descriptor sweet cassava starch in a display that retains the Portuguese product name. Do not interpret doce as added sugar or a universal sweetness/process specification. Do not add aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, conversions, yields, substitutions, or recipe links; do not map sweet tapioca starch or unqualified tapioca starch globally.

Record Yoki's manufacturer-declared 20 g per 1 colher de sopa as a source-specific portion on the existing polvilho doce identity. Retain the Portuguese spoon wording without converting it to a standardized Canadian tablespoon or inferring a filling method. The Québec-facing Marché Brésil listing supplies local product context but is out of stock and gives no measure. Keep default density null, unit mappings empty, substitution research not yet researched, and the separate polvilho azedo and generic tapioca/cassava-starch identities unchanged; do not add a reusable conversion, form, package yield, recipe link, or substitution.

Keep Doce substitution research blocked. The comparative study and general guidance do not directly authorize this directional replacement, and the half-swap tip appears in a full indexed publisher-page snapshot for one recipe version while the directly accessible canonical page serves a different formula. Preserve the version conflict, both active identities, and R688 measurement evidence; retain R716’s separately owned sour-to-sweet biscuit finding; and add no active substitution rule or recipe link.

substitutionFindings.context: Potential sweet-to-sour replacement in the full indexed publisher snapshot of Ana Maria Braga’s named pão de queijo recipe; applicability is unresolved because the clean canonical page serves a different formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: The full publisher-page snapshot lists 1 kg polvilho doce and gives a recipe-specific tip to replace half with polvilho azedo for a softer crust. It therefore documents the direction and stated purpose for that captured recipe version. The clean canonical route opened on 2026-10-19 instead lists 500 g polvilho azedo, yields 40 units, and has no sweet-polvilho line or tip. This page-version conflict blocks claiming that the snapshot instruction applies to the currently served recipe. The Pereira study compares formulas but does not itself authorize a directional replacement in a named recipe; general Globo guidance gives no direction-specific formula or amount.
expectedEffects: The captured page says the tip aims for a softer crust; it reports no comparative or controlled result for that effect.
limitations: The finding remains blocked because the full indexed publisher snapshot and the clean canonical page opened on 2026-10-19 serve different recipe formulas.
Treat the half-swap instruction as applying only to the captured Ana Maria Braga page version; do not claim that it applies to the currently served canonical recipe or other pão de queijo formulas.
The captured formula lists 1 kg polvilho doce but the tip does not state a revised full formula or the resulting sour-polvilho amount or basis. Do not calculate a replacement quantity or ratio.
The softer-crust effect is the snapshot’s stated aim, not a measured or independently verified outcome.
The comparative paper’s blend groups do not independently establish a one-way substitution, and the Globo explainer supplies no direction-specific formula or amount.
This review concerns the inverse direction in cheese bread only. It does not reopen R716’s sour-to-sweet biscuit result or complete the polvilho substitution-family review.
Do not create an active global/contextual rule, recipe-line link, density, unit mapping, measure, or conversion.

quantity.unitConvention: The WSU source’s unqualified cup; not converted to RecipeBook’s cup convention.

substitutionFindings.context: The Washington State University / Clark County Extension mix-and-match meatloaf framework for 1 1/2 lb ground meat, using its single one-cup binder choice. Quick oats are one of the listed oat options; the source also lists breadcrumbs as a choice.
substitutionFindings.basis: The WSU framework offers a one-cup choice of breadcrumbs or oats (quick or regular). The Kitchn separately names quick-cooking oats as replacing traditional breadcrumbs in its own meatloaf. Together these support the one-cup quick-oat option only within the WSU framework, not a controlled or universal ratio.
adjustments: The WSU framework directs mixing the selected binder with its other ingredients and gives the framework’s bake/rest instructions; it states no oats-specific soaking, liquid, fat, salt, temperature, or timing adjustment. Do not transfer The Kitchn recipe’s 1/3 cup milk because that quantity belongs to its separate formula.
expectedEffects: The WSU source reports no comparative result. In The Kitchn’s own formula, the author says quick oats act as a binder and help the loaf hold its shape when sliced; keep this outcome attached to that recipe.
limitations: The source cup convention is unspecified; do not convert this source quantity to RecipeBook’s cup convention or infer mass, density, or a mass-to-mass ratio.
The breadcrumb form is unspecified; do not bind the evidence to fresh or dried breadcrumbs.
Do not activate a global or contextual rule: the evidence is limited to the named meatloaf binder framework, and the current resolver cannot enforce that binder role or a meatloaf dish type.
Do not generalize the reported texture, moisture, or cooking outcome to other meatloaves, meatballs, coatings, stuffing, or baking uses.

decisions.reason: Accept a narrow identity for flour made from Artocarpus altilis flesh. The regional French source names farine de fruit à pain; add no aliases, forms, numeric data, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions. No bundled recipe line matched.

Keep breadfruit flour as a separate identity for dried, milled edible Artocarpus altilis flesh; do not merge it with fresh fruit, breadnut seed flour, hybrid-only scope, or extracted breadfruit starch. Study-specific bulk-density values are not standardized kitchen-volume measures; no reliable product-specific household measure or general density is supported. Keep defaultDensity null, unitMappings empty, and do not convert study measurements into recipe quantities.
Broad wheat-flour replacement advice supplies no ratio. A partial replacement result applies only to one tested cake formula and does not support a global substitution or another recipe context.

Retain `breadfruit flour / farine de fruit à pain` as a provisional display. OQLF supports fruit à pain for the fruit and a French Pacific leaflet uses the exact flour phrase, but Québec flour usage was not located. Preserve the existing Artocarpus altilis scope and existing source-specific bulk-density observations without activating a default.

sources.supports: Documents one Québec breakfast-sausage product made with pork and beef, sold as 110 portions of 45 g, with freezer storage. Product-specific evidence only; it does not define a universal species, portion conversion, or recipe 027 product.

sources.title: Johnsonville Canada, Saucisses à Déjeuner de Porc et Bœuf
sources.locator: French product name, Québec manufacture, description, and product-specific ingredient statement.
sources.supports: Uses the French product name saucisses à déjeuner for a Québec-made pork-and-beef breakfast-sausage product. Product-specific naming and composition; does not establish a universal formula or a recipe conversion.

sources.title: John Kanell, Preppy Kitchen, Breakfast Casserole
sources.locator: “What You Need to Make This Recipe,” sausage paragraph; recipe-card ingredients and instructions; “Pro Tips For Making This Recipe,” meat-free bullet and recipe-card note.
sources.supports: The current 12-serving, 9×13-inch formula lists 2 lb ground pork sausage. Its meat-free note says to skip the sausage and replace it with a vegetable such as mushrooms for umami flavour. It gives no mushroom amount, ratio, preparation, or adjustment. This source record supports only the named formula and is separate from the existing cheddar-specific record for the same URL.

decisions.reason: Verify the existing breakfast sausage / saucisse à déjeuner identity as a named product class. CFIA distinguishes breakfast/uncooked sausage from preserved/cured sausage; OQLF and current Québec product usage support the bilingual class name. Preserve the active reference, aliases, recipe 027#1 link, saved quantity, and unit. Do not infer one species, a universal formula, a fresh/cured form, a portion conversion, or a substitution.

substitutionFindings.context: Preppy Kitchen’s current 12-serving, 9×13-inch Breakfast Casserole formula with ground pork sausage, hash browns, bell pepper, green onion, eggs, milk, and cheddar. The meat-free note suggests mushrooms for this formula. RecipeBook 027#1 is not attached: its saved eight-serving formula and method differ materially despite sharing the source URL.
substitutionFindings.basis: The author’s “Pro Tips For Making This Recipe” and recipe-card notes name mushrooms as one vegetable option when omitting the sausage. The source gives no mushroom amount.
adjustments: The source gives no mushroom-specific preparation, skillet order, fat or liquid replacement, seasoning change, temperature, timing, or other adjustment. Do not transfer the sausage browning and retained-drippings instructions to mushrooms.
expectedEffects: The author describes mushrooms as an umami-flavoured meat-free option; no evidence establishes matching flavour, texture, structure, protein, yield, moisture, or cooking result.
limitations: Limit the finding to the current named Preppy Kitchen formula and its stated meat-free option.
Do not infer an amount, ratio, inverse direction, or recommendation for RecipeBook 027#1, another casserole, other sausage identities or species, other vegetables, or other methods.
The source labels the variation meat-free; this does not establish vegan, allergen-safe, nutrition-equivalent, or food-safety claims.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List, full lookup results
sources.locator: Full list rows for Abramis brama (TSN 163666), Boops boops (TSN 169218), and Parabramis pekinensis (TSN 639626).
sources.supports: The Fish List pairs Bream / Brème with Abramis brama, Bream / Bogue with Boops boops, and White Amur Bream / Brème with Parabramis pekinensis. It shows bream wording across distinct taxa. These are Canadian fish-labelling names, not culinary-equivalence or substitution evidence.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only bream / brème as a species-neutral name group with a visible multi-species qualifier. CFIA assigns bream wording to distinct fish taxa. Keep the marine sea-bream / dorade group separate. Add no aliases, taxon, forms, density, unit mappings, recipe links, measures, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: RECYC-QUÉBEC, Réemploi et suprarecyclage
sources.locator: Nourrir des gens; examples of food reuse through processing.
sources.supports: Uses farine issue de drêches de brasserie as a Québec human-food reuse example. Supports the proposed descriptive French display and food-use context, not one standardized grade, recipe formula, measure, or product specification.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, drêche sèche (GDT)
sources.locator: Term, related terms, domain, and English translations.
sources.supports: Supports the Québec French lexical base drêche(s) for spent brewery grain. Its technical note concerns a dated material and does not establish human-food use, a universal flour grade, or a transferable bran substitution.

sources.title: Tiziana Amoriello et al., Technological Properties and Consumer Acceptability of Bakery Products Enriched with Brewers’ Spent Grains
sources.locator: Materials and Methods §§2.1–2.4; bakery-product trials.
sources.supports: Primary study dries, mills, and sieves one fresh barley brewers’ spent-grain sample into flour and tests it in wheat-flour blends for bread, breadsticks, and pizza. The sample, drying endpoint, particle size, analytical findings, and 5%/10% experimental blend results remain specific to this study and do not establish general recipe amounts, composition, or substitution ratios.

sources.title: E. Ktenioudaki et al., Brewer’s spent grain as a functional ingredient for breadsticks
sources.locator: Abstract and study of brewers’ spent grain in breadstick formulations.
sources.supports: Primary study evaluates brewers’ spent grain in baked breadsticks and corroborates human-food use. Its formulation, processing, and product outcomes are study-specific; it does not set a general ingredient replacement direction, ratio, or adjustment.

substitutionFindings.context: Use of brewers’ spent-grain flour as a replacement for ordinary recipe flour, without a specified target dish or formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed studies test source-specific experimental bakery blends and report changes in dough behavior and product properties. They do not establish a generally applicable replacement ratio or adjustment for ordinary recipes.
limitations: Do not generalize the study-specific 5% and 10% flour-blend levels to other recipes or spent-grain samples.
No target recipe, flour function, processing state, ratio, or adjustment is supported for a contextual replacement rule.
The Québec human-food example establishes reuse context only; it does not establish a substitution recommendation.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic brewers’ spent grain flour / farine issue de drêches de brasserie. Keep the process-defined flour separate from fresh spent grain, distillers’ grains, bran, malt flour, and extracted BSG ingredients. The Québec human-food example and primary baking studies support identity; no aliases, forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or active substitutions are added.
No reusable kitchen measure, mass-volume conversion, density, yield, or standard flour grade is supported. Study preparation details and blend percentages remain source-specific.
Keep recipe substitution research blocked pending contextual evidence; the reviewed bakery blends do not establish a general replacement ratio or adjustment.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards, Volume 7 — Dairy Products
sources.locator: Source as cited in the proposal source register; see supports for the cited scope.
sources.supports: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards, Volume 7 — Dairy Products (https://inspection.canada.ca/en/about-cfia/acts-and-regulations/list-acts-and-regulations/documents-incorporated-reference/canadian-food-compositional-standards-0). Canadian standards for named varieties, cream cheese/spread, cottage/creamed cottage, and cheddar aging; composition values in this proposal are regulatory limits only.

sources.title: OQLF, Brie
sources.locator: Source as cited in the proposal source register; see supports for the cited scope.
sources.supports: OQLF, Brie (https://vitrinelinguistique.oqlf.gouv.qc.ca/fiche-gdt/fiche/10423418/brie). English and French name.

decisions.reason: Keep Brie as a named identity distinct from Camembert and the broader soft-ripened family.

substitutionFindings.context: No global substitution is established by the reviewed identity sources.
limitations: No exact linked recipe demand or supported amount is present in the bundle.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service, 2021–2023 Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies Documentation
sources.locator: FoodWeights description, page 13
sources.supports: States that portion weights are edible portions as consumed and are estimates for generic or composite foods; they may not account for every size of a specific product. It provides no matching raw brioche slice weight for the unspecified brioche in recipe 075 ingredient 4.

decisions.reason: For recipe 075 ingredient 4 (5 to 8 slices brioche bread), preserve the range and keep count-to-mass measurement blocked pending a source that matches the brioche product, slice size, and raw/as-consumed basis. The USDA documentation describes generic/composite portion estimates that may not cover all product sizes; no matching source or slice mass was verified. Add no numeric observation, conversion, density, substitution, or recipe edit.

sources.title: OQLF, brocoli
sources.locator: Preferred French/English terms and distinction from chou-brocoli
sources.supports: Pairs brocoli with broccoli/sprouting broccoli and distinguishes ordinary broccoli from chou-brocoli related to cauliflower.

decisions.reason: Reviewed the existing brocoli / broccoli identity against OQLF and activated only the source-listed sprouting broccoli term. Keep Chinese broccoli and chou-brocoli distinct.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension, Growing broccoli in home gardens
sources.locator: Broccoli identity and edible-leaf culinary-use statements.
sources.supports: Identifies ordinary broccoli as Brassica oleracea var. italica, states its leaves are edible, and describes using them like kale or collards. Supports the plant-part identity; the comparison is not a general substitution rule or measurement.

sources.title: Oregon State University Extension, Broccoli
sources.locator: Culinary-use section describing raw and cooked broccoli leaves.
sources.supports: Independently describes broccoli leaves as usable raw or cooked like kale or collards. Supports culinary use only; no substitution ratio, form model, or reusable amount is established.

sources.title: Catena Farm, Brocoli + Feuilles de Brocoli
sources.locator: French page heading and broccoli-leaf culinary/cooking sections.
sources.supports: Attests the French wording feuilles de brocoli and describes culinary use of broccoli leaves. Storage, nutrition, taste, and preparation details remain specific to this source and are not transferred to generic data.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, brocoli (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred French base term and taxonomic scope.
sources.supports: Supports the Québec French base term brocoli and ordinary-broccoli taxonomic scope. It does not standardize the full plant-part phrase feuilles de brocoli.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only broccoli leaves / feuilles de brocoli for the culinary leaves of ordinary cultivated broccoli. Keep it separate from broccoli florets and stalks, Chinese broccoli, baby broccoli, rapini, other Brassica crops, and sprouts. The kale/collard comparison is contextual use only. Add no form, measure, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Canada Border Services Agency, Customs Tariff, Chapter 10 (2026, English)
sources.locator: Chapter 10, tariff item 1006.40.00, rice
sources.supports: Names tariff item 1006.40.00 “Broken rice,” separate from husked/brown rice and semi-milled or wholly milled rice. Federal commodity nomenclature; paired with the French schedule for the bilingual term. Does not establish measurements or cooking behavior.

sources.title: Agence des services frontaliers du Canada, Tarif des douanes, chapitre 10 (2026, français)
sources.locator: Chapitre 10, numéro tarifaire 1006.40.00, riz
sources.supports: Nomme le numéro tarifaire 1006.40.00 « Riz en brisures », distinct du riz cargo/brun et du riz semi-blanchi ou blanchi. Nomenclature fédérale des marchandises; jumelé au tarif anglais pour le terme bilingue. N’établit ni mesures ni comportement à la cuisson.

sources.title: OQLF, brisures de riz (1982)
sources.locator: Brewing component-of-beer domain; definition and associated term
sources.supports: Defines broken rice grains used as starch substitutes and gives brisures de riz / broken rice, while explicitly scoping the entry to brewing.

sources.title: OQLF, brisures de riz (1986)
sources.locator: Brewing component-of-beer domain; definition and English translations
sources.supports: Describes grains fragmented longitudinally or transversally during milling; lists brewer's rice, broken rice, rice grits, and rice screenings, all within a brewing-domain entry. Do not globalize those associated terms.

sources.title: Codex Standard for Rice CXS 198-1995 (English)
sources.locator: Scope, sections 2.1.1 and 4.1.1–4.1.5
sources.supports: Covers rice for direct human consumption, defines rice as whole and broken Oryza sativa kernels, and distinguishes head rice, large/medium/small broken kernels, and chips. Supports the edible physical boundary but does not decide catalog identity versus form.

sources.title: Government of Canada, CUSMA Canadian Tariff Schedule (French)
sources.locator: Tariff item 1006.40.00
sources.supports: Uses riz en brisures as a separate French commodity name from milled rice and rice flour classifications; supports terminology, not culinary behavior.

sources.title: Marché Afritibi, Brisures de riz au jasmin Parfumé
sources.locator: French product name, ingredient declaration, and cooking directions
sources.supports: Québec retailer sells brisures de riz au jasmin parfumé as 100% jasmine rice and provides consumer cooking directions; supports a human-food product listing while retaining the jasmine qualifier.

sources.title: Marché Afritibi, Jasmine Broken Rice
sources.locator: English product name and ingredient declaration
sources.supports: English product listing names Jasmine Broken Rice and declares 100% jasmine rice, paired with the French retailer page [WP03-S65].

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Rice (CXS 198-1995)
sources.locator: Section 4.1, broken-kernel classes
sources.supports: Defines broken-kernel size classes as fragments measured against whole kernels. Supports broken rice as a physical/milling grade rather than a cooking-state form; does not settle recipe-facing catalog allocation or French wording.

sources.title: USDA Economic Research Service, Growing Demand for Broken Rice for Feed and Food
sources.locator: Introduction and broken-rice milling/food-use discussion, pp. 1–2
sources.supports: Describes broken rice as fragments/byproduct of milling and documents food use, including West African dishes. Supports processing boundary and food use, not universal culinary equivalence.

sources.title: Marché Afritibi, Brisures de riz au jasmin parfumé
sources.locator: Product title/description and related product listing
sources.supports: A Québec retailer uses brisures de riz for a food product and lists riz cassé 2 fois separately. Supports local market wording but not a global equivalence among brisures de riz, riz cassé, and generic broken rice.

sources.title: Organic Mandya, Broken Rice
sources.locator: Product description and FAQ, “What is broken rice called in different languages?”
sources.supports: The producer describes broken rice as milling fragments and lists Hindi Tukda Chawal. This is producer wording, not a Hindi terminology standard or a claim about every market.

sources.title: Sports Authority of India, Procurement of Dry Ration
sources.locator: Dry ration procurement listing, “Rice Tukda” item; indexed PDF text.
sources.supports: Lists an unbranded Rice Tukda procurement item. Direct PDF retrieval did not complete; the item corroborates procurement wording but gives no product or grain specification.

decisions.reason: The evidence supports intentionally sold edible broken rice / brisures de riz, but the OQLF term entries are scoped to brewing and Codex treats broken kernels as rice quality classes, not necessarily a separate recipe identity. Keep brewer's rice, rice grits, rice screenings, cracked rice, riz cassé, and riz brisé inactive as global aliases. Resolve identity-versus-form treatment with WP01's dry/cooked rice model before allocating an active row; import no numeric data.

Codex classifies broken kernels by physical fragment size and USDA ERS documents broken rice as a milling byproduct with food use; the product boundary is therefore clearer than in the earlier review, and brokenness is not a preparation-state form. Keep the candidate out of the active catalog because no bundled recipe requests it and generic Québec French wording remains unresolved: OQLF brisures de riz records are brewing-scoped, while Québec retail wording distinguishes brisures de riz from riz cassé 2 fois. Do not add a broken-rice form under generic rice or activate brewing terms as aliases.

The current 2026 Canadian Customs Tariff pairs “Broken rice” / “Riz en brisures” at tariff item 1006.40.00. The Codex rice standard applies to rice for direct human consumption and defines both whole and broken kernels, supporting an edible physical/milling-grade identity. Broken rice is not a dry/cooked preparation form; create a separate identity with no aliases, forms, numeric data, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions. No bundled recipe currently requests it, but recipe demand is not required to include a verified ingredient identity. Keep the OQLF brewing-scoped brisures de riz terms, brewer’s rice, rice grits, rice screenings, cracked rice, riz cassé, and riz brisé inactive as aliases; do not infer variety or cooking behavior.

Add only the exact romanized Hindi search alias tukda chawal to the existing broken-rice identity. Organic Mandya identifies Tukda Chawal as Hindi for its broken-rice product; the indexed Sports Authority procurement item “Rice Tukda” is corroborating wording only. Do not add bare tukda, tukda rice, rice tukda, a French alias, or any new identity, form, measurement, conversion, recipe association, or substitution.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, omble de fontaine (GDT)
sources.locator: Edible-fish and ichthyology domains; preferred term, English and Latin equivalents, and notes on non-retained Québec fish-product terms.
sources.supports: Normalizes omble de fontaine, pairs it with brook trout and Salvelinus fontinalis, and lists speckled trout in English. Truite mouchetée is a context term not retained for Québec fish-product marketing; it is stored only as an internal search alias, while the normalized display remains omble de fontaine.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Omble de fontaine
sources.locator: French and English common names, alternate names, scientific name, similar species, and food-market aquaculture note.
sources.supports: Pairs Omble de fontaine / Brook trout / Salvelinus fontinalis, lists brook charr, speckled trout, and truite mouchetée as alternate names, and distinguishes rainbow trout, touladi, and omble chevalier. Food-market aquaculture context does not establish current retail stock or a specific product; biological size and weight are not culinary measures.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, omble de fontaine anadrome (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition of the anadromous form and note on the broader use of truite de mer.
sources.supports: Defines anadromous brook trout as a migratory form of Salvelinus fontinalis and notes that truite de mer can also name migratory forms of other salmonids. This supports keeping the form and broad sea-trout wording out of aliases; it does not establish a recipe form or substitution.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List query for Brook Trout
sources.locator: Search result for TSN 162003, Salvelinus fontinalis, and related common-name entries.
sources.supports: Lists Brook Trout / Omble De Fontaine and Speckled Trout for Salvelinus fontinalis and uses the unqualified Trout label for multiple salmonid taxa. Canadian fish-label common-name evidence, not a recipe taxonomy or substitution standard.

decisions.reason: Accept brook trout / omble de fontaine as an identity-only PROTEIN reference for Salvelinus fontinalis. Preserve the OQLF-normalized French display. Add brook charr and speckled trout as English search aliases and truite mouchetée only as a search alias; it is not the Québec fish-product display. Keep generic trout/truite, char/charr/omble, anadromous wording, and sibling taxa distinct. Add no forms, default measures, density, unit mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions. The 114-recipe corpus has no matching demand, and no reusable culinary measurement is supported.

sources.title: OQLF, Grand dictionnaire terminologique — Bouillon
sources.locator: Term record, culinary definition, and English translation.
sources.supports: Supports the Québec French term bouillon and English broth for the ordinary culinary liquid; it separately names consommé terminology and does not equate broth with stock.

sources.title: Cotter Crunch, Lindsay Cotter, African Peanut Stew
sources.locator: Recipe card and Ingredients and Substitutions; optional meat and broth lines; page updated 2022-07-20.
sources.supports: The publisher card lists optional one-pound (450 g) diced stew-meat choices (chicken, beef, or pork). It also lists two cups of broth and describes vegetable or chicken broth or stock for this stew, with less broth in the meatless version. This supports the local recipe wording only; it does not define generic broth, establish global broth/stock equivalence, or provide a transferable measurement or substitution.

decisions.reason: Accept generic broth / bouillon for an ingredient line that names broth without a type (recipe 090#9). Keep it distinct from named beef/chicken/vegetable broth references, beef stock, broth concentrate, powders, and consommé. The publisher page also mentions broth or stock for this particular stew, but that contextual recipe wording is not a global equivalence or substitution rule. No form, measurement, density, conversion, or substitution is established.

Keep broth concentrate / concentré de bouillon as a provisional exact-text owner for recipe 044#5 pending direct evidence for a generic concentrate class and Québec French display. Remove Better Than Bouillon aliases; the branded recipe line 099#3 now links to its separate family identity.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, barbotte (GDT)
sources.locator: Normalized Québec edible-fish term, English translations, species, and commercial-label note.
sources.supports: Normalizes barbotte for Québec fish-product marketing and maps it to Ameiurus nebulosus, brown bullhead, catfish, and common catfish. Says barbotte brune was not retained for Québec fish-product marketing; the catalog uses it only as a qualified search alias.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List brown bullhead query
sources.locator: Species-linked common-name result and neighboring bullhead/catfish entries.
sources.supports: Lists Ameiurus nebulosus as Brown Bullhead / Barbotte and shows the species scope of Canadian fish-label names. Neighboring entries assign related common terms to other taxa, so no bare catfish or bullhead alias is activated.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Barbotte brune species profile
sources.locator: Bilingual species names, Ameiurus nebulosus, alternate names, neighboring taxa, and commercial exploitation.
sources.supports: Identifies Ameiurus nebulosus as brown bullhead, lists brown catfish and barbotte as alternate names, distinguishes yellow bullhead, stonecat, and channel catfish, and reports commercial exploitation in the St. Lawrence. Whole-fish size observations are not kitchen measures.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Portrait de la pêche commerciale
sources.locator: Current overview of principal freshwater commercial species and the St. Lawrence/Lake Saint-Pierre fishery.
sources.supports: Lists brown bullhead among commercially harvested freshwater fish in Québec. The overview does not provide species-specific current landings, retail stock, or recipe quantities.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Barbotte — Simmer International
sources.locator: Current Québec product listing, fish presentations, Lac Saint-Pierre provenance, and bulk-format wording.
sources.supports: Lists eviscerated, skinned, and skinless frozen fillet products as Barbotte from Lac Saint-Pierre. The displayed bulk format 4.54 has no explicit unit and is not a reusable kitchen quantity.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec / MAPAQ, Permis de pêche commerciale en eau douce
sources.locator: Commercial freshwater species and legal sale for consumption.
sources.supports: Lists brown bullhead among Québec freshwater commercial species and describes legally caught fish sold for consumption. This is market-pathway evidence, not culinary measurement or recipe evidence.

substitutionFindings.context: General recipe use for Ameiurus nebulosus; the complete bundled recipe corpus has no matching fish request.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed terminology, fishery, and product sources establish a locally marketed species but provide no tested replacement, recipe method, or ratio. Shared catfish terminology or taxonomic relationship does not establish culinary interchangeability.
limitations: The reviewed source set establishes no global or contextual substitute.
Keep channel catfish, other bullhead species, and other catfish taxa separate; do not infer cooking or food-safety equivalence.

decisions.reason: Add one identity-only PROTEIN reference for Ameiurus nebulosus, displayed brown bullhead / barbotte. Use only the qualified search aliases brown catfish and barbotte brune. Keep generic catfish and bullhead terms, channel catfish, yellow bullhead, and stonecat distinct. The 4.54 product-page format has no unit, and whole-fish biological weights do not support kitchen measures. Add no forms, density, unit mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Agriculture et Agroalimentaire Canada, La graine de moutarde : situation et perspectives
sources.locator: Bimonthly Bulletin 14(8), pp. 1–2; mustard types, uses, and French terms.
sources.supports: Names brown mustard seed as a Canadian type, distinguishes it from yellow and oriental seed, and describes its food use. The report’s historic market statistics and oil percentage are not recipe measures.

sources.title: OnlineOrganics, Graines de moutarde brune biologique
sources.locator: French product title and product description.
sources.supports: A Canadian French product listing names brown mustard seeds and identifies Brassica juncea; its SKU and package details do not establish a reusable measure.

sources.title: Canadian Food Focus, Canadian Ingredient Spotlight: Mustard
sources.locator: Mustard type descriptions and culinary use.
sources.supports: Distinguishes yellow/white from brown and oriental mustard seed types in a Canadian culinary overview; it does not establish household conversions.

decisions.reason: Add brown mustard seeds / graines de moutarde brune as a source-supported food seed class. Keep it distinct from oriental mustard seed even though Canadian sources place both under Brassica juncea; add no regional or transliterated aliases.

The reviewed evidence does not establish a reusable household measure, density, mapping, or yield for this mustard-seed type. Agricultural figures, source package amounts, and branded serving information are not transferred into active recipe behavior.
No reviewed source establishes a tested, scoped ratio or method for replacing this mustard-seed type with another seed or spice. Keep substitution behavior empty.

sources.title: TERMIUM Plus, brown rice / riz brun
sources.locator: Milling and Cereal Industries record for RIZ INTEGRAL
sources.supports: Lists brown rice as the correct English term and riz brun as the correct French term; defines brown rice as rice with the hull removed and the bran retained. Also lists riz complet and riz intégral, which are not activated as aliases pending Québec review.

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Rice CXS 198-1995
sources.locator: Section 2.1.1.2–2.1.1.3 and Annex A
sources.supports: Defines husked (brown) rice by removal of the husk only and milled (white) rice by removal of all or part of the bran and germ; grain-length classification is a separate axis.

sources.title: Government of Canada, Spécifications sur la qualité des aliments – Riz
sources.locator: SQA-22, paragraphs 5–9
sources.supports: Names Riz Brun as a whole-grain rice distinction, states that long-, short-, and glutinous rice can be consumed brown, and specifies long-grain brown rice by default when no length is given.

sources.title: OQLF, riz cargo
sources.locator: Definition, note, and English term
sources.supports: Defines riz cargo as rice without its husk, pairs it with the English term hulled rice, and explicitly identifies it in the note as brown rice. These are the only activated aliases.

sources.title: La Moisson, Riz brun long biologique — Abénakis Gourmet
sources.locator: French product description: “Le riz long brun, aussi appelé riz complet”; product grain/milling description
sources.supports: A Québec retailer explicitly uses riz complet for its intact long brown rice product and describes the retained bran layer. Supports this French search alias for the brown-rice milling identity; it is product-language evidence, not an OQLF preference, generic grain-length claim, or measure.

sources.title: Dainty, Basmati brun
sources.locator: French product description, “Qu’est-ce que c’est” section
sources.supports: The Canadian manufacturer calls brown basmati “un riz complet à grains entiers” and says only the hull is removed while bran and germ remain. Supports Canadian French product usage for the brown-rice milling distinction; variety-specific wording, not a recipe measure or conversion.

decisions.reason: Add brown rice / riz brun as an identity-only milling distinction in GRAIN_AND_CEREAL. TERMIUM gives the display pair; OQLF directly supports hulled rice and riz cargo as same-identity aliases. Keep cargo rice, riz décortiqué, riz complet, riz intégral, and riz non usiné inactive pending broader regional review. Brown is a milling axis that can overlap long-, medium-, short-grain, and glutinous rice; keep this identity separate from brown rice flour and do not create grain-length × milling × cooked-state rows or forms. Add no density, unit mapping, measurement, yield, conversion, or substitution data. The 114 bundled recipes contain no brown-rice request.

Add riz complet as one French search alias on the existing brown-rice milling identity. The existing TERMIUM source WP03-S115 lists the term under its brown-rice milling record; Québec retailer and Canadian manufacturer sources use it for intact long brown rice and brown basmati. Keep brown rice / riz brun as the display and retain hulled rice / riz cargo. Do not add riz intégral or other unreviewed variants; keep qualified red-rice and rice-flake wording separate. No forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions are added.

sources.title: Eden Foods, Brown Rice Flakes organic
sources.locator: Product title, ingredient declaration, and manufacturer details.
sources.supports: Names brown rice flakes, identifies organic short-grain brown rice as the ingredient, and describes this product as roasted and rolled. Product-specific processing, package size, and cooking claims do not establish a generic measure or substitution.

sources.title: Eden Foods, Canadian product image catalogue
sources.locator: Cereal » Flakes entry 183055.
sources.supports: The Canadian bilingual product listing pairs Brown Rice Flakes with Flocons de Riz Brun Rond and identifies it as whole grain. The round/short-grain qualifier and package details are product-specific, not identity-level aliases or measures.

substitutionFindings.context: The cake batter in King Arthur Baking's Cinnamon-Streusel Coffee Cake only. The source says its brown sugar can be replaced with granulated sugar because the brown-sugar amount is small relative to the granulated sugar and the formula uses baking powder.
substitutionFindings.basis: The source formula lists 1 1/2 cups (298 g) granulated sugar and 1/3 cup (71 g) brown sugar in the cake batter. The article permits the directional swap for this formula but does not state the replacement quantity or whether to match by mass or volume; no ratio is encoded.
expectedEffects: King Arthur says the small brown-sugar proportion does not affect this cake's structure. Replacing brown sugar also removes some brown-sugar color and caramel flavor.
limitations: Applies only to the named coffee-cake batter formula and its brown-sugar line; it is not linked to the separate RecipeBook coffee-cake recipe.
Do not infer a same-mass or same-volume amount, transfer the finding to another cake or muffin formula, or use it for cookies.
King Arthur warns that in cookies brown sugar's acidity helps activate baking soda; replacing it with granulated sugar can require acid/leavener changes and may alter spread.

substitutionFindings.context: The filling in King Arthur Baking's Cinnamon-Streusel Coffee Cake only. The source identifies its separate filling as 1 cup brown sugar with cinnamon and cocoa and says granulated sugar is structurally acceptable in a filling that has no structure.
substitutionFindings.basis: The recipe lists 1 cup (213 g) packed brown sugar in the filling and no granulated sugar there. The article permits granulated sugar for this filling but gives no replacement quantity or mass/volume basis; no ratio is encoded.
expectedEffects: The source says the filling will lose brown sugar's caramelized flavor if granulated sugar is used.
limitations: Applies only to the named coffee-cake filling; keep this separate from the cake-batter finding and do not transfer it to structured batters, cookies, or other fillings.
Do not infer a same-mass or same-volume amount or link the source formula to a RecipeBook recipe.

sources.title: Eren and Akkaya, Effect of different forms of buckwheat addition on the physicochemical and sensory properties of bread
sources.versionOrDate: Czech Journal of Food Sciences 42(3) (2024), 216-223; DOI 10.17221/36/2024-CJFS
sources.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods, Material and Bread production; Table 1; Conclusion.
sources.supports: Primary study tests 10%, 20%, and 30% buckwheat-flour substitution in one white-wheat-bread formula, using common buckwheat groats ground below 500 micrometres to whole flour at 100% yield. It identifies 20% as the most appropriate flour level within that study and reports lower bread volume for all buckwheat-added samples than control. The tested flour and formula do not establish a general recipe rule.

decisions.reason: Accepted buckwheat flour as a distinct milling product using Canadian bilingual labels. It is not wheat flour; no substitutions or numeric data were added.

Added the source-backed English search aliases kuttu atta, kuttu ka atta, and kuttu flour to the existing buckwheat-flour identity. Retained the preferred Québec display farine de sarrasin, excluded bare kuttu and unsupported French regional spellings, and added no form or numeric behavior.

Add only the independently attested hyphenated English search alias soba-ko to the existing buckwheat-flour identity. Keep the fused sobako spelling unallocated because the current picker normalizes case and the official SOBAKO concept uses the same fused key for a distinct 0%-buckwheat product. Keep the Québec French display, forms, density, mappings, measurement state, and substitution state unchanged.

Keep fused sobako unallocated: it is a Japanese common noun for buckwheat flour, but the official SOBAKO concept uses the same case-folded exact search key for a distinct 0%-buckwheat multi-ingredient soba-style product. No current Canadian listing for that brand was found; capitalization cannot resolve the external-name collision in the picker.

Record the 2023 Agrobio catalog's 1/4 cup (40 g) nutrition portion as product-specific evidence on the existing generic buckwheat-flour row. The current product listing does not independently confirm that serving. One dated label statement supports no generic measure, density, mapping, or conversion; keep substitution research unreviewed and active catalog data unchanged.

Complete the deferred substitution review by retaining the government guidance, test-kitchen starting levels, and one formula-specific bread trial as a blocked source-scoped finding. Their contexts and partial-replacement amounts cannot be represented safely as a reusable ingredient-to-ingredient rule. Keep the active catalog and all ingredient naming and numeric behavior unchanged.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Coop Agrobio organic buckwheat flour, the named product in the cooperative's 2023 catalog.
measurementObservations.foodState: Dry flour as sold; serving reported in the product catalog.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: The catalog's Nutrition Facts panel states 1/4 cup (40 g); it gives no fill, compaction, or weighing procedure.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One catalog-reported nutrition portion for the named Agrobio product only. Do not transfer this value to generic buckwheat flour or derive density or a unit mapping.

sourceQuantity.unitConvention: Source-stated 1/4 cup; the catalog does not specify cup capacity or fill method.

substitutionFindings.context: Use of buckwheat flour to replace part of wheat flour in recipes, including non-yeasted baked goods and yeasted bread.
substitutionFindings.basis: Health Canada offers buckwheat flour as an option to try instead of wheat flour for gluten-free needs and notes possible texture and other-ingredient adjustments. King Arthur Baking suggests starting at 25% replacement in non-yeasted recipes and 15% in yeasted bread, by weight or volume. Eren and Akkaya test 10%, 20%, and 30% common whole buckwheat flour in one white-wheat-bread formula, favoring 20% within that study while finding lower loaf volume for every buckwheat-added sample than control.
limitations: The Health Canada advice has no replacement amount, recipe type, or tested result; it is general adjustment guidance.

King Arthur's 25% and 15% values are starting guidance for two recipe contexts, not a validated maximum or instruction for every flour product. The source explicitly discourages replacing all wheat flour.

The primary trial is one yeasted white-bread formula and uses common buckwheat whole flour milled from whole groats below 500 micrometres. Its 10%, 20%, and 30% results do not transfer to generic home recipes or the separate dark, light, sprouted, Tartary, and whole-flour identities.

The current contextual-rule model has no field to represent replacing only a stated fraction of a recipe's wheat-flour quantity while retaining the remainder. A single ratio would either imply full-line replacement or omit the un-replaced flour amount.
No matching bundled recipe line supplies a recipe role, amount, or method for a recipe-specific substitution.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only white canjica maize / maïs blanc pour canjica as a source-defined white class of degerminated Zea mays grain, with canjica white as its only English alias. MAPA defines the product and white class, Yoki documents a current manufacturer product, Canadian retail evidence uses Canjica White, and Québec retail wording supports maïs blanc pour canjica. The Yoki 50 g / ⅓ xícara de chá label serving is retained only as a source-specific portion observation; it does not create an app unit mapping or density. Keep this dry grain distinct from corn kernels, hominy corn / maïs lessivé, hominy grits, crushed yellow canjiquinha, and prepared canjica/mungunzá dessert. Accept the exact CNF 2026 source-specific small-carrot portion (14 cm long = 50 g). This does not resolve the recipe’s size-unspecified “small carrots” line and does not create a reusable count mapping.

decisions.reason: Add chana sattu / farine de sattu as the source-defined roasted Bengal gram (Cicer arietinum) flour identity. Keep it separate from generic chickpea flour/besan, which eNAM lists separately. Use only source-backed roasted-grain names; do not assign the unqualified terms sattu, gram flour, besan, or chickpea flour as aliases because they can obscure the grain or preparation boundary. Add no density, unit mapping, form, conversion, yield, measurement, or substitution data.

Retain the source-defined roasted Bengal gram (Cicer arietinum) flour identity and its existing scoped aliases. The reviewed official definition, separate besan commodity listing, and Canadian product wording support keeping it distinct from generic chickpea flour and unqualified roasted-gram names. Do not add a broad roasted-gram alias or any form, amount, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Retain the chana-sattu identity and its current scoped aliases without adding `besan`, `besan flour`, `gram flour`, `desi besan`, or unqualified `roasted gram flour`. The official standard defines Sattu from roasted gram, and current commodity/manufacturer listings keep it distinct from Besan. The existing phrase `roasted Bengal gram flour` continues to make the broad `gram flour` query a multi-result search after the generic chickpea-flour alias is added. Add no measurement, form, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution data.

sources.title: Raczyk et al., Effect of Coconut and Chestnut Flour Supplementations on Texture, Nutritional and Sensory Properties of Baked Wheat Based Bread
sources.locator: Sections 2 and 3.2; tested flour contribution levels 5%, 10%, 15%, 30%, and 50% by weight
sources.supports: The study reports that chestnut-flour supplementation at 5%, 10%, and 15% remained good quality in its bread formula, while 50% produced a very sweet loaf with low specific volume and was not advisable in that bread-making technology. Marianna Raczyk is first author and Bartosz Kruszewski is second author.

sources.title: Gallego et al., Effects of adding chickpea and chestnut flours to layer cakes
sources.locator: Sections 2.2–2.4 and Tables 1–3; WF100 and WF50-CF50 comparisons
sources.supports: In the tested layer-cake formula, the 50% wheat / 50% chestnut blend had lower specific volume and lower consumer overall acceptability than the wheat-only control. The 100% chestnut-flour sample was not consumer-scored; the flour was sieved below 130 μm.

decisions.reason: Add chestnut flour / farine de châtaigne as an identity-only FLOUR_AND_STARCH reference. Keep it separate from whole edible chestnuts, chestnut paste, unspecified chestnut powder, and water-chestnut products. The active row has no aliases, forms, reusable numeric behavior, or active substitutions; R269 records source-specific recipe portions and study findings in the ledger only.

Record the two recipe-specific flour portions and two formulation-specific wheat-replacement study findings as research-ledger evidence. They support no generic cup mass, default density, unit mapping, or reusable substitution rule; keep active catalog behavior unchanged.

replacements.roleInCompound: Study-specific partial replacement material for wheat flour.

substitutionFindings.context: Experimental single-phase wheat bread; chestnut flour replaced wheat flour at 5%, 10%, 15%, 30%, or 50% by weight.
substitutionFindings.basis: Raczyk et al. report that 5–15% chestnut-flour bread remained good quality in the tested formula; the 15% loaf had favorable overall acceptance. The 50% loaf was very sweet, had low specific volume, and was not advisable in the study’s bread-making technology.
expectedEffects: Outcome varied with the tested chestnut-flour percentage and the bread process; the 50% sample had low specific volume and very sweet flavor.
limitations: Specific flour samples, single-phase bread formula, process, and study panel; do not generalize as a household bread ratio or equal-volume replacement.

replacements.roleInCompound: 50% replacement component for wheat flour in the tested WF50-CF50 layer-cake formula.

substitutionFindings.context: Experimental layer cakes with wheat-only, chestnut-only, and wheat/chestnut/chickpea formulas; the consumer comparison included wheat-only and a 50% wheat / 50% chestnut blend. The 100% chestnut sample was not consumer-scored.
substitutionFindings.basis: Gallego et al. report lower specific volume for the 50/50 wheat/chestnut blend than for wheat-only cake and lower consumer overall acceptability (6.88 ± 1.41 versus 7.82 ± 0.99).
expectedEffects: In the tested layer-cake formula, the 50/50 wheat/chestnut blend had lower specific volume and lower consumer overall acceptability than the wheat-only control.
limitations: The comparison is specific to the 50/50 blend and wheat-only control. The commercial chestnut flour was sieved below 130 μm; do not generalize to other cake types, flour brands, or household recipes.

sources.title: Correia et al., The effect of starch isolation method on physical and functional properties of Portuguese nuts starches. I. Chestnuts (Castanea sativa Mill. var. Martainha and Longal) fruits
sources.locator: Abstract and results comparing chestnut starch isolated by alkaline and enzymatic methods from Portuguese chestnut varieties.
sources.supports: Primary study isolates starch from Castanea sativa fruit and evaluates it as a food ingredient. It reports method- and variety-specific functional properties, not a retail grade, household measure, density, or general substitution.

sources.title: Correia and Beirão-da-Costa, Starch isolation from chestnut and acorn flours through alkaline and enzymatic methods
sources.locator: Abstract, isolation-method comparison, optimized recovery and purity results for Castanea sativa chestnut starch.
sources.supports: Primary study distinguishes starch isolated from chestnut flour from the starting flour and from acorn starch. The reported recovery and purity figures are specific to optimized laboratory extraction methods and do not establish kitchen yield or a flour-to-starch conversion.

sources.title: Fang et al., Analysis of the Physicochemical and Structural Properties of Chestnut Starch After Thermal Processing
sources.locator: Abstract and sections 2.1–2.2 on Castanea mollissima source material, starch extraction, and dry-heat treatment.
sources.supports: Primary study isolates starch from a specified Castanea mollissima chestnut sample and analyzes raw and dry-heat-treated material. Treatment results do not define a general commercial grade, reusable measure, or substitution.

sources.title: The Oxidative Extraction of Starch from Chestnut (Castanea sativa Mill.) Byproducts: A Valorization Strategy for a Sustainable Food Industry
sources.locator: Abstract and materials/methods describing Castanea sativa cultivars, flour/byproduct starting material, and isolated starch treatments.
sources.supports: Primary study distinguishes chestnut flour and kernel material from starch isolated through specific oxidative/alkaline routes and discusses potential food use. The byproduct, treatment, yield, and product-performance findings are experimental and do not establish a general market specification or reusable recipe measure.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only chestnut starch / amidon de châtaigne as a distinct FLOUR_AND_STARCH product for starch isolated from Castanea chestnut fruit. Keep the French display provisional because no reviewed Québec product source attests the exact compound. Keep whole-ground chestnut flour, whole sweet chestnuts, chestnut purée/spread, and Eleocharis/Trapa water-chestnut products separate. Do not add aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.supports: Root integration recheck of the official current results table confirmed repeated exact Clam / Palourde labels across species rows. This supports label overlap only, not a taxon, complete membership list, or culinary-equivalence rule.

decisions.reason: Hold pending a product or recipe target. Québec commercial terminology distinguishes multiple clam species and names, so do not select a broad palourde/clam identity without a clear scope.

Promote the existing generic clam candidate in place only to a visibly qualified name group for the repeated Clam / Palourde label pair across multiple CFIA species rows, supported by a mixed-species raw-clam CNF food entry. This is a source-bounded generic culinary-search label group, not a taxon, Québec-standardized compound, or culinary-equivalence claim. Preserve the earlier unresolved decision for assigning bare clam/palourde to one species and preserve all species-specific holds. CNF portions remain code-specific. Add no forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

Hold as a source-market product candidate; Cornish protected-product boundaries must not be generalized, and there is no exact recipe demand.

sources.locator: Annex III, family-level Cardiidae row and separate Clinocardium ciliatum entry.
sources.supports: Lists Cardiidae (Family) as Cockle unspecified / Bucarde (coque) non spécifié, separately from Clinocardium ciliatum Iceland cockle / Coque d’Islande. Historical survey classification; not a current retail label, recipe identity, edible yield, or measure.

sources.title: TERMIUM Plus, COQUE search results, records 12–13
sources.locator: Records 12–13: Cerastoderma edule and Clinocardium ciliatum.
sources.supports: Record 12 pairs European cockle/coque européenne with Cerastoderma edule and records English cockle as a commercial name; record 13 pairs Clinocardium ciliatum with hairy/Iceland cockle and French coque. Species-scoped terminology supports name overlap, not one species-neutral biological identity or aliases for a specific species.

decisions.reason: Hold the unqualified cockle/coque ingredient identity. OQLF's species-specific food entry supports coque/cockle for Clinocardium ciliatum, but the current CFIA Fish List also assigns French Coque to Clinocardium nuttallii. Current Canadian and Montréal product pages use unqualified coques without identifying a species, and the bundled recipes contain no cockle/coque ingredient line. Do not add an active reference or generic aliases from this evidence. Reopen with a species-qualified recipe or target-product label; a future Clinocardium ciliatum row should be reviewed as coque d'Islande / Iceland cockle, with bare cockle/coque alias scope decided separately. Keep this candidate distinct from ingredient-ref-clam and its Mya arenaria / Venus mercenaria terminology boundary.

Promote the existing candidate in place only as a visibly qualified, species-neutral culinary-market name group used for multiple cockle species. Do not treat it as a taxon, imply that every use worldwide belongs to the group, or infer equivalence or substitution. The earlier unresolved decision remains accurate for assigning bare cockle/coque to one species; keep species-specific holds and generic clam separate.

sources.supports: Describes the young leafy shoots as a cooked green and includes them in two named recipes. Amounts, methods, nutrition information, and cooked-quantity estimates remain source-specific; this is not a Québec availability or plant-identification guide.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, ansérine Bon-Henri (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition; preferred French terms; English and Latin term sections.
sources.supports: Pairs the French ansérine Bon-Henri with English Good King Henry and the historical scientific name Chenopodium bonus-henricus. The entry also lists wild spinach and explicitly defines it as a term used for several Chenopodium plants, so that ambiguous phrase is not used as an alias. This is terminology evidence, not culinary-use evidence.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only common lamb’s-quarters / chénopode blanc for the leafy culinary use of correctly identified Chenopodium album L. Keep it separate from Good King Henry, garden orach, amaranth greens, spinach, quinoa seed, and other named leafy identities. Use only the source-attested qualified display names; omit ambiguous common-name aliases. The extension recipes’ amounts and methods remain source-specific. Add no aliases, forms, reusable measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or active substitutions.

sources.title: Canadian VASCAN, Syringa vulgaris
sources.locator: Accepted taxon and vernacular names.
sources.supports: Supports Syringa vulgaris and the vernacular names common lilac and lilas commun. It does not establish culinary use or a flower-part compound.

sources.title: Université du Québec à Chicoutimi, Forêt nourricière, Lilas commun, Syringa vulgaris
sources.locator: Species heading; harvest-part and culinary-use sections for the flowers.
sources.supports: Identifies Syringa vulgaris, the flower as the harvested part, and culinary uses for fleurs de lilas. The floral timing and sensory details remain source-specific; no exact edible floral structure or standardized full ingredient name is established.

sources.title: Colorado State University Extension, Edible Flowers
sources.locator: Table 2, Syringa vulgaris / lilac row.
sources.supports: Lists Syringa vulgaris in its edible-flower table and says it candies well. Use only for the species-bounded flower identity; preserve existing source allocations for other flowers and do not generalize to other Syringa taxa.

sources.title: Télé-Québec, Cuisinez, Cocktail Lilas
sources.locator: Homemade lilac liqueur ingredient list and infusion directions.
sources.supports: Uses the Québec culinary phrase fleurs de lilas and reports 500 ml of freshly picked flowers for one named infusion method. The recipe does not identify a species; its quantities and two-stage infusion remain recipe-specific and are not reusable measures, density, or substitution evidence.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only common lilac flowers / fleurs du lilas commun for the flower part of Syringa vulgaris. Keep the French compound descriptive and provisional; preserve exact species and plant-part boundaries, with no aliases, floral-structure claim, forms, or recipe links.
No transferable household measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, or yield is supported. The Télé-Québec flower-to-alcohol amount belongs only to its named infusion recipe.
The reviewed sources describe culinary uses but support no global or contextual replacement ingredient, direction, ratio, or dish-role rule.

sources.title: OQLF, millet commun
sources.locator: Definition, preferred terms, translations, and Latin name

sources.title: Health Canada, Residue Chemistry Crop Groups
sources.locator: Cereal grains, crop group 15-21E; millet, proso listed with Panicum miliaceum subsp. miliaceum separately from other millet taxa
sources.supports: Places proso millet in the cereal-grain subgroup and lists its taxon separately from foxtail, pearl, little, finger, and barnyard millet; this supports the species boundary, not a product measurement.

sources.title: FAO, Sorghum and millets in human nutrition
sources.locator: Table 1 and Common millet section
sources.supports: Maps Panicum miliaceum to proso/common millet, distinguishes it from foxtail and pearl millet, and describes its grain in a human-nutrition source.

sources.title: FAO, A propos de l’Année internationale du mil 2023
sources.locator: Section Millet commun; species and food-grain description
sources.supports: Uses the French name millet commun for Panicum miliaceum and treats it as a distinct edible millet species.

sources.title: ICAR–Indian Institute of Millets Research: Millets Information
sources.locator: Proso Millet entry; Bengali and Punjabi Cheena, Gujarati Cheno, and Hindi Chena / Barri regional names; page footer updated 2026-07-07.
sources.supports: Maps Bengali and Punjabi Cheena, Gujarati Cheno, and Hindi Chena / Barri to English Proso Millet. Supports these regional grain-name crosswalks only, not Canadian naming, flour-qualified names, or recipe measurements.

sources.title: A1 Indian Grocery Online, Proso Millet 2.2LB (Chena / Cheno / Barri)
sources.locator: Product title, Add to cart control, and Barrie, Ontario store address.
sources.supports: Canadian retailer title lists Proso Millet (Chena / Cheno / Barri), supporting the exact title spellings as product-search wording. The listing is not a package ingredient declaration; identity is supported by the IIMR crosswalk, inventory can change, and package size is not a kitchen measure.

sources.title: Mayrand, Graines de millet crues 1 kg
sources.locator: Product listing and store-availability section; stock shown in Anjou, Laval, Brossard, and Saint-Jérôme.
sources.supports: Current Québec retail page uses generic French grain wording and showed store stock. It does not identify Panicum miliaceum or use Chena; package weight and availability are not recipe measures or stable stock claims.

sources.title: Translation Bureau, Government of Canada, TERMIUM Plus: BROOM MILLET
sources.locator: Botany and Grain Growing; universal entry Panicum miliaceum; English term cheena millet.
sources.supports: Lists cheena millet as a correct, standardized English term for Panicum miliaceum. Terminology supports the species-qualified grain phrase, not current consumer frequency or a product label.

sources.title: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, GRIN-Global-CA: Panicum miliaceum L. subsp. miliaceum
sources.locator: Common names and economic uses sections.
sources.supports: Lists India common names cheena and chin for Panicum miliaceum L. subsp. miliaceum and human food use as cereal. This supports the species/name connection, not current Canadian product naming or a recipe measure.

sources.title: Desertcart Canada, Superior Proso Millet 1 kg
sources.locator: Product title and alternate-name wording; indexed page was crawled about three weeks before review.
sources.supports: Canada-facing marketplace copy names Cheena among alternate names for a Superior Proso Millet grain item. Desertcart purchases products on buyers’ behalf from other markets; this is not a verified Canadian package label or stable stock record. Package mass is not a recipe measure.

sources.title: BuyNearby Calgary, Proso Millet (Panivaragu)
sources.locator: Search-indexed local-store product card titled “Proso Millet (Panivaragu) 2lb”; direct retrieval failed during review.
sources.supports: Provides Canada-market grain search wording pairing Proso Millet and Panivaragu. It is a product card, not an inspected package ingredient declaration or continuing stock evidence; 2 lb is package mass, not a recipe measure.

sources.title: ICAR–Indian Institute of Millets Research, Chapter 7: Proso millet
sources.locator: Chapter 7, Proso millet (*Panicum miliaceum L.*); indexed text gives panivaragu as a Tamil and Malayalam name. Direct PDF retrieval failed during review.
sources.supports: Supports the closed spelling panivaragu as a regional name for Proso millet. The indexed text supports grain naming only, not flour terminology, Canadian retail stock, French terminology, or a recipe measure.

decisions.reason: Accept common millet / millet commun as the species-qualified cereal grain Panicum miliaceum; use proso millet as its sole English alias. Omit bare millet and mil, which overlap the existing generic millet identity and multiple millet taxa; omit unsupported millet proso and feed-associated labels. Assign the project GRAIN_AND_CEREAL category. Add no density, unit mappings, forms, yields, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links.

Add only chena as an English search alias to the existing common millet / millet commun grain. IIMR maps Hindi Chena to proso millet, and a current Barrie retailer lists Proso Millet (Chena / Cheno / Barri). Preserve the OQLF-backed French display; current Québec retail wording is generic and does not establish local Chena usage. Package sizes are not measures. Add no flour alias, form, density, unit mapping, yield, recipe link, conversion, or substitution.

Add only barri as an English search alias to the existing common millet / millet commun grain. ICAR-IIMR maps Hindi Barri to proso millet, and the current Barrie retailer title pairs Proso Millet with Chena / Cheno / Barri. Preserve the OQLF-backed French display and existing aliases; add no flour alias, French alias, form, measure, density, unit mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only cheno as an English search alias to the existing common millet / millet commun grain. ICAR–IIMR maps Gujarati Cheno to proso millet, and the current Ontario A1 listing uses Cheno in a Proso Millet grain title. Preserve the OQLF-backed French display and existing aliases; add no flour alias, French alias, form, measure, density, unit mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only cheena and cheena millet as English search aliases on the existing common millet / millet commun grain. ICAR–IIMR maps Bengali and Punjabi Cheena to proso millet; AAFC lists cheena for Panicum miliaceum, and TERMIUM standardizes cheena millet for that species. A Canada-facing marketplace listing corroborates the spelling but is not treated as a verified Canadian package label. Preserve the OQLF-backed French display and existing flour row; keep flour-qualified Cheena terms unassigned. Add no form, measure, density, unit mapping, yield, recipe link, conversion, or substitution.

Add only panivaragu as an English search alias to the existing common millet / millet commun grain. ICAR–IIMR maps the spaced Pani varagu to Proso millet and separately maps Varagu to Kodo; its 2026 chapter and a Calgary local-store product card support the closed spelling for Proso grain. Keep the spaced pani varagu form inactive because it would make pani an exact phrase hit and suppress four existing substring results. Preserve the OQLF-backed French display and all numeric, form, recipe-link, and substitution fields.

sources.title: OQLF, bigorneau (GDT)
sources.locator: Edible-mollusc domain, preferred term, English translation, Latin name, and fishery note
sources.supports: Normalizes bigorneau for Québec; maps the edible mollusc and English common periwinkle to Littorina littorea; says littorine was not retained for fish-product marketing to avoid confusion.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Bigorneau species profile
sources.locator: Latin name and northeastern North American range
sources.supports: Identifies bigorneau as Littorina littorea and gives its Atlantic range from Newfoundland and Labrador south to New Jersey; taxonomy and range do not establish recipe identity or product state.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List lookup results
sources.locator: Littorina rows: Winkle and Periwinkle / Bigorneau; marine-toxin hazard flag
sources.supports: CFIA lists the English/French product names under genus Littorina, not a species-specific Littorina littorea row. The list is a Canadian fish-label naming reference, not evidence that a vendor or recipe phrase names this exact species.

sources.title: CFIA, Guidance on determining common names for fish sold or processed in Canada
sources.locator: Sections 1 and 4, CFIA Fish List purpose and scope
sources.supports: The Fish List provides common names for Canadian fish labeling, and the common name listed for the actual species is used for that species sold or processed in Canada. This does not infer a species from unqualified culinary wording.

sources.title: MAPAQ, Répertoire des poissons et fruits de mer du Québec — commercial-name glossary
sources.locator: Glossary table entries for Bigorneau and Buccin
sources.supports: The directory pairs Bigorneau / Periwinkle / Littorina littorea and lists bigorneau among names not retained for Buccin / Whelk. This older Québec glossary corroborates terminology, not current vendor contents.

sources.title: Frandon Seafoods, Produits
sources.locator: French fresh-fish A-Z listing and daily-delivery description; English counterpart https://frandon.ca/language/en/products/
sources.supports: A Québec seafood supplier lists BIGORNEAU on its French page and PERIWINKLE on its English page. Neither list states the species, product package, or a periwinkle-specific product state.

sources.title: Seafood Depot, Winkles
sources.locator: Product title and characteristics
sources.supports: Canadian vendor lists Winkles / Littorina, also known as Periwinkles, and describes fresh/frozen, wild, Canada and U.S. products. This is genus-level product evidence and does not identify Littorina littorea.

sources.title: Les Fruits de Mer Madeleine, Buccins crus, congelés
sources.locator: Species, product title, alias wording, and Québec sales area
sources.supports: Québec processor identifies its raw frozen product as Buccinum undatum but says it is also called Bigorneau. This proves current colloquial/product-name overlap; it does not make Buccin and Littorina the same identity or override OQLF's normalized term.

decisions.reason: Add an identity-only reference scoped to Littorina littorea as common periwinkle / bigorneau. OQLF provides a normalized Québec edible-mollusc term for this species, DFO independently confirms the species, and current Québec/Canadian suppliers list the bilingual or genus-level market product. Keep the reference taxon-scoped: CFIA's listing and several current product listings are broader, and one Québec buccin seller uses bigorneau for Buccinum undatum. Do not link unqualified recipe or vendor text to this row without species evidence. The recipe corpus has no periwinkle demand. Add no aliases, forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, pourpier (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred French terms, English terms, Latin name, and culinary notes.
sources.supports: Lists pourpier and pourpier commun as preferred French terms, purslane and common purslane as English terms, and Portulaca oleracea as the Latin name. Notes that the plant is edible and ordinarily sold as leaves, with culinary use in salads and soup. The entry is old and is used for terminology and identity, not current retail availability or measurements.

sources.locator: French, English, and Latin names.

sources.supports: Identifies common purslane as Portulaca oleracea and describes its history as a food plant and continued cultivation and culinary use. Supports generic identity only; no quantity or conversion is transferred.

Keep the identity separate from waterleaf (Talinum fruticosum), other Portulaca species, and parsley; do not activate pursley because of its picker collision risk. No recipe demand, form, measure, density, mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported.

decisions.reason: Accept the common sorrel identity and source-listed aliases. Keep wood sorrel (Oxalis) and roselle / oseille de Guinée (Hibiscus sabdariffa) distinct; do not add an unqualified substitute or form.

decisions.reason: Accept compound coating as a product distinct from standardized chocolate and couverture. Keep compound chocolate, chocolate coating, candy melts, and brand names out of aliases.

sources.supports: Defines compressed yeast as fresh, not dried, yeast formed into a cake; lists compressed, cake, pressed, and fresh English terms and French levure comprimée, levure fraîche pressée, levure fraîche, and levure pressée. Keep manufacturer cake sizes and packet equivalences in evidence only; do not activate a cross-format mapping or substitution.

The protected geographic identity, current Québec retailer names, and Québec recipe use support this narrow display and one exact French search alias. Keep Gruyère and other regional cheeses distinct. Do not add forms, reusable measures, density, unit mappings, yields, conversions, recipe links, or substitutions; substitution research remains open.

sources.locator: TSN 72554 Lobatus gigas and TSN 72555 Strombus spp. rows.
sources.supports: The exact English/French common-name pair Conch / Conque appears for both listed gastropod taxa. Supports a visibly qualified internal search name group only; it is not a taxon, species membership list, product state, CFIA-approved catalog display, or culinary-equivalence claim.

sources.locator: Section 4 and section 5.2.2: actual-species Fish List scope and possible consideration of group names.

This does not approve the catalog-authored qualifier or establish culinary equivalence.

sources.supports: Supports food use only for the named Queen Conch species. The historical enforcement notice is not evidence of current import legality, other taxa, product form, edible portion, preparation, or generalized culinary behavior.

Use the Queen Conch source only for species-specific food context and the OQLF entry only for the stated Strombus genus context. Preserve candidate-conch, its unresolved decision and all 13 sources, species/product boundaries, and product-specific observations unchanged. Add no forms, measures, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

Use descriptive Québec recipe wording for racines de coriandre without claiming an OQLF entry for the compound; keep the recipe amount and preparation source-specific. sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, maïs

sources.supports: Identifies maïs as the preferred French term and gives Canadian English corn; marks maize as United Kingdom usage. It supports the base word in the display, not the complete regional food name arraw de maïs.
