decisions.reason: Add finger-millet flour separately from finger millet grain and generic millet flour. Keep bare ragi attached to the active grain identity; the exact ragi-flour phrase may resolve to this flour. Add no form, hydration, density, mappings, recipe links, or substitutions.

Add nachni flour as an English alias on the verified finger-millet flour row, based on FSSAI roti ingredient wording and current Canadian product headings that group Nachni with Ragi/Finger Millet flour. Retain the existing display pair and ragi flour alias; keep bare nachni, nachni atta, and farine de nachni out. Add no forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

Add only ragi atta as an English alias on the verified finger-millet flour row. Retain finger millet flour / farine de ragi, ragi flour, and nachni flour; keep bare ragi on finger millet grain, and keep sprouted ragi atta and unsupported phrase variants out. Add no identity, form, French alias, recipe link, measurement, density, mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only kurakkan flour as an English alias on the existing finger-millet flour identity, retaining farine de ragi and all existing aliases. Keep roasted and sprouted Kurakkan flour names outside the unqualified alias. Preserve the study density values only as source-specific observations with the table-unit inconsistency explicit; keep defaultDensity null and unitMappings empty. Keep general wheat replacement blocked, with no active substitution rule.

Add only mandua flour and mandua ka atta as English aliases on the existing finger-millet-flour identity. The existing FSSAI standard defines ragi flour from dried mature Eleusine coracana grains; Himachal Pradesh and the Government of India's Department of Science and Technology connect Mandua with finger millet and its flour; APEDA lists Mandua Flour; the Canadian-facing listings support the qualified product phrases. Retain all source-specific density observations and the existing blocked wheat-replacement finding; keep defaultDensity null, unitMappings empty, and add no form, active measurement, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only mandua atta as an English-search alias on the existing finger-millet-flour identity. Two makers use the exact phrase for finger-millet flour; the existing FSSAI cereal standard supports the Mandua–finger-millet crop boundary. Retain farine de ragi, all other aliases, the source-specific density observations, and blocked wheat-replacement finding. Add no French alias, identity, form, active measure, mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

Add only ragulu pindi as an English-search alias on the existing finger-millet-flour identity. The maker explicitly identifies its product as finger-millet flour and lists Ragulu Pindi (Telugu) as a name; the Indian Institute of Millets Research separately verifies Ragulu as a finger-millet grain name. Retain the current display, aliases, source-specific density observations, and blocked wheat-replacement finding. Add no French alias, form, active measure, mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic fish cheeks / joues de poisson as an edible fish-part identity across species where the cut is marketable or harvested. Keep joues de poisson descriptive rather than claiming OQLF standardization. Preserve the Atlantic cod and Atlantic halibut cheek holds and every species-specific entry; do not add species-qualified aliases, forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Bon Appétit, Fish Collars

sources.title: Epicurious, For the Most Succulent Fish, Cook the Collar

decisions.reason: Add one identity-only generic fish-collar cut, displayed as fish collars / colliers de poisson, with only the singular French alias collier de poisson. Government, Canadian terminology, and culinary sources support the cut boundary and generic usage across species. Keep fish heads, cheeks, bones, frames, trimmings, skin, stock, fillets, steaks, species identities, and the salmon-collar/kama hold separate. Recipe-specific counts, masses, temperatures, and methods remain within their sources; no reusable measure or structured substitute is supported. Add no English singular alias, forms, recipe links, conversions, yields, or active substitution rules.

The DFO industrial amount is not transferred as a household measure.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic fish heads / têtes de poisson as a fish part used as food, separate from fish bones, fish stock, named fish species, and formed seafood products. The bilingual Metro recipe directly names the head with bones for stock, although its French ingredient line says whole fish; the Northwest Territories guide provides the French plural and documents fish-head culinary use in its northern traditional-food context. Preserve its 75 g cooked-whitefish-head nutrient-table portion as a source-specific published observation only; add no generic head measure, form, recipe link, density, mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Add flattened rice (poha) / flocons de riz (poha) as an identity-only processed rice product, distinct from generic rice, crispy rice cereal, and puffed rice. CFTRI and CSIR document the flaking process and regional product names; current Canadian French sources support the display. Keep aliases empty until rice-flake synonyms and regional grades receive collision and Québec scope review. No bundled recipe uses poha, so no recipe link, form, density, mapping, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution is added.

Accept the source-documented English terms rice flakes, flaked rice, and beaten rice, plus Canadian French riz aplati and riz battu, as aliases for the same flattened rice product. CSIR identifies the English terms in the poha/rice-flake name family, and Canadian French product/recipe sources use riz aplati and riz battu. Keep chiwda and region-specific transliterations out because their food/snack and regional scope needs separate review. No bundled recipe uses poha.

Add thin, medium, and thick poha as separately labeled commercial thickness-grade forms, supported by Canadian retailer listings in English and French. The sources do not define standardized physical cutoffs. Do not add super-thin, nylon, paper, red-rice, or maize-poha variants as aliases or forms in this review.

Do not infer interchangeability among thin, medium, and thick poha. Product pages describe grade-specific texture or uses but provide no cross-grade substitution recommendation, dish/method scope, or adjustment ratio.

Keep bare chiwda/chivda out of flattened-rice aliases and do not create a global prepared-snack ingredient reference. CSIR records a regional rice-flake synonym sense, while current Canadian recipe and retail sources use the same term family for prepared poha-based and cornflake-based snacks. No bundled recipe requests the terms; the existing poha identity, aliases, and grade forms remain unchanged.

Accept `chiura` only as an English alias of existing `ingredient-ref-flattened-rice-poha`: Nepalese technical and standards sources identify it as beaten rice flakes, and current Canadian English listings pair chiura with beaten rice. Keep the current English/French displays and French aliases unchanged. Do not add color/cultivar/crispness-qualified products, prepared dishes, forms, numeric behavior, recipe links, or substitutions.

Add only aval as an English alias of flattened rice (poha), supported by regional technical naming and Canadian product listings. Keep Québec French display and aliases, product grades, forms, recipe links, measurements, and substitution status unchanged.

Add only atukulu as an English search alias on the generic flattened-rice (poha) identity. An official Indian technical handbook identifies it as Telugu for flaked rice, and Canada-facing retailer listings pair it with white and red poha. Keep color and thickness boundaries, all numeric fields, forms, French aliases, recipe links, and substitution state unchanged.

Add only avalakki as an English search alias for the existing generic flattened-rice (poha) identity. The official technical handbook identifies it as Kannada for flaked rice and a Canada-facing white-poha listing independently includes it among regional names. Keep the current displays, French aliases, thickness forms, red-rice and maize-poha boundaries, null active density, and empty unit mappings. Prepared-dish and composite-mix uses do not broaden the alias. The reviewed industrial grade/process figures and mix directions do not provide a household measure for plain flattened rice.

Add only chira as an English search alias on the existing flattened-rice (poha) identity. Bangladesh Rice Research Institute, manufacturer, and Canadian retail sources use it for flattened rice; keep the Québec French display and aliases, existing grades, and neighboring rice-flake identities unchanged. Record the FAO / BBF 60 g / 3 fistfuls only as the complete Chirar Polao formula amount for one 230 g cooked bowl and two servings, not per serving or as a generic conversion. Keep default density null, unit mappings empty, and substitution research blocked.

Add only bare chuda as an English search alias on the existing flattened-rice (poha) identity. Odisha government and food-heritage sources, a plain-product label, and a Canada-facing Poha listing support the regional product name. Keep French displays and aliases, thin/medium/thick grades, forms, active numeric behavior, the existing recipe-specific Chirar Polao observation, and blocked substitution research unchanged. The Odisha menu’s 50 g amount lacks dry/prepared state and measurement method, so it is not recorded as a generic measurement. No recipe demand or links were found.

Add only sira as an English search alias for the existing flattened-rice (poha) identity. Assam government sources pair sira with flat or flattened rice, while the processing handbook supports the established flaked-rice product class. Preserve chira as a separate spelling alias on the same row; do not add sira as a French alias or create a new product for the qualified Malbhog Sira listing. Keep all displays, numeric fields, forms, recipe links, measurements, and substitution state unchanged.

Accept only bare Konkani phovu as an English search alias for the existing flattened-rice (poha) identity. The Central Bank of India food-grains table pairs Phovu with rice flakes, and current GSB cooking sources use bare phovu for the ingredient while using compound names for prepared dishes. Keep English and Quebec French displays, French aliases, forms, numeric fields, recipe links, and blocked grade-substitution state unchanged. The bundled corpus has no phovu term or flattened-rice link; recipe-specific cup quantities do not establish a reusable measure or conversion.

Add powa, pawa, pauwa, pauaa, and paunva as English-search aliases on the existing flattened-rice (poha) identity. The Supreme Court of India record and current product pages support the Powa spelling and related flattened-rice terms; the Government of India NIFTEM presentation directly lists Paunva as Gujarati and identifies pawa with flaked rice, and current seller/exporter pages attest Pauwa and Pauaa. Keep these regional names in aliasesEn, not aliasesFr, and map none to a thin, medium, or thick grade. Keep displays, forms, numeric data, recipe links, and blocked grade-substitution status unchanged. The bundled corpus has no matching demand.

Keep poya unassigned. It appears only in a broad Rani alternate-name list and a secondary list that says it was taken from Wikipedia; no independent current product or regional-authority evidence establishes the term or its language scope.

sources.title: McWatters et al., Physical and sensory characteristics of sugar cookies containing mixtures of wheat, fonio (Digitaria exilis) and cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) flours
sources.locator: Publisher-hosted full text, p. 404, “Cookie formula” subsection (base recipe quantities and eight flour-component formulations); p. 407, sensory evaluation results and ratings; article conclusion.
sources.supports: The full text lists the base formula as flour 75.5 g, granulated cane sugar 75.0 g, hydrogenated vegetable shortening 47.0 g, whole fresh egg 24.0 g, cream of tartar 1.6 g, baking soda 1.0 g, cinnamon 0.5 g, and salt 0.4 g; its eight flour-component formulations include 50% wheat / 50% fonio. Percentages are given for the flour components, but the text does not state whether those component shares are by mass or volume. The sensory results report flavor 6.7 and overall acceptability 6.5 for the 50/50 formulation, versus 7.1 and 6.9 for the 100% wheat control; the other six formulations scored below 6 on both measures. This single study does not establish a general substitution rule.

sources.title: Sobowale, Omotoso & Agbawodike, Effect of fermentation duration on microstructure and quality of acha flour and its cookies acceptability
sources.locator: Table 1; §2, Materials and Methods, native-flour preparation and bulk-density method
sources.supports: Reports 0.57 ± 0.00 g/mL loose and 0.84 ± 0.01 g/mL tapped bulk density for native Acha flour. The sample was made from market-purchased Acha, winnowed, washed/desstoned, dried at 45 °C, attrition-milled, and sieved through 50 μm. The method is attributed to Adeleke et al. but is not reproduced; the sample species is unspecified although the article describes Acha as Digitaria exilis and Digitaria iburua. These laboratory observations do not support a white-fonio default density or household measure.

quantity.unit: reported share of the flour-component blend; mass/volume basis unspecified

replacements.roleInCompound: Fonio half of the tested wheat/fonio flour blend

substitutionFindings.context: One basic sugar-cookie formulation using white fonio (Digitaria exilis) and plain all-purpose wheat flour; the method gives 75.5 g flour in the base recipe and lists 50% wheat / 50% fonio among eight flour-component formulations.
substitutionFindings.basis: The 0.5 share is the fonio fraction of the reported flour-component blend, not of total dough. Although the method gives 75.5 g flour for the base formula, it does not state whether component percentages are by mass or volume; do not calculate component grams or convert this study-specific share into a general ratio, recipe amount, or active runtime rule.
expectedEffects: Among the tested formulations, the 50% wheat / 50% fonio cookie and the 100% wheat control had the highest flavor and overall-acceptability ratings; the 50/50 formula scored 6.7 and 6.5, respectively, versus 7.1 and 6.9 for the control.
limitations: One experimental basic sugar-cookie context only; do not generalize to other cookies, bread, cakes, or home recipes.
The study names white fonio (Digitaria exilis); do not transfer the result to black fonio (Digitaria iburua), roasted fonio flour, precooked fonio flour, or uncharacterized products.
The full text provides the base recipe quantities, including 75.5 g flour, but does not identify whether the flour-component percentages are based on mass or volume; do not derive component amounts.
No active contextual or form-substitution rule is supported by this evidence record alone.

decisions.reason: Source-backed products establish fonio flour as a milling product, but descriptions differ on whole versus dehulled grain and Québec sources sell roasted and precooked flour variants. Decide whether generic fonio flour is a distinct identity or discovery family with process-specific products, and obtain an independently reviewed generic fr-CA name before allocating an active reference. No measurements or substitutions are inferred.

Promote generic fonio flour / farine de fonio as an identity-only milling product. Retain the single English alias acha flour, but not bare acha or fonio. Whole versus dehulled grain, roasted and precooked products, and any process equivalence remain separate or unresolved; the French display remains provisional pending independent Québec review.

Record only the reported 50% fonio share of the flour-component blend and its measured outcome in one basic sugar-cookie study as formula-specific substitution evidence. Keep measurement research not yet done and add no active substitution rule or broader wheat-flour replacement claim.

Complete the bounded measurement review. The 2025 Acha study reports loose and tapped laboratory bulk densities for a market-sourced sample whose species is unspecified and cites, but does not reproduce, the measurement method. Current species-resolved white-fonio flour pages provide cup-based use instructions without a verified paired gram amount; package weights are not recipe portions. No reusable household mass/volume measure, default density, unit mapping, or conversion is supported, and measurement observations remain empty.

decisions.reason: Accept foxtail millet / millet d'Italie as a species-qualified food-grain identity distinct from generic millet and pearl millet. OQLF supports millet d'Italie and foxtail millet for Setaria italica; FAO supports its food-grain scope, and Health Canada lists millet d'Italie among cereal crops. Omit millet, millet des oiseaux, petit mil, and other broad or bird-feed-associated alternatives from aliases as a conservative catalog boundary. Assign the project's GRAIN_AND_CEREAL category. sources.title: Associated Press, Handfuls of fresh herbs enliven Sardinia’s fregola-studded soup
sources.locator: Sardinian Herb Soup with Fregola and White Beans (S’erbuzzu) recipe headnote and ingredient list.
sources.supports: In this four-serving soup, AP republishes Milk Street guidance to replace fregola with an equal amount of pearl couscous and cook it for five minutes before adding beans, parsley, and garlic. The recipe lists 3/4 US cup fregola; this is one recipe-specific substitution, not a general pasta interchange rule.

quantity.unitConvention: US customary recipe cup

substitutionFindings.context: Only for Associated Press / Milk Street’s four-serving Sardinian Herb Soup with Fregola and White Beans (S’erbuzzu), whose ingredient list calls for 3/4 cup fregola.
substitutionFindings.basis: The recipe headnote explicitly says to use an equal amount of pearl couscous; the fixed recipe amount is therefore 3/4 cup in this dish.
adjustments: Cook the pearl couscous for five minutes before adding the beans, parsley, and garlic, following the recipe headnote.
limitations: Context-specific finding only; do not infer a global fregola-to-pearl-couscous ratio for other soups, seafood dishes, salads, or pasta recipes.
Do not transfer the five-minute instruction to other pearl couscous brands, shapes, or recipes without their package and recipe guidance.
This evidence does not authorize reciprocal or transitive substitutions.

decisions.reason: Backfill the verified regional pasta identity and record the AP/Milk Street pearl-couscous replacement only for the named S’erbuzzu soup. The recipe provides no reusable mass-volume conversion, and the finding remains ledger-only.

sources.supports: Product 059749994569 and 340 g package, paired with S03 by product number. Supports an exact Québec French product-name variant; it does not identify the species or establish a general product measure.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List, TSN 79456, Mytilus galloprovincialis
sources.locator: TSN 79456 naming rows; CFIA Fish List overview on Canadian fish-labelling common names.
sources.supports: Associates Mytilus galloprovincialis with Mussel / Moule Méditerranéenne and a second misspelled Mediterannean Mussel / Moule row. Generic mussel and moule names are also used for other taxa, so only the species-qualified display is retained.

sources.title: Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Pêcheries et de l’Alimentation du Québec, Les mollusques du Québec
sources.locator: Blue-mussel species and product-format tables, including the cooked-mussel-meat and smoked-product rows.
sources.supports: Identifies blue mussel as Mytilus edulis and lists cooked mussel meat formats including individually frozen product, alongside smoked product in varied formats. This older Québec producer-format evidence does not prove current production, current retail stock, the species of retailer SKUs, or a reusable household measure.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only frozen cooked mussel meat / chair de moule cuite surgelée as a species-neutral prepared-product group. Retain only the two exact shell-free product-title variants as aliases; do not assign a species, universal shell state, readiness, or cooking instructions. Keep named mussel species, smoked, brined, escabeche, dried, and mixed seafood products separate. Package amounts remain product-specific; add no forms, reusable measures, density, unit mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Normes d'identité canadiennes : Volume 4 – Produits de fruits ou de légumes transformés
sources.locator: Article 53(1)-(2), frozen peas and carrots; reversed carrots-and-peas class.
sources.supports: Defines pois et carottes congelés as 52-75% peas and 25-48% carrots by weight, and separately defines carottes et pois congelés with the larger share reversed. Supports a distinct pea-first frozen mixture identity and French regulatory product term; does not give this recipe's exact ratio, cup mass, or conversion.

sources.title: The Wholesome Dish, The Best Classic Shepherd's Pie
sources.locator: Ingredient card and method; note on unavailable frozen mixed peas and carrots.
sources.supports: The linked recipe page lists 1 cup frozen mixed peas & carrots, its method names frozen peas and carrots, and its note suggests 1/2 cup frozen peas plus 1/2 cup frozen sliced carrots if the mix is unavailable. Supports the exact product wording and one source-specific workaround only; it does not establish a general substitution or cup-to-mass conversion.

sources.locator: Légumes surgelés, item FZ003016.
sources.supports: Lists Petits pois et carottes surgelés under the same FZ003016 item and 12x750G pack as the English catalog. Supports the current French-language product wording and bilingual Canadian-market SKU pairing; it does not establish the recipe's brand, component ratio, or cup mass.

decisions.reason: Accept a separate frozen peas-and-carrots mixture identity for the exact unlinked 078#14 row. The current Canadian standard, linked recipe source, and bilingual Canadian-market SKU identify the mixed product; do not map it to peas alone. Keep the recipe quantity and frozen preparation unchanged and add no ratio, measurement, yield, form, or substitution data.

decisions.reason: Add fructose syrup / sirop de fructose as a distinct syrup product; no concentration, density, or conversion to pure fructose or another syrup is inferred.

sources.title: OQLF Grand dictionnaire terminologique, ketchup
sources.locator: Definition and note on qualifying nonstandard ketchup products.
sources.supports: Defines unqualified ketchup as the common tomato product and says other ketchup types, including fruit and green variants, should be qualified. Supports separate named product identities, not a universal composition for fruit ketchup.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Fruit ketchup
sources.locator: Product display, condiment category, Québec-prepared label, and producer.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Ketchup aux fruits

sources.supports: Uses the exact French product name Ketchup aux fruits and describes a Québec-made condiment used with stews, tourtière, and meat pies. Supports the fr-CA display without assigning a recipe composition.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Québec fruit ketchup / ketchup aux fruits, separate from unqualified tomato ketchup. Recipes and retail products vary, including their use of tomatoes; the identity does not assert a fixed ingredient formula or make the product tomato-free. No recipe row or numeric behavior is inferred.

sources.title: Lazzaris, Fruit Mostarda

sources.title: Lazzaris, La Mostarda
sources.locator: Sections on what mostarda is and regional Italian styles
sources.supports: The manufacturer describes a fruit, sugar, and mustard preparation while distinguishing regional recipes and piece/puree styles. This is producer guidance, not a regulatory or universal definition.

sources.title: Comune di Cremona, Le DE.CO. di Cremona
sources.locator: La Mostarda tradizionale di Cremona
sources.supports: Defines Cremona's traditional mostarda as candied fruit with mustard and describes serving it with meats and cheeses. It documents one local style, not all mostardas.

sources.title: Regione Lombardia, Mostarda
sources.locator: Definition, regional varieties, preparation, and serving sections
sources.supports: Describes fruit candied in syrup and mustard-flavoured, names distinct local varieties including Cremona, Mantova, and Voghera, and discusses pairings. It is regional culinary information, not a single market standard.

sources.title: Elio Importing, Lazzaris Mostarda Fruit

sources.title: Elio Importing, Our Company

sources.supports: The importer states that its wholesale orders ship across Canada and lists Québec among its service regions. This is the distributor's service claim, not independent confirmation of item inventory.

sources.title: Hôtel Le Bonne Entente, L’expérience Bulle menu (French)
sources.locator: Carpaccio de bœuf and plateau de charcuteries
sources.supports: A Québec French-language menu uses the borrowed term mostarda alongside meat, cheese, grape must, and charcuterie. It supports local menu usage, not an OQLF ruling, product formula, or supplier identity.

decisions.reason: Add an identity-only fruit mostarda / mostarda reference in SAUCE_AND_CONDIMENT using the source-attested English product name and provisional Québec borrowed French display. Keep regional recipes, vegetable mostarda, ordinary prepared mustard, chutney, ketchup, and piccalilli distinct; do not infer a common texture, formula, or conversion across fruit-piece and puree styles. Add no forms, measures, density, unit mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.locator: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Fukujinzuke — Traditional Foods in Japan

Its historical story gives several possible curry origins and is not used to infer chutney substitution. Its product description does not define every commercial SKU

decisions.reason: Add the named fukujinzuke preserve identity. Regional recipes, manufacturer formulations, and Québec product listings do not establish universal numeric or substitution behavior.

sources.supports: Describes furikake as a savory rice seasoning/topping class with varied ingredients and dry or soft-moist products; not a universal formula.

sources.title: Japan MEXT, Food Composition Database: furikake with egg
sources.locator: Food-group entry and item name.
sources.supports: Identifies one food-composition-table item as furikake / seasoning mix for rice containing dried seaweed and egg; the entry is product-class evidence, not a universal ingredient profile.

Add only the specific English furikake rice seasoning alias; do not generalize to rice seasoning or toppings. Keep component foods and other Japanese rice seasoning products separate; formulas and product states vary. No recipe line, form, or numeric behavior is supported.

sources.title: OQLF, fusilli
sources.locator: Alimentation > pate alimentaire; definition, preferred French term, plural, and English term
sources.supports: Defines fusilli as short spiral-shaped pasta, gives fusilli as the preferred French and English term, and states the French plural fusillis. Notes that spirale is sometimes used for this pasta shape.

decisions.reason: Accept fusilli as an identity-only pasta shape. Use the OQLF-supported French plural fusillis as the sole French alias. Although OQLF notes that spirale is sometimes used for this shape, omit this broad descriptive common noun from aliases to reduce false matches. Assign the project's existing GRAIN_AND_CEREAL category for pasta shapes without asserting grain, egg, fresh/dry, or cooked composition. Add no forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, yields, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links.

sources.locator: Definition, note on usual spice components, preferred French terms, and English equivalents.
sources.supports: Defines garam massala / garam masala as an aromatic ground-spice blend used in Indian cuisine and lists both spellings in French and English term lists. Supports adding garam massala as a spelling alias in both search languages. The typical component note is descriptive and is not adopted as a universal formula.

sources.title: Metro, McCormick Garam Masala 48 g
sources.locator: Product title, number 066200004040, description, and ingredient declaration.

sources.supports: Current Canadian manufacturer page names a South Asian spice blend and lists its own formula, including corn maltodextrin, ginger, bay leaf, and anise seed. Its ingredient declaration differs from the McCormick retail listing; the formulas remain SKU-specific.

sources.title: Santé Canada, Cari aux pois chiches et aux légumes
sources.locator: Ingredient list and method.
sources.supports: The current Canada Food Guide recipe lists poudre de cari and garam masala as separate ingredients and adds them at different steps. Supports keeping these compound identities distinct in recipe search; no amount or cooking rule is generalized.

decisions.reason: Verify the existing garam masala / garam masala identity and add the OQLF-attested garam massala spelling as a French and English search alias. Keep it distinct from curry powder, curry paste, panch phoron, and Chinese five-spice. The bundled butter-chicken recipe 086 already links its exact 2 tsp garam masala line to this reference; leave that line unchanged. Recipe 048 is a separate source-specific homemade blend recipe whose ingredient rows list component spices, not a universal formula. Current Canadian product pages show SKU-specific formulations. Add no form, measurement, density, unit mapping, package yield, conversion, or substitution.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: cresson alénois
sources.locator: French headword, English and Latin equivalents, preferred terms, and culinary-use note.
sources.supports: Supports cresson alénois / garden cress and Lepidium sativum; lists passerage cultivée and nasitort as preferred French terms and describes young plants as a salad and sauce condiment and garnish. The entry notes that cresson de jardin is ambiguous in horticultural use. It does not establish current retail availability.

sources.supports: Describes garden cress as cultivated for leaves used in salads, sandwiches, soups, and as baby greens. Cultivar and growing information is not used as ingredient variants or measurement evidence; medicinal statements are not used.

Use only the OQLF-listed French aliases passerage cultivée and nasitort; omit ambiguous cresson de jardin, bare cress/cresson, and broad common-name aliases. CNF serving observations remain tied to Food Code 2084 and do not establish a generic density, universal sprig weight, or trim yield. sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Solanum aethiopicum
sources.locator: Accepted-name record and cultivated-origin statement.
sources.supports: Accepts Solanum aethiopicum and gives its native range as a cultigen from northeast tropical Africa. Taxonomy and range only; not culinary or Québec naming evidence.

sources.title: PROTA / Pl@ntUse, Solanum aethiopicum (French account)
sources.locator: Vernacular-name list; fruit/leaf uses in West Africa and other regions; cultivar-group names; substitution note.
sources.supports: Lists aubergine écarlate and the English names garden egg and scarlet eggplant; describes immature-fruit use in humid West Africa and separate leaf uses/names by region and cultivar group. It states African eggplant fruits may be replaced by common eggplant, without recipe scope or amount.

sources.title: PROTA / Pl@ntUse, Solanum aethiopicum (English account)
sources.locator: English account common-name and use sections; fruit substitution note.
sources.supports: English account supports garden egg / scarlet eggplant usage, edible fruit use, and a qualitative common-eggplant replacement statement. The statement lacks dish, form, or quantity scope and does not support a runtime rule.

sources.title: Aguessy et al., Ethnobotanical characterization of scarlet eggplant varieties cultivated in Benin (West Africa), Journal of Agriculture and Food Research 5 (2021)
sources.locator: Abstract: edible-fruit crop, rural appraisal in 680 households across 92 villages, and cultivar context.
sources.supports: Primary Benin field research describes scarlet eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum) as an edible-fruit crop and reports 680 households across 92 villages. It supports regional food identity, not Québec naming or kitchen measures.

sources.title: Nkansah, Some physiological features of the African eggplant, Solanum aethiopicum group Gilo, Scientia Horticulturae 90 (2001), 181–186
sources.locator: Introduction: African-eggplant ambiguity, Ghana Gilo common name, and fruit use in soups/stews.
sources.supports: Primary Ghana research says the Gilo group is popularly known as garden eggs, is found in tropical West Africa, and its fruit is used in soup and stew. It also states African eggplant can refer to both Solanum aethiopicum and Solanum macrocarpon, supporting rejection of that broad alias.

sources.title: Marchés publics de Montréal, Les légumes du marché qui évoluent
sources.locator: French-language article dated 2025-06-16; paragraph on small African aubergines and West African/Caribbean cooking.
sources.supports: Local market article uses the borrowed English product wording “Garden Egg” in French copy. It supplies Montréal market context but does not identify the species or a French equivalent.

sources.title: Adekeye et al., Osmotic Dehydration of Garden Egg (Solanum aethiopicum): The Shrinkage and Mass Transfer Phenomena, Journal of Analytical Techniques and Research 2(1) (2020)
sources.locator: Methods §§2.2.1 and 2.3.1; results §3.1 and Table 1.
sources.supports: Reports 1.05 g/mL for raw garden egg material collected at Mojere market, Ado-Ekiti, Nigeria. A 10 g sample was measured by water displacement in a volumetric cylinder in triplicate; cultivar and maturity are not reported. Preserve as study-specific research only, not a default density or household measure.

sources.title: Walsh Medical Media, indexed copy of Osmotic Dehydration of Garden Egg
sources.locator: Bibliographic heading for the article title and author list.
sources.supports: The page labels the same title under Journal of Food Processing & Technology with a different DOI. It is a metadata discrepancy check only, not independent confirmation of the 1.05 g/mL finding.

sources.title: Santé Canada, Groupes de cultures et propriétés chimiques de leurs résidus
sources.locator: French residue-chemistry crop group 8-09 and subgroup 8-09B; aubergine entries for Solanum melongena, S. macrocarpon, and S. aethiopicum.
sources.supports: Lists aubergine écarlate (Solanum aethiopicum) separately from aubergine d’Afrique (S. macrocarpon) and aubergine (S. melongena). This is regulatory crop terminology, not a Québec culinary naming ruling.

sources.title: Oyedoyin et al., Variation Among Agronomic Traits and Mineral Contents in 15 Accessions of Garden Egg Plant (Solanum aethiopicum) in Southwest of Nigeria, Journal of Agricultural Science and Environment, 2020
sources.locator: Article title and abstract; common name garden egg plant attached to Solanum aethiopicum.
sources.supports: Uses garden egg plant for Solanum aethiopicum in the cited Nigerian study. This is a boundary example, not an exhaustive regional naming claim.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Raw garden egg material (Solanum aethiopicum), collected at Mojere market in Ado-Ekiti, Nigeria.
measurementObservations.foodState: Raw; cultivar group and fruit maturity are not specified.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: The study measured the displacement of a 10 g sample in distilled water in a volumetric cylinder; the experiment was conducted in triplicate.

substitutionFindings.context: PROTA says African eggplant fruits can be replaced by common eggplant in dishes.
substitutionFindings.basis: The statement does not identify dishes, cultivar, preparation state, culinary role, quantity, ratio, or expected result.
limitations: Do not activate a global or contextual substitution rule from this unscoped statement.
Do not add a replacement link, warning, quantity adjustment, form conversion, or recipe-line link.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only garden egg / aubergine écarlate for the West African edible fruit product of Solanum aethiopicum. Keep the French display provisional for fr-CA; do not put scientific names, African eggplant, bitter tomato, regional leaf names, generic eggplant, or jiló into aliases. Keep fruit separate from S. macrocarpon gboma leaves and generic S. melongena eggplant. Record the single-market density only as a study-specific observation and the qualitative replacement claim only as a blocked finding; activate no density, measure, conversion, or substitution. Add no forms, recipe links, yields, or other runtime numeric behavior.

sources.supports: Cross-references the Québec crop name Arroche with Atriplex hortensis. This is a Québec commodity-name/species crosswalk, not an OQLF ruling, culinary-use source, or evidence of retail availability.

Keep other Atriplex species, spinach, and other spinach-named greens separate; do not add plant-part assumptions beyond the supported edible leaves, measurements, forms, density, mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.supports: Defines gari as a processed cassava product and retains the product name gari in French.

sources.title: Endo Foods, Product Information

sources.supports: Defines gari as sweetened pickled ginger and lists beni shoga separately; does not address West African cassava gari.

sources.locator: Definition / accompaniment wording

decisions.reason: Accepted as the named processed cassava product gari. Keep it distinct from edible cassava flour and extracted tapioca starch. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.
Add the English spelling alias garri to the existing gari identity based on a Nigerian manufacturer’s cassava product naming. Keep the French display gari and add no numeric or substitution data.

Resolve the prior Japanese gari hold by adding a separate Japanese gari (pickled ginger) reference with a sushi-specific French display and search labels. Keep this cassava reference unchanged as the West African product gari / garri; do not add Japanese gari as an alias to the cassava row. The plain gari query now returns two distinct labels, while sushi-specific queries return only the Japanese condiment. Keep beni shoga separate. No matching preserved-ginger recipe rows, forms, measurements, mappings, conversions, yields, or substitutions were added.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Glebionis coronaria

substitutionFindings.context: Replacement of finished gat kimchi in an unspecified recipe role and preparation state.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed sources establish gat kimchi identity and document particular preparations, but no source recommends a replacement for finished gat kimchi in a defined dish role. Bundled recipes contain no demand that would identify a target method or quantity basis.
limitations: Do not infer replacement by generic kimchi, kkakdugi, dongchimi, baek-kimchi, pickled mustard greens, or takana-zuke from shared condiment use or mustard-leaf wording.
Recipe-level ingredient changes within a particular gat-kimchi formula do not establish substitutes for the finished condiment.
No reviewed evidence establishes a matching dish role, preparation state, quantity basis, ratio, or adjustment for a contextual rule.

rejectedCandidates.reason: The generic kimchi identity is broader than this named mustard-leaf type, and no source recommends it as a replacement for finished gat kimchi.
Kkakdugi is a separately named radish kimchi type; no source recommends replacing gat kimchi with it.
Dongchimi is a separately named radish-water kimchi type; no source recommends replacing gat kimchi with it.
Baek-kimchi is a separately named white-cabbage kimchi type; no source recommends replacing gat kimchi with it.
The broader pickled-mustard-greens identity does not establish the named Korean fermented kimchi type or a substitution direction.
Takana-zuke is a separate named Japanese preserve; shared mustard-family wording does not make it a substitute for gat kimchi.

decisions.reason: Accepted as a source-backed identity-only row with the exact bilingual display pair. OQLF records riz gluant and glutinous rice as names for a distinct sticky rice type. No alternate aliases or rice-state conversions are activated. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.

Reject `sticky rice` as a global alias for glutinous rice / riz gluant. OQLF and TERMIUM support the terminology equivalence, but Canadian manufacturer and retailer sources also use Sticky Rice / Riz Collant for short-grain sushi rice and a separate ready-to-heat rice product. Keep the active glutinous-rice display unchanged and the alias inactive until product-specific context establishes dry glutinous grain. No bundled recipe uses this wording; no recipe links or quantities change.

Add waxy rice and sweet rice as English aliases and riz glutineux and riz doux as French aliases on the existing glutinous-rice grain identity, retaining glutinous rice / riz gluant as the display. OQLF and USDA NAL terminology plus Canadian product/specification evidence support these terms. Keep sticky rice / riz collant withheld under the existing Canadian product-boundary decision; do not add sweet brown rice, regional/variety-qualified titles, flour aliases, measurements, forms, conversions, yields, substitutions, or recipe links. The full 114-recipe corpus has no matching demand.

Add mochigome as an English-search alias to the existing glutinous rice / riz gluant identity. Keep all display names and current aliases, the black-glutinous-rice identity, forms, measurements, and other data unchanged. Do not encode the unbounded regular-rice replacement statement as a substitution rule.

substitutionFindings.context: A Japan National Tourism Organization page says mochigome can replace regular rice, but supplies no dish, role, quantity, or method boundary.
substitutionFindings.basis: This is a broad use statement, not enough evidence for a reusable directed or contextual recipe substitution rule.
limitations: Do not add an active global or contextual substitution rule.
Do not transfer a ratio or cooking method from the statement.

sources.title: OQLF, acide gras saturé (GDT)
sources.locator: Usage note for nominal gras.
sources.supports: OQLF notes nominal gras is common in Québec and gives gras d’oie as an example; it is not a dedicated goose-fat terminology record.

decisions.reason: Add goose fat / graisse d’oie as an identity-only cooking-fat reference. Use gras d’oie as a Québec French alias supported by OQLF usage and a Canadian product label. Do not claim rendering or clarification; keep goose fat separate from duck fat and other poultry species. No matching recipe rows, forms, measures, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, groseille à maquereau (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred terms, English equivalent, and notes distinguishing gooseberry from currants.
sources.supports: Supports gooseberry / groseille à maquereau and explains that bare groseille has different Québec and European usage.

decisions.reason: Add gooseberry / groseille à maquereau as a distinct FRUIT identity. Preserve source-qualified synonyms and regional boundaries; add no forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Industrial Development Board, “Goraka Paste.”
sources.locator: Goraka rind use and separate paste product description.
sources.supports: Describes goraka rind use and a processed paste containing other ingredients; it does not resolve a safe global identity or shelf-life claim.

sources.title: Sri Lanka Export Development Board, goraka product listing.
sources.locator: Goraka product listing and paste-product context.
sources.supports: Supports Sinhala goraka and Garcinia paste context; insufficient to merge goraka with kokum.

sources.title: DailyLife.lk, “Village Style Dried Fish Recipe.”
sources.locator: Dried-fish curry ingredient list and method.
sources.supports: Supports one local Sri Lankan recipe context; it does not define exact ingredient forms or a universal formula.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online, Garcinia quaesita Pierre
sources.locator: Accepted name, species status, and native range.
sources.supports: Accepts Garcinia quaesita Pierre as a species native to Sri Lanka. Establishes current taxonomic identity; it does not define a food product or culinary use.

sources.title: Food and Agriculture Organization, The State of the World’s Forest Genetic Resources: Country Report Sri Lanka
sources.locator: Annex 8, species profile for Garcinia quaesita, pp. 115–116.
sources.supports: Names Garcinia quaesita and gives Sinhala common names including Goraka and Rath Goraka; describes the edible fruit’s sun-dried rind as a Sri Lankan curry condiment and fish-curing ingredient. The report documents older use of Garcinia cambogia and other names as synonyms; those historical names are not adopted as catalog aliases.

sources.title: Liyanagamage et al., Correlation between Antioxidant Activity and the Garcinol Content Released from Fruit Rinds of Endemic Garcinia quaesita Pierre on Different Cooking Conditions, Journal of Food Quality
sources.locator: Introduction and plant-material section.
sources.supports: Identifies G. quaesita as locally known as Rathgoraka and says its dried fruit rind is used as a souring spice in traditional curries; the plant material was taxonomically authenticated at Sri Lanka’s National Herbarium. It distinguishes G. quaesita from G. gummi-gutta (formerly G. cambogia), which is used in other regional cuisines. Laboratory sample amounts are not recipe measures.

sources.title: Institute of Chemistry Ceylon, Chemistry in Sri Lanka, Vol. 42 No. 2
sources.locator: Abstract 2025_273, p. 35.
sources.supports: Reports commercially available dried Garcinia quaesita fruit rinds collected in Sri Lanka and identifies Goraka as the local name; describes the rind as a flavour enhancer and food preservative. This is not a household measure or recipe formula.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online, Garcinia gummi-gutta (L.) N.Robson
sources.locator: Accepted name and synonym list.
sources.supports: Accepts G. gummi-gutta and lists Garcinia cambogia among its synonyms. In combination with the accepted G. quaesita record and the Sri Lankan culinary study, this keeps the old G. cambogia label out of goraka aliases and avoids conflating goraka with Malabar tamarind.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only dried goraka rind / pelure séchée de goraka as the dried fruit rind of Garcinia quaesita used as a Sri Lankan souring spice. Use goraka and the source-backed Rath Goraka spelling only; do not add Garcinia cambogia, Malabar tamarind, kokum, tamarind, or paste as aliases. Keep the compound paste candidate separate. Add no form, recipe link, measure, conversion, yield, or active substitution.

No reusable household measure, density, unit mapping, portion relationship, or yield is supported. The country report’s annual household consumption figure and research-paper laboratory quantities are not recipe measures.

sources.title: European Commission, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/1595, French official text and single document

sources.locator: Product description and production section.
sources.supports: Current English Consortium wording for Gorgonzola PDO and the Gorgonzola dolce and Gorgonzola piccante styles. Supports the bilingual display and phrase aliases; it is not a Canadian regulatory source.

Delivery is restricted to the designated business area, availability can change, and direct page retrieval returned a cache miss; use only for listing wording, not current stock.

sources.title: Metro Canada, Fromage gorgonzola, product 239139
sources.locator: French-language product title and selected-store listing.
sources.supports: Supports the exact French retail title. The listing does not identify PDO status, so the phrase is not an alias for the PDO-bounded row. Its approximately 165 g cut-piece amount is retailer-specific; the selected store context showed out of stock.

sources.title: Metro Canada, Gorgonzola Cheese, product 239139
sources.locator: Paired English-language listing for the same Metro product.
sources.supports: Supports the exact English retail title. It is the same SKU as the French page and does not identify PDO status, so the title is not an alias for the PDO-bounded row.

sources.title: Mayrand Québec, Gorgonzola coupé 400 g, Castello item 08491
sources.locator: Québec-facing product title, blue-cheese category, and store listings.
sources.supports: Supports local French product wording and point-in-time store availability. The product page does not identify PDO status; the approximate 400 g cut package is SKU-specific and is not a reusable measure.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only Gorgonzola AOP / Gorgonzola PDO with Gorgonzola DOP and the source-backed French and Italian style phrases as aliases. Keep generic blue cheese, Roquefort, Fourme d’Ambert, and other named blue cheeses distinct. Metro’s unqualified English and French product titles and Mayrand’s unqualified Castello SKU do not establish PDO status, so they are not aliases. Product-specification wheel and maturation details and retailer package sizes do not support recipe measures, densities, forms, mappings, conversions, or yields. No bundled recipe demand or supported substitution was found. Add no forms, measures, recipe links, conversions, package yields, or substitutions; reuse existing generic blue-cheese source WP04-Q-CHEESE-20261010-S16 without duplicating it.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards
sources.locator: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards, Volume 12, sections 12.1.3–12.1.4.
sources.supports: Current incorporated Canadian standard. Section 12.1.4 defines Graham flour as flour with part of the bran and other wheat-berry constituents added and gives the moisture-free ash range. Section 12.1.3 separately defines whole-wheat flour. Regulatory criteria are not imported as cooking measurements or conversions.

sources.locator: Preferred term and English equivalent
sources.supports: Directly pairs grain sorghum with sorgho à graine. The grain identity remains separate from sorghum flour; regional names are not added.

sources.locator: English and Latin equivalents; preferred Québec French term.
sources.supports: Identifies sorgho as the preferred Québec French term for Sorghum bicolor and pairs it with English sorghum. It does not establish milo as a Québec food-grain term.

sources.locator: Sections 2.4 and 4.3: common names, name scope, Canadian uses.
sources.supports: Lists milo among common English names for Sorghum bicolor and cautions that common names may apply to narrower subspecies, races, or uses. sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Canadian Feed Ingredients Table
sources.locator: Entries 1-201-014 and 1-201-015; bilingual French table also reviewed.
sources.supports: Separates generic sorghum grain from sorghum milo grain (or milo), defined as whole grain of the milo variety. This is an animal-feed ingredient definition, not a human-food synonym standard.

sources.title: Agence canadienne d’inspection des aliments, Tableau canadien des ingrédients des aliments du bétail
sources.locator: Entries 1-201-014 and 1-201-015, French wording.

sources.title: FAO, Sorghum and millets in human nutrition
sources.locator: Sorghum section: food-grain classes and kernel colour variation.
sources.supports: Describes milo as one of several grain-sorghum types grown primarily for food and says sorghum kernel colour ranges from white through shades of red and brown to yellow and purple-brown. decisions.reason: Accepted as a source-backed identity-only row with the exact bilingual display pair. Directly pairs grain sorghum with sorgho à graine. The grain identity remains separate from sorghum flour; regional names are not added. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.

Retain grain sorghum / sorgho à graine as the existing identity-only row and hold bare milo, sorghum milo grain, and grain de sorgho milo outside its aliases. CFIA uses milo both as a broad botanical common name and as a narrower feed-table grain class, while FAO describes milo as one food-grain class among several. Current Québec terminology supports sorgho but does not settle milo as a food alias. Keep source-specific milo-variety products and feed meanings separate; add no forms, recipe links, measures, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

Add sorgho en grains and sorgho en grain as French aliases for the existing grain-sorghum identity, keeping the Québec OQLF display pair unchanged. Retain the three Health Canada CNF 2015 portions as food-code-specific observations only because the CNF entry does not identify grain preparation or packing. Do not activate a density, unit mapping, form, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only jowar whole as an English alias on the existing grain-sorghum identity. The Government of India's 2024 rules identify Sorghum (Jowar) among whole or dehulled millets for direct human consumption, and a current Ontario retailer uses the exact qualified product phrase and describes whole sorghum grains. Keep bare jowar unstored; its picker result may show the clearly labeled grain, flour, and semolina options. Preserve Québec French naming and all existing source-specific grain observations; add no form, active density, mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

Add `guinea corn` as an English alias on the existing grain-sorghum reference. Nigeria’s National Agricultural Sample Census identifies Guinea corn with sorghum, while the Canadian product listing keeps the distinct Ogi Baba powder boundary visible. Retain the Québec French display, existing grain-code observations, identity, and active numeric and substitution behavior; do not add a flour or powder alias to the grain row.

Keep `mabele`, `mabele meal`, `mabele flour`, `amabele`, `amabele flour`, and Canadian spelling `mabela` out of active aliases. Regional crop sources identify mabele with sorghum, but South African guidance and research use Mabele for a dry-milled meal/breakfast cereal with a variable meal-versus-finer-flour boundary; Canadian Mabela porridge wording does not establish composition, and `amabele` is also attested for pearl millet. Preserve the verified grain identity and all current fields. Do not transfer grain-code measures or add a new identity, French name, form, measure, conversion, recipe link, or substitution.

Add `red sorghum` as an English alias to the existing grain-sorghum identity because a current Ontario retailer lists Red Sorghum (Jowar) as a grain product. Keep the grain and flour choices distinct; do not add red jowar, French red-sorghum wording, or a red-specific identity. Red is a colour descriptor within sorghum, not a separate cultivar or specification. No recipe link or numeric behavior is added.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether Ardent Mills granular flour has a source-supported, actionable replacement relationship for household recipes, including its stated dusting and thickening applications.
substitutionFindings.basis: Ardent Mills' current bilingual product pages list bakery products, premium dusting flour, and sauce/gravy thickening as applications. Its February 2023 English and French portfolios describe Talisman Granular as an instant blending flour best used for dusting or thickening. None identifies an ingredient to replace, a replacement direction, quantity, ratio, or process. These uses do not establish a tested or actionable substitute relationship.
limitations: Do not convert the manufacturer's application list into a substitution claim.
The words 'thickening agent' and 'instant blending flour' do not identify a displaced ingredient, formula, quantity, ratio, or method.
Do not infer a relationship with cornstarch, all-purpose flour, Farina/spring-wheat semolina, Wheatlets, durum semolina, or another flour from functional overlap or product wording.

The pages describe an industrial product available in 20 kg bags and totes and state that Ardent Mills does not sell directly to home bakers or consumers; this finding does not establish home-recipe behavior.
No global or contextual substitution rule or bundled recipe link is supported by the reviewed sources.

sources.title: Maple from Canada, The Versatility of Maple Syrup

sources.supports: Recommends equal amounts of maple syrup and sugar for most recipes and reducing other liquid by 1/4 cup per cup of sugar; the page says this may not suit pastry recipes using large amounts of sugar. This is producer-association guidance, not a tested recipe conversion.

sources.title: Colorado State University Extension, Ingredient Substitutions

sources.supports: Lists 1 cup corn syrup for 1 cup sugar but cautions never to replace more than half of the sugar called for in a recipe, reducing other liquid by 1/4 cup. Also lists 13/16 cup honey per cup sugar with a liquid reduction and pinch of baking soda, 3/4–1 cup maple syrup with a liquid reduction, and 1 cup molasses or sorghum with leavener/liquid adjustments. These broad table entries do not establish recipe-tested universal rules or resolve generic molasses identity.

decisions.reason: Removed source-less draft density and unit-mapping values from the active bundled catalog. Restore a value only with source, exact food/form, unit convention, method or basis, and reviewer disposition.

Preserve the distinct published 1-cup observations of 200 g (USDA SR28, Sugars, granulated) and 198 g (King Arthur, Sugar (granulated white)). The source cup conventions and row-specific filling methods are not stated, so neither value is activated as a generic cup-to-mass mapping or density and the values are not averaged.

Add the five Health Canada CNF 2015 food code 4318 metric-volume portions as source-specific observations. Keep the observations ledger-only: the source does not state a volume-filling or packing method, and it does not resolve the distinct USDA SR28 and King Arthur source-cup conventions. Do not infer or activate a density, unit mapping, conversion, or recipe quantity; do not average or reconcile across sources.

Record the source-bounded, one-way granulated-sugar-to-generic-corn-syrup partial-replacement guidance. Retain the maximum one-half recipe-sugar limit and liquid adjustment; keep the candidate ledger-only because the runtime model cannot enforce them.

Keep honey and maple-syrup replacements blocked: reviewed sources disagree on their ratios and liquid/leavener/temperature adjustments. Do not average their instructions, activate a rule, or link a bundled recipe. Maple syrup’s ingredient identity also awaits review. Do not assign generic molasses guidance while that identity remains unresolved.

substitutionFindings.context: Partial replacement of granulated sugar with generic corn syrup in cooking or baking; Colorado State Extension limits the substituted share to at most half of the recipe’s sugar.
substitutionFindings.basis: Colorado State Extension and Utah State Extension each list a one-cup-for-one-cup volume replacement. Colorado State explicitly caps corn syrup at no more than half of the sugar called for; Utah State does not state that cap. These are general substitution tables rather than tested source-recipe formulas.
adjustments: Colorado State Extension says to reduce other liquid by 1/4 cup per cup of corn syrup; Utah State Extension also says to reduce recipe liquid by 1/4 cup for its listed cup replacement.
limitations: Keep the Colorado State maximum of one-half of the recipe’s sugar; do not infer support for replacing all sugar.

substitutionFindings.context: Honey as a liquid-sweetener replacement for granulated sugar in cooking and baking guidance; no single transferable ratio or adjustment set is resolved.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur Baking and the Utah State archive recommend about 3/4 cup honey per cup of granulated sugar; Colorado State lists 13/16 cup; the newer Utah State page recommends 1/2 cup. Their liquid, soda, and oven adjustments also differ, so the ratios and adjustments remain source-specific and must not be averaged.
adjustments: King Arthur Baking: reduce liquid by 3–4 tablespoons per cup of sugar replaced, or add flour if the recipe has no liquid; avoid baking above 350°F.
Utah State archive: reduce recipe liquid by 1/4 cup and add 1/2 teaspoon baking soda per cup of honey.
Colorado State: reduce liquid by 3 tablespoons per cup of honey and add a pinch of baking soda.
Utah State 2025: reduce each liquid by 25%, lower oven temperature by 25°F, and add 1/4 teaspoon baking soda per cup of honey.
expectedEffects: King Arthur describes honey as sweeter than sugar, relatively acidic, and prone to faster browning; its test-kitchen guidance warns that creamed cakes can become denser and that honey scorches above 350°F.
limitations: Do not select, average, or convert the competing ratios or leavener adjustments into one general rule.
These general guides do not specify a single recipe, role, mixing method, or exact product; no active contextual rule or recipe-line link is supported.
The runtime model cannot express the necessary liquid, flour, oven-temperature, and leavener adjustments together.

substitutionFindings.context: Maple syrup as a liquid-sweetener replacement for granulated sugar; reviewed sources disagree on the volume ratio and recipe adjustments.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur Baking and Maple from Canada recommend equal volumes for most recipes; University of Maine Cooperative Extension recommends 3/4 cup syrup per cup sugar; Colorado State Extension gives a 3/4–1 cup range. Keep these recommendations separate. The maple-syrup identity is also still unreviewed in the catalog.
adjustments: King Arthur Baking: reduce liquid by 3–4 tablespoons per cup syrup, or add about 1 tablespoon flour per 1/4 cup syrup if no liquid is used.
Maple from Canada: reduce other liquid by 1/4 cup per cup of sugar; its guidance excludes pastry recipes with large amounts of sugar.
University of Maine: reduce liquid by 2–4 tablespoons per cup syrup, add baking soda except when cultured dairy supplies acidity, and reduce oven temperature by 25°F.
Colorado State: reduce other liquid by 3 tablespoons.
expectedEffects: King Arthur’s maple-sweetened soft cookies were moister and more cake-like and could spread more than the granulated-sugar version.
limitations: Do not average or choose among the conflicting ratios or liquid adjustments.
The candidate replacement identity has not completed catalog review.
The source guides do not establish a single recipe context or compatible adjustment set; keep the evidence out of runtime rules and recipe-line links.

decisions.reason: Accept Greek-style yogurt / yogourt grec as a distinct dairy identity, retaining the existing candidate ID. Complete a source-bounded substitution review for sour cream and plain Greek-style yogurt. Keep directions and uses in separate evidence findings, preserve source amount/method/fat limits, and leave the runtime rule arrays and bundled recipe lines unchanged because those constraints are not enforceable by the current model.

Record the Health Canada CNF portions as separate source-specific observations for plain Greek-style yogurt at 2% M.F. and for the distinct rich product at 8–12% M.F. The exact product codes do not establish one generic density, a common Greek-style-yogurt composition, the recipe cup convention, or an active ingredient mapping. Keep default density and unit mappings empty and recipe lines unchanged.

decisions.reason: Accept as a distinct flour identity. Keep generic lentil flour, other lentil colors/preparations, forms, aliases, measurements, conversions, recipe links, and substitutions outside this row.

Complete bounded measurement and substitution research for this identity. No reviewed source supports a product-matched household measure or reusable density. replacements.roleInCompound: Replaces part of the oat flour in the named experimental muffin formula.

substitutionFindings.context: The Geraldo et al. 2024 oat and lentil muffin comparison, followed by the 2026 sensory study. The lentil muffin uses 50% green lentil flour in its flour blend; the 2026 study used green lentils milled in-house and says the formulation was selected after internal trials.
substitutionFindings.basis: The 2024 study describes green lentil flour as a partial substitute for oat flour. Its tested muffin formulation also changes other ingredients and process variables. The 2026 follow-up reports similar flavour, texture, and overall acceptance, with lower appearance and smell ratings for the lentil muffin.
adjustments: The reported result depends on the complete study formulation; several ingredient amounts, including sweetener, leavening, oil, water, and vanilla, differ from the oat-only control.
expectedEffects: The study muffin contains green lentil flour alongside oat flour at the reported 50% flour-blend level.
The 2024 paper reports higher protein and fibre and lower fat than its oat-only comparator.
The 2026 sensory follow-up reports similar flavour, texture, and overall acceptance, with lower appearance and smell scores.
limitations: This is a controlled, study-specific muffin formulation using a particular green-lentil flour preparation; do not apply its 50% level to other muffins, baking formulas, breads, or dishes.
The other formula changes mean the study does not support replacing oat flour alone in an arbitrary recipe or a reusable mass/volume ratio.

sources.supports: Supports banane plantain as a Québec French fruit term; it does not approve a full flour compound.

sources.title: Parce Canada, MD Plantain Flour — Farine de Plantain
sources.locator: Canadian product title.
sources.supports: Documents a Canadian French retail label farine de plantain; the page does not establish the product maturity or authorize it as an alias for the green-qualified reference.

sources.title: OQLF, farine de banane (GDT)
sources.locator: GDT entry, last updated 1982.
sources.supports: Pairs farine de banane with banana meal and discusses broad banana maturity. Adjacent historical evidence only; it does not identify green banana or plantain flour.

sources.title: Basmex, Nos produits
sources.locator: Listings for Tropiway farine de taro and farine de plantain; Montréal distributor.
sources.supports: Attests local product wording but gives no composition for these fufu flour listings.

sources.title: Tropical Foods / Tropiway, Making Fufu
sources.locator: Product description and ingredients context.
sources.supports: Describes plantain and cocoyam fufu flours as products made from processed tropical produce blended together; does not establish pure green plantain or whole-taro flour.

sources.title: OQLF, banane (GDT), and TERMIUM Plus plantain record
sources.locator: Fruit-name terminology records.
sources.supports: Supports banane and banane plantain as fruit wording; neither source establishes the complete green-plantain-flour compound.

sources.title: Le Pro 1600, Mountain Delight, Farine de plantain / Plantain flour, 340 g
sources.locator: French product page; parallel English page: https://lepro1600.com/en/products/delight-farine-de-plantain-340g-delight-plantain-flour-340g
sources.supports: The bilingual product pages use the exact French label farine de plantain and English label plantain flour, and describe the product as dried, finely ground green plantains. This supports aliases for this green product, not every unqualified plantain flour product.

sources.title: Épicerie La Hacienda, Laval, Mountain Delight plantain flour listing
sources.locator: Product listing for the 340 g Mountain Delight item.
sources.supports: A Laval retailer lists the bilingual product wording plantain flour / farine de plantain for the same brand and package size. The retailer listing supports naming but does not itself state maturity or composition.

decisions.reason: Add green plantain flour as an identity-only product separate from plantain fruit, green banana flour, ripe plantain flour, and isolated plantain starch. Keep the display maturity-explicit and leave unqualified plantain flour inactive as an alias. The French label is a provisional descriptive compound pending independent Québec review. Leave density, mappings, forms, recipe links, conversions, yields, and substitutions unset.

Retain `green plantain flour / farine de banane plantain verte` as a provisional descriptive display. Québec evidence names a Tropiway fufu flour and the maker says its regional fufu flour is blended; no exact Québec source establishes a single-source green-plantain flour. Keep broad flour terms inactive as aliases and add no forms or numeric or substitution behavior.

Add only the exact Canadian retail aliases plantain flour / farine de plantain to the existing green plantain flour identity. Le Pro identifies its bilingual-label product as flour made from dried green plantains, and a Laval retailer uses the same labels for the same brand and package. Keep the maturity-qualified canonical displays and separate green banana flour; leave broad banana-flour wording, forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, and substitutions unset.

sources.title: OQLF, pois cassé, Grand dictionnaire terminologique
sources.locator: Definition and note for pois cassé; color terms pois jaune cassé / yellow split pea and pois vert cassé / green split pea.
sources.supports: Defines a split pea as a dry pea whose two cotyledons have been separated and gives the green and yellow French terms with English equivalents. Supports identity and Québec terminology only; no measurement or recipe mapping.

sources.title: Mayrand, Riz et grain
sources.locator: Product listings for Pois jaunes cassés and Pois verts cassés, alongside separate Pois jaunes entiers listings.
sources.supports: Québec retailer lists green and yellow split peas as distinct products and distinguishes them from whole yellow peas. Supports market terminology and identity only; no quantities or conversions are inferred.

sources.title: Loblaws, French-locale green split pea search results
sources.locator: French-locale search results list Pois verts cassés and Pois jaunes cassés as separate packaged products.
sources.supports: Corroborates distinct green and yellow split-pea retail names in French. Search-result availability is changeable; supports product naming only.

sources.title: Artisan Tradition, Pulses
sources.locator: Organic Yellow Split Peas and Organic Green Split Peas product sections; whole yellow peas are listed separately.
sources.supports: Québec pulse producer lists separate green and yellow split-pea products and a separate whole yellow pea product. Supports identity and product distinction only.

sources.title: Diefenbaker Spice & Pulse, Special Crop Products
sources.locator: Green Split Peas and Yellow Split Peas product descriptions; separate Whole Yellow Peas section.
sources.supports: Pulse supplier distinguishes green and yellow split-pea products from whole yellow peas. Supports identity and product distinction only; no recipe measures or catalog form rules are inferred.

decisions.reason: Add the identity-only green split-pea reference using the OQLF color term and corroborating Québec retail and pulse-producer listings. Keep it separate from the generic legacy split-pea candidate and from whole yellow peas. Add no forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, conversions, yields, substitutions, or recipe links.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards, Volume 17 §17.1.4
sources.locator: Standard for green tea.
sources.supports: Supports a named dry tea product type; no matcha equivalence is inferred.

sources.title: OQLF, thé vert (GDT)
sources.locator: Québec French term and English translation green tea.
sources.supports: Supports the bilingual product name; no matcha or herbal-infusion alias is added.

decisions.reason: Add green tea / thé vert as a dry Camellia sinensis product identity. Keep matcha, other tea types, herbal infusions, and prepared drinks separate; add no aliases or recipe links because no matching recipe row exists.

sources.title: OQLF Grand dictionnaire terminologique, ketchup
sources.locator: Definition and note on qualifying nonstandard ketchup products.
sources.supports: Defines unqualified ketchup as the common tomato product and says other ketchup types, including fruit and green variants, should be qualified. Supports separate named product identities, not a universal composition for green ketchup.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Si-Bon Ketchup vert genre maison
sources.locator: Bilingual product listing for UPC 055429500228 and ingredient list.
sources.supports: The Québec retailer lists the French product as Ketchup vert and English as Homestyle Green Ketchup; ingredients identify green tomatoes as the principal named vegetable. Supports the local display and matching bilingual product class.

sources.title: La petite bette, Le ketchup vert délicieux de ma maman
sources.locator: Product discussion and terminology sections, including “Ketchup aux tomates vertes”.
sources.supports: Québec culinary publisher defines the product as a condiment made from green tomatoes picked before ripening and uses ketchup vert / ketchup aux tomates vertes. It notes chow-chow overlap and explicitly reports variable naming; do not adopt chow-chow as an alias.

sources.title: Wildly Canadian, Green Tomato Ketchup
sources.locator: Product title and Ontario-grown-preserves product description.
sources.supports: Current Canadian product listing uses the exact English phrase Green Tomato Ketchup. This corroborates the English product wording; the source is Ontario market evidence, not Québec terminology authority.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only green tomato ketchup / ketchup vert for the preserved condiment made with green tomatoes. Use the directly attested French alias ketchup aux tomates vertes; leave chow-chow inactive because Québec sources report variable overlap with relish terminology. Keep regular tomato ketchup and fruit ketchup separate; no recipe row or numeric behavior is inferred.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, flétan du Groenland (GDT)
sources.versionOrDate: Last updated 2012; preferred term normalized July 2004
sources.locator: Preferred terms, Latin name, and terms used in certain contexts
sources.supports: Identifies Reinhardtius hippoglossoides, normalizes flétan du Groenland, and lists flétan noir as a preferred term. It says turbot and turbot du Groenland were not retained for Québec fish-product marketing to avoid consumer-label confusion, and distinguishes European turbot.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA Fish List lookup for Reinhardtius hippoglossoides
sources.locator: TSN 172930 and the listed English/French common names
sources.supports: Maps Reinhardtius hippoglossoides to Greenland halibut / flétan du Groenland and lists flétan noir among the species names. The lookup also lists trade names containing turbot; the OQLF consumer-product boundary is used to keep those terms out of aliases.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Greenland halibut species profile
sources.locator: Latin name and species description; French profile titled Flétan noir - flétan du Groenland
sources.supports: Identifies Reinhardtius hippoglossoides and distinguishes Greenland halibut from Atlantic halibut. The paired French DFO profile uses flétan noir - flétan du Groenland. Biological size and weight descriptions are not edible yields or recipe measures.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, 2026 Gulf of St. Lawrence Groundfish Integrated Fisheries Management Plan
sources.locator: Species list and Annex L general overview
sources.supports: Lists Atlantic halibut and Greenland halibut as separate species and identifies Greenland halibut as Reinhardtius hippoglossoides. Records that a fresh Greenland-halibut market developed in the mid-1970s; fishery landings and stock data are not retail portions or ingredient measures.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File food 3013: raw Greenland halibut
sources.locator: Food name, available serving sizes, and refuse
sources.supports: For the raw CNF food record “Fish, halibut, Greenland (turbot), raw” / “Poisson, flétan, Groenland (flétan noir), cru”, lists 1/2 fillet = 204.0 g, one Food Guide serving = 90.0 g, and 64% total refuse. These are source-specific observations; the edible/as-purchased basis must not be generalized to other products or cuts.

sources.title: Québec Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, Poissons de fond et pélagiques du Québec
sources.locator: Greenland-halibut product descriptions, average size/weight, and general information
sources.supports: Names Reinhardtius hippoglossoides / Greenland halibut and flétan du Groenland, also uses flétan noir, describes several fresh, frozen, whole, head/carcass, “dentelle”, and smoked product states, and calls the species a good substitute for several fish. Its 50–55 cm and 1–1.5 kg whole-fish profile and product sizes are not recipe portions; the broad substitute note supplies no recipe role, method, or replacement quantity.

substitutionFindings.context: MAPAQ describes Greenland halibut as a good substitute for Atlantic halibut, sole, haddock, cod, and plaice, without naming a dish, ingredient role, preparation state, or replacement quantity.
substitutionFindings.basis: Source-specific qualitative culinary note from the MAPAQ 2009 product brochure.
