decisions.reason: Add Greenland halibut / flétan du Groenland (Reinhardtius hippoglossoides) as a species-scoped PROTEIN identity with flétan noir as its sole French alias. Use OQLF and CFIA naming while excluding turbot expressions from Québec consumer-product aliases. Keep Atlantic and Pacific halibut separate. Preserve the two CNF portions only as source-specific observations, with no active measure, form, density, mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution rule; the broad MAPAQ substitute note remains blocked pending recipe and quantity scope.

sources.title: The Wholesome Dish, The Best Classic Shepherd's Pie
sources.locator: Recipe introduction and meat-filling ingredient list
sources.supports: The source line reads 1 lb. 90% lean ground beef -or ground lamb, and the author says the recipe is written for either ground beef or ground lamb. This supports the exact wording and this dish-specific choice only; it is not a product label, composition analysis, portion conversion, or general substitution relation.

sources.title: OQLF, bœuf haché
sources.locator: Preferred term, definition, and English translation
sources.supports: Directly pairs bœuf haché with ground beef and defines the specific ground product.

sources.title: OQLF, viande de bœuf
sources.locator: Definition and note
sources.supports: Defines viande de bœuf as a general butchery term, distinguishing generic beef from the specific ground-beef identity.

decisions.reason: Removed the generic French alias bœuf because the source distinguishes general beef from the specific ground-beef term bœuf haché. Existing recipe references explicitly say ground beef; no numeric data was added.

Preserve the exact source qualifier 90% lean in Shepherd's Pie recipe 078#3 while retaining the existing 1 lb amount, ground-beef identity, and recipe-local ground-lamb note. The source does not establish a catalog composition field, form, portion mapping, or general substitution; no such data is added.

Record the exact ground-lamb option in The Wholesome Dish’s Shepherd’s Pie formula as a recipe-scoped finding. Keep its one-pound amount and beef-only 90% lean qualifier tied to that source line; do not generalize the option or activate runtime substitution.

quantity.unitConvention: The Wholesome Dish’s one-pound amount for the shared ground-meat slot in this named six-serving formula; no conversion to other recipes is implied.

substitutionFindings.context: The Wholesome Dish’s six-serving The Best Classic Shepherd’s Pie formula. The ground-meat choice is browned with seasonings, simmered with broth and vegetables, topped with mashed potato, and baked.
substitutionFindings.basis: The source explicitly lists 1 lb 90% lean ground beef or ground lamb in the same recipe line. The one-pound amount belongs to this formula; the 90% lean qualifier applies only to the beef wording.
adjustments: The source gives the same formula method for either option and reports no lamb-specific seasoning, liquid, fat, or timing adjustment.
The 6–8 minute browning step is source-specific to this formula and is not a general cooking-time claim.
expectedEffects: The author describes the traditional Shepherd’s Pie version as using lamb and says lamb is their special-occasion choice; no comparative sensory, texture, yield, or cooking result is reported.
limitations: Restrict this finding to the named formula and RecipeBook recipe 078#3. Do not transfer it to chili 034#4, meatloaf 074#1, other recipes, other ground-meat identities, or an inverse lamb-to-beef direction.
The active replacement reference is generic lamb and does not preserve the source’s ground qualifier. Do not create a ground-lamb alias/form or infer lamb’s fat percentage from 90% lean.
This recipe option is not a controlled comparison, mass conversion, product equivalence, or general ground-meat ratio.
Do not infer nutritional, allergen, dietary-safety, or product equivalence.
The resolver cannot enforce a named-recipe limit for a contextual rule; do not add an active rule or recipe-line substitution link.

Record USDA SR28 and Health Canada CNF 2015 ground-cinnamon portions separately and exactly as published. Keep their reported units and release context; no active density, unit mapping, or recipe conversion is supported.

The four source-specific portions do not establish current CNF 2026 values or a generic fill, leveling, or spoon-volume convention. Keep measurement research blocked and active density and unit mappings empty. Do not extend these values to bare cinnamon recipe lines or other cinnamon forms.

sources.title: Visit Trinidad, Street Food Favourites: How to Make Trini Doubles
sources.locator: Ingredient names in the doubles recipe.
sources.supports: Directly pairs chadon beni with culantro and geera with cumin powder; one local recipe, not a universal formula.

decisions.reason: Accept exact phrase geera powder for ground cumin from the source pair Geera/Cumin Powder. Do not add bare geera, cumin seeds, or a whole-spice alias.

sources.title: MTL Meats, Grouper
sources.locator: Current Greater Montréal delivery listing: Grouper — 1.8 kg, wild-caught and frozen, with delivery across Greater Montréal.
sources.supports: Supports a current Montréal-facing grouper product and the broad English market name. The listing supplies no scientific name or French label; the approximately 1.8 kg box is product-specific, not a kitchen measure.

sources.title: Health Canada, Updating the Existing Risk Management Strategy for Mercury in Retail Fish
sources.locator: Section 3.4.3, Grouper: the report says CFIA Fish List records several Serranidae taxa, including Epinephelus adscensiosis, E. guttatus, and E. itajara, that may be presented as grouper.
sources.supports: Documents a federal Health Canada report summary of the CFIA Fish List showing grouper wording across multiple Serranidae taxa. This historical naming evidence does not establish culinary equivalence, a current product, or a safety claim.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List, grouper query results
sources.locator: Query results pair grouper common-name wording with multiple taxa, including Cephalopholis, Epinephelus, and Mycteroperca.
sources.supports: Shows that Canadian fish-labelling use of grouper spans multiple fish taxa. It supports a broad name group, not a single species, culinary equivalence, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, GDT: mérou
sources.locator: Edible-fish and ichthyology entry; preferred term and broad definition.
sources.supports: The OQLF prefers mérou and defines it broadly for Serranidae, particularly Epinephelus and Mycteroperca. It does not define the term as one species or establish a culinary-equivalence rule.

sources.title: Poissonnerie La Mer, arrival list dated 2026-04-28
sources.locator: Filets row: FILET DE MEROU NOIR / BLACK GROUPER FILLET, origin Florida, sold by KG.
sources.supports: Documents a bilingual supplier product phrase for a black grouper fillet. It provides no scientific name and does not support adding the species-flavoured phrase as an alias to the generic group or using KG as a household measure.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List, Canadian fish common names
sources.locator: Search results for tilapia entries and associated scientific names.
sources.supports: The official fish list shows multiple Oreochromis species under the broad market name tilapia, including distinct Mozambique and Nile tilapia entries. It supports keeping generic tilapia separate from this species row; it is a labeling source, not recipe-equivalence guidance.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only grouper / mérou as a visibly qualified, species-neutral market-name group. CFIA applies grouper wording across multiple fish taxa and OQLF uses mérou broadly for the family; current Montréal listings do not identify one taxon. Keep Red Grouper, Black Grouper, and other species-specific wording out of this group. Add no aliases, taxon, forms, density, unit mappings, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

Canadian standards for named varieties, cream cheese/spread, cottage/creamed cottage, and cheddar aging; composition values in this proposal are regulatory limits only.

sources.supports: OQLF, emmental (https://vitrinelinguistique.oqlf.gouv.qc.ca/fiche-gdt/fiche/45766/emmental). French spelling variant and Swiss cow-milk cooked-pressed cheese description.

sources.supports: European Commission, French Gruyère PGI specification (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52010XC1104%2802%29). Distinct geographic product with raw cow milk, cooked-pressed body, holes, salt range, and 120-day minimum maturation.

decisions.reason: Retain the existing unqualified Gruyère identity and correct its English display accent. Do not infer the French PGI from the recipe spelling or merge it with Emmental or Swiss cheese.

sources.title: European Commission, Amatriciana Tradizionale TSG specification application
sources.locator: Amatrice pork-jowl ingredient definition
sources.supports: Identifies Amatriciano-type guanciale as pork jowl matured for the named regional dish; not a universal guanciale specification.

sources.title: Mayrand, Bajoue de porc salé à sec guanciale
sources.locator: Québec retailer product title and description
sources.supports: Current Québec product listing names guanciale and describes it in French as dry-salted pork jowl. Supports local product wording, not an OQLF-preferred synonym or curing standard.

decisions.reason: Add guanciale as a distinct matured pork-jowl identity. Use the source-attested product name in both language fields; no descriptor alias is activated pending independent Québec terminology review. Keep it separate from pancetta and fresh pork cheek. No numeric or substitution data is inferred.

sources.locator: Named French entries for gomme d’acacia, gomme de caroube, carraghénine, gomme gellane, gomme de guar, méthylcellulose, pectine and alginate de sodium.

sources.title: MAPA Portaria MAPA nº 70/1982
sources.locator: sections 3.7–3.13 and 4.1–4.2
sources.supports: Primary product standard. Defines em grão, em bastão, and em pó as distinct presentation groups; distinguishes fruit processing from seed/kernel products. It is a Brazilian product standard, not a recipe-use standard or Canadian product rule.

Do not generalize its protected-product terminology or process as the definition of every Brazilian guarana product.

sources.title: Brazil Ministry of Health Alimentos regionais brasileiros, 2nd ed.
sources.locator: 2015, Guaraná entry, p. 53, culinary-use section
sources.supports: Identifies the Amazonian food and says processing the seed yields powder, sticks, extracts, and syrups. Regional-food overview; does not make these products compositionally interchangeable.

sources.title: Embrapa Amazônia Ocidental Cultura do guaranazeiro no Amazonas, 4th ed.

sources.supports: Explains stick processing, em rama roasted seeds, and ground powder uses in drinks and foods. Regional production guide; its descriptions are not universal recipe conversions or current legal requirements.

sources.title: Health Canada Caffeine in Foods

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only gukganjang / gukganjang as a named Korean soy-sauce cooking type used for soups, stews, and namul. decisions.reason: Accept identity-only gundruk as a named generic Himalayan fermented leafy-vegetable food, distinct from sinki, salt-and-vinegar pickled radish, pickled mustard greens, fermented bamboo shoots, and other nearby preserves. Keep the borrowed French display provisional and add no broad fermented-leaf aliases. Preserve regional variation and do not encode a universal plant-part rule. Study and survey processing conditions, times, acidity, and sample observations remain source-specific. Add no aliases, forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.supports: Documents one commercial bagel formula using HI-MAIZE 260 in place of part of hard-wheat flour, with added gluten, more water, and flavour modulation. Table 8 reports 25.4 g resistant starch per 119.8 g RS bagel versus 6.83 g per 124.2 g control bagel. These are source- and formula-specific results, not a reusable substitution ratio or measure.

replacements.roleInCompound: source-specific starch component replacing part of the wheat-flour fraction in the commercial study bagel

substitutionFindings.context: Commercially produced resistant-starch bagel formulation in a University of Guelph study; HI-MAIZE 260 replaced a portion of hard-wheat flour.
substitutionFindings.basis: The RS bagel batch used 168 kg HI-MAIZE 260 and 112 kg hard-wheat flour, versus 280 kg hard-wheat flour in the control. The RS formula used 224 kg water versus 136.1 kg in the control and added 28 kg gluten; a flavour modulator was used to address slight bitterness. Table 8 reported 25.4 g resistant starch per 119.8 g RS bagel and 6.83 g per 124.2 g control bagel.
adjustments: The study formula increased water and added gluten; its flavour-modulator work is specific to that commercial bagel formulation.
expectedEffects: The study measured greater resistant starch content per bagel in the RS treatment than in the control; the measured values belong to those tested products and methods.
limitations: This is one commercial, source-specific bagel formula, not a general 60% replacement recommendation.
Do not transfer the formula, water adjustment, gluten amount, or flavour treatment to other recipes or other starches.
No runtime substitution rule, generic ratio, density, or unit mapping is supported.

decisions.reason: Add hominy corn / maïs lessivé as an identity-only named processed-corn product, with lyed corn as its only English alias. OQLF supplies the direct English/French pair and describes mature dry yellow or white maize in preservative liquid; CFIA confirms the French name under Maïs hominy; TERMIUM distinguishes lye-treated and pearled kernels and identifies grits as a ground product. The Haudenosaunee educator directly equates lyed corn with hominy, and Six Nations sources document current regional product use. Use VEGETABLE_AND_AROMATIC with the existing corn-kernel identity. Add no other aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions. Keep unqualified hominy, lye hominy, pearled hominy, hominy grits, corn grits, cornmeal, masa harina, and pozole corn unmerged pending separate product/name review. No bundled recipe uses this wording.

decisions.reason: Add hominy grits / gruau de maïs as an identity-only GRAIN_AND_CEREAL product. Statistics Canada directly maps the human-food classification Hominy grits to Gruau de maïs. OQLF supplies the preferred French term but its entry is brewing-scoped, so it is corroboration rather than sole food-use evidence; Ricardo and La Moisson show Québec culinary use of the wording for generic corn grits, not specifically hominy. Codex separates hominy grits from standard degermed corn grits and alkaline-treated maize products. Keep the ground product separate from whole hominy corn / maïs lessivé, cornmeal / semoule de maïs, and generic grits. Do not activate semoule de maïs de type grits or gruau hominy as aliases. Add no aliases, forms, default density, unit mappings, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions. No bundled recipe wording or exact normalized-key collision was found. Independent Québec French review remains open.

Retain hominy grits / gruau de maïs as the current bilingual identity. Federal human-food coding directly pairs the terms; OQLF is brewing-scoped and Québec culinary use overlaps generic coarse corn grits, so keep the display provisional and aliases empty. Keep it distinct from generic grits, cornmeal, polenta, and whole hominy corn. Do not reuse recipe-specific measures or alternatives.

Record Pearl Milling Company Quick Grits 1/4 cup (37 g) as one named-product dry serving portion on the existing hominy-grits row. Keep the observation specific to this product and manufacturer label; do not derive a generic grits measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, form, recipe link, yield, or substitution. No bundled recipe demand was found. Preserve the current bilingual identity and neighboring corn-grits, cornmeal, and whole-hominy identities.

Retain the manufacturer's explicitly directional Quick Grits-to-regular/enriched hominy grits note as a blocked, source-local finding only. The current recipe's liquid conflict and the lack of a current product/SKU crosswalk prevent an executable adjustment or a mapped ingredient relation. No fromIngredientRefId or replacements are recorded; no active catalog mapping or substitution rule is added.

decisions.reason: Accepted as a source-backed identity-only row with the exact bilingual display pair. Directly pairs hulled barley with orge mondé and defines removal of the outer hull. This does not establish equivalence for every product sold as pot barley. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.

Add only hulless barley and naked barley as English aliases and orge à grains nus as a technical French search alias on ingredient-ref-hulled-barley. The Canadian Grain Commission identifies the hulless/naked type and its French term; the federal bilingual food specification describes hulled, whole, or hull-less barley as whole grain with only the inedible outer husk removed, matching the existing OQLF-backed hulled-barley identity. This search route denotes the edible whole-kernel product and does not claim a mechanical dehulling process. Keep the Québec display orge mondé. Do not add orge nue, which can route an ambiguous search toward the separate orge nue germée maltée product, or orge entière, which overlaps the existing whole-barley-flour phrase. Add no row, form, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution; leave measurement and substitution states unchanged.

Add only the English alias barley groats to the existing hulled-barley / orge mondé identity. A Canadian mill and retail listing apply the exact phrase to whole hulled barley; the CBSA uses groats for fragmented cereal products within tariff heading 11.03, so keep this alias product-matched and do not add generic groats, a French alias, or a new row. Preserve barley grits / gruau d’orge and unresolved barley meal as separate items. No recipe demand, measurement, form, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution is added.

decisions.reason: Add one FRUIT identity for jackfruit, using OQLF jaque and the scoped spelling aliases jacque / jakfruit. Do not alias the tree name or short jack, add maturity forms, or assign ripe/unripe state to unqualified jackfruit. No measurements, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links.

Do not activate green, young/tender, unripe, or processed-product forms until ingredient-stage wording and product boundaries can be represented without collapsing source-distinct stages. Keep source wording and candidate form research in the proposal.

Keep the verified generic jackfruit / jaque identity and its current spelling aliases. No current bundled recipe requests jackfruit maturity, seeds, canned/frozen fruit, or jackfruit flour. Do not add maturity aliases/forms or processed-product identities without exact demand and source-qualified product details. Stage names remain descriptive/source-specific, and fruit-bulb flour and seed flour remain separate candidate product scopes. No density, unit mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported by this review.

sources.title: Trejo Rodríguez et al., Physicochemical Properties, Antioxidant Capacity, Prebiotic Activity and Anticancer Potential in Human Cells of Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) Seed Flour

sources.supports: Reports individual seed weights of 6–8 g for seed material from 15 jackfruits sampled in Huasteca Potosina, Mexico. The methods describe weighing before cleaning and freezing. The sample range is not a culinary portion, cooked weight, or general count conversion; the exact seed-covering basis is unstated.

sources.title: Khan, Effects of seed mass on seedling success in Artocarpus heterophyllus L., a tropical tree species of north-east India

The 4–14 g viable-seed subset is not substituted for the full-sample range. This ecological sample does not establish culinary preparation, edible yield, or a general count conversion.

sources.title: Cook with Kushi, Jackfruit Seed Curry / Bikkand Gashi

It gives no alternative amount or quantity basis; the recipe-specific seed count cannot be transferred to replacements.

valueIntervals.unitConvention: Source-reported gram mass; no kitchen volume convention applies.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Artocarpus heterophyllus seeds from 15 fruits sampled in Huasteca Potosina, Mexico.
measurementObservations.foodState: Study seed material weighed before the subsequent cleaning and freezing steps; exact seed-covering basis is not stated.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: The authors report weighing each seed; balance, precision, and detailed weighing protocol are not stated.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One seed within this 15-fruit study sample only. The sample range is not a source-neutral kitchen value, portion, cooked mass, or edible-yield measure.

valueIntervals.unitConvention: Source-reported gram mass; no kitchen volume convention applies.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Artocarpus heterophyllus seeds extracted from ripe fruits sampled in North Lakhimpur forest range, Assam, India.
measurementObservations.foodState: Fresh, unprepared seeds weighed individually in an ecological seed-mass study.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: About 6,000 seeds were extracted from a random sample of ripe fruits and weighed individually; balance, precision, and detailed weighing protocol are not stated.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One seed within the full ecological sample range only. Do not substitute the study’s 4–14 g viable-seed subset. This is not a culinary portion, cooked mass, or source-neutral conversion.

substitutionFindings.context: The six-serving Konkani jackfruit-seed curry (Bikkand Gashi) in the cited recipe, whose source-specific formula uses 20–30 peeled jackfruit seeds before adding coconut-spice gravy.
substitutionFindings.basis: The recipe explicitly suggests potato, yam, or eggplant and says to cook an alternative until tender. It gives no replacement amount or count, mass, or volume basis, so the seed quantity cannot be transferred to any alternative.
adjustments: The source distinguishes the seed pressure-cooking time from cooking alternatives until tender, but gives no quantified method or liquid adjustment for a replacement.
limitations: The 20–30 seeds are a quantity for the named recipe only; do not infer an equal count, mass, volume, or serving-scaled replacement amount.
Do not generalize the suggestion beyond this curry context or create an active substitution rule without a supported replacement quantity and basis.

decisions.reason: Add generic jackfruit seeds as an identity-level edible-part ingredient for Artocarpus heterophyllus. Keep it separate from the whole-fruit identity, brined young-fruit form, and held seed-flour/starch candidates; add no cooked-state form.
The crop seed-count and source-recipe quantities do not establish a reusable measure, density, conversion, or yield.
Present in the legacy RecipeKeeper catalog but absent from the canonical bundled seed; reconcile identity and aliases before acceptance.

OQLF supports the generic base terms, while Canadian French references use farine de blé tendre for a broader flour family and distinguish cake and pastry flour as more specific products. measurementObservations.foodDescription: Greenmax-Adlay Powder, Natural Blue retailer listing P016/IND082G03; ingredient listed as Adlay; named-product observation only.

sourceQuantity.unitConvention: Retailer prints “2 spoon”; spoon size and capacity are not stated. Do not normalize to teaspoon, tablespoon, or another unit.

substitutionFindings.context: Watanabe et al.'s cookie trials only: a 100 g flour control made with Nisshin Flower wheat flour (`薄力小麦粉`, Japanese weak wheat flour); a 100 g flour blend of 50 g wheat flour plus 50 g Job's-tears flour; a 100 g all-Job's-tears-flour formula; and a separate all-Job's-tears formula with additional butter replacing part of the added water.
substitutionFindings.basis: The 50% Job's-tears-flour cookie received preference ratings similar to the wheat-flour control. The unmodified 100% Job's-tears-flour cookie was significantly smaller in volume, harder, and less preferred. In a second formula, the authors used 100 g Job's-tears flour, 46.4 g butter, and 11.5 g added water (compared with 30 g butter and 23 g added water in the unmodified 100% formula); its overall acceptance was similar to the control, with improved hardness preference. These are distinct tested formulas, not one scalable replacement rule.
expectedEffects: Within the study's 50% cookie formula, preference ratings were similar to the wheat-flour control.
Within the study's unmodified 100% formula, cookies were smaller, harder, and less preferred.
Within the study's butter-adjusted 100% formula, acceptance improved compared with the unmodified 100% formula.
limitations: The study uses one refined Aki Shizuku flour sample from Oyama, Tochigi, milled through a 100 μm screen; the results do not establish behavior for all Job's-tears flours or milling processes.
The comparator is Nisshin Flower `薄力小麦粉`, linked at the Japanese weak-wheat class level. Do not describe the result as guidance for generic cake flour, all-purpose flour, or every wheat-flour class.
The cookie ingredient quantities and water/butter adjustment belong only to the tested formulas. Do not turn 50% or 100% into a reusable recipe recommendation or runtime rule.
Sensory results came from 50 female university students with a mean age of 20; they are not a broad consumer-preference study.
No bundled recipe supplies demand, a matching cookie role, or a line to link to these trial formulas.

substitutionFindings.context: Watanabe et al.'s single crepe formula only: 25.0 g of either Nisshin Flower wheat flour (`薄力小麦粉`, Japanese weak wheat flour) or refined Job's-tears flour, with 25.0 g egg, 83.7 g milk, 7.5 g sugar, and 3.7 g butter. Batters were rested for 0, 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes and cooked on a 160°C hot plate for 3 minutes per side.
substitutionFindings.basis: The same 25.0 g flour amount was used for either flour in this fixed crepe formula. Across the tested batter-rest times, Job's-tears crepes had significantly lower fracture stress than wheat-flour crepes and were less preferred. A 30-minute Job's-tears batter rest was reported as easier to prepare; this describes the study batter, not a general resting instruction.
expectedEffects: The tested Job's-tears crepes were easier to fracture than the wheat-flour crepes.
The tested Job's-tears crepes had lower preference ratings than the wheat-flour control.
limitations: This is one fixed crepe formula using 25.0 g of one refined Aki Shizuku flour sample from Oyama, Tochigi, milled through a 100 μm screen.
The comparator is Nisshin Flower `薄力小麦粉`, linked at the Japanese weak-wheat class level; do not generalize to generic cake flour or other wheat-flour classes.
The 25.0 g amount and 30-minute batter observation are not a reusable measure or recipe substitution instruction.
Sensory results came from 50 female university students with a mean age of 20.
No bundled recipe supplies demand, a matching crepe role, or a line to link to the study formula.

substitutionFindings.context: A study-specific 20% replacement of total flour mass with bran from one Khorasan wheat sample in an experimental common-wheat type 00 bread formula.
substitutionFindings.basis: The 2025 study identifies one Khorasan sample as Triticum turgidum subsp. turanicum, prepares and analyzes its bran, and uses that bran at 20% of total flour content in common-wheat bread. Water is optimized separately for each formula. These conditions describe the one study sample and its experimental breadmaking process only.
limitations: One study sample does not establish that the results represent all Khorasan bran or milling grades.

Keep Khorasan grain, flour, flakes, semolina, puffed wheat, and generic wheat bran distinct. Keep the single-sample bread trial and laboratory values source-scoped. decisions.reason: Accept kudzu starch as a source-named extracted-starch identity. The OQLF kouzou entry does not identify a Latin species, so no species assertion or Japanese-arrowroot alias is made; keep the product scope source-neutral only at the commercial class level pending terminology review.

Add only the exact English alias “kudzu flour” to the existing extracted kudzu-starch reference. Japan MEXT explicitly classifies kudzu flour as kudzu starch; MAFF describes the named kudzu powder/flour as extracted and refined root starch. Keep “kuzu flour”, “Japanese arrowroot powder”, and French flour/starch wording out of aliases; retain the unresolved botanical scope.

Whole-root kudzu root powder is a distinct milled-root material, but its Québec product name and exact recipe demand remain unresolved; do not map it to extracted kudzu starch. No reusable household measure, density, yield, or substitution is established.

Record a bounded taxonomic crosswalk for MEXT food item 02029: its Pueraria lobata name is a homotypic synonym of Kew’s accepted Pueraria montana var. lobata. This resolves the name mapping for that specific table item only. Keep the active commercial kudzu-starch identity at needs_clarification because OQLF and MAFF do not identify a species for the broad class and Kew recognizes other varieties under P. montana. Do not add scientific names as picker aliases or alter active catalog data.

sources.supports: Defines lasagne as a long, flat pasta with straight or wavy edges, usually about 5–7 cm wide; gives French preferred singular lasagne, plural lasagnes, and English terms lasagna and lasagne. This distinguishes the pasta shape from an assembled dish.

sources.title: Barilla Canada, Oven-Ready Lasagne.
sources.locator: Product description, package information, ingredients, and directions.
sources.supports: Describes its oven-ready product as thin flat pasta sheets, rolled flat and intended to be layered and baked without boiling; names semolina. Its cooking directions, composition, sheet count, package details, and nutrition portions are specific to this product.

sources.title: Barilla Canada, Lasagne prête à cuire.
sources.locator: French product title and description, product ingredients, and instructions.
sources.supports: Uses Québec-facing wording feuilles de pâtes lasagne for flat sheets intended to be layered and baked without precooking. This is one product and does not establish a class-wide preparation state or measure.

sources.title: Catelli Canada, Classiques Lasagne.
sources.locator: Québec French product title, product description, ingredients, and nutrition portion.
sources.supports: Calls the product Classiques Lasagne, describes feuilles de lasagne for oven-baked dishes, and lists durum semolina. Its ingredient statement and package portion apply to this product only.

substitutionFindings.context: Global and contextual substitutions for the lasagne pasta shape.
substitutionFindings.basis: The terminology and product sources establish a pasta shape and product-specific preparation details but no replacement ingredient, quantity, role, or method. The bundled recipe corpus has no matching lasagne ingredient demand.
limitations: Do not infer interchangeability with other pasta shapes, fresh pasta, gluten-free pasta, or the assembled lasagna dish.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only lasagna sheets / lasagne as a GRAIN_AND_CEREAL reference for the broad, flat pasta shape, including straight or ruffled edges. Keep it separate from generic pasta, composition-qualified pasta, other shapes, and the assembled lasagna dish. Use only the supported shape terms; add no forms, recipe links, measures, density, unit mappings, conversions, yields, or active substitutions.

Product-specific no-boil directions and package portions do not establish a general preparation state, household measure, sheet count, density, cooking yield, or recipe substitution. Keep those behaviors unavailable.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Le lavash
sources.locator: French indexed official description.
sources.supports: The French record describes lavash as a traditional thin bread. Direct page opening returned a verification challenge; this entry uses the official indexed wording only and does not generalize all commercial variants.

sources.title: Super C, Lavash pain mince
sources.locator: Search-indexed Québec product listing, product 797153446631.
sources.supports: The indexed Québec retailer listing uses Lavash pain mince; direct page returned HTTP 403, so this supports local product wording only.

sources.title: Canadian Intellectual Property Office, 2017 Trade-marks Journal, Vol. 64, No. 3277
sources.locator: Page 652, application 1,804,776, French goods/services wording.
sources.supports: Uses pain pita and pain lavash separately and also names pain plat; Canadian attestation only, not a terminology recommendation or product standard.

sources.title: Ozery Bakery, French Canadian product catalog
sources.locator: Separate Mini-Pitas and Craquelins lavash product names.
sources.supports: The French Canadian manufacturer catalog lists pita products and craquelins lavash separately; supports keeping lavash crackers distinct from lavash bread.

decisions.reason: Add lavash bread / pain lavash as a distinct identity-only bread product. Keep lavash crackers and generic flatbread / pain plat separate; no form, measure, conversion, yield, substitution, or recipe link is established.

sources.title: OQLF, saindoux de panne (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and English term.
sources.supports: Pairs saindoux de panne with leaf lard and identifies it as a specific internal-fat product, distinct from general lard.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Food Compositional Standards, Volume 8 — Fats and Oils
sources.supports: Defines lard, leaf lard, and suet by animal source or source part, and distinguishes semi-solid shortening from water-in-fat margarine. No regulatory numeric criteria are imported.

sources.title: ACIA, Normes canadiennes de composition des aliments, Volume 8 — Graisses et huiles
sources.supports: French counterpart for the named Canadian product standards and fat/spread distinctions cited in the English standard. No numeric criteria are copied into the catalog.

decisions.reason: Accept leaf lard / saindoux de panne as a distinct identity-only product made from specified internal abdominal fat. Keep separate from general lard; add no forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: OQLF, laitue frisée
sources.locator: Preferred French and English terms; loose-leaf/cutting distinction
sources.supports: Pairs laitue frisée and laitue à couper with leaf lettuce, cutting lettuce, loose-leaf lettuce, and curled lettuce; distinguishes leaf lettuce without a head from headed lettuce.

decisions.reason: Accepted leaf lettuce / laitue frisée with cutting and loose-leaf terms. Keep distinct from generic lettuce and headed types.

sources.title: Quezon City Government, La Loma Lechon Area
sources.locator: Description of Ping Ping's Lechon and its trademark liver-based lechon sauce.
sources.supports: The city government's account identifies lechon sauce as a named accompaniment associated with the local lechon trade and documents one liver-based restaurant version. It does not establish that every lechon sauce uses liver.

sources.title: Philippine Department of Health, East Avenue Medical Center, 2026 procurement list
sources.locator: Item 150, Lechon Sauce, 1 kg pouch.
sources.supports: The hospital procurement list treats lechon sauce as a food-product category and specifies a retail-style pouch size. The size is not a kitchen measure, and the listing does not define composition.

sources.title: Mama Sita's, product folio: Sarsa ng Lechon All Purpose Sauce
sources.locator: Sarsa ng Lechon product entry, description, and suggested uses.
sources.supports: The manufacturer presents regular and hot Sarsa ng Lechon all-purpose sauces as a vinegar, cane-sugar, and spice blend for lechon and other meats. This commercial formula is not generalized to homemade or other brand versions.

sources.title: Canadian Intellectual Property Office, Journal des marques de commerce, Vol. 63 No. 3223
sources.locator: Mama Sita's goods list includes 'sauce pour lechon'; the accompanying notice says use in Canada since 2010.
sources.supports: Provides a Canadian French product-category wording for lechon sauce and evidence of Canadian commercial use. The trademark listing is not treated as a recipe or regulatory definition.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Sauce tout usage originale Mang Tomas
sources.locator: French product title, Filipino sauce description, and product-specific ingredient statement.
sources.supports: Documents Québec retail availability of Mang Tomas all-purpose sauce and one product's breadcrumb, cane-sugar, vinegar, and spice formulation. This brand-specific label is not generalized to every lechon sauce.

sources.title: Skip Canada, Kalapaw menu, Dollard-des-Ormeaux
sources.locator: Lechon Kawali listing in the bilingual menu: French 'sauce léchon maison' and English 'homemade lechon sauce'.
sources.supports: A Québec Filipino restaurant uses 'sauce léchon' for a house-made accompaniment, supporting the descriptive French display without claiming an OQLF-preferred term.

decisions.reason: Add lechon sauce / sauce léchon as a Filipino sauce identity, with sarsa ng lechon and the Canadian French wording sauce pour lechon as search aliases. Québec menu and Canadian French commercial sources support the displays. The sources document liver-based, breadcrumb-based, and vinegar/sugar/spice commercial variants, so do not impose one recipe or require liver. Keep the category separate from toyomansi, banana ketchup, and spiced vinegar; do not map it to a brand. No recipe links, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are established.

The 56% refuse figure remains a qualifier; do not treat 89 g as gross untrimmed leek mass or a general conversion.

sources.locator: Definition, English equivalent, and Latin identification.
sources.supports: Maps French citron to English lemon and Citrus limon; it does not support English citron as an alias for lemon.

sources.title: The Kitchn, Korean Soy-Marinated Jammy Eggs
sources.locator: Current ingredient card and step 5; recipe file 066#13 is timestamped 2026-04-04.
sources.supports: The current card says 1/2 medium lemon and instructs thinly slicing it over the eggs. It does not say whether peel is removed, give slice count or mass, or say whether the lemon is eaten or removed; its update postdates the bundled recipe file.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2026
sources.versionOrDate: 2026 distribution; Food Code 1587 component rows retain historical update dates
sources.locator: Food Code 1587, Lemon, raw, without peel / Citron, cru, sans pelure; food_name.csv and joined measure-name, measure-type, and measure-weight-conversion rows. The official online portion view is https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/serving-portion?id=1587.
sources.supports: The joined CNF portion rows report 58 g for one medium 5.4 cm fruit, 84 g for one large 6 cm fruit, and 7 g for one wedge or slice of a medium fruit; the record is raw lemon without peel with 47% total refuse. Historical row update dates predate the 2026 file distribution. These are not a peel-included thin-sliced half-fruit match.

sources.title: USDA ARS, SR28 Food Group 09, NDB 09150
sources.versionOrDate: Standard Reference Release 28 (2015), Food Group 09, pp. 487–488
sources.locator: Lemons, raw, without peel; common measures are explicitly reported as amounts in the edible portion.
sources.supports: Reports 58 g for one 2-1/8-inch fruit, 84 g for one 2-3/8-inch fruit, 7 g for one medium-fruit wedge or slice, and 47% refuse. The food is raw and without peel; the source does not match the recipe’s unspecific peel status or thin-sliced half-medium amount.

decisions.reason: Accept the bounded bilingual ingredient identity and aliases supported by the cited sources. Do not infer a recipe link, form, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Preserve bundled recipe 066#13 exactly as 1/2 lemon, thinly sliced (quantity 0.5, unit item, ingredient-ref-lemon). The current publisher version specifies a medium lemon but postdates the saved recipe and does not state peel status or whether slices are eaten or removed. CNF 2026 and USDA SR28 portions are for raw lemon without peel and do not establish a matching thin-sliced half-fruit mass. Keep measurement blocked pending evidence that matches the bundled line; do not derive mass, slice count, or purchase weight, and do not change the recipe or activate a mapping.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Melissa officinalis
sources.locator: Accepted name, Uses, and Common Names sections.
sources.supports: Accepts Melissa officinalis and records food use; the common-names section includes lemon balm. This is the taxonomic and general food-use anchor, not the Québec display-name source.

sources.title: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, Lemon Balm
sources.locator: Latin Name; Uses and Markets; Harvest; Post harvest; Storage Conditions.
sources.supports: Identifies Melissa officinalis as a culinary herb used for flavouring, teas, and candies, and describes fresh-leaf harvesting and dried-leaf production. The older agricultural profile supports culinary identity, not kitchen measures or current Québec retail availability.

sources.title: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, Mélisse officinale
sources.locator: Autres noms usuels; Nom latin; Utilisations et marchés; Récolte.
sources.supports: Identifies Melissa officinalis, lists mélisse and mélisse-citronnelle as common names, and describes culinary uses including flavouring, tea, and candy. It also documents fresh-leaf harvest and dried-leaf production. The compound name is evidence only and is not adopted as a picker alias.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: mélisse (entry attributed to AFNOR)
sources.versionOrDate: Entry attributed to Association française de normalisation, 1975.
sources.locator: Botanical domain; French term; English and Latin translations.
sources.supports: Pairs French mélisse with English balm and lemon balm and Latin Melissa officinalis. The GDT record is attributed to AFNOR, not presented as an OQLF-authored preferred-term ruling.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: citronnelle
sources.locator: Botanical and food domains; Latin and English translations.
sources.supports: The OQLF-authored entry maps bare citronnelle to Cymbopogon citratus and English lemongrass. It supports excluding the short French term from the lemon-balm picker identity; it does not prove that all speakers use the word only this way.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: verveine citronnelle
sources.locator: Preferred term; English and Latin translations; note on infusion.
sources.supports: Maps verveine citronnelle to Lippia citriodora and English lemon verbena; the note says its infusion resembles lemon balm. Supports keeping this similar name and separate taxon outside the proposed lemon-balm identity.

sources.title: Croque Paysage, Mélisse — Plant Bio
sources.locator: Product heading and French culinary-use description.
sources.supports: The Québec edible-plant nursery labels its plant Mélisse and names Melissa officinalis / Lemon balm; its description says the leaves and flowers are edible and gives culinary uses. This is Québec naming and food-use evidence for a plant listing, not a fresh-leaf product or current fresh-herb availability.

sources.title: Health Canada, List of non-novel determinations for food and food ingredients
sources.locator: Lemon balm determination: raw leaves for tea use.
sources.supports: The listed determination is limited to raw Melissa officinalis leaves for tea, whole or minimally processed. It is food-history context only, not blanket evidence for all preparations, uses, or doses.

sources.title: LiquidShop / Liquid Solution, Lemon Balm Powder (Mélisse) — Bulk Food Grade
sources.locator: Product title, botanical name, French wording, and food-grade listing.
sources.supports: The Québec supplier identifies a dried Melissa officinalis powder as Lemon Balm Powder / Mélisse and states food-grade use. This is one supplier-specific processed product and naming corroboration, not a fresh-leaf measure or universal powder form.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only HERB reference for the culinary leafy herb Melissa officinalis, displayed as lemon balm / mélisse officinale, with mélisse as its sole French alias. Keep lemongrass and lemon verbena separate. Exclude citronnelle and mélisse-citronnelle because the reviewed French uses conflict and the phrase-first picker matches a word inside a longer alias. No form, measure, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution is supported; the bundled recipe corpus has no matching candidate wording.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, crème au citron (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition, preferred French term, and English equivalents.
sources.supports: Defines a creamy preparation of eggs, sugar, butter, lemon juice, and zest used as a tart or cake filling or as a spread. Gives crème au citron as the preferred French term and lists lemon curd among the English equivalents. Does not establish a generic household measure, composition standard, or substitution.

sources.title: Independent City Market, PC Black Label Lemon Curd, 250 ml
sources.locator: Current product heading, description, package size, ingredient list, and 34 ml labelled serving.
sources.supports: Lists a current Canadian PC Black Label product as Lemon Curd, 250 ml, and describes its use in tart shells, on scones, in cakes, and as a dessert topping. Its sugar, egg yolk, butter, and lemon-juice ingredients are consistent with the GDT identity. The 250 ml package and 34 ml labelled serving are SKU-specific and do not establish a reusable measure, mass, or density.

sources.title: Loblaws, French search results for lemon curd
sources.locator: French product result for PC Collection noire Crème de citron, 250 ml; adjacent lemon spread and pie-filling results.
sources.supports: The French retailer listing presents PC Collection noire Crème de citron as a 250 ml Canadian-prepared item in the lemon-curd search results. It supports crème de citron as an exact Québec retail label for this product class. The same page distinguishes Bonne Maman tartinade de citron and E.D. Smith garniture pour tarte au citron; those distinct products are not aliases. Listing details, stock, and price can vary by location and time.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only lemon curd / crème au citron as a source-defined lemon dessert filling and spread. Keep the Québec retail wording crème de citron as one exact French alias. Leave the OQLF-listed English terms lemon cheese, lemon cheese curd, and lemon butter out of picker aliases because the cheese and butter terms would broaden unrelated base-ingredient searches. No bundled recipe line needs this reference. The Canadian package and serving values are SKU-specific and support no reusable measurement, density, or unit mapping. Add no form, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution; substitution research remains open.

sources.supports: Uses jus de citron and jus de lime labels and fresh-juice wording; branded bottled-product ingredients are product-specific and do not establish a generic bottled-juice alias, conversion, or substitution.

sources.title: ACIA, Normes canadiennes de composition des aliments, volume 10
sources.locator: Sections 10.3.2–10.3.16: jus de pomme, jus de raisin, jus de pamplemousse, jus d’orange, jus d’ananas, and the same-fruit reconstitution rule.
sources.supports: Provides the exact French names for the five named-fruit juice classes and defines reconstituted/from-concentrate juice as water added to concentrate from the same named fruit. It does not establish a kitchen dilution ratio, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, jus de citron concentré (GDT)

sources.supports: Supports the Québec French name for lemon juice concentrate; the Canadian same-fruit rule determines that reconstituted ready-to-use juice remains lemon juice.

sources.supports: Reports 244 g per 1 cup, 30.5 g per 1 fl oz, and 48 g per 1 lemon yields for Lemon juice, raw. Cup capacity, filling method, fruit size, and extraction method are not specified.

sources.title: King Arthur Baking, Ingredient Weight Chart

sources.supports: Publishes a source-specific lemon-juice portion of 14 g per tablespoon; the chart does not identify raw/fresh versus another preparation.

decisions.reason: Removed source-less draft density and unit-mapping values from the active bundled catalog. Restore a value only with source, exact food/form, unit convention, method or basis, and reviewer disposition.

Retain the existing plain lemon/lime juice identity and accept only the reviewed fresh-juice alias coverage. The manufacturer page supports Québec French juice wording; recipe wording supplies the exact fresh preparation. Do not infer a generic bottled-juice identity or product equivalence.

Add only same-fruit ready-to-use from-concentrate/reconstituted aliases to the existing plain juice identity. The Canadian standard defines these as juice made by adding water to concentrate of the same fruit; do not map the water-removed concentrate to this row, and do not add a generic juice-from-concentrate alias. No recipe links or numeric behavior changed.

Preserve the source-specific USDA SR28 raw lemon-juice portions and King Arthur chart tablespoon portion as separate observations. USDA does not specify the cup capacity/filling method or fruit yield method, and King Arthur does not identify the juice preparation. These observations do not support an active density, generic unit mapping, or a universal lemon-to-juice yield; do not generalize the raw USDA item to bottled or reconstituted juice.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: verveine citronnelle
sources.locator: Preferred French term, contextual term, English and Latin translations.
sources.supports: Gives preferred French verveine citronnelle, contextual verveine odorante, English lemon verbena, and Latin Lippia citriodora. This older botanical entry supports naming, not a retail product, kitchen measure, or medical claim.

decisions.reason: Add lemongrass / verveine des Indes as a distinct identity in HERB. Keep the species/product boundary described by its sources; add no forms, default density, unit mappings, conversions, or substitutions.

sources.supports: The audited catalog and archive contained no active lentil-starch owner, form, ledger candidate, legacy owner, focused prior proposal, or matching recipe line; R120 mentions lentil starch only as a comparator.

decisions.reason: Accept the distinct food-ingredient identity lentil starch / amidon de lentille as an identity-only FLOUR_AND_STARCH reference. The Canadian product-finder listing and separate manufacturer product entry support the named ingredient, while Canadian cultivar research distinguishes isolated starch from lentil flour. Keep the French display descriptive and provisional because no reviewed Québec source attests the exact compound or a local package label; keep whole lentils, lentil flour, and starch-rich lentil flour distinct.

The reviewed product thresholds, general pulse composition/process ranges, and cultivar-specific laboratory results do not establish a bulk-powder density, household measure, generic yield, or reusable unit mapping. Leave default density null and unit mappings empty; add no measurement observation unless same-product kitchen-scale evidence becomes available.

No reviewed source establishes a product-specific or tested recipe replacement ratio for lentil starch. Functional thickening/binding descriptions and related starch research do not support a global or contextual substitution; keep substitution findings empty unless a same-product replacement study or tested recipe relationship is found.

decisions.reason: Retain the broad base identity only. Keep class and variety descriptors out of its aliases so the generic row remains distinct from the accepted green, French green, red, and black Beluga rows; keep brown/yellow boundaries and all whole/split/dehulled forms unresolved.

Keep unqualified brown lentils / lentilles brunes and yellow lentils / lentilles jaunes out of active references and aliases. Brown describes seed-coat types including narrow Spanish Brown/Pardina, while at least one Canadian supplier also uses brown lentils for whole red lentils. Yellow describes a cotyledon colour shared across types and also appears in a supplier-defined split/dehulled product. Québec retail titles attest lentilles brunes but do not define a seed class; no stable Québec standalone yellow-lentil class or recipe need was established. Reopen only for an exact scoped recipe/product need. Add no forms or numeric/substitution behaviour.

decisions.reason: Add the distinct human-food product lima bean flour / farine de haricots de Lima in FLOUR_AND_STARCH. The English display is supplier-attested, while the French compound is attested in the supplier catalogue and remains provisional for Québec because no Québec flour label was found. Keep the whole Lima-bean identity separate; add no aliases, forms, or recipe links.

Retain the reported dehulled and undehulled bulk-density results only as study-specific observations. The paper conflicts between 0.80 ± 0.02 g/mL in its table and 0.82 g/mL in prose for dehulled flour; no value is matched to the catalog product or a household packing convention. Keep defaultDensity null and unitMappings empty.

Keep the tested bread and cookie blends out of general substitution rules. The manufacturer describes milling dried raw beans, which is not evidence that the flour is ready to eat uncooked; general FDA/EFSA preparation guidance is not a product-specific heat-treatment determination or recipe instruction.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only sacred lotus seeds (Nelumbo nucifera), distinct from Euryale ferox makhana, lotus root, and lotus-root starch. Keep the French botanical display provisional pending Québec review and keep alias arrays empty.

Retain the USDA dried-seed cup observation as historical, product-specific evidence only. Do not activate default density, unit mappings, a form, or a conversion; the raw-seed entry includes shell refuse and is not applied to edible kernels.
Do not merge makhana/fox nut/gorgon nut with Nelumbo seeds or add lotus-seed aliases to the existing makhana reference/form; retail wording is not botanical equivalence.

Add the English search alias sacred lotus seed as a singular, species-qualified variant of the existing whole-seed display. This preserves the whole-seed result alongside the new sacred-lotus seed-flour identity for singular lotus seed searches. Add no French singular alias pending Québec terminology review.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only lovage / livèche for the leafy culinary herb in HERB, with leaf-qualified English and French aliases. Keep celery-like vernacular names, roots, stems, seeds, essential oil, and prepared products outside this reference; preserve their distinct product boundaries. UQAC mentions a qualitative celery replacement only in salted-herb mixtures or celery salt, without an amount, ratio, or broader role. Record this context as evidence but add no active substitution. The recipe bundle has no matching demand; add no forms, measurements, density, mapping, conversion, yield, or recipe link.

substitutionFindings.context: UQAC mentions lovage as a celery replacement only in salted-herb mixtures or celery salt. No bundled recipe requests lovage.
substitutionFindings.basis: The source gives no amount, ratio, or test result, and the named preparations are narrower than a general celery substitution. This contextual mention does not support an active global or contextual rule.
limitations: Do not substitute lovage for celery generally.
Do not encode the salted-herb or celery-salt mention as a quantified replacement without recipe-specific evidence.

decisions.reason: Add an identity-only reference for the named hand-rolled Palestinian maftool product with display names maftool (Palestinian couscous) and maftoul (couscous palestinien). Keep maftool distinct from generic and pearl couscous, bulgur, and wheat flour; do not infer a universal formulation. Add no aliases, forms, recipe links, or numeric data.

Keep measurement research blocked. The 500 g value and preparation directions are specific to one Canadian seller listing, and its “parts” basis is unspecified. No reviewed source establishes a reusable mass-volume measure, density, mapping, cooked form, or yield.

Keep substitution research blocked. The sources do not provide a tested, scoped replacement ratio or method for substituting maftool for generic or pearl couscous, bulgur, durum semolina, or whole-wheat flour.

sources.title: Aslam et al., Utilization of malted barley flour as replacement of wheat flour to improve technological, rheological, physicochemical, and organoleptic parameters of fortified breads
sources.versionOrDate: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 7 (2023), article 1230374; published 2023-09-27; DOI 10.3389/fsufs.2023.1230374.
sources.locator: Methods on flour preparation and bread trials, Table 1, and conclusion.
sources.supports: Original research produced a custom malted barley flour from named barley varieties and tested 0%, 2.5%, 5%, 7.5%, and 10% wheat-flour replacement in one controlled yeast-bread formula. The authors recommend 5% for acceptable bread when proper malting, dough development, and baking protocols are followed. This recommendation is limited to the study flour, formula, and process; it supplies no household measure or general home-recipe substitution rule.

decisions.reason: Add malted barley flour / farine d'orge maltée as a distinct FLOUR_AND_STARCH identity made from malted barley. Use OQLF's malt barley flour as an English search alias for the chosen display name malted barley flour. Keep it distinct from general barley flour, malted wheat flour, malt extract, and malt syrup; do not add a broad malt flour alias or activate diastatic/non-diastatic variants as forms. Add no density, unit mapping, measurement, conversion, or substitution data.

Complete bounded measurement and general wheat-flour replacement research for the existing malted-barley-flour identity. No reusable household measure, density, mapping, or conversion is supported. Preserve the study authors’ conditioned 5% bread recommendation as evidence only; it does not establish a general home-recipe replacement rule. Keep the active reference and all forms, aliases, and rules unchanged.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether unspecified malted barley flour has a reusable wheat-flour replacement amount across home-recipe dish types and ingredient roles, beyond the cited authors’ conditioned recommendation for their bread experiment.
substitutionFindings.basis: The authors tested a custom-prepared malted barley flour in one controlled yeast-bread formula at 2.5%–10% replacement and explicitly recommended 5% for acceptable bread when proper malting, dough development, and baking protocols are followed. This is a source-backed recommendation for that study’s flour, formula, and process, not a transferable home-recipe ratio. Current manufacturer descriptions are qualitative and product-specific.
limitations: Preserve the 5% recommendation only as study-specific, conditioned evidence; do not encode it as a general ratio or active contextual rule.
Do not infer water, leavening, fermentation-time, texture, or yield adjustments for home recipes.
Do not transfer the study to Arva’s product, non-diastatic malted barley flour, other malted or roasted cereal flours, or other bread formulas without matching flour and process evidence.

sources.supports: The current author-controlled card specifies canned sweetened mango pulp. A reader comment gives three mangos with powdered sugar and milk as a fresh-pulp alternative, matching the bundled count context but providing no size, cultivar, preparation state, or mass.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2015, Mango, raw, food code 1603
sources.locator: Interim online CNF serving-portion page: 1 fruit = 207.0 g and 29% refuse (seeds and skin).
sources.supports: Documents a source-specific generic raw-mango portion. It does not identify the size or variety of the recipe fruit or establish its edible/as-purchased and puree basis. No measurement observation or recipe conversion is derived.

sources.title: USDA ARS, SR28 Food Group 09: Fruits and Fruit Juices
sources.locator: NDB 09176, Mangos, raw, printed pp. 520–522; measures include 165 g per cup pieces and 336 g per fruit without refuse; 29% seeds and skin.
sources.supports: Documents a separate USDA SR Legacy edible-portion measure and cultivar footnote. It does not establish the saved variant’s size, cultivar, as-purchased mass, or puree yield; no value is applied to the recipe.

sources.title: USDA ARS, Home and Garden Bulletin 72, Table 9
sources.locator: Row 319, printed p. 38: raw mango without skin and seed; one mango = 207 g; about 1½ per lb with skin and seed.
sources.supports: Documents a distinct 2002 edible-part portion; it does not resolve the SR28 value or match the reader’s fruit size/cultivar. No mass is assigned to the saved recipe.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2026 dataset and resource files; CNF overview
sources.locator: CNF 2026 dataset/resource files and the CNF overview describing the online-interface transition.
sources.supports: Establishes dataset-version context only. No current 2026 whole-mango count row was verified for this review, so no current numeric portion is attributed to it.

sources.title: USDA ARS, FoodData Central downloads
sources.locator: Current “Latest Downloads” table, checked 2026-10-11: Foundation Foods 04/2026, FNDDS 10/2024 (2021–2023), and SR Legacy 04/2018.
sources.supports: Establishes current USDA downloadable-data version context only. No verified current whole-fruit measure was found for this recipe line; older SR28/HG72 values remain separate.

sources.title: USDA AMS, PDP Laboratory Operations SOP
sources.locator: Section 5.3.27, Mangoes; sample-preparation handling and unit counting.
sources.supports: Provides laboratory sample-preparation guidance, not a culinary portion, household count weight, or mango-puree yield for this recipe.

decisions.reason: Keep recipe 052#1 as 3 mangos with no structured unit, mass, or count conversion. The linked current publisher card specifies canned mango pulp; the bundled fresh-mango alternative follows a 2016 reader comment that gives no fruit size, cultivar, peel/pit state, or weight. Generic CNF and USDA raw-mango portions are conflicting source-specific edible-part values and do not establish this variant’s count-to-puree basis. Do not combine, select, multiply, or activate any value; preserve the recipe text.

sources.title: OQLF, mangoustan (GDT)
sources.locator: mangosteen/mangoustan and its listed alternate term.
sources.supports: mangosteen/mangoustan and its listed alternate term. Identity and Québec terminology evidence only; no measurement, yield, or substitution data.

decisions.reason: Accept mangosteen / mangoustan as a distinct identity-only FRUIT reference using the OQLF-supported Québec term and English equivalent. Keep documented near-neighbour and product boundaries separate. No forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are established.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, beurre d’érable (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred French term, definition, English terms maple butter / maple cream / maple spread, and product-composition note.
sources.supports: Defines beurre d’érable as a spread prepared from maple syrup, lists the English terms maple butter, maple cream, and maple spread, and states the Québec product standard restricts it to maple-sap products without substitutes. Supports a separate maple product identity and exact English aliases; no numeric behavior is inferred.

sources.title: Érable du Québec, Beurre d’érable
sources.locator: Product heading, no-butter/no-dairy statement, sap origin, and current kitchen uses.
sources.supports: Current Québec maple-producer association page identifies beurre d’érable as a maple-sap product, says it contains neither butter nor dairy, and names culinary uses as a topping and recipe ingredient. Supports separation from dairy butter; no portion, density, or conversion is adopted.

decisions.reason: Add maple butter / beurre d’érable as a distinct SUGAR_AND_SWEETENER identity, separate from maple syrup, maple sugar, and dairy butter. Use only the OQLF-supported English aliases maple cream and maple spread. Add no forms, measurements, density, mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Érable du Québec, Flocons d’érable
sources.locator: Product description and suggested culinary uses.
sources.supports: The Québec maple producers’ association names flocons d’érable, describes freeze-drying/dehydrating maple syrup, and lists finishing, dessert, savory, fish, and breading uses. It gives a 3:1 panko-to-flakes ratio for a specific breading mixture. This is association product guidance, not an identity standard or universal conversion.

sources.title: Maple from Canada, Maple Flakes
sources.locator: English product page and suggested uses.
sources.supports: The English-language counterpart uses Maple Flakes for the association’s freeze-dried/dehydrated syrup product and describes finishing, breading, cocktail, and sweet-salty uses. It is the same association’s English page, not independent corroboration.

sources.title: Maple from Canada, The Ultimate Smoked-Tea Maple Salmon
sources.locator: Ingredient list and step 7.
sources.supports: The published recipe lists maple flakes and directs the cook to sprinkle them on cooked salmon as a garnish without an amount. This is one recipe-specific use, not a measure, identity standard, or substitution.

sources.title: Érable du Québec, Sucre d’érable
sources.locator: Product process, texture, and granulation descriptions.
sources.supports: The association describes maple sugar as crystallized maple syrup that is boiled, cooled, and filtered, with multiple granulations, pieces, and compact forms. Supports a boundary from a separately named flake product but does not define how every flake product is made.

sources.title: Mayrand, Decacer Pure Maple Flakes 800 g
sources.locator: SKU name and package listing; adjacent separate Pur Maple Sugar SKU.
sources.supports: Mayrand separately lists Decacer Pure Maple Flakes 800 g (SKU 34109) and Pur Maple Sugar 800 g (SKU 34822) under its maple-sugar category. Retailer classification is not proof of synonymy or a product standard; package mass is SKU-specific.

sources.title: Amber Maple Products, Maple flakes
sources.locator: Product name, ingredient declaration, package, and suggested uses.
sources.supports: A Québec producer lists Maple flakes with 100% pure Quebec maple syrup as the sole ingredient, a 120 g package, and garnish/breading uses. This is evidence for that producer’s product, not a universal manufacturing specification or reusable amount.

sources.title: Ma Cabane en Gaspésie, Flocons d’érable purs
sources.locator: Search-indexed product description; direct page retrieval returned a cache miss.
sources.supports: The indexed listing describes crystallized pure maple syrup under the flocons d’érable name and mentions food uses and package options. The page could not be fetched directly; retain this only as an unresolved discrepancy lead, not as a representative process claim.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Labelling requirements for maple products
sources.locator: Overview and common-name sections.
sources.supports: CFIA gives broad maple-product labeling examples, including maple sugar, soft maple sugar, maple butter, and maple taffy, and guidance for common names of other maple products. It does not name maple flakes or establish a flakes-specific standard.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only maple flakes / flocons d’érable as a separately named dry maple product with no aliases. The Québec maple association and its English-language counterpart use the bilingual product name and describe finishing/breading uses; a Québec producer lists a standalone product made with pure maple syrup, and a Québec recipe uses flakes as an unquantified garnish. Keep maple flakes distinct from maple syrup and maple sugar. Process descriptions are not universal or consistent, so do not encode a manufacturing method or a syrup/sugar form. Package masses remain product-specific. No bundled recipe demand was found. Add no form, density, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

substitutionFindings.context: No bundled recipe requests maple flakes. The external maple-salmon recipe uses an unspecified quantity as a garnish, and association guidance gives a 3:1 panko-to-flakes mixture for one breading preparation.
substitutionFindings.basis: The garnish recipe gives no amount. The panko ratio is local to a breading mixture and does not establish replacement equivalence. Guidance about replacing sugar with syrup or maple sugar does not apply to flakes; no tested, quantified substitution is supported.
limitations: Do not substitute maple flakes for maple syrup, maple sugar, granulated sugar, icing sugar, panko, or breadcrumbs without recipe-specific evidence.
Do not convert package mass or the one breading ratio into a general measure or replacement rule.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, sucre d'érable (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred term, definition, notes, and English translation; see the North American WP06 proposal source register.
sources.supports: Defines sucre d’érable as maple syrup cooked and then stirred until it forms a uniform crystal, with soft through very hard consistencies, and gives maple sugar as the English translation. Supports a distinct solid maple sweetener identity only; it does not support ingredient forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, conversion, or substitution.

decisions.reason: Add maple sugar / sucre d’érable as a distinct SUGAR_AND_SWEETENER identity, separate from maple syrup and generic granulated sugar. Keep the rare Québec terms sucre du pays and sucre d’habitant out of unscoped global aliases. Add no form, numeric, conversion, or substitution data.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2015 serving-size page, Food Code 4326
sources.locator: Available serving sizes for “Sweets, syrups, maple, bulk”: 15, 30, 100, 125, and 250 mL entries.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT “sirop d’érable”
sources.locator: Preferred term, English equivalent, definition, and usage note.
sources.supports: OQLF identifies sirop d’érable as the preferred French term and maple syrup as its English equivalent. The dated entry also lists sirop du pays as a context-specific, old term; that term is not proposed as a global alias.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Importing maple syrup and maple products
sources.locator: Overview definition of maple syrup; page modified 2026-01-13.
sources.supports: CFIA describes maple syrup as a pure, single-ingredient food obtained by concentrating maple sap or diluting/solving another maple product in potable water. This supports the product boundary only, not measurements or substitutions.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2026, Measure Weight Conversion file
sources.locator: Food_Code 5917; Measure Codes 341, 383, 415, 1457, and 750; exact weights and row-updated dates.
sources.supports: The official Measure Weight Conversion CSV reports 100 mL = 78.191 g, 125 mL = 97.739 g, and 250 mL = 195.477 g for Food Code 5917, with row dates 2011-06-14. It also contains a mass-labelled 140 g row and a zero-weight total-refuse row; neither is a volume-to-weight edible portion.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File
sources.locator: Data in the Canadian Nutrient File; 2026 files and access to the 2015 online file.
sources.supports: Health Canada states that the 2026 CNF is published as relational CSV files and that the 2015 online search remains available only as an interim measure while a more user-friendly 2026 access method is developed. This page establishes the current dataset context but supplies no cooked-quinoa measure; item-level 2026 rows remain to be checked.

decisions.reason: Removed source-less draft density and unit-mapping values from the active bundled catalog. Restore a value only with source, exact food/form, unit convention, method or basis, and reviewer disposition.

Verify the existing maple syrup / sirop d’érable identity using OQLF’s preferred bilingual terminology and CFIA’s current single-ingredient product boundary. Record the CNF 2015 Food Code 4326 bulk and 6175 prepackaged portions separately as historic, source-specific observations. Keep the two code classes separate; do not derive a generic density, cup weight, active unit mapping, or conversion. CNF 2026 is the current dataset, but the Measure Weight Conversion CSV could not be inspected through available retrieval, so measurement review remains blocked pending exact review of the maple row and related measure joins. Leave substitutions not yet researched and recipe lines unchanged.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, tire d’érable (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred Québec term, English terms, definition, and explicit distinction from tire à l’érable / maple taffy blend.
sources.supports: Defines tire d’érable as maple confectionery and maple taffy as its English term. The OQLF distinguishes it from tire à l’érable / maple taffy blend containing commercial glucose. Product identity only; no temperature, percentage, serving, or conversion value is imported.

sources.title: Érable du Québec, Tire d’érable
sources.locator: Current product heading and description of concentrated maple syrup, seasonal context, and culinary uses.
sources.supports: Current Québec maple-producer association page names tire d’érable, describes it as concentrated maple syrup, and shows it as a topping and cooking ingredient beyond snow service. It does not establish an ingredient measure or equivalence to glucose-containing maple taffy blend.

decisions.reason: Add maple taffy / tire d’érable as a distinct SUGAR_AND_SWEETENER identity for the OQLF-defined maple-syrup confection. Keep maple syrup, maple butter, maple sugar, and glucose-containing tire à l’érable / maple taffy blend separate. Add no aliases, forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: EPPO, Aristotelia chilensis
sources.locator: Common names
sources.supports: Provides English maqui berry / Chilean wineberry and French maqui du Chili for Aristotelia chilensis.

sources.title: Chile Ministry of Agriculture, SIMEF native forest species and uses
sources.locator: Aristotelia chilensis, maqui, direct fruit use
sources.supports: Pairs Aristotelia chilensis with maqui and records direct fruit use separately from jam and syrup.

decisions.reason: Add maqui berry as the fresh fruit of Aristotelia chilensis using EPPO English and French names and Chilean food-use evidence. Keep jam, syrup, honey, leaves, and extracts separate. No numeric or substitution data is inferred.

sources.title: FAO, Milk composition
sources.locator: Equine-milk entry; horse and donkey milk food use.
sources.supports: Identifies horse milk separately from donkey milk under equine milk and states that equine milk is mostly consumed fermented. Supports the horse/mare milk identity and food context only; it does not support an active fermented form, measurement, or substitute.

sources.title: FAO, La composition du lait
sources.locator: Species entry for lait de jument within equine milk; fermented consumption context.
sources.supports: Names lait de jument and says mare and donkey milks are mostly consumed fermented. Supports the French display and food identity; the comparative composition and fermentation notes do not establish a reusable measure or processed form.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, lait de jument (GDT)
sources.locator: Alimentation/lait entry; preferred French term and English equivalent.
sources.supports: Pairs the preferred French term lait de jument with English mare's milk. Supports Québec-facing bilingual terminology only, not a measure or substitution.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only mare milk / lait de jument, with the OQLF-backed mare's milk alias and the FAO-attested horse milk alias. Keep it distinct from donkey milk and fermented mare-milk products such as koumis. Do not transfer FAO composition or processing descriptions into measures, forms, conversions, or substitutions; no bundled recipe demand was found.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, Grand dictionnaire terminologique: marjolaine
sources.locator: Food/spice domain, definition, preferred French terms, English translations, and Latin name
sources.supports: Places marjolaine in the food, spice, and seasoning domain; defines it as an aromatic plant; lists marjolaine and grand origan as preferred French terms; gives marjoram, sweet marjoram, knotted marjoram, and Origanum majorana. It describes marjolaine as a close relative of origan with a somewhat milder flavour, supporting separate identities.

decisions.reason: Present in the legacy RecipeKeeper catalog but absent from the canonical bundled seed; reconcile identity and aliases before acceptance.

Promote the existing legacy candidate to the identity-only HERB reference marjoram / marjolaine for culinary Origanum majorana. Add OQLF-listed English aliases sweet marjoram and knotted marjoram and French alias grand origan. Keep it separate from oregano; the broad French query origan returns both this row and the existing dried-oregano row, while origan séché remains specific to dried oregano. Remove the promoted candidate from legacy-import-identities.v1.json. No matching bundled recipe demand was found. Add no forms, measures, density, mappings, conversions, recipe links, yields, or active substitutions; measurement and general substitution research remain not_yet_researched.

decisions.reason: Verify marshmallow crème / crème de guimauve as a spread identity distinct from whole marshmallows. Keep the recipe’s 7 oz line unchanged; the branded serving is not a generic conversion. Add no aliases, forms, measurements, mappings, yields, or substitutions.

sources.locator: Preferred term and definition of the confection.
