decisions.reason: Verify marshmallows / guimauves as the active identity. Keep whole marshmallows separate from marshmallow crème, retain “white” as recipe-line wording, and add no aliases, forms, measurements, mappings, yields, or substitutions.

sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp02-gianduja-praline-paste-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.

decisions.reason: Accept masa harina / farine de maïs nixtamalisée as a distinct maize-flour identity defined by nixtamalization. Keep brand names, corn color, grind, measurements, conversions, and substitutions out of the general identity.

2026-10-18 review: the available studies document only their controlled wheat-bread and chapati formulations, and the accessible publisher material does not resolve the botanical millet identity. Keep the evidence formula-specific; add no active substitution rule, general replacement ratio, or hydration adjustment.

sources.title: Sanz-Penella et al. - Impact of the addition of resistant starch from modified pea starch on dough and bread performance
sources.versionOrDate: European Food Research and Technology 231 (2010), 499-508; published 2010-06-09.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; subscription-gated full text.
sources.supports: Abstract reports one PeaP wheat-bread study: flour replacement up to 20% did not significantly hinder dough machinability, while 30% negatively affected mixing and overmixing; acceptable quality changes were reported through 10-20%.

sources.title: Roquette - LYCOAT RS 780 modified pea starch as binder for wet granulation
sources.locator: Materials and methods and Table 1, granules' main characteristics.
sources.supports: Reports bulk and tapped densities for finished pharmaceutical mannitol/maize-starch granules with 3% pregelatinized hydroxypropyl pea-starch binder; these are not pea-starch powder values.

substitutionFindings.context: One wheat-bread study used the high-resistant-starch modified pea starch PeaP as a partial wheat-flour replacement; the study's wheat-flour source is not mapped to an existing reference.
substitutionFindings.basis: The publisher abstract reports flour replacement up to 20% without significant hindrance to dough machinability, with 30% negatively affecting mixing and overmixing; acceptable bread-quality changes were reported through 10-20%.
limitations: This is a study-specific formulation result, not a general flour or starch substitution, kitchen conversion, or active recipe rule.
The study product is not identified as the Selection candy ingredient or as equivalent to all modified pea-starch grades.
The full paper is subscription-gated on the publisher page; do not infer omitted methods or formula details.

decisions.reason: Add modified pea starch / amidon de pois modifié as a distinct identity from the existing native/general pea-starch row. Keep aliases and forms empty, density null, and unit mappings empty. Record the single high-resistant-starch bread-study finding as source-specific only; add no active conversion, substitution rule, or recipe link.

sources.title: Ali et al. — Extraction and characterization of starch from low-grade potatoes and formulation of gluten-free cookies containing modified potato starch
sources.locator: Methods sections 2.4 and 2.12–2.13; results sections 3.2.7–3.2.9.
sources.supports: Primary study modifies starch from Asterix, Kruda, and Mosaic potatoes using lintnerization plus repeated autoclaving/cooling. Its gluten-free-cookie formula uses 15 g starch/modified starch; the control substitutes an additional 15 g gram flour for the modified starch. Sensory scores were not significantly different overall, while texture effects differed from native starch.

sources.title: 100x100 Ingredients — CUSTARD COLD
sources.locator: Product description, uses, dosage, and product-specific recipe links.
sources.supports: Describes one branded cold custard product as basically composed of modified potato starch, with product dosage of 40–80 g/kg and use as an alternative to corn starch's thickening function. This product-specific formulation claim is not a pure-ingredient conversion or reusable substitution rule.

substitutionFindings.context: One 2023 laboratory gluten-free-cookie formula used 15 g of study-modified potato starch; the control used an additional 15 g gram flour instead. The starch was extracted from Pakistani Asterix, Kruda, or Mosaic potatoes and modified by lintnerization and repeated autoclaving/cooling.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study's methods say the control cookies replaced the modified-starch amount with additional gram flour. Cambridge defines gram flour as flour made from chickpeas, and Norway's official food table identifies gram flour as Cicer arietinum / FoodEx2 Chickpea flour. The study reports no significant overall sensory difference among control, native-starch, and modified-starch cookie groups, while modified starch changed cookie hardness relative to native starch.
limitations: This is one study-specific formulation and one laboratory modification process; it does not establish a general cookie substitution or the behavior of commercial modified potato starch grades.
The study's 15 g amount is a recipe mass, not a volume measure, density, or reusable conversion.
The study does not identify its gram flour as a particular chickpea variety or milling state; link only to the existing broad chickpea-flour identity, not Desi chickpea flour or roasted chana sattu.
No `SubstitutionRule`, `ContextualSubstitutionRule`, recipe-line substitution, or bundled-recipe link is proposed.

decisions.reason: Add modified potato starch / amidon de pomme de terre modifié as a plant-qualified identity distinct from ordinary potato starch and the other modified botanical starch rows. Retain the French fécule variant as a source-attested alias. Record the single laboratory cookie-formula replacement only as a bounded research finding; keep measures, default density, mappings, forms, recipe links, conversions, yields, and active substitution rules empty.

decisions.reason: Add the separately named modified rice starch identity as modified rice starch / amidon de riz modifié. CFIA supplies the plant-qualified English naming construction, and current Québec-facing ingredient declarations use the French phrase. Keep ordinary rice starch separate. Do not add aliases or equate native pre-cooked grades, product SKUs, or process-specific grades with this identity.

No reviewed source establishes a reusable household measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, or yield for the identity class. SKU packaging, finished-food case size, and one test formula proportion remain source-specific. Keep defaultDensity null and unitMappings empty.

The reviewed documents describe different grades and functions but do not establish a generally safe or equal-amount substitution with ordinary rice starch, another starch, or flour. Add no global or contextual substitution rule.

substitutionFindings.context: Only Nicole Hunn's Gluten Free Sopapillas recipe; the formula calls for 1/4 cup (36 g) Expandex modified tapioca starch.

limitations: The recipe note does not clarify whether `equal amount` means equal volume or equal mass. Record no replacement quantity and do not create a reusable rule.
This is one recipe-specific outcome for Expandex and the author's dough method; it does not establish interchangeability with all modified tapioca starch grades.
The same author explicitly rejects regular tapioca starch as a replacement for modified tapioca starch in the Bakes Bread recipes; substitution behavior is recipe-specific.

The preparation method and composition results remain specific to study samples.

sources.locator: Oat processing section; groat structure and milling.
sources.supports: Describes oats as most commonly processed as whole grain because the softer groat is not easily converted into separate germ, endosperm, and bran fractions. Supports a processing limitation and the decision not to claim common standalone retail availability or routine consumer use.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only oat germ / germe d’avoine as a distinct generic grain fraction with food-ingredient potential supported by primary research. sources.title: Oliinyk et al., “Studying the influence of meats from wheat and oat germs, and rose hips, on the formation of quality of rye-wheat dough and bread”
sources.locator: Eastern-European Journal of Enterprise Technologies 1(11 (103)) (2020), 59–65; abstract, methods, and results.
sources.supports: Primary food study describes oil-production meal use in rye-wheat dough. It tests oat germ meal as an addition at 10–20% of flour mass; its recommendation of no more than 15% is limited to the study's bread formula and quality findings, not replacement or household-use guidance.

decisions.reason: Promote the held candidate to the identity-only consumer ingredient octopus / pieuvre, with poulpe as the sole French alias. OQLF supports both French terms and identifies pieuvre as familiar in Quebec; CFIA applies the names across generic and species-specific octopus entries, and current Canadian and Quebec product listings corroborate the consumer category. This does not select a species, cut, preparation, or harvest origin. Keep squid/calamari and cuttlefish/seiche separate; exclude tako, named species, baby or size-specific products, and prepared products. Add no forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

Add a cooked-octopus-tentacles form under generic octopus, based on a Québec retailer’s paired English/French SKU and OQLF terminology. Keep the unqualified tentacles query effect visible, and add no species claim, reusable measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution; seller-specific previously frozen/thawed wording does not define a universal preparation rule.

sources.title: Labuckas, Lamarque, and Maestri, Partially defatted peanut flour: a functional ingredient to improve nutritional value of bakery products
sources.locator: Methods, bread and cookie formulas, results, and conclusions.
sources.supports: Primary study of flour prepared from dehulled Runner market-type peanuts by partial n-hexane extraction (11.5% oil). It tested 10% and 20% wheat-flour replacement in one bread formula and peanut flour replacing the wheat-flour component in one cookie formula with substantially increased shortening. These findings are limited to the tested flour and formula/process; not a generic replacement ratio or adjustment.

decisions.reason: Accept only the explicitly partially defatted peanut flour identity. Keep whole ground peanuts, peanut meal, peanut butter, powdered peanut-butter mixes, protein isolates, unqualified cross-product aliases, forms, measurements, conversions, recipe links, and substitutions outside this row.

Complete bounded measurement and substitution research for the existing partially defatted peanut-flour identity. Keep the Protein Plus/Mill Creek 1/4 cup (30 g) label portion listing-specific and density/mappings unset. Record the two Labuckas bread/cookie flour replacements as formula-specific evidence-only findings with no active rule; do not generalize to commercial grades or arbitrary recipes.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Protein Plus bulk roasted defatted peanut flour as repackaged and described by Mill Creek; label lists roasted peanuts; defatting grade, roast grade, cup standard, and filling method are unspecified.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Reproduced Nutrition Facts label serving declaration on the Mill Creek listing.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: The listing declares 1/4 cup (30 g) for this repackaged product. Cup capacity and filling method are unstated; retain only as a product-listing-specific portion, not a reusable conversion.

replacements.roleInCompound: Replaces 10% or 20% of wheat flour in the named experimental bread formula; no general recipe ratio.

substitutionFindings.context: Labuckas et al. bread made with laboratory flour from dehulled Runner market-type peanuts, partially extracted with n-hexane (11.5% oil), desolventized at 30 °C and milled so 90% passed a 100-mesh screen. PFB1/PFB2 replaced wheat flour at 10%/20% of the 63.4% flour fraction. The formula also used 34.3% water, 0.65% shortening, 0.65% brewer's yeast, and 1.0% salt; the dough was mixed, fermented 3 h, shaped into 10 cm cylinders, and baked at 190 °C for 1 h.
substitutionFindings.basis: The authors conclude that this partially defatted flour may replace up to 20% of wheat flour without adversely affecting dough handling, baking performance, loaf volume, crust and crumb color, or texture. Both tested peanut-flour breads had increased protein and fiber compared with the all-wheat bread.
expectedEffects: In this formula only, 10% and 20% wheat-flour replacement increased bread protein and fiber.
The study reports no adverse effect through the tested 20% level on the listed dough and bread qualities.
limitations: The flour was laboratory-made from one Runner market-type peanut source and one extraction/milling process; it was not matched to a commercial grade or SKU in this catalog class.

This finding is bounded to the tested bread formula, mixing, fermentation, shaping, and baking process. Do not generalize the tested percentages as a recommendation for other bread formulas or dishes.
It does not establish a volume conversion, hydration correction, arbitrary-recipe substitution, or active global/contextual rule.
adjustments: The paper reports no additional liquid or shortening adjustment beyond the listed study formula; do not infer a correction for other bread recipes.

replacements.roleInCompound: Replaces the 10.5% formula-basis wheat-flour component with peanut flour in the study formula; cornstarch remains.

substitutionFindings.context: Labuckas et al. peanut-flour cookie formula: 10.5% flour, 42.0% cornstarch, 15.7% shortening, 2.2% water, 11.8% egg yolk, 15.7% sugar, and 2.1% baking powder; dough rolled to 5 mm, cut to 60 mm, and baked at 180 °C for 12 min. The authors state shortening was increased substantially relative to the standard ACC formula to improve spread, but do not report the numeric adjustment from that baseline.
substitutionFindings.basis: The authors conclude that peanut flour can totally replace wheat flour in a cookie formulation when shortening is increased. Their peanut-flour cookies showed good spread and similar sensory results to wheat-flour cookies except for a higher texture score.
expectedEffects: The tested peanut-flour cookie replaces its wheat-flour component while retaining cornstarch.
The authors report the shortening adjustment improved cookie spread in this formulation.
limitations: One laboratory-made flour and a single cookie formula; the paper does not give the numeric shortening increase relative to the standard ACC baseline.
This finding concerns replacement of the wheat-flour component only; do not treat it as replacement of cornstarch or as an instruction for other cookie recipes.
It does not establish a reusable shortening correction or active global/contextual rule.
adjustments: Shortening was increased substantially relative to the standard ACC formula to maximize peanut-flour addition and improve spread; the numeric increment is not reported.

decisions.reason: Accept pea starch / amidon de pois as a distinct ingredient identity and keep native pea starch as a narrow English alias. Confirm amidon de pois as the Québec French display: OQLF prefers amidon generally and describes fécule as more specific to starch in tubers or underground organs, while a current Montréal food label declares amidon de pois. This applies OQLF general guidance; it is not an exact compound headword. Do not add fécule de pois, amidon natif de pois, or modified pea-starch wording as aliases. sources.locator: Methods §§2.2.1–2.2.2.4; bulk-density method and Table 2.

sources.title: Maktouf et al., Evaluation of dough rheological properties and bread texture of pearl millet-wheat flour mix

sources.locator: Materials and methods; results and conclusion for Tunisian bread formulation.

decisions.reason: Accepted as an identity-only product with the Codex English / Québec French display pair “pearl millet flour / farine de mil chandelle”. Defines pearl millet flour as a distinct milling product and gives the official French product name farine de mil chandelle. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.

Add only the exact source-named English alias bajra flour to the existing pearl-millet-flour identity. Keep the existing Québec French display, category, and identity boundary unchanged. Under current phrase search, bare bajra returns both grain and flour choices, while bajra flour returns flour only. Add no French alias, form, measurement, conversion, yield, substitution, or recipe link.

Add only the exact French search alias farine de millet perlé to the existing pearl-millet-flour row. Canadian French-facing product sources support this wording for pearl-millet flour; OQLF and Usito provide grain-name context but do not establish the flour phrase as an official preferred term. Keep farine de mil chandelle as the Codex-based display, retain only the live English alias bajra flour, and add no measurement default, unit mapping, form, recipe link, or active substitution.

Add the exact English alias bajri flour to ingredient-ref-pearl-millet-flour. Canadian mill and retail sources pair this phrase with pearl-millet flour; retain the existing display, bajra flour alias, French alias, category, null density, empty unit mappings, and existing measurement and substitution research. Add no new identity or numeric behavior.

Add only the exact English alias sajjalu flour to the existing pearl-millet-flour identity. The current listing pairs Pearl Millet Flour with Sajjalu and says it is made from Pearl Millet (Sajjalu). Keep the existing Québec display, aliases, category, measurement observation, null density, empty unit mappings, and blocked substitution research unchanged; do not treat the 500 g package as a recipe measure.

Add only kambu flour as an English search alias to the existing pearl-millet-flour row. A current Shastha Canada ingredient declaration explicitly names Pearl Millet (Kambu) Flour. Keep the French display and alias, other English aliases, category, source-scoped measurement evidence, and blocked substitution research unchanged; add no grain alias, form, active measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution from this flour source.

Add only sajje hittu as an English search alias to the existing pearl-millet-flour identity. The Canada-localized Kalagura product page directly pairs Kannada Sajje Hittu with Pearl Millet Flour; its seller is based in Telangana and it does not establish Québec French wording. Retain the existing display, French alias, other aliases, null active density, empty unit mappings, source-scoped measurement observation, and blocked substitution research. Add no sajje flour alias, form, measure, conversion, yield, recipe link, or active substitution.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Whole pearl-millet flour sample used in the study.
measurementObservations.foodState: Laboratory-prepared whole pearl-millet flour.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: A dry 100 mL measuring cylinder was filled with 50 g of flour; its base was gently tapped until the volume no longer decreased.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Reported mean ± SD: 0.63 ± 0.01 g/mL. Study- and sample-specific bulk density; not a household volume-to-mass mapping or product-independent default.

substitutionFindings.context: Replacing wheat flour with pearl-millet flour outside the single Tunisian bread formulation studied by Maktouf et al.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study tested 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10% by-weight replacement in one wheat-bread formula and reported 5% as optimal for its measured dough and bread outcomes. The formula-specific finding does not establish a general replacement ratio.
limitations: Do not use the study percentages as a general wheat-flour substitution range.
The trial covers one wheat flour, one pearl-millet flour sample, and one bread formula; it does not establish behavior in other breads, flatbreads, cakes, sauces, or thickening.
No active substitution rule or recipe-line substitution is justified.

sources.title: Ferme Maxiel, Perles de maïs
sources.locator: Product title, product description, usage and intended users.
sources.supports: The current Québec-facing product is dried, shelled maize intended as a treat for birds and small rodents. Its similar wording is an animal-food homonym, not a human-food pearled-hominy label or a transferable moisture/density specification.

decisions.reason: A distinct dry-milled human-food product is supported and TERMIUM distinguishes it from lye-treated hominy. However, the only Canadian French wording found for hominy perlé is in a feed-byproduct definition; OQLF’s semoules du maïs entry is broader and overlaps the existing cornmeal wording. A Québec food article also uses maïs perle for a broad maize type but does not define the product or connect it to dry-milled pearled hominy. Do not add a row or alias until a human-food source supports the Québec French product name. Keep it separate from canned/preserved maïs lessivé, hominy grits, cornmeal, and masa harina. The Canadian classifications separate pearled corn from unprocessed corn and list pearled corn separately from white hominy; Québec human-food naming and equivalence to pearled hominy remain unresolved. The reviewed French forms are broad, import-classified, feed-scoped, or a different animal-feed product. No reusable kitchen measure or substitution is supported.

sources.title: OQLF, penne
sources.locator: Alimentation > pâte alimentaire; product definition, preferred term, French plural, English term, and surface variants
sources.supports: Defines short pasta shaped like a small tube with bevelled ends; gives penne as the preferred French and English term, pennes as a French plural, mostaccioli as an English term, and smooth or ridged surfaces as variants.

decisions.reason: Accept penne as a shape-specific pasta identity with the OQLF-supported French plural pennes and English alias mostaccioli. Keep smooth and ridged surface variants within the same identity; do not adopt the sometimes-used French plume term. Assign the project’s existing GRAIN_AND_CEREAL category for pasta shapes without asserting a specific grain composition. Add no forms, numeric values, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Perilla frutescens
sources.locator: Accepted taxon name and status
sources.supports: Accepts Perilla frutescens as a species. This supports botanical identity only; it is not a food-label standard, measure, or substitution source.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online: Perilla frutescens var. crispa
sources.locator: Accepted variety and common-name section
sources.supports: Accepts Perilla frutescens var. crispa and records shiso as a common name. It does not show that all perilla leaves are this variety or that variety-specific products are interchangeable.

sources.title: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, Specialty Cropportunities: Perilla
sources.locator: Common names, botanical name, leaf uses, and green/purple crop types
sources.supports: Identifies Perilla frutescens, lists shiso among common names, and documents culinary raw and cooked leaf uses. It notes that green and purple types serve different end uses and markets; this older Ontario crop profile is not a Québec terminology ruling or measure source.

sources.title: Health Canada, List of non-novel determinations
sources.locator: Perilla frutescens leaf entry dated 2017-05-12
sources.supports: Lists perilla leaf as whole or minimally processed separately from seed and leaf oil. This records a history-of-food-use determination, not a general safety or dosage conclusion and not a Québec naming ruling.

sources.title: Pépinière.ca, Périlla en pot — Fine herbe asiatique
sources.locator: Product name, shiso wording, and culinary leaf description
sources.supports: Uses accented Périlla, says it is also called shiso, identifies Perilla frutescens, and describes culinary leaf use. This is Québec horticultural wording, not a fresh-food SKU or official terminology ruling.

sources.title: Doshrock, Montréal, De notre jardin à votre table
sources.locator: Fresh leaf-wrap ingredient wording
sources.supports: Uses feuilles de périlla for leaves grown and eaten in a Korean wrap context. This supports observed Montréal culinary wording but does not establish that every Korean cultivar is identical to Japanese shiso.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only perilla leaves / feuilles de périlla for culinary leaves of Perilla frutescens as a HERB reference. Kew supports the species and records shiso for var. crispa; OMAFRA documents culinary leaf use, and Health Canada lists leaf separately from seeds and leaf oil. Pépinière.ca and a Montréal restaurant support Québec wording. Keep perilla seeds as a separate identity; do not add seed powder, oils, preserved dishes, botanical names, cultivar-specific forms, measures, mappings, density, conversions, recipe links, yields, or active substitutions. No matching bundled recipe demand was found. Measurement and general substitution research remain unresolved.

sources.title: Health Canada, List of non-novel determinations for food and food ingredients
sources.locator: 2017-05-02 Perilla (Perilla frutescens) seeds entry; introductory scope notes.
sources.supports: Lists whole or minimally processed Perilla frutescens seeds and records a history of safe use as food. Health Canada states these listings did not undergo a food-use safety assessment; this is not preparation advice.

sources.title: Santé Canada, Liste des déterminations d’aliments et d’ingrédients alimentaires qui ne sont pas nouveaux

sources.supports: Uses Graine de perilla and Graine de perilla entière ou minimalement transformée. Supports French singular wording and species; not a Québec OQLF preference.

sources.locator: Uses and Markets section.
sources.supports: Identifies Perilla frutescens and says seeds are eaten cooked or pressed for oil, separately from culinary leaf use. It gives no recipe measure, density, or substitution.

sources.supports: A Québec retailer lists a named 200 g perilla-seed powder product. Package weight is not a whole-seed measure or conversion.

sources.supports: Lists Poudre de périlla and Poudre de périlla molle for perilla-powder products. Supports Québec wording for powders only, not whole seeds or a kitchen conversion.

sources.locator: Common name, botanical identification, and culinary description.
sources.supports: A Québec horticultural retailer uses the accented plant name Périlla and identifies Perilla frutescens; its culinary description concerns leaves, not a seed product label.

decisions.reason: Accept an identity-only perilla seeds / graines de périlla reference for food seeds of Perilla frutescens. Keep leaves, oil, seed powder, sowing seed, and sesame separate; add no measurements, forms, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.supports: Describes selva cecina as dried and smoked meat traditionally used to preserve meat, and says Peruvian jungle varieties differ by animal species, seasonings, and smoking method. Government science-education source, not a technical product specification.

sources.supports: Studies pork cecina in Pucallpa using local fuelwood and differing smoke times; the abstract reports that producer smoke times were not standardized. This local pork study is not a national definition or numeric ingredient measure.

sources.supports: Records charqui and charque as French dried-meat terms and jerky/charqui as English terms; its general definition is broader than the integrated source-defined camelid identity. These terms are not cecina aliases.

sources.title: Argentina, Joint Resolution 15/2023 amending the Argentine Food Code
sources.locator: Articles 289 and 292
sources.supports: Outside Peru, defines Argentine cecina across pork, beef, and other edible species and defines charqui separately. Comparative evidence that cecina scope varies by jurisdiction; it does not define Peruvian cecina.

sources.title: INACAL, Trámites y servicios
sources.locator: NTP virtual reading-room link and targeted cecina search
sources.supports: The NTP reading-room search performed for this review did not locate a cecina-specific standard. The search was targeted, not exhaustive; this does not establish that no such standard exists.

decisions.reason: Add one source-named, Peru-Amazon-qualified PROTEIN identity displayed as Peruvian Amazon cecina (smoked, dried meat) / cecina de l’Amazonie péruvienne (viande séchée et fumée). CONCYTEC describes the Peruvian Amazon family as dried and smoked and reports variation in species, seasonings, and smoking methods; recipe and regional sources show common pork examples without making pork invariant. Keep this family distinct from source-defined camelid charqui, charque, jerky, and generic dried or smoked meat; do not use unqualified cecina for other countries' product standards. Add no aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, conversions, substitutions, package yields, or recipe links.

sources.locator: Québec Peruvian-food menu description of chicha morada.
sources.supports: A Québec Peruvian-food service describes chicha morada as a pineapple-and-maïs-mauve beverage. Supports local French culinary wording and Peruvian context, not a standalone kernel product name or a measure.

sources.locator: Current Canadian retailer product title and description.
sources.supports: Lists a prepared popcorn snack made from purple-kernel popcorn corn. Used only to distinguish popping corn from the proposed Peruvian non-popping dry-grain product; no identity or measurement is transferred.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Peruvian purple corn kernels / grains de maïs mauve péruvien for dry, food-grade whole kernels marketed as Peru-sourced maíz morado. Keep it distinct from generic and color-qualified maize, purple popcorn, flour, meal, cob/coronta, pigment, and prepared products. Add no Spanish aliases, forms, measurements, density, mappings, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions; no bundled recipe demand or supported household measure was found.

sources.supports: The same Classico product is labelled Basil Pesto in English and Pesto au basilic in French; supports product-name search aliases only.

sources.supports: Names a sun-dried tomato pesto variant, supporting its boundary from classical basil pesto; no formula is generalized.

Keep tomato pesto as a distinct variant, do not generalize formulas, and leave forms, measurements, conversions, yields, substitutions, and recipe links unset.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only piccalilli / piccalilli as a named English-style vinegar-and-mustard vegetable condiment in SAUCE_AND_CONDIMENT. Use the OQLF-supported term in both locales. Add no aliases, recipe links, forms, measurements, density, unit mappings, yields, conversions, or substitutions.

replacements.roleInCompound: In the cited experimental treatments only, replaces a portion of 80:20 ground beef and is paired with an equal mass of water.

substitutionFindings.context: Felker et al. tested raw pinto bean flour and, separately, jet-cooked/drum-dried pinto bean flour in 100 g 80:20 ground-beef patties. The 6 g, 12 g, and 18 g flour treatments used 88 g, 76 g, and 64 g beef, respectively, plus the same mass of water as flour. Do not combine the two flour processes in one treatment.
substitutionFindings.basis: Primary controlled study of pinto bean flour in ground-beef patties; the reported replacement and added-water amounts are the tested formula.
expectedEffects: The flour treatments changed cooking loss, cooked dimensions, and cooking time versus untreated patties.
The jet-cooked/drum-dried 18% treatment had the largest cooked diameter and shortest cook time in this study.
limitations: The authors milled purchased pinto beans in the laboratory; the study does not identify a match to Avena's commercial flour specification.
The amounts apply only to the tested 80:20 ground-beef patty formulation and its processing conditions.
Raw and jet-cooked/drum-dried flours are distinct research materials with different behavior.
This finding is not a general meat-free replacement, flour-for-flour substitution, density, measure, or runtime rule.

substitutionFindings.context: Replacing potato flour with cornstarch in yeast breads, based on King Arthur Baking’s White Sandwich Bread test and recommendation for yeast recipes.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur reports that cornstarch kept the tested bread moist but lacked the subtle potato-flour flavor and color; the resulting loaf was paler and less flavorful.
expectedEffects: Bread is paler and less flavorful than with potato flour; moisture retention is described as similar.
limitations: Test-kitchen guidance for yeast bread only; no rule is established for cakes, sauces, gluten-free baking, or other uses.
The volume ratio is not a mass ratio, density, or active unit conversion.
Do not activate as a runtime substitution rule or attach to recipe lines.

quantity.unitConvention: King Arthur states 1:1 by volume in yeast recipes; cup convention and any mass equivalence are not specified.

substitutionFindings.context: Replacing potato flour with all-purpose flour in yeast breads, based on King Arthur Baking’s White Sandwich Bread test and recommendation for yeast recipes.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur says potato flour absorbs more liquid. It advises beginning at the lower end when the recipe gives a water range and adding flour only if dough remains too sticky to handle.
adjustments: Begin at the low end of a recipe’s water range; add a small amount of all-purpose flour only if dough remains too sticky to handle.
expectedEffects: The dough may initially be stickier; the loaf is drier, paler, less flavorful, and stales sooner than with potato flour.
limitations: Test-kitchen guidance for yeast bread only; no rule is established for cakes, sauces, or other uses.
The volume ratio is not a mass ratio, density, or active unit conversion.
Do not activate as a runtime substitution rule or attach to recipe lines.

substitutionFindings.context: Potato starch used in place of potato flour solely to retain moisture in yeast breads.
substitutionFindings.basis: King Arthur describes the two as roughly interchangeable for retaining moisture in yeast bread, while noting that potato starch lacks potato flour’s flavor and warm color and that a little less starch may be appropriate. No precise ratio is supplied.
expectedEffects: Moisture retention may be similar in yeast bread; flavor and warm color from potato flour are lost.
limitations: Qualitative and approximate guidance only; no precise ratio or measurement basis is supplied.
King Arthur says they are not interchangeable in gluten-free baking.
Do not add a potato-flour/starch conversion or runtime substitution rule.

substitutionFindings.context: One White Sandwich Bread test using unseasoned mashed potatoes in place of potato flour; King Arthur reports that the loaf may collapse and recommends this approach for rolls instead.
substitutionFindings.basis: The source example uses 3/4 cup mashed potatoes for each 1/4 cup potato flour and reduces added recipe liquid by 50%. Potato moisture varies by cooking method, making the dough hard to predict.
adjustments: Reduce added recipe liquid by 50%; adjust flour or liquid as needed for a soft, non-sticky dough, following the source’s formula-specific guidance.
expectedEffects: Very moist dough; the tested loaf collapsed as it cooled. King Arthur suggests rolls because their structure is more stable.
limitations: One tested formula only; mashed-potato water content varies with baking or boiling and is not represented by a catalog form.

decisions.reason: Pozolero corn is a real specialty whole-kernel maize product, but available sources cover both dry regional posole corn and canned precooked/nixtamalized pozolero corn. The canned Québec-market product is also labeled hominy, overlapping the existing maïs lessivé identity, and no authoritative English–Québec French food-term pair was found. Keep the candidate unallocated until product state and display wording are narrowed; do not alias it to hominy corn, hominy grits, cornmeal, or masa harina.

The R114 Canadian and Québec retail recheck strengthens the dry-versus-prepared product boundary: a Canadian bulk supplier distinguishes dried raw kernels from processed hominy, while local listings use Maíz pozolero or Maïs Pozolero Blanc without consistently stating product state. One Montréal retailer explicitly presents Maïs Pozolero Blanco as ready-to-serve hominy; no Québec-facing French name for the dry raw kernels is established. Keep the candidate unallocated and separate from the existing hominy-corn identity until product state and French display are resolved.

R318 rechecked current Canadian and Québec product wording, regional use, active ownership, picker behavior, and the bundled corpus. Québec listings include ready-to-use or precooked hominy marketed for pozole and listings whose state is unstated; the Canadian dry-raw offer remains a quote-based umbrella without a Québec French product name. Regional sources also use pozolero across maize races and states. Keep the candidate ledger-only and needs_clarification; do not allocate pozole/posole wording to hominy corn, add an active identity or alias, or infer a dry-product display. No form, reusable measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, recipe link, yield, or substitution is supported. Retail package sizes remain SKU-specific evidence, and the previously recorded regional hominy alternative is not a universal substitution.

sources.title: P.A.N. USA, Nutritional Information: Pre-Cooked White Corn Meal 1 kg
sources.locator: Product title, ingredients declaration, and Nutrition Facts serving-size line for PRE-COOKED WHITE CORN MEAL 1KG.
sources.supports: The official P.A.N. USA page identifies the product as PRE-COOKED WHITE CORN MEAL 1KG, declares PRE-COOKED WHITE CORN MEAL ENRICHED as its ingredient, and states serving size 3 Tbsp. (30g). This is a manufacturer-label portion for this named product only. No spoon preparation method, metric volume, SKU/GTIN, or general flour conversion is stated.

decisions.reason: Accept precooked corn flour / farine de maïs précuite as a separate maize-flour identity defined by the precooking product process. Technical review distinguishes precooked refined maize flour from dehydrated nixtamalized flour; manufacturer and Québec-market evidence support the English and French product wording. Keep it separate from masa harina, untreated whole-kernel corn flour, cornmeal, and cornstarch. Do not activate brand, color, or precooked-cornmeal aliases. Density, unit mappings, measurements, and substitutions remain unresearched.

Record the P.A.N. 1 kg label’s 3 Tbsp. (30 g) serving as manufacturer evidence for that named pre-cooked white-corn product on the existing precooked-corn-flour ledger row. Preserve the product scope; do not infer density, a generic serving, an active conversion, or a substitution.

sourceQuantity.unitConvention: The label prints 3 Tbsp.; it gives no metric volume or spoon-preparation method.

decisions.reason: Add source-qualified pregelatinized potato starch / fécule de pomme de terre prégélatinisée as an identity-only FLOUR_AND_STARCH reference. Keep whole-potato flour separate; the reviewed supplier example is a different material and does not establish a Canadian/Québec pregelatinized-flour product. No household measure, reusable density, conversion, or replacement ratio is supported, so add no forms, measures, mappings, recipe links, yields, conversions, or substitutions.

decisions.reason: Accept a separate proso/common-millet flour identity, distinct from common-millet grain and generic millet flour. The French display follows OQLF’s millet commun and current Canadian French flour wording; no aliases, forms, numeric behavior, recipe links, or substitutions are established. Measurement and substitution research remains not_yet_researched.

Add only the qualified English alias proso millet atta to the existing proso-millet-flour reference. The maker identifies atta as finely milled proso millet, with corroborating Canada-facing product wording and Canadian proso-flour retail context. Keep displays, French aliases, category, forms, null active density, empty unit mappings, and recipe links unchanged. Measurement research found no supported household flour measure; the 0.79 g/mL value is intact grain. Preserve both bread studies as formula-specific blocked findings with no active substitution.

Add only barri flour as an English search alias to the existing proso-millet-flour reference. Two supplier product listings pair Barri with proso millet flour, and ICAR–IIMR maps Hindi Barri to proso millet. Preserve the current displays, proso millet atta alias, category, null active density, empty unit mappings, forms, measurements, recipes, and blocked substitution research; add no Barri Atta alias or product form.

Keep barri atta unassigned pending stronger food and local product evidence. The only exact proso-flour page reviewed with this phrase had every listed size sold out, and a 2018 ethnobotanical paper uses the same exact phrase for an unidentified medicinal plant rather than food. Neither establishes current Canadian or Québec usage.

Add only panivaragu maavu as an English search alias to the existing proso-millet-flour identity. The current Organic Mandya maker page names Panivaragu Maavu, and Sempulam identifies Pani Varagu Maavu as proso flour; a Canada-localized Silkrute snapshot provides limited corroboration of the closed Panivaragu spelling. Keep spaced pani varagu maavu and the Mavu spelling out of active aliases to preserve picker behavior and exact spelling support. Preserve existing displays, null active density, empty unit mappings, forms, recipe links, and blocked substitution research.

substitutionFindings.context: Partial replacement of 87.50%-extraction wheat flour with proso millet flour in the studied Egyptian balady-bread formulas.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study tested 10–25% proso-millet-flour blends and reported its highest overall acceptability at 15% in that balady-bread system.
limitations: Study-specific formula and consumer context; it does not support replacement in arbitrary bread, chapati, roti, cakes, cookies, pastry, or thickening.
Do not convert the tested percentages into an active recipe rule or assume another flour extraction, grind, hydration, or process behaves the same way.

substitutionFindings.context: Optimized wheat/proso-millet composite bread formula using emulsifiers and enzymes.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study optimized an experimental 50:50 wheat/proso composite with emulsifiers and enzymes; its abstract notes that higher millet additions required higher dough moisture.
limitations: The result depends on a specified experimental bread system and additives; it does not establish an arbitrary recipe substitution or transferable hydration correction.
No active replacement quantity, form conversion, recipe-line substitution, or general dough adjustment is supported.

substitutionFindings.context: General replacement of Pupuru in the tested traditional cassava-flour and cooked-dough setting, including fufu and lafun.
substitutionFindings.basis: The comparative study reports significant functional differences among fufu, lafun, and pupuru flours and concludes that their flours and cooked doughs cannot suitably substitute for one another in the tested market and consumer setting. No replacement ratio is inferred.
limitations: The conclusion is limited to the study’s tested traditional products and settings; it does not evaluate every possible recipe use or establish that no context-specific substitute exists.
No runtime substitution rule is activated.

rejectedCandidates.reason: The comparative study does not support these products as suitable substitutes for Pupuru in its tested market and consumer setting.

decisions.reason: Add Pupuru as a distinct smoked, fermented cassava product in FLOUR_AND_STARCH. Use pupuru in both display fields, with the French display provisional pending independent Québec review; add only the English alias pupuru flour. Keep generic cassava flour on its existing identity and leave pukuru unassigned because the broader naming source conflicts with the focused product comparison. Add no forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitution rules.

Independent Québec French wording review retains pupuru as the provisional borrowed French display and keeps aliasesFr empty. The reviewed French thesis uses Pupuru outside Québec, the Canadian English product listing is from Ontario, and OQLF farine de manioc is a broader dry-ground root-flour term. No Québec-specific display or French alias is established.

sources.title: Kurek, M.A., and Sokolova, N. Optimization of bread quality with quinoa flour of different particle size and degree of wheat flour replacement
sources.locator: Publisher abstract; §§2.1–2.3 materials and bread preparation; §§3.2–3.6 results and optimized bread; conclusion.
sources.supports: Primary study of quinoa-flour particle size and wheat-flour replacement in bread. The authors report local-supplier wheat and quinoa flour, prepare quinoa particle-size classes, and test a response-surface design spanning 1.1–17.4% substitution. The selected lab-bread optimum is 219 μm quinoa flour and 5.41% substitution. The paper does not identify a wheat-flour grade, quinoa cultivar/color, or matching commercial flour, and the optimized result is not a reusable home-recipe ratio.

decisions.reason: Add red rice / riz rouge as an identity-only GRAIN_AND_CEREAL entry scoped to edible red-bran rice used as food. The federal bilingual food specification has separate Red Rice / Riz rouge entries and describes a generally unhulled or partially hulled grain whose red bran colors the cooked dish; USDA defines red rice by appreciable red bran. CFIA’s survey groups red, black, and unspecified rice under its analytical Riz – Autre category, which does not erase the directly documented product identity. Agricultural literature also uses red rice for weedy rice; do not match agronomic weed references, red-rice vinegar, red yeast rice, or named regional/cultivar products to this unqualified food identity. Brown is a separate, potentially overlapping milling axis. Add no aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions. No bundled recipe wording or exact normalized-key collision was found. Independent Québec French review remains open.

Reconfirm red rice / riz rouge for edible red-bran rice using the federal bilingual food specification and current Metro Québec product listing. decisions.reason: Keep one generic rice identity and represent the recipe-relevant dry and cooked states as forms. The current linked recipe lines are explicitly cooked and now carry the cooked form. Keep named rice types and milling distinctions out of a Cartesian product; no aliases, density, unit mapping, conversion, cooking yield, or substitution are inferred.

Add only chawal as an English-search alias on the existing generic rice identity. An official regional source identifies it as a Hindi name for Oryza sativa, and a Canadian rice retailer applies it to a named whole-rice product. Keep the generic rice / riz display, all named varieties, milling distinctions, dry/cooked forms, numeric data, and substitution state unchanged. Add no Dhan/Chamal spellings, French alias, dish phrase, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution.

Add only uruchi rice and uruchimai as English-search aliases on the existing generic rice identity. Government of Japan and MAFF sources support uruchi rice as ordinary table/common Japanese rice distinct from glutinous rice; Tiger attests Uruchimai as a spelling but specifically describes short-grain rice. Route both queries to rice / riz without adding a new identity, French alias, or grain-length, Japonica, or sushi claim. Keep existing forms, numeric fields, measurement research state, and substitution research state unchanged; add no recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

expectedEffects: The study reports changes to dough rheology and several pizza-base physical and nutritional properties as the rice bean flour proportion increases.

Record that reviewed evidence does not support a reusable wheat-flour replacement across the white/brown rice-flour family. Keep the white- and brown-rice study outcomes formula-specific; add no active substitution rule, replacement amount, hydration adjustment, or recipe link.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether unqualified rice flour, covering the white- and brown-rice source grades identified by OQLF, has a reusable wheat-flour replacement across recipe types and ingredient roles.

sources.title: Kohyama et al., Changes in starch, β-glucan, physicochemical properties, and flavor compounds in barley flour by roasting
sources.versionOrDate: Food Science and Technology Research 28(5) (2022), 363–371; DOI 10.3136/fstr.FSTR-D-22-00054.
sources.locator: Materials and Methods, water-absorption test; Table 4; Conclusion.
sources.supports: Original research on flour made from one barley cultivar under controlled roasting and milling conditions. The study reports water absorption of 1.78–2.27 mL/g dry weight after 90 minutes at 25°C and 4.98–2.46 mL/g after 30 minutes at 90°C across the raw and roasted samples. These are laboratory water-uptake tests, not bulk density, a household measure, or a recipe replacement amount; the authors say further study is needed for food-product conditions and sensory acceptance.

decisions.reason: Keep roasted barley flour / farine d'orge torréfiée as a distinct FLOUR_AND_STARCH product from a Québec mill, separate from general and malted barley flour. Add `toasted barley flour` as its English alias: Eurogerm's manufacturer catalogue identifies a barley product by that term, and its Parfen specification defines the product family as roasted cereal flour made by milling roasted cereal [WP02-S144–S145], matching the basic barley-plus-roasting-and-milling identity of the Québec mill's product [WP02-S123–S124]. This is a name/class equivalence, not a claim of identical brand-specific processing or performance. Keep `hattai-ko` and `mugikogashi` unresolved and off this row because Japanese sources document regionally variable cereal inputs and no Québec French naming or equivalence to the Québec product [WP02-S141–S143]. Leave density, unit mappings, forms, conversions, yields, measurements, and substitutions inactive.

Independent Québec review retains farine d’orge torréfiée as the existing display and keeps the exact English toasted barley flour alias on this row only. Feminine agreement is correct if farine is characterized as roasted; the Québec mill describes its own thermal process but does not clearly state whether the grain or resulting flour is treated. No universal process equivalence with other roasted barley products is inferred. The bundled corpus has no matching row or direct link.

Complete the evidence-state review while keeping reusable measures, conversions, and home-recipe replacement behavior unsupported. Manufacturer use descriptions and commercial addition guidance do not establish a household quantity or replacement basis, and the roasting study reports laboratory water absorption under controlled conditions rather than recipe guidance.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether the existing roasted barley flour has a reusable household measure or replacement amount, especially as a wheat-flour replacement across home-recipe types and ingredient roles.
substitutionFindings.basis: The Québec manufacturer gives qualitative baking uses but no quantities. Eurogerm gives an indicative 0.5–5% addition for its commercial Parfen range, with a 25 kg bag and 100 kg minimum order, but does not state the percentage denominator or replacement basis. One original study measures laboratory water absorption of flour made from a single barley cultivar and controlled roasting/milling process; it calls for further work on food-product conditions and sensory acceptance.
limitations: Do not encode Eurogerm's range as a household dose, replacement percentage, or denominator.
Do not infer density, cup mass, hydration adjustment, baking performance, or a substitute amount from laboratory water-absorption values.
Do not transfer the study to the Québec product, other roasting profiles, malted barley flour, whole barley flour, or a home recipe without matching product/formula evidence.

decisions.reason: Accept the exact Canadian Nutrient File product name as a narrow GRAIN_AND_CEREAL identity for buckwheat groats, roasted, dry / gruau de sarrasin, rôti, sec. Keep it distinct from buckwheat flour and the prepared gruel kacha / kasha; those prepared-dish names are not activated as aliases. Revise only the Québec French picker display to grains de sarrasin rôtis et secs. The current Canadian Nutrient File wording gruau de sarrasin, rôti, sec is documented and understandable, but OQLF records the familiar dish sense of gruau as cooked porridge and a technical grits sense scoped to malt crushing; a Québec product listing directly describes the roasted kernels as grains de sarrasin rôtis. This is a descriptive catalog label, not an OQLF-prescribed term. Keep the English display and identity unchanged, retain the separation from buckwheat flour and prepared kacha/kasha, and add no aliases, forms, measurements, densities, mappings, yields, recipe links, conversions, or substitutions. The current bundled corpus has no matching recipe line or mention.

Add the two CNF 2026 Food Code 4412 type-6 volume rows as separate edition-specific portion observations on the existing roasted, dry buckwheat-groats identity. Leave the type-9 Yield 36.04 entry uninterpreted and exclude the mass-only and refuse rows. These observations do not establish a reusable measure, density, mapping, conversion, cooking yield, recipe amount, or substitution; keep the prior CNF 2015 page values separate.

Keep the display grains de sarrasin rôtis et secs and add only the French search alias sarrasin grillé to the existing roasted dry buckwheat-groats identity. Québec producer and retailer wording supports the phrase for roasted grains. Do not activate kacha/kasha: the reviewed sources use it for both dry roasted grains and an OQLF-defined cooked gruel, so the unqualified term remains ambiguous for the picker. The recipe’s 40 g / 1/4 tasse amount is formula-specific; add no measurement observation, form, density, mapping, conversion, cooking yield, recipe link, or substitution.

sources.title: Kaur, Sukhmandeep, and Navjot Kaur. Development and sensory evaluation of gluten free bakery products using quinoa (Chenopodium Quinoa) flour
sources.versionOrDate: Journal of Applied and Natural Science 9(4), 2449–2455 (2017); DOI 10.31018/jans.v9i4.1552
sources.locator: Abstract: tested roasted quinoa flour levels, 10/45/45 gluten-free flour blend, and panel size.
sources.supports: Primary article reports roasted quinoa flour tested at 5%, 10%, and 15% in gluten-free cookies, cakes, muffins, pies, and tarts. Its abstract reports high acceptance for a 10% roasted-quinoa, 45% rice, 45% oat flour blend in a semi-trained panel of 10. It gives no household flour measure or mass-volume conversion and does not identify the flour as the Moulins product.

sources.title: Park, Sang Ha, Tomoko Maeda, and Naofumi Morita. Effect of Whole Quinoa Flours and Lipase on the Chemical, Rheological and Breadmaking Characteristics of Wheat Flour
sources.locator: Abstract; materials and methods; bread formula; Tables 3 and 4.
sources.supports: Primary study compares stone-mortar quinoa flour and roller-milled/roasted quinoa flour (RMRQ) in bread. It reports 10%, 20%, and 30% (w/w) replacement levels, a 280 g total-flour breadmaker formula, decreasing loaf volume as quinoa substitution rose, and experimental farinograph water-absorption results. The RMRQ sample is sourced from imported Peruvian quinoa and is not identified as the Moulins product; the formula is not a household measure or general replacement instruction.

decisions.reason: Add a distinct, source-bounded roasted quinoa flour identity from the Québec mill, separate from generic quinoa flour [WP02-HATTAI-KOGI-FUNCTIONAL-FLOUR-20261010-S06–S08]. Use the grammatically agreeing fr-CA display farine de quinoa torréfiée; keep aliases empty and independent Québec terminology review open. The recipe audit found no matching bundled line, so make no recipe link. Leave density, unit mappings, forms, conversions, yields, measurements, and substitutions inactive.

Independent Québec review retains farine de quinoa torréfiée as a provisional display. The manufacturer’s French headings use masculine torréfié, which can characterize quinoa before milling; the reviewed pages do not establish whether roasting occurs before or after milling. Do not settle that process by agreement alone, and add no alias or product equivalence. The bundled corpus has no matching row or direct link.

Record the completed research review on the existing verified Moulins-product row. The available study formulas do not establish a reusable household measure or a general home-recipe replacement for this source-bounded product; keep active numeric and substitution behavior unchanged.

substitutionFindings.context: Whether the Moulins de Soulanges roasted quinoa flour has a reusable home-recipe measure or a transferable flour-replacement instruction.
substitutionFindings.basis: The mill pages give qualitative absorption/performance claims and suggested uses, without a quantity. Kaur and Kaur tested 5%, 10%, and 15% roasted quinoa flour in gluten-free baked goods, with a 10% quinoa, 45% rice, 45% oat flour blend rated highly by a semi-trained panel of 10. Park et al. tested study-prepared RMRQ at 10%, 20%, and 30% (w/w) in one 280 g flour breadmaker formula; loaf volume decreased as substitution increased, and the RMRQ material was not identified as the Moulins product.
expectedEffects: In Park et al.'s experimental bread formula, increasing the study-prepared RMRQ share reduced loaf volume; the reported lipase response varied by substitution level.
Kaur and Kaur report high sensory acceptance for their tested 10% roasted-quinoa, 45% rice, 45% oat gluten-free blend; the result is formula- and panel-specific.
limitations: The tested flour materials and processing are not established as the Moulins de Soulanges product represented by this reference.
Do not treat experimental blend percentages as general home-recipe replacements, a household measure, or a mass-volume conversion.
Do not activate a global or contextual substitution rule or attach a recipe-line substitution; the bundled corpus has no matching quinoa-flour line.

decisions.reason: Hold the broad salt-pork identity: OQLF pairs salt pork with petit salé / lard salé but describes a commonly sold salted-and-cooked pork product, while the cited Canadian labeling source names salt pork without defining its composition. Do not activate the French terms as global aliases until the intended recipe/product scope is fixed. No numeric or substitution data is inferred.

A follow-up review confirms both OQLF terminology and current Québec salt-pork-labelled products, but these sources cover a cooked petit-salé product and distinct brined lard-salé belly products. The evidence still does not establish the cut or ready-to-eat state for every recipe use. Retain the broad candidate unresolved; keep it distinct from bacon, pancetta, guanciale, ham, and prosciutto. Do not activate names or aliases or infer safety, storage, conversion, or substitution.

sources.supports: Lists Eel / Anguille for A. dieffenbachii, A. japonica, and A. rostrata; separately lists American eel / Anguille américaine for A. rostrata, a more qualified Short-finned Eel / Anguille d’Australie for A. australis, and Conger Eel for Conger spp. This is Canadian fish-label naming evidence, not a recipe synonym or culinary-equivalence rule.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Guidance on determining the common names for fish sold or processed in Canada
sources.locator: Purpose and CFIA Fish List common-name instructions.
sources.supports: Describes the Fish List as the source of English and French common names used to label commercial fish in Canada. It governs labeling naming scope; it does not prescribe recipe search aliases or establish a single culinary identity for every use of the word eel.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked eel / anguille fumée as a species-neutral finished-food market group, not a species identity or a form under American eel. Preserve the existing American-eel reference and unqualified-eel candidate; keep unagi and kabayaki boundaries separate. Add no aliases, forms, reusable measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, flétan du Groenland (GDT)
sources.versionOrDate: Last updated 2012; preferred term normalized July 2004
sources.locator: Preferred terms, Latin name, and terms used in certain contexts
sources.supports: Identifies Reinhardtius hippoglossoides, normalizes flétan du Groenland, and lists flétan noir as a preferred term. It says turbot and turbot du Groenland were not retained for Québec fish-product marketing to avoid consumer-label confusion, and distinguishes European turbot.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA Fish List lookup for Reinhardtius hippoglossoides
sources.locator: TSN 172930 and the listed English/French common names
sources.supports: Maps Reinhardtius hippoglossoides to Greenland halibut / flétan du Groenland and lists flétan noir among the species names. The lookup also lists trade names containing turbot; the OQLF consumer-product boundary is used to keep those terms out of aliases.

sources.title: Québec Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, Poissons de fond et pélagiques du Québec
sources.locator: Greenland-halibut product descriptions, average size/weight, and general information
sources.supports: Names Reinhardtius hippoglossoides / Greenland halibut and flétan du Groenland, also uses flétan noir, describes several fresh, frozen, whole, head/carcass, “dentelle”, and smoked product states, and calls the species a good substitute for several fish. Its 50–55 cm and 1–1.5 kg whole-fish profile and product sizes are not recipe portions; the broad substitute note supplies no recipe role, method, or replacement quantity.

decisions.reason: Add the species-qualified smoked Greenland-halibut finished-food identity separately from raw Greenland halibut. Keep the manufacturer carton and mixed-trio amount product-specific; add no aliases, forms, reusable measures, mappings, conversions, package yields, recipe links, or active substitutions.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, gades fumés (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and note distinguishing a single smoked fish (including aiglefin fumé) from mixed gades fumés / Finnan haddie, and warning about the canned product name.
sources.supports: For a single fish in the product family, the OQLF directs the writer to the species-specific term, including aiglefin fumé. It reserves gades fumés for a mix of listed gadids and distinguishes the canned Finnan haddie product from a split, smoked, lightly salted haddock preparation. It does not establish a universal product formula or preparation state.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Aiglefin species profile
sources.locator: Species heading, Latin name, and Canadian range.
sources.supports: Identifies aiglefin as Melanogrammus aeglefinus and documents the species in Canadian Atlantic waters. Biological species evidence; it does not define the smoked product or its recipe behavior.

sources.title: Real Atlantic Superstore, smoked-fish product listings (French and English storefronts)
sources.locator: Current indexed product listing for Sea Bright Smoked Haddock / Aiglefin fumé, Sea Bright; prepared-in-Canada label and per-weight prices.
sources.supports: The French listing uses Aiglefin fumé and the English listing uses Sea Bright Smoked Haddock. The item was out of stock in the selected listing. The storefront page returned 403 to direct retrieval; the indexed current listing supplied the displayed titles and price basis. This supports market wording only, not a common UPC, formula, stock at other locations, or processing details.

sources.title: Fisherman's Market, Frozen Cold Smoked Haddock Fillets
sources.locator: Current product page title, description, package amount, and availability note.
sources.supports: Halifax seafood retailer lists frozen cold-smoked haddock fillets smoked by its Seabright Smokehouse, in a one-pound package. It is one named product example; its cold-smoked, frozen, fillet, and package details are not generalized to the identity. The seller says availability and prices vary with landings and seasonality.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked haddock / aiglefin fumé as a named PROTEIN product scoped to the existing haddock species identity. Keep plain haddock separate and omit Finnan haddie / gades fumés, which OQLF uses for a broader or mixed/canned product boundary. Current Canadian listings support the product name, but not a universal smoke method, storage state, measure, yield, or substitution; the bundled corpus has no matching line. Add no forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: CFIA, Canadian Grade Compendium: Volume 8 — Fish
sources.locator: Fish Grade Requirements, Interpretation, definition of herring.
sources.supports: Defines herring for this Canadian fish-grade compendium as Clupea harengus or Clupea pallasii. This supports leaving unqualified herring unresolved across species, not treating Atlantic and Pacific herring as equivalent.

sources.title: OQLF, GDT: bouffi.
sources.locator: Definition for the edible-fish term and its listed French and English equivalents.
sources.supports: Defines the edible-fish term as whole salted and smoked herring; lists bouffi, craquelot, and hareng bouffi, with English bloater. Terminology source, not a current retail specification.

sources.title: DFO, Plan de gestion intégrée des pêches au hareng de l’Atlantique dans la région des Maritimes — Zone 15.

sources.supports: Provides Québec production and trade context for smoked herring called hareng bouffi. It is historical management-plan evidence, not current store inventory or a package specification.

sources.title: Leslie Leger & Sons Ltd., Salted/Smoked Herring Choice Bloaters (Whole or Split).

sources.supports: A current New Brunswick producer describes locally caught Atlantic herring, salt-brine cure, slight desalting, a 4–6 week smokehouse process, and an 18 lb box. Species, process, and package details are producer-specific; title includes whole or split presentations.

sources.title: Merex Inc., Contact.

sources.supports: Toronto retailer lists an option labelled Whole Herring (Bloaters), approximately 1 lb or 3–4 pieces. The option was crossed out at access, so stock is unconfirmed and package wording is not a reusable measure.

sources.title: Intercambio Canada, Hareng.
sources.locator: French supplier product description, whole-fish and process statements.
sources.supports: Calls its Canadian product salted/smoked herring and names Clupea harengus for that product. Its approximate fish weights, case size, durations, and nutrition basis are supplier-specific; no general measurement is adopted.

sources.title: Translation Bureau, TERMIUM Plus: craquelot.
sources.locator: Terminology entry for craquelot and bloater.
sources.supports: Lists bouffi and craquelot for the herring product, notes Canadian use of bloater for hareng saur, and notes the freshwater-fish use of bloater for Coregonus hoyi. Supports qualified naming; it does not replace the CFIA/OQLF product definition.

substitutionFindings.context: No bundled recipe identifies a substitution context for whole salted-and-smoked round herring bloaters.
substitutionFindings.basis: The Intercambio supplier suggests using its product like anchovies but gives no matched recipe, quantity, or ratio. Reviewed sources do not establish a replacement for raw herring, oil-packed smoked herring fillets, kippers, Matjes, rollmops, or other fish products.
limitations: Do not encode a global or contextual substitution without recipe-specific evidence and a supported replacement basis.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked herring bloater / hareng bouffi as a species-neutral PROTEIN market group for salted-and-smoked round herring. CFIA distinguishes bloaters from bloater fillets and defines herring across Clupea harengus and C. pallasii; do not assign a species or merge fillets, split kippers, oil-packed fillets, Matjes, rollmops, sauces, or composite spreads. Use only bloaters, bouffis, and craquelot as source-backed aliases. Retain no measures, forms, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions; the corpus has no demand.

sources.title: Rügen Fisch, Bücklingsfilets in Pflanzenöl

sources.supports: The manufacturer describes smoked herring fillets packed in rapeseed oil and own juice; its ingredient list names Clupea harengus (75%), rapeseed oil, salt, and beechwood smoke. These are facts for this maker’s SKU only and do not assign species or formula to the wider market group. Search indexing supplied the product content; direct retrieval timed out.

sources.supports: The retailer uses the exact French product wording for the named Rügen Fisch oil-packed smoked-herring fillets. It supports local market naming, not species, universal processing details, or a package measure.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked herring fillets in oil / filets de hareng fumés à l’huile as a finished-food market group. Canadian retail listings support the English and Québec-facing French names, and the manufacturer documents one matching product. Keep it separate from plain herring species, herring in tomato sauce, whole smoked herring, kippers, and other smoked-fish identities. The manufacturer’s species, fish percentage, ingredients, and the retailer package amount remain SKU-specific. No bundled recipe demand; add no aliases, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA Fish List search for Lake Whitefish
sources.locator: Species rows for Coregonus clupeaformis and broad whitefish.
sources.supports: Lists Coregonus clupeaformis under multiple common-name rows and also assigns Whitefish / Poisson Blanc wording to broad whitefish, Coregonus nasus. Supports the species boundary; do not copy broad names as aliases.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, grand corégone (GDT)
sources.locator: Grand dictionnaire terminologique; zoology and edible-fish domains.
sources.supports: Directly pairs grand corégone, lake whitefish, and Coregonus clupeaformis; identifies grand corégone as the Québec standardized term and explains that poisson blanc is not species-specific.

substitutionFindings.context: General recipe substitution review for smoked lake whitefish, bounded to the reviewed Canadian and Québec sources and bundled recipe corpus.
substitutionFindings.basis: The Ontario dip gives an amount only for its own recipe method, the corpus has no matching recipe, and the reviewed sources do not compare a directional replacement with quantity or method adjustments.
limitations: This finding covers only the sources and bundled corpus reviewed; it is not proof that no substitute exists.
Do not infer equivalence between smoked and raw lake whitefish or between species-qualified and species-unknown smoked whitefish.
Do not infer cooking or food-safety equivalence.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked lake whitefish / grand corégone fumé as a species-qualified finished-food reference for Coregonus clupeaformis. Keep generic smoked whitefish and species-unknown Canadian listings unallocated; preserve the Québec OQLF species term and add no aliases, forms, reusable measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or supported substitutions.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked mackerel / maquereau fumé as a finished-food market product group, separate from raw mackerel species. Current Québec producers and retailers use both base-language names, while source-specific products differ in cut, seasoning, smoking method, package amount, and storage state. Keep those details product-specific; do not infer species, universal smoke method, readiness, storage, measure, yield, or substitution. No bundled recipe demand was found.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked mussels / moules fumées as a named finished-product group. Current manufacturer and distributor pages use this bilingual wording, MAPAQ documents smoked formats for Québec blue mussels, and the manufacturer reports more than one Mytilus source scope for its own product. The recipe bundle has no matching demand; add no aliases, forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

substitutionFindings.context: Global and contextual substitutions for finished smoked sardine fillets.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed market and manufacturer sources establish product names and package-specific details, not tested quantity-preserving replacements. The bundled recipe corpus has no matching ingredient demand.
limitations: Do not infer equivalence with canned sardines, fresh or raw sardines, whole smoked sardines, herring, kippers, or other smoked fish.
A future contextual rule would require a named dish, ingredient role, preparation method, and tested replacement amount.

decisions.reason: Add species-neutral identity-only smoked sardine fillets / filets de sardines fumés in PROTEIN, with only golden-smoked and fillet-qualified aliases. Keep it distinct from the broad canned-sardine group, raw sardine species, herring identities, and the unresolved Brunswick Kippered product. Do not infer one taxon, universal smoking process, or common formula.

Retain the Brunswick 80 g drained Nutrition Facts basis, Metro 92 g package listing, and Wild Canadian Seafood 180 g format only as source- and product-specific observations. Do not infer a common can size, drained yield, reusable measure, density, or conversion.

Keep broad smoked-sardine wording off the aliases because the reviewed market includes an oil-packed smoked product with no stated fillet cut. Preserve the existing Brunswick Kippered hold because its species and smoking process remain unverified.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only smoked trout / truite fumée as a finished-food market product group, separate from raw trout species and from smoked-trout spread or pastry. Current Québec producer and retailer listings support the bilingual product wording, while product-specific sources show cold-smoked and hot-smoked presentations, different cuts, and package sizes. sources.supports: Supports Trichosanthes cucumerina L. as the accepted species and its placement in Cucurbitaceae. This taxonomic backbone does not by itself establish food use or a local common name.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Plants of the World Online, Trichosanthes cucumerina var. anguina
sources.locator: Synonym section.
sources.supports: Supports treating Trichosanthes cucumerina var. anguina as a synonym of the accepted T. cucumerina subsp. cucumerina, rather than as a separate accepted species or catalog identity.

sources.supports: Supports T. cucumerina as a vegetable crop and records snake gourd, serpent gourd, club gourd, wild snake gourd, concombre serpent, couleuvre végétale, patole, and serpent végétal as common names. sources.title: Institut agronomique néo-calédonien, Agripedia, Courge serpent

sources.supports: Supports the French name courge serpent for T. cucumerina and the culinary scope: the immature fruit is cooked and eaten as a vegetable, while the mature fruit changes color and becomes fibrous and bitter. It also names leaves, young shoots, seeds, and mature pulp as separate uses; it supplies no household measure or conversion.

sources.title: International Plant Protection Convention, Fresh Fruits and Vegetables Import Manual, List of Approved Names
sources.locator: Entries for edible snake gourd and pointed gourd.
sources.supports: Separates Trichosanthes anguina/T. cucumerina from pointed gourd T. dioica and assigns patole and related spellings to pointed gourd in this manual. The naming conflict is sufficient reason to keep patole out of a global alias array.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Medicinal Plant Names Services, patola

sources.supports: Shows patola associated with multiple accepted Luffa and Trichosanthes taxa, including Luffa acutangula, Luffa aegyptiaca, T. dioica, and T. cucumerina. It is lexical-ambiguity evidence, not a culinary or retail standard.

decisions.reason: Accept snake gourd / courge serpent as the cultivated immature-fruit food identity of Trichosanthes cucumerina. Kew accepts the species and treats var. anguina as a synonym under the species; IAC documents immature fruit cooked as a vegetable; and a Québec retailer provides the matching bilingual Chichinda seed-cultivar labels. Use edible snake gourd and serpent végétal as the only proposed aliases. Keep source-conflicted or regional alternatives out of the default aliases, including patole/patola, serpent gourd, club gourd, snake cucumber, and melon serpent. Add no form, measurement, conversion, substitution, or recipe link.

The descriptive qualifiers make the scope explicit. Keep red, gray, and yellowtail snapper and their qualified French names outside aliases; do not assign a taxon or imply species interchangeability. decisions.reason: Add identity-only snow crab sections / sections de crabe des neiges for the marketable section/cluster assembly. Do not claim a species, add a standalone snow crab alias, or reopen the R12 species hold. Keep crab legs, picked meat, claws, other crab products, and freshwater crayfish separate. Source-specific serving and package amounts remain evidence only; add no forms, measures, density, mappings, package or edible yield, recipe links, conversions, or substitutions.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only soubressade / sobrasada as a PROTEIN reference, with the OQLF French phrase and TERMIUM English spelling variant as the only aliases. decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic sorghum bran / son de sorgho as a grain milling fraction with documented human-food use.
