sources.title: Sharanagat et al. Effect of sorghum pre-processing (roasting and germination) on the replacement level and quality of sorghum-wheat bread: bread characteristics, digestibility, consumer acceptability and microbiological analysis
sources.versionOrDate: Journal of Food Science and Technology 61(2) (2024), 253–267; first published 2023-09-27; DOI 10.1007/s13197-023-05810-3
sources.locator: Materials and Methods: Material, Processing of sorghum, Table 1; Results and discussion; Conclusion.
sources.supports: Primary experimental study of sorghum–wheat bread. The authors identify cultivar HJ-513, mill unprocessed control sorghum through a 212 μm sieve, and test composite bread formulas with rice flour fixed at 10%, control sorghum flour at 10–40%, and refined wheat flour at 80–50%. The control-sorghum bread is reported as acceptably rated up to 20% sorghum flour in this formula family. These results are limited to the study cultivar, milling, co-ingredient, additions, method, and sensory assessment; they do not establish a general wheat-flour replacement ratio.

decisions.reason: Accepted as an identity-only product with the Codex English / Québec French display pair “sorghum flour / farine de sorgho”. Confirms sorghum flour as a named milling product distinct from sorghum grain and provides the official French product name. No aliases, measurements, or substitutions were added.

Add jowar flour as one English alias on the existing sorghum flour / farine de sorgho identity. FSSAI defines the paired jowar/sorghum flour product from Sorghum bicolor, and a current Canadian mill uses the paired product name. OQLF and Canadian French retail wording support retaining farine de sorgho. Keep bare jowar, jowar atta, and farine de jowar out of this decision; keep grain sorghum separate. No forms, recipe links, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are added.

Hold milo flour off the sorghum-flour aliases because current phrase search would make a bare milo query return sorghum flour alone despite a distinct current Canadian Milo chocolate-malt drink product. Keep the existing jowar flour alias and bilingual display; add no French alias, form, measure, density, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution. The qualified flour phrase is supported on specific Canadian retail listings but not established as a safe unqualified search term.

Add `jowar atta` as the only new English alias on the existing sorghum flour / farine de sorgho identity. ICAR–IIMR identifies Jowar Atta as sorghum flour, and two Canadian retailers pair the exact phrase with sorghum flour. Keep bare jowar, unqualified sorghum atta, multigrain atta, and French aliases out of this decision. No forms, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions are added.

Add `guinea corn flour` as an English alias on the existing sorghum-flour reference. The manufacturer and regional research sources support the phrase while the studied process remains source-specific. Keep `farine de sorgho`, forms, density, mappings, and active rules unchanged; retain the manufacturer-labeled 3 tbsp (30 g) serving only as a product-specific ledger observation, and do not infer a universal ratio or density.

Keep `mabele flour` and `amabele flour` unallocated. Regional sources support sorghum as the crop but do not establish a stable boundary between Mabele meal and the standardized sorghum-flour identity; one study uses Mabele Meal for a particular flour sample, while other evidence describes a breakfast cereal/meal. Canadian Mabela listings do not establish composition, and the current Québec product wording remains generic `Farine de Sorgho`. Preserve the current identity, French display, aliases, measurement observation, and blocked substitution research. Do not generalize the 3 tbsp (30 g) manufacturer observation to Mabele, or add any active alias, measure, conversion, form, recipe link, or substitution.

Add only `sweet white sorghum flour` and `farine douce de sorgho blanc` as exact bilingual search aliases on the existing `ingredient-ref-sorghum-flour`. Bob’s Red Mill’s Canadian product list pairs the English Sorghum Flour name with the French wording, and current Canadian and Montréal-facing listings corroborate the exact phrases. This is a name update, not a new identity, cultivar, separate milling process, sweetener, or standardized flour class. Keep `white sorghum flour` and other shorter/broader variants unstored; the picker matches the qualified phrases within the aliases. Keep the existing display, forms, density, unit mappings, measurement observation, and blocked substitution research unchanged. The retailer’s 623 g is package mass; the manufacturer serving and blend suggestion do not establish candidate-specific density, unit mapping, or replacement ratio.

Keep jowari flour off the active sorghum-flour aliases. Canadian product descriptions connect jowari with sorghum in a flour context, and FSSAI identifies Jwari as a regional sorghum name, but the reviewed Canadian pages do not title a product Jowari Flour. Adding the qualified phrase would make a bare jowari query return only the flour row while the grain-sorghum row remains unaliased. Preserve current displays, aliases, forms, measurement observations, and substitution research; reconsider after a grain-scoped query decision or qualifier-preserving search behavior.

Add `red sorghum flour` as an English alias to the existing sorghum-flour identity. Current Canadian distribution and a miller listing use the exact product name, with the miller identifying red sorghum grain as the source. Keep the French display and aliases unchanged; do not create a red-specific flour identity or add shorter red jowar terms. Preserve all existing measurements and blocked substitution research without transferring product-specific recipe quantities.

Record Sharanagat et al.'s untreated HJ-513 sorghum-flour bread trial as one formula-scoped finding on the existing generic sorghum-flour row. The fixed rice-flour share, specific flour sample and process, and unidentified refined-wheat class do not support a reusable wheat-replacement rule. Preserve the existing measurement evidence and Westpoint finding; keep active catalog behavior and recipe links unchanged.

substitutionFindings.context: Westpoint says its Organic Sorghum Flour has texture and taste similar to wheat, lists baking uses, and suggests combining it with tapioca starch, cornstarch, or legume flours.
substitutionFindings.basis: The manufacturer supplies qualitative use guidance but no replacement quantity, ratio, controlled recipe, or method-specific adjustment.

The page concerns one organic whole-grain sorghum-flour product and does not establish behavior for all sorghum or Guinea-corn flour products.
No global or contextual substitution rule or recipe-line link is supported.

substitutionFindings.context: One yeasted composite-bread study using untreated HJ-513 sorghum flour with refined wheat flour and a fixed rice-flour addition.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study compares a 100% refined-wheat control with composite flour bases containing 10% rice flour, 10–40% untreated control sorghum flour, and 80–50% refined wheat flour. It reports control-sorghum bread as acceptably rated up to 20% sorghum flour within this formula family. Water was set according to farinograph analysis, and the bread formula also includes yeast, oil, sugar, and salt.
limitations: The sorghum sample is from one HJ-513 grain lot and is milled through a 212 μm sieve; the result does not establish behavior for every commercial sorghum flour.
All composite formulas include 10% rice flour. The study therefore tests a multi-flour reformulation, not sorghum as the only replacement for wheat flour.
The comparator is described only as local-market refined wheat flour. Do not map it to all-purpose flour or another active wheat-flour reference.
The flour proportions and sensory finding belong to one experimental yeasted-bread process with fixed added ingredients and farinograph-directed water; they are not a home-recipe replacement rule.
No bundled recipe has matching sorghum-flour demand or the study's flour role, quantities, and method. No recipe-line link is supported.

sources.title: Badem, A., Yörük, A., and Şahin, N. Evaluation of the effects of Triticum spelta flour and Ahlat pear flour on the physical, chemical, textural, and sensory properties of bread
sources.versionOrDate: Journal of Food Measurement and Characterization 20, 9510–9522 (2026); published 2026-04-28; DOI 10.1007/s11694-026-04420-9
sources.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods: Materials, Experimental design, Composite flour rheology, Bread production, Sensory analysis; Results: sensory properties; Conclusion.
sources.supports: Primary study of bread formulas using locally purchased common-wheat and Triticum spelta flours, with Ahlat pear flour as a separate factor. The design tests five spelt shares (0–100%) and three Ahlat-pear shares (0–10%) in a 100% total flour blend. The 50% wheat / 50% spelt formula and a distinct 70% wheat / 25% spelt / 5% pear-flour formula have the highest comparable overall-acceptability results in this experiment. Water is adjusted by Mixolab analysis. The samples, formula set, and laboratory process do not establish a general home-recipe replacement ratio.

substitutionFindings.context: One laboratory bread study using local-market Triticum spelta and common-wheat flours, with Ahlat pear flour as a 0–10% formulation factor.
substitutionFindings.basis: The study tests five spelt shares (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%) across formulas with 0%, 5%, or 10% Ahlat pear flour, for a 100% total flour blend. The 50% wheat / 50% spelt formula and a separate 70% wheat / 25% spelt / 5% pear-flour formula receive the highest comparable overall-acceptability results. Water is adjusted from Mixolab rheology; seven trained evaluators assess sensory attributes on a five-point scale. The 100% spelt bread scores lowest for several sensory measures.
limitations: Both wheat flours are local-market samples from Karaman, Türkiye. The article does not name a supplier, cultivar, extraction rate, or milling grade; do not assign the comparator to an active wheat-flour reference or transfer the result to whole-, white-, or another qualified spelt-flour row.

The best-rated pear-containing formula includes a third flour and is not evidence for a stand-alone 25% spelt substitution. The 50% result is one formula in this specific bread experiment, not a home-baking starting ratio.
Water is adjusted by Mixolab, and the laboratory dough process, baking conditions, and seven-person trained panel limit transfer to other breads and recipes.
No bundled RecipeBook recipe matches the flour blend, bread process, or sensory study context; no recipe-line link or active substitution rule is supported.

substitutionFindings.context: King Arthur Baking's R&D tests of spelt as one of eight ancient-grain flours in selected breakfast-baking formulas.
substitutionFindings.basis: The account says the R&D team tested equal-amount 25%, 50%, and 100% substitutions in banana bread, muffins, scones, pancakes, and cinnamon bread. It calls 25% a useful starting point that worked in many recipes without significantly changing flavor and texture; it also advises against more than 50% ancient-grain flour in yeast breads. Quick breads and pancakes were the most adaptable categories in the tested set.
limitations: The tested spelt sample is not identified by brand, cultivar, extraction rate, or other milling grade, and the page does not report separate numeric results for each spelt/formula combination.

The 25% and yeast-bread statements summarize King Arthur's mixed ancient-grain test set and test-kitchen advice; they do not establish one transferable ratio for all generic spelt flour or every dish.
The page does not provide a matching RecipeBook recipe-line context. Keep the guidance source-scoped and do not create an active replacement rule or recipe link.

sources.locator: See proposal source register for the cited term, food, product, or data table.
sources.supports: Uses squash and zucchini blossoms as the ingredient name and gives 8–10 in its own recipe. Does not generalize blossom counts.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Fleurs de courgettes
sources.locator: See proposal source register for the cited term, food, product, or data table.
sources.supports: Québec retailer's product listing supports the exact French market name. The listing's `1 un` is not a weight.

decisions.reason: Add squash blossoms / fleurs de courgettes with the source-supported flower-name aliases. Recipe-specific counts do not establish a universal portion or mass; no form or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, sriracha
sources.locator: Definition and preferred French and English terms, including accepted English misspellings.
sources.supports: Defines sriracha as Thai chili sauce and supports sriacha / sriacha sauce; no equivalence to sambal or sweet chili sauce.

decisions.reason: Removed source-less draft density and unit-mapping values from the active bundled catalog. Restore a value only with source, exact food/form, unit convention, method or basis, and reviewer disposition.

Verify the existing sriracha identity and add OQLF-listed French and English spellings. Keep it distinct from sambal, sweet chili sauce, and generic chili paste. Add no forms, density, unit mapping, package yield, measurement observation, conversion, or substitution rule in this batch.

sources.title: Sempio, Ssamjang, Korean Soybean Dipping Paste
sources.locator: Product description and ingredients
sources.supports: Manufacturer describes ssamjang as a dipping paste blending soybean paste (doenjang), red chili paste (gochujang), sesame, and vegetables. This is one product formulation.

sources.title: Canadian Intellectual Property Office, Trademarks Journal, 2026-02-18 (French)
sources.locator: French goods listing
sources.supports: Canadian French goods wording includes pâte de soya fermentée au piment fort (gochujang), pâte de soya fermentée (doenjang), and pâte de haricots assaisonnée (ssamjang). This is trademark terminology, not an OQLF recommendation or food standard.

sources.title: Haisue, Sempio collection (French)
sources.locator: Sempio product titles in Canadian French collection
sources.supports: Retail titles include Korean chili paste Gochujang, Korean soybean paste Doenjang, and Ssamjang Korean soybean dipping paste. Product-title wording only; pages show stock state separately.

sources.title: OQLF, soya
sources.locator: Preferred French terms and regional usage note
sources.supports: Lists soya and soja and notes that Québec uses soya more often while Europe more often uses soja. Supports local spelling, not the Korean product names.

sources.title: Haisue, Sempio Ssamjang Korean Soybean Dipping Paste (French product page)
sources.locator: French product title
sources.supports: Canadian French product title supports the local soybean dipping-paste wording for ssamjang. The title is not a terminology authority or universal formula.

decisions.reason: Add ssamjang as a separate named compound condiment, not an alias for doenjang or gochujang. Keep the blend composition product-specific and do not add broad soybean-paste aliases.

sources.title: OQLF, carambole (GDT)
sources.locator: carambola/star fruit/carambole and fruit étoile.
sources.supports: carambola/star fruit/carambole and fruit étoile. Identity and Québec terminology evidence only; no measurement, yield, or substitution data.

decisions.reason: Accept star fruit / carambole as a distinct identity-only FRUIT reference using the OQLF-supported Québec term and English equivalent. Keep documented near-neighbour and product boundaries separate. No forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are established.

sources.title: Kraft Heinz Canada, Original Steak Sauce
sources.locator: Product title, description, and 1 tbsp (15 mL) nutrition serving
sources.supports: The current Canadian manufacturer page identifies A.1. Original Steak Sauce and describes its product-specific serving and ingredient composition. These support the English product-family name but do not establish a generic measurement or shared formula.

sources.title: Heinz Canada, Sauce à bifteck originale
sources.locator: French product title, description, ingredient list, and product-specific serving panel
sources.supports: The French page for the same Canadian product ID names it Sauce à bifteck originale. Its portion and ingredients are specific to A.1. and are not generic kitchen measures or a universal steak-sauce formula.

sources.title: Kraft Heinz Canada, A1 - Sauce à steak
sources.locator: French A.1. brand-page title and product-family copy
sources.supports: The Canadian French brand page uses Sauce à steak in its page title and discusses A.1. sauces for meats, supporting the narrow French search alias without establishing a shared formula.

sources.title: Your Independent Grocer, Sauces BBQ et à bifteck
sources.locator: French condiment category and current listings for A1, HP, and The Keg
sources.supports: The Canadian retailer places A1 and HP sauce à bifteck products and The Keg sauce à steak under its BBQ-and-steak-sauce category. This supports current French retail usage and product diversity, not formula equivalence or a universal standard.

sources.title: Canadian Beef, Merveilleuses marinades pour les biftecks à mariner
sources.locator: Mucho mexicaine and Quatre-épices de la Jamaïque marinade ingredient lists
sources.supports: The French Canadian beef recipes use sauce à bifteck as a named marinade ingredient in recipe-specific quantities. They do not provide a reusable measure or define all steak sauces.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, bifteck
sources.locator: Preferred French terms and usage note
sources.supports: OQLF lists bifteck as a preferred Québec French term for steak and accepts the loanword steak. This supports local terminology only, not a sauce definition.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only steak sauce / sauce à bifteck as a commercial condiment-family reference with the source-attested French alias sauce à steak. The sources support the market names but not a shared formula or reusable measure. Keep barbecue sauce, Worcestershire sauce, and broad brown-sauce questions separate; add no form, measurement observation, density, mapping, recipe link, conversion, package yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Azuma Foods (Canada), Ankimo / Steamed Monkfish Liver, product 63142
sources.locator: Product name, product number, paired French title, main ingredients, and package statement.
sources.supports: Pairs Ankimo, Steamed Monkfish Liver, and Foie de baudroie cuit à la vapeur. Lists monkfish liver and salt as main ingredients and 15 pieces / 190 g / case. The basis of the 190 g figure is unclear; it is not a count conversion, serving, or package yield.

sources.title: Azuma Foods (Canada), Ankimo (Monkfish Liver) Ramen
sources.locator: Two-serving recipe ingredient list and preparation.
sources.supports: For a two-serving recipe, lists 20 g ankimo in broth and 2 slices steamed ankimo as topping. Record only the 20 g broth amount as a recipe-specific observation; the slices have no stated mass. The page lists no substitute, which is only a page-level observation.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: baudroie
sources.locator: Preferred Québec term, English equivalent, and Latin-name note.
sources.supports: Prefers Québec baudroie, gives English monk fish and Lophius sp., and notes that L. piscatorius and L. americanus may occur in commerce. The Azuma product does not identify either species.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: lotte
sources.locator: Preferred term, English and Latin equivalents, and note distinguishing lotte from baudroie.
sources.supports: Defines Québec lotte as burbot / Lota lota and warns against using lotte for baudroie. Reuses the source ID already registered on ingredient-ref-burbot; it supports keeping foie de lotte off this product.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Monkfish
sources.locator: Latin name and Canadian species profile.
sources.supports: Identifies Lophius americanus as one Canadian monkfish species. It does not identify the Azuma product species and is retained only as taxonomic context.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Ankimo as named in Azuma Foods (Canada)'s Ankimo Ramen recipe; the recipe does not identify a product SKU.
measurementObservations.foodState: Recipe-listed ankimo in broth; the recipe does not specify handling state.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Azuma's two-serving recipe lists 20 g ankimo for the broth.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One source-listed amount for the complete two-serving Ankimo Ramen recipe only; not a per-person amount or general ankimo portion.

decisions.reason: Add the product-level identity steamed monkfish liver / foie de baudroie cuit à la vapeur with ankimo as the only alias. Keep it species-neutral and distinct from whole monkfish, freshwater burbot / lotte, roe, and other fish-liver products. The broad monkfish, baudroie, liver, and foie queries expose this specific prepared product as a singleton, so its product-qualified label must remain visible. Record only Azuma’s two-serving 20 g broth amount as a recipe-specific observation. Do not infer a per-person serving, count weight, package basis, cooking yield, density, or substitution. Keep substitution research open.

sources.title: OQLF, avoine découpée
sources.locator: Preferred French term, English equivalent, definition, and discouraged synonym
sources.supports: Provides the preferred Québec French name avoine découpée and English steel-cut oats; defines the product as whole oats cut into pieces with steel blades. Explicitly discourages avoine épointée.

sources.title: RICARDO, Gruau irlandais à l'autocuiseur
sources.locator: Note de l'équipe Ricardo; description de l'ingrédient et remplacement proposé.
sources.supports: Identifies avoine irlandaise as a name for whole oats cut into small pieces. Its 180 g (1 cup) line and large-flake replacement are specific to this recipe; the prepared gruau title and the source's discouraged avoine épointée wording are not adopted as aliases.

sources.title: Bob's Red Mill Canada, Flocons d'avoine coupée biologiques
sources.locator: Description of the Canadian French-language steel-cut-oats product.
sources.supports: Describes the product as whole-grain oats cut into small pieces and says it is also called flocons d'avoine irlandais. Corroborates the cut-oat relationship in Canadian French product usage; the broader flake phrase is not added as an alias.

decisions.reason: Accepted steel-cut oats / avoine découpée as a distinct identity-only processed oat product. Keep it separate from rolled and quick oats. Do not activate avoine épointée or infer measurements, cooking yields, forms, or substitutions.

Add Irish oats and pinhead oats as English aliases and avoine irlandaise as a French alias on the existing steel-cut-oats identity. Retain steel-cut oats / avoine découpée as the display. Keep Irish oatmeal, prepared gruau irlandais, avoine écossaise, avoine épointée, and broad flake wording outside the alias set; add no form, reusable measure, conversion, recipe link, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, stévia (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and English term
sources.supports: Identifies stévia as the name of a plant and the English term; it does not equate the plant with refined extract or carrier-containing products.

sources.title: Health Canada, Sugar Substitutes
sources.locator: Stevia ingredient distinctions
sources.supports: Distinguishes fresh, dried, and powdered stevia leaves and crude aqueous extracts from purified extracts containing at least 95% steviol glycosides; no recipe interchangeability is established.

decisions.reason: Add stevia leaves / feuilles de stévia as plant material distinct from crude extracts, purified glycosides, and retail blends; no form or sweetening conversion is inferred.

sources.title: Health Canada, Sugar Substitutes
sources.locator: Stevia ingredient distinctions
sources.supports: Distinguishes fresh, dried, and powdered stevia leaves and crude aqueous extracts from purified extracts containing at least 95% steviol glycosides; no recipe interchangeability is established.

sources.title: CFIA, Étiquetage des glycosides de stéviol
sources.locator: Authorized label synonyms and product specification
sources.supports: Describes purified steviol glycosides and conditional label synonyms for products meeting specifications; conditional synonyms are not activated as broad catalog aliases.

decisions.reason: Add steviol glycosides / glycosides de stéviol as the purified product class; do not activate conditional CFIA label synonyms as unconditional aliases.

sources.title: Cotter Crunch, Lindsay Cotter, African Peanut Stew
sources.locator: Recipe card and Ingredients and Substitutions; optional meat and broth lines; page updated 2022-07-20.
sources.supports: The publisher card lists optional one-pound (450 g) diced stew-meat choices (chicken, beef, or pork). It also lists two cups of broth and describes vegetable or chicken broth or stock for this stew, with less broth in the meatless version. This supports the local recipe wording only; it does not define generic broth, establish global broth/stock equivalence, or provide a transferable measurement or substitution.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Beef wholesale nomenclature — 100 series
sources.locator: Item 135A, Beef for stewing.
sources.supports: Canadian institutional specification applies to diced beef for stewing, including qualified piece-size and fat limits. It does not define chicken or pork stew meat or the exact product used in the recipe.

sources.title: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications: Fresh Beef, Series 100
sources.locator: Item 135A, Beef for Stewing, PDF p. 43.
sources.supports: US institutional specification is limited to beef for stewing and corroborates a beef-only product boundary. It does not establish a cross-species household ingredient or the publisher’s product.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Meat cuts manual
sources.locator: Meat cut nomenclature exemptions.
sources.supports: CFIA says anatomical cut terms need not be used for products such as stewing beef, pork fondue, or other meat broken into small pieces. This is cut-name context, not proof of one interchangeable product.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, bœuf en cubes (GDT)
sources.locator: Food domain, viande de bœuf; dated 1982; definition, notes, and English equivalents.
sources.supports: Maps bœuf en cubes and bœuf à ragoût to beef-specific stewing beef and describes a boneless cubed product. The historical dimensions and fat limits do not apply to the recipe’s chicken or pork choices.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, veau à ragoût (GDT)
sources.locator: Food domain, viande de veau; updated 1983; definition and species-label note.
sources.supports: Provides the separate Québec term veau à ragoût / English stewing veal and says the animal species belongs in meat-label wording. It does not define generic stew meat or the recipe’s named species.

decisions.reason: Keep the existing stew-meat reference and recipe 090#8 link, but mark the identity needs_clarification. The publisher groups optional chicken, beef, or pork under one local stew-meat line; Canadian/Québec and USDA stewing-product specifications reviewed here are species-scoped and do not validate a generic Québec product name. Preserve the publisher’s 450 g statement separately from the bundled 454 g amount. Add no alias, form, measurement observation, conversion, yield, recipe edit, or reusable substitution.

sources.title: Filière des plantes médicinales biologiques du Québec, L’ortie dioïque — Guide de production sous régie biologique
sources.locator: 2009 guide, pp. 5–6.
sources.supports: Identifies Urtica dioica L., gives ortie dioïque and stinging nettle among its names, and describes young leaves in culinary use. The guide also reports irritating hairs and that young leaves lose their stinging property when cooked, dried, or transformed; retain these as source-specific limits, not general safety instructions.

sources.title: Oregon State University Extension Service, “Wild Edibles: Stinging Nettle”
sources.locator: Peer-reviewed extension publication; botanical identification, culinary use, preparation discussion, and substitution sentence.
sources.supports: Identifies stinging nettle as Urtica dioica, describes young leaves as edible, and lists culinary uses. Its broad spinach/kale replacement sentence is retained only in the blocked substitution finding; measurements, preparation directions, and stinging-hair warnings remain source-specific.

substitutionFindings.context: S02 broadly suggests properly prepared stinging nettle leaves in recipes using spinach or kale.
substitutionFindings.basis: Direct online searches on 2026-10-19 found S02 as the selected peer-reviewed extension source; it provides no replacement amount or transferable ratio and does not scope the broad claim to a defined dish role or method.
limitations: The broad phrase “almost any recipe” does not establish a safe contextual rule for all spinach or kale uses.
The source does not specify a dish role, named recipe/method, replacement amount basis, required adjustments, or expected effects.
Keep stinging-hair and processing statements source-specific; do not turn them into a general preparation or foraging-safety instruction.

rejectedCandidates.reason: The source's broad “almost any recipe” scope is too broad for a contextual replacement rule and provides no amount or adjustments.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only stinging nettle leaves / feuilles d’ortie dioïque for young culinary leaves of Urtica dioica L. Keep other Urtica species and plant parts separate. The French plant-part wording is descriptive, not an OQLF-standardized term. Preserve the source-specific handling notes and do not infer retail prevalence or a general safety instruction.

Keep the broad spinach/kale replacement suggestion blocked pending dish-role, form, amount-basis, and adjustment evidence. Do not activate a runtime rule, replacement link, or recipe link; preserve the handling cautions as source-specific only.

sources.title: Food and Agriculture Organization, International exports of fishery commodities by commodity, 2007, table A-4
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp04-salt-cod-stockfish-boundary-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Separates cod dried unsalted (stockfish) from cod salted and dried (klipfish) and records French and Spanish product phrases: morue, séchée, non salée; bacalao, seco, sin salar; morue, salée et séchée; bacalao, salado y seco. These are commodity descriptions, not proposed aliases.

sources.title: Norwegian fish-product regulation, English translation hosted by FAOLEX, Regulations on quality of fish and fishery products, §§ 1-2(42), 12-1, and 13-1
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp04-salt-cod-stockfish-boundary-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Defines stockfish as dried without added salt/additives and permits a set of cod-family species (cod, haddock, saithe, ling, blue ling, tusk), with an exceptional allowance for other species. The salted-fish/klippfish section also has a multi-species scope.

sources.title: Norwegian Seafood Council / Nielsen, Italian stockfish consumer study 2024, p. 9
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp04-salt-cod-stockfish-boundary-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Reports self-reported stockfish substitutions among Italian consumers (including fresh cod and baccalà). Survey behavior is not tested substitution guidance and supplies no usable rule or ratio.

decisions.reason: Accept stockfish as a named unsalted-dried fish product whose Norwegian legal scope includes several species. Keep it separate from salt cod and retain the English loanword provisionally in fr-CA.
No source-qualified Québec French display for the multi-species stockfish product was found; independent review remains open.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Fish List crab query
sources.locator: Rows for TSN 98811 and TSN 98810; English search for crab
sources.supports: Lists Stone crab / Crabe caillou for Menippe mercenaria and separately for Menippe spp.; the same query distinguishes Lithodes maja / crabe épineux. The CFIA display names support a Canadian market-group identity, not a claim about the Metro SKU species.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Guidance on determining the common names for fish sold or processed in Canada
sources.locator: Sections 1–4, purpose, scope, common-name definition, and CFIA Fish List use
sources.supports: Explains that the CFIA Fish List collects French and English common names for Canadian fish labeling and that the names listed for a species should be used for fish sold or processed in Canada.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, crabe épineux | Grand dictionnaire terminologique
sources.locator: Preferred term, English translation, and Latin-name links
sources.supports: Pairs crabe épineux with Northern stone crab, deep-sea king crab, and Lithodes maia. This OQLF name belongs to a different taxon and is excluded from the Menippe row.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Pinces de crabe de pierre cuites surgelées
sources.locator: Product 058973933757, French product title and package listing
sources.supports: Uses crabe de pierre for cooked frozen stone-crab claws and lists a 680 g package. The listing gives no scientific name, claw count, composition, or yield; the French phrase is retained only as a retail wording alias.

sources.title: Metro Canada, Frozen Cooked Stone Crab Claws
sources.locator: English product title for product 058973933757
sources.supports: Confirms the English stone-crab wording for the same 680 g SKU as the French listing. It does not identify a scientific name or support a recipe measure or edible yield.

sources.title: Seafood Depot, Stone Crab
sources.locator: Canadian supplier product identity and characteristics
sources.supports: Identifies a Menippe mercenaria product and lists claws or meat, fresh or frozen. This supplier page is scoped to that product and does not define the entire Menippe market group or the Metro SKU.

sources.title: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Stone Crab: Menippe mercenaria or Menippe adina
sources.locator: Current commercial stone-crab page title and market scope
sources.supports: Names Menippe mercenaria or Menippe adina under the stone-crab market heading. This supports a multi-species market boundary; fishery rules and claw sizes are not kitchen measures.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only stone crab / crabe caillou for the CFIA Menippe spp. market group; CFIA also lists the same bilingual names for M. mercenaria. Retain crabe de pierre only as the documented Metro Québec retail wording. Keep Northern stone crab / crabe épineux under Lithodes separate. Add no forms, measures, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Health Canada, Residue Chemistry Crop Groups — English.
sources.locator: Identity and terminology support summarized in the linked proposal packet.
sources.supports: Edible-fungi list gives Bunashimeji / H. marmoreus, Chinese mushroom / V. volvacea, Pom Pom / H. erinaceus, Shimeji / T. conglobatum, and White jelly fungi / T. fuciformis. Also lists Blewitt (Lepista nuda) under edible fungi. A regulatory crop table, not a current retail synonym authority.

sources.supports: French crop terms include Bunashimeji, Volvaire asiatique / V. volvacea, Hydne hérisson / H. erinaceus, Shimeji / T. conglobatum, and Trémelle blanche / T. fuciformis. Also lists Pied bleu (Lepista nuda) under edible fungi. Regulatory naming evidence; no recipe measures or product-state mappings.

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius, Classification of Foods and Animal Feeds, CXA 4-1989.
sources.locator: Identity and terminology support summarized in the linked proposal packet.
sources.supports: Commodity names include Straw mushroom / V. volvacea, Wood ears mushroom / Auricularia polytricha, and Shimeji under a different taxonomic treatment. This is a commodity classification and its taxonomic labels may be dated.

decisions.reason: Scope to Volvariella volvacea from the English/French Canadian and Codex sources; do not add Chinese mushroom alias.

sources.title: General Mills / Cheerios Canada, Cheerios Fraises et bananes
sources.locator: French-language product title, ingredient declaration, package size, and Valeur nutritive panel.
sources.supports: The Canadian French manufacturer page identifies the same ready-to-eat cereal, supplies the exact French display, lists a 317 g package, and gives a 1 tasse (39 g) serving. It directs consumers to the package if online data differ.

sources.title: General Mills / Cheerios Canada, Our Products
sources.locator: Canadian product list and result count.
sources.supports: Lists 17 current Canadian Cheerios products, including Strawberry Banana Cheerios, Multi-Grain Cheerios, and three Oat Crunch variants. This documents product-family scope, not an equivalence or need to add all siblings.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Céréales à saveur de fraise et banane Cheerios, 317 g
sources.locator: Current indexed Québec listing, package amount, product number 065633188518, and ingredient statement.
sources.supports: The current indexed Québec retailer listing corroborates the local French descriptive wording, matching 317 g product, and product number. The retailer phrase remains evidence only and is not added as an alias.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Strawberry Banana Cheerios, Canadian manufacturer Nutrition Facts serving.
measurementObservations.foodState: Dry ready-to-eat cereal, as sold.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Manufacturer Nutrition Facts serving-size label.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Product-specific nutrition serving only; not a generic cereal measure, density, or unit conversion.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Strawberry Banana Cheerios / Cheerios Fraises et bananes as a named Canadian ready-to-eat cereal. Use the current manufacturer titles and keep both alias arrays empty; do not treat cereal components as a formula or map them to ingredient identities. Record 1 cup (39 g) only as a product-specific Nutrition Facts observation, not a generic cereal measure, density, or conversion. Add no forms, legacy mapping, active measurement, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions. The bundled recipe corpus has no matching demand.

sources.title: CFIA, Labelling requirements for processed fruit or vegetable products
sources.locator: Common name section, Strawberry Jam example.
sources.supports: Identifies Strawberry Jam as the common name under the Canadian generic jam standard. Supports the English identity and product class, not a French term or a measure.

sources.locator: Sections 74–78, standards for jam and jelly.
sources.supports: Defines separate standards for named-fruit jam and named-fruit jelly. Supports keeping jam and jelly as separate product identities, not interchangeable aliases.

sources.locator: Definition of confiture as a spreadable preparation made from whole or cut fruit cooked with sugar.
sources.supports: Provides the GDT definition of confiture; helps distinguish standard terminology from broader descriptive food writing but does not define kaya.

sources.supports: Identifies CNF 2026 as the current downloadable relational dataset and says the 2015 online CNF remains available as an interim measure. The exact 2026 thyme food and serving-measure rows were not verified in this review.

sources.supports: The author lists strawberry jam as an alternative to raspberry jam in this specific Linzer-cookie filling at 1/2 cup (120 mL). Seedless guidance is stated for raspberry jam; neither passage establishes a mass conversion or a general substitution rule.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, tartinade de fruits (GDT)

sources.supports: Defines fruit spread / tartinade de fruits as similar to jam but lower in sugar and distinguishes it from regulated confiture in Canada. Supports keeping fruit spread outside this jam identity.

decisions.reason: Promote the reviewed legacy candidate as strawberry jam / confiture de fraises, retaining confiture de fraise as a source-attested French alias. Keep the identity separate from fresh strawberries, strawberry purée, raspberry jam, jelly, and lower-sugar fruit spreads. Record the strawberry-for-raspberry option only for the cited Linzer-cookie formula; add no active substitution rule, form, recipe-line link, density, unit mapping, or reusable conversion. Measurement research remains blocked pending a verified current strawberry-jam-specific source.

replacements.roleInCompound: jam filling for Linzer cookies

substitutionFindings.context: Only the Linzer-cookie filling in John Kanell / Preppy Kitchen's cited source formula, which explicitly offers strawberry jam or raspberry jam, strained.
substitutionFindings.basis: The source lists 1/2 cup (120 mL) of raspberry jam or strawberry jam for this filling. This is a formula-specific alternative, not a general jam replacement ratio.
limitations: Do not generalize to other fillings, recipes, fresh fruit, purée, jelly, or fruit spread.
The source's seedless guidance refers to its raspberry jam wording; do not transfer that preparation adjustment to strawberry jam.
No active contextual substitution rule is created.

sources.title: Sally's Baking Addiction, Homemade Strawberry Cake
sources.locator: Strawberry puree method and ingredient list.
sources.supports: The source recipe blends fresh strawberries, reduces the puree on the stove, and adds 1/2 cup of reduced strawberry puree to the cake. Supports this recipe-specific intermediate and exact line; not a universal yield, density, or purchased-product equivalence.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, purée de fruits (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition and preferred term.

sources.title: Gouvernement du Québec, Culture des fraises et des framboises
sources.locator: Description of Québec strawberry and raspberry processing products.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Purée de fraises 10% sucre ajouté
sources.locator: Product heading, description, and available formats.
sources.supports: Uses the French name purée de fraises for a Québec-made frozen strawberry puree product with added sugar. Product-specific identity evidence; no equivalence to the recipe-made reduced puree is inferred.

sources.title: Aliments du Québec, Purée de fraises sans sucre ajouté
sources.locator: Product heading, description, and available formats.
sources.supports: Uses the same French product-class wording for a Québec-made frozen strawberry puree without added sugar. Product-specific evidence only; it does not establish an active sugar-state form or a substitution.

decisions.reason: Add strawberry puree / purée de fraises as a separate FRUIT identity from fresh strawberries, jam, and freeze-dried strawberries. Link only recipe 051 ingredient 12 to this identity and record the recipe-specific reduced / réduite preparation. Preserve the authored original text, ingredientName, amount, unit, and group. Do not infer purchase totals from the fresh-strawberry line or activate a form, density, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Tokushima Sudachi GI summary
sources.locator: GI no. 129, registered fruit identity and culinary use.
sources.supports: Identifies sudachi as a distinct registered Tokushima citrus fruit; no cross-citrus aliases are asserted.

decisions.reason: Accept the bounded bilingual ingredient identity and aliases supported by the cited sources. Do not infer a recipe link, form, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution.
Present in the legacy RecipeKeeper catalog but absent from the canonical bundled seed; reconcile identity and aliases before acceptance.

sources.title: Post Consumer Brands Canada, Original Sugar Crisp
sources.locator: Current Canadian manufacturer product page, product name, and available box sizes.
sources.supports: Names the Canadian product Sugar Crisp and lists 365 g and 550 g boxes. The page does not expose a readable ingredient panel or serving mass; package sizes are product presentations only.

sources.title: Post Consumer Brands Canada, Sugar-Crisp, French-Canadian product page
sources.locator: French-Canadian product page title and available box sizes.
sources.supports: Uses the French-Canadian brand wording Sugar-Crisp and lists the same 365 g and 550 g box sizes. This manufacturer wording supports the product display but is not a Québec terminology ruling.

sources.title: Post Consumer Brands Canada, Céréales Sugar-Crisp — Notre histoire
sources.locator: French-Canadian brand history, Sugar-Crisp product and cross-market/historical naming discussion.
sources.supports: Describes the Canadian Sugar-Crisp as sweetened puffed-wheat cereal and contrasts the Canadian name with historical names and the current U.S. name Golden Crisp. This supports the finished-cereal boundary and not activating those historical or cross-market names as aliases.

sources.title: Super C, Céréales de blé au miel, Sugar-Crisp, 365 g, item 628154138006
sources.locator: Québec product page title, item number, package size, and product listing.
sources.supports: Current Québec retailer listing names the finished product Céréales de blé au miel, Sugar-Crisp, 365 g and provides a product-specific ingredient list. Retailer category wording and ingredient formula are not generalized to all Sugar-Crisp packages.

sources.title: Provigo, Céréales Sugar Crisp, 365 g
sources.locator: Indexed Québec product listing, title, description, serving panel, and product number 20071915001_EA.
sources.supports: The current indexed retailer listing describes Sugar Crisp cereal as sweetened puffed wheat, gives a 365 g package size, and shows a nutrition-panel serving of 1 cup (40 g). Direct text extraction returned no page text in this review; retain the serving only as a retailer-listing-specific portion observation and do not infer a generic cup measure or transfer it across products without a verified crosswalk.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Post Sugar Crisp cereal, Provigo listing 20071915001_EA
measurementObservations.foodState: Dry ready-to-eat cereal as sold in the named retailer listing.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Provigo indexed nutrition panel lists 1 cup (40 g); physical measuring method and fill are not stated.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: This is a source-specific serving for Provigo product listing 20071915001_EA only. It is not a reusable household cup measure, density, volume-to-mass conversion, or serving value for another Sugar-Crisp package.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Sugar Crisp cereal / Céréales Sugar-Crisp for the named finished Canadian cereal. Keep it separate from plain puffed wheat and do not use the product page’s historical, U.S., or character names as aliases. The single Provigo 1 cup (40 g) nutrition-panel portion remains a source-specific ledger observation; it does not activate a cup mapping, density, or conversion. No forms, component links, reusable measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions are supported.

sources.title: NOAA Fisheries, Sugar Kelp
sources.locator: Species name and food-use overview; blade anatomy; nutrition panel basis.
sources.supports: Identifies sugar kelp as Saccharina latissima and describes food use. Blade dimensions, U.S. availability, and the 100 g raw nutrition-panel basis remain source-specific and do not establish a reusable recipe measure or Québec supply claim.

sources.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Guide de bonnes pratiques pour une récolte durable et sécuritaire des algues marines au Québec
sources.locator: Species list and commercial-interest species table naming Laminaire sucrée (Saccharina latissima).
sources.supports: Uses the French name laminaire sucrée for Saccharina latissima in a Québec seaweed harvesting guide. It supports the species-linked French wording only, not a recipe measure, culinary substitution, or commercial-product roster.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, laminaire saccharine (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred Québec French name, Latin translation, and note on broad goémon/varech harvest terms.
sources.supports: Standardizes laminaire saccharine and pairs it with Laminaria saccharina. Its English translation kelp is broad; the OQLF note says goémon/varech can describe mixed shoreline algae and does not make those terms aliases for this species.

sources.title: Ocean Biodiversity Information System, Laminaria saccharina taxon record
sources.locator: Taxon status and accepted-name cross-reference.
sources.supports: Lists Laminaria saccharina as unaccepted and Saccharina latissima as its accepted name. This taxonomic cross-reference supports the narrow Latin alias only.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only sugar kelp / laminaire sucrée for Saccharina latissima. Keep it separate from kombu, wakame, winged kelp, and the unresolved broad kelp candidate; do not add the broader kelp/varech/goémon terms as aliases or add forms.
The reviewed biological dimensions, U.S. nutrition basis, harvest details, and market context do not establish a reusable household measure, density, conversion, or yield.
The reviewed sources establish identity and food use but do not establish an interchangeable replacement or recipe-independent ratio with other seaweeds.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, bonbons décoratifs (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred Québec French term and definition; lists vermicelles, nonpareilles, and perles de sucre as types.
sources.supports: Defines the broad sugar-decoration class corresponding to sprinkles and identifies sugar pearls as one type; the named types are not synonyms for every sprinkle.

sources.title: Wilton, White Sugar Pearl Sprinkles
sources.locator: Product name and use description.
sources.supports: Identifies sugar pearls as an edible cake decoration that can be used alone or mixed with other sprinkles; no measure or synonym relation is established.

decisions.reason: Add sugar pearls / perles de sucre as a named decoration type, distinct from the generic sprinkles identity and pearl sugar / sucre perlé. Link only Fraisier recipe 045’s exact sugar-pearl row. Add no alias, form, measurement, mapping, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Kyo Tsukemono — Traditional Foods in Japan
sources.locator: Kyoto pickle list, suguki-zuke description, ingredients, fermentation, and customary serving context.
sources.supports: Lists suguki-zuke as a distinct Kyoto pickle and describes suguki as a Kyoto turnip type preserved with salt and lactic fermentation. Root and leaves are cut separately for serving. Production steps and serving context do not establish a standard measure or substitution.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Sugukizuke — Our Regional Cuisines
sources.locator: Page title, Kyoto region, source-attested English names, and traditional-food description.
sources.supports: Attests the fused spelling Sugukizuke and phrase Suguki Pickles. Its parenthetical “turnip greens” gloss is not adopted as an alias; another official MAFF account and Kyoto Prefecture identify suguki as a turnip type. Its process details remain source-specific.

sources.title: Kyoto Prefecture, すぐき菜（すぐき）
sources.locator: Local cultivar description and preserved-food preparation overview.
sources.supports: Describes suguki-na as a local Kyoto turnip cultivar and suguki as a salt-fermented preserve made from that vegetable. The specific production steps are not transferred as catalog defaults.

sources.title: Voyages à Kyoto, Gastronomie et boissons
sources.locator: Pickles section referring to suguki (navet) among emblematic Kyoto pickles.
sources.supports: Provides French-language regional culinary usage of suguki (navet). It is not a Québec terminology decision and does not establish navet as a unique French alias for this preserve.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, navet (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred specialized term navet and note limiting rabiole to a turnip variety.
sources.supports: Supports navet as the Québec French specialized term for turnip and describes rabiole as a particular variety. It does not define the Kyoto preserve or supply a Québec name for suguki-zuke.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only suguki-zuke as a named regional Kyoto preserve. Use the borrowed display pending Québec-specific terminology evidence and retain only narrow source-attested English aliases. Keep fresh turnip, turnip greens, shibazuke, takuan, and generic pickled radish separate; add no process default, measure, form, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Green Gold Gourmet, Suka Pinakurat FAQ
sources.locator: What is Suka Pinakurat; product composition; distinction between the brand and wider spiced-vinegar names.
sources.supports: Brand owner identifies Suka Pinakurat as a branded blended spiced coconut-sap vinegar and describes fermented coconut sap, bird's-eye chiles, and spices including garlic, onion, ginger, and sweet peppers. It explicitly distinguishes the brand from the broader spiced-vinegar family and from Sinamak as a regional name.

sources.title: WOW Food Distributor, Pinakurat Spiced Vinegar
sources.locator: Product title, product description, and category listing.
sources.supports: Distributor identifies Pinakurat Spiced Vinegar as coconut vinegar infused with chile and spices and describes dipping and marinade uses. Package/case data are not treated as kitchen measures.

sources.title: Skip Canada, Pinoy Meaty Mart menu
sources.locator: Sauces section, Pinakurat Spiced Vinegar listing.
sources.supports: Canadian retail delivery menu lists the Pinakurat product and describes its coconut-sap vinegar base and Iligan origin. The product title is English; the French-language site chrome is not treated as evidence for a French product name.

decisions.reason: Add a product-specific Suka Pinakurat identity for the named spiced coconut-sap vinegar. Keep it distinct from plain coconut vinegar, generic spiced vinegar, and Sinamak. Use only aliases that retain the Pinakurat product name. French wording is descriptive pending independent Québec review. Add no forms, measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Government of Canada, Department of National Defence, Food Quality Specifications: Dried Fruits (English)
sources.locator: Raisins product row: Sultana and golden-coloured dried-grape wording; any grape kind may be used. Federal departmental procurement specification, not a universal standard of identity.
sources.supports: Supports Sultana as a marketed dried-grape type and documents procurement-context use of Sultana/golden terminology; does not fix a cultivar. No measurement or conversion data used.

sources.title: Ministère de la Défense nationale, Spécifications sur la qualité des aliments : Fruits séchés (français)
sources.locator: Rang Raisins secs : raisins sultana et raisin de Smyrne; toute sorte de raisin peut servir à produire des raisins sultana. Federal departmental procurement specification, not a universal standard of identity.
sources.supports: Supports Québec French product wording raisins sultana and records the procurement-context golden/Smyrna overlap; does not fix a cultivar. No measurement or conversion data used.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, raisin sec (GDT)
sources.locator: Termes privilégiés and note on common dried-raisin types.
sources.supports: Supports raisin sec as the general Québec French dried-grape term and lists sultana among dried-raisin types; does not make Sultana the meaning of generic raisins. Identity and terminology only.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, raisin de Corinthe (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred term and English translation note concerning dried Vitis currants.
sources.supports: Supports the separate dried Corinth/Zante grape product and distinguishes it from fresh Ribes currants; used to preserve the existing dried-currant boundary.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, raisin de Smyrne (GDT)
sources.locator: Domain classification, preferred French term, English translation, and note about Smyrna varieties used to make dried raisins.
sources.supports: Supports raisin de Smyrne / Sultana raisin terminology but spans botanical and food-fruit domains; does not establish a universal dried-product alias.

sources.title: Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Raisins CXS 67-1981
sources.locator: Scope and labelling section, clauses 1 and 7.1.
sources.supports: Defines the standard scope for dried Vitis vinifera grapes, excludes dried currants, permits Sultanas where that name is used for certain raisin types, and uses Golden as a possible descriptor for bleached raisins. Identity/label boundary only.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Common name on food labels
sources.locator: General common-name guidance for foods without a prescribed name.
sources.supports: General label-naming guidance; supports keeping an established named subcategory explicit where a broader name is too wide. Not raisin-specific evidence.

sources.locator: Current Québec product sheet name, ingredients, and last-updated date 2026-09-28. Product data supplied via GS1.
sources.supports: Supports current Québec-market wording for a distinct Premium Sultana Raisins product. Retail listing does not define a universal cultivar or regulatory synonym set.

sources.title: PRANA Foods, Raisins sultana biologiques (French)
sources.locator: Current product title and description.
sources.supports: Supports Québec-facing retail wording raisins sultana as a distinct marketed dried-grape type. Seller’s substitution claim is not used as an ingredient-substitution rule.

sources.locator: Bilingual dried-fruit product listing for Sultana, Thompson, California Flame, and Zante currant raisins.
sources.supports: Supports current Canadian market naming for Sultana raisins as one of several named dried-raisin products; not botanical-equivalence evidence.

decisions.reason: Accept sultana raisins / raisins sultana as a distinct identity-only marketed dried-grape type, with only the English plural sultanas as an alias. Do not assign a grape cultivar or add golden-raisin or raisin-de-Smyrne aliases: available sources use these terms in product- or labelling-specific ways. Keep generic raisins and dried currants separate. No forms, measurements, yields, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links are established.

sources.title: OQLF, sumac (GDT)
sources.locator: Definition, note on Middle Eastern cooking, and English term.
sources.supports: Defines the culinary identity as aromatic purple powder made from berries of a Mediterranean shrub and lists Middle Eastern cooking use; notes it is an ingredient of zaatar.

decisions.reason: Accept the existing sumac legacy candidate as a standalone culinary spice identity. Keep it distinct from the zaatar compound blend that can contain sumac, and from ornamental or toxic wild-sumac products, extracts, and seasoning blends. The supported identity itself is the ground culinary powder; no separate preparation form, numeric conversion, package yield, or substitution is supported.

sources.locator: Accepted species name and vernacular-name list.
sources.supports: Accepts Satureja hortensis and lists sarriette des jardins, summer savory, and summer thyme. The latter is source-attested but omitted from active aliases because it would add this row to existing thyme searches.

sources.supports: Names Satureja hortensis, sarriette d’été, sarriette des jardins, and sarriette commune; documents culinary uses and cautions against confusing summer and winter varieties. Crop guidance is not a kitchen measure.

sources.title: La Brouette Maraîchère: Sarriette d’été
sources.locator: Botanical information, common names, and culinary description.
sources.supports: Québec producer listing names Satureja hortensis, sarriette d’été, sarriette commune, and Summer Savory; describes culinary use and drying leaves. The plant listing was sold out when reviewed, so this is terminology and product-scope evidence, not availability or a measure.

sources.title: Save-On-Foods: McCormick Summer Savory Leaves, 14 g
sources.locator: Retail product title and product information.
sources.supports: Canadian retailer wording uses Summer Savory Leaves for a packaged spice. Supports the qualified English alias only; product package size and inventory are not reusable measures or availability guarantees.

sources.title: Espace pour la vie, Montréal Botanical Garden: Sarriette vivace
sources.locator: Botanical name, French and English common names, and culinary use.
sources.supports: Identifies Satureja montana as sarriette vivace / winter savory and distinguishes it by name and plant characteristics from Satureja hortensis. Supports keeping winter savory separate.

decisions.reason: Add one identity-only HERB reference, ingredient-ref-summer-savory, for culinary Satureja hortensis L., displayed as summer savory / sarriette d’été. Keep winter savory (Satureja montana) separate. Use only source-supported bilingual terms; omit summer thyme because it would broaden the current thyme picker results, and omit generic sarriette retail wording that is not species-qualified. The bundled recipes have no matching ingredient demand. Add no forms, measures, unit mappings, density, conversions, recipe links, yields, or active substitutions; measurement and substitution research remain not_yet_researched.

sources.supports: Supports summer squash / courge d’été as a broad maturity and skin category, not a synonym for zucchini or another individual member.

decisions.reason: Accept summer squash / courge d’été as a distinct source-backed produce identity. Keep neighboring varieties, processed products, forms, measurements, and substitutions separate unless their own evidence is reviewed.

decisions.reason: Add sunflower oil / huile de tournesol with OQLF-attested English seed-oil variants. Keep modified fatty-acid profiles outside this generic source identity. No bundled recipe line names this oil.

sources.locator: Product details: ingredient list and added-sugar statement; page marked sold out on 2026-10-16.

sources.locator: Preferred term, definition, note, and English equivalent.

sources.supports: Identifies sunflower as Helianthus annuus and describes sunflower seedlings grown in trays and harvested as microgreens for salads and sandwiches. Supports species, stage, and culinary use; does not establish a Québec term or kitchen amount.

sources.locator: Sunflower row in Table 1 and general harvest directions.

substitutionFindings.context: Replacement for sunflower shoots in an unspecified recipe role and preparation state.

Keep the French display and crop-qualified micropousses alias provisional; do not alias generic shoots, microgreens, sprouts, or germinations. No reusable kitchen measure, mass-volume conversion, density, yield, or standard harvested form is supported. The Utah growing data and Cornell smoothie amount remain scoped to their respective sources.

replacements.roleInCompound: 20% of the dry-matter flour blend in the named study; the study separately tested 0%, 2%, 3.5%, and 5% vital gluten by total flour weight. Formula-specific finding only; no general replacement ratio.

substitutionFindings.context: Pleming et al. tested commercial Australian sweet lupin flour (Lupinus angustifolius) from Western Australia in 20:80 dry-matter blends with Perfection Bakers Flour (Allied Mills, Australia). Bread was made by rapid and sponge-and-dough processes; the lupin-enriched formulas tested 0%, 2%, 3.5%, or 5% vital gluten relative to total flour weight.
substitutionFindings.basis: The primary study reports that 5% gluten improved average loaf volume by about 20% and crumb softness by 30–50% across the tested lupin sources and breadmaking methods; L. angustifolius weakened the base-flour blend less than L. albus, and sponge-and-dough was more suitable for lupin inclusion.
expectedEffects: Effects belong to the named experimental bread formula and commercial flour samples.
The study supplies no reusable home recipe replacement rule.
limitations: One commercial Australian sweet-lupin flour source and one Australian commercial baker’s flour base; not the Lupina product listed in the portion source.
The 20:80 blend is a tested dry-matter formulation, not a general wheat-flour substitution ratio.
Gluten additions and the two breadmaking methods are experimental conditions; do not translate them into a runtime or recipe-level instruction.
Do not generalize to sweet white lupin (L. albus), other lupin species, non-bread roles, or other bread formulas.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Ecoideas Organic Lupin Flour 400 g; organic white lupin; product-specific nutrition-label serving.

expectedEffects: In the tested formula, increasing the white-lupin flour proportion changed dough and bread properties.

Tested amounts are experimental blend levels. Do not treat them as a recipe replacement recommendation outside this formula.

sources.supports: Defines tahini as paste made from ground sesame seeds; supports beurre de sésame, tahini, tahin, tahina, and English tahini/tahina.

decisions.reason: Present in the legacy RecipeKeeper catalog but absent from the canonical bundled seed; reconcile identity and aliases before acceptance.

Promote the stable legacy ID as tahini / beurre de sésame and correct its unreviewed FAT_AND_OIL categorization to SAUCE_AND_CONDIMENT. OQLF defines ground sesame paste and supports the listed variants. Do not alias generic East Asian sesame pastes without separate crosswalk evidence. Add no forms, density, unit mapping, package yield, measurement observation, conversion, or substitution rule in this batch.

Keep the existing tahini / beurre de sésame identity. OQLF confirms that the canonical English term tahini is also a French term and remains searchable through bilingual lookup; do not duplicate it in aliasesFr. Do not alias generic sesame paste, sesame butter, or black sesame paste.

sources.title: Ozawa Canada, Frozen Takana Shiozuke (Salted Mustard Greens)
sources.locator: Product heading and item number TU-2032.
sources.supports: A Canadian Japanese-food distributor names a frozen Takana Shiozuke product and describes it as salted mustard greens. This is product-specific trade evidence, not a general form or state default.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Setaka no Takana Zuke
sources.locator: Product overview and ingredients.
sources.supports: Identifies a Fukuoka regional pickle made from takana, a leaf mustard, using salted layered leaves and stems with regional aging. It supports a named product identity, not one global formula.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Aso Takana-zuke
sources.locator: Product overview and preparation notes.
sources.supports: Describes Aso takana pickles and distinguishes short-aged products from older products fermented for about six months. It supports preserving the named product without asserting one process state.

sources.title: Nightlife Montréal, “Nakamichi: un nouveau spot à ramen au centre-ville”
sources.locator: Donburi description: feuilles de moutarde marinées (takana).
sources.supports: A Montréal restaurant article uses takana as the source-qualified name for leaves described in French as feuilles de moutarde marinées. This supports local descriptive context, not an official French compound term.

decisions.reason: Add the named Japanese takana-zuke identity separately from generic pickled mustard greens. Retain the borrowed Japanese name as the French display to avoid making the generic French label return both identities; the Québec descriptive wording remains documentation-only. Source descriptions distinguish regionally variable preparations, so add no process form, aliases, recipe links, measurements, density, unit mappings, yields, conversions, or substitutions.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Pickled — Traditional Foods in Japan
sources.locator: Takuan section; classification table for vegetables pickled in rice bran; production description.
sources.supports: Identifies takuan as a typical Japanese pickle made from daikon radish pickled in rice-bran paste, and classifies it among rice-bran pickles. This describes a traditional product class, not every commercial takuan formula or a recipe measurement.

sources.title: Ozawa Canada, Kimura Takuwan (Pickled Radish)
sources.locator: Product title, Pickled Yellow Radish description, Tsukemono category, and Montreal office listing.
sources.supports: Current Canadian distributor lists Kimura Takuwan as a yellow pickled-radish product in its Japanese tsukemono category and provides a Montreal office. The product page is evidence for this commercial item and Canadian distribution, not a universal formula.

sources.title: Ozawa Canada, Product Catalogue, July 2025
sources.locator: Tsukemono / pickled vegetables section: Takuwan Japanese Style and Sweet Takuan Korean Style.
sources.supports: A Canadian distributor distinguishes Japanese-style takuwan from a separate sweet Korean-style takuan product. This supports keeping the named Japanese product bounded and does not establish a global synonym for Korean pickled radish.

sources.title: Hungry Ninja, RFG Tokai Takuwan Taro Tokyo Pickle Radis
sources.locator: French Canadian retail listing; product title, French product description, ingredients, and country of origin.
sources.supports: An Ottawa retailer uses the product name Takuwan/Takuwan Taro Tokyo alongside French radis mariné wording and identifies a Japan-origin item. Its formula and commercial title are SKU-specific; no aliases or ingredient behavior are generalized from it.

sources.title: Iru Izakaya, French Menu
sources.locator: Chirashi listing; restaurant locations in Brossard, Québec City, and Montréal.
sources.supports: A current Québec French-language Japanese restaurant menu uses takuan as a named ingredient in chirashi. It supports local borrowed-name use, not a retail formula or recipe amount.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, daïkon (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred terms for the edible radish, including daïkon and radis daïkon.
sources.supports: Supports the Québec French spelling daïkon and the term radis daïkon used descriptively in the localized product display. It does not define takuan or an official compound name for the pickle.

decisions.reason: Add the bounded Japanese preserved-radish identity takuan. Use the borrowed name with a concise descriptive English/French display; OQLF supports daïkon wording while Canadian French product/menu sources attest takuan/radis mariné use. Keep it separate from generic daikon, generic pickled radish, and the separately marketed sweet Korean-style takuan product. Add no aliases, forms, measurement values, unit mappings, yields, conversions, or substitutions; no bundled recipe requests it.

sources.title: European Commission, Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/955
sources.locator: Approval of non-minor amendments to the Taleggio PDO product specification
sources.supports: Approves non-minor amendments to the protected Taleggio designation; the legal text identifies the registered name as a protected designation of origin.

sources.title: European Commission, Official Journal C 72/10, Taleggio single document
sources.locator: Sections 1–4; product description, cheese class, and concise geographical definition
sources.supports: Defines Taleggio PDO as a soft raw-paste table cheese made from whole raw or pasteurized cow’s milk, rennet, salt, and lactic starter cultures; specifies the milk-origin and production/maturation/portioning geography. Its whole-cheese weight and process requirements are product specifications, not kitchen measures.

The European Commission defines the protected Taleggio PDO product, while current Québec retailer and cheese-shop wording supports the bilingual display and aliases. Keep Québec-made Taleggio Localé separate. The external arancini quantity remains recipe-specific evidence only. No bundled recipe demand or reusable measure was found; add no forms, density, unit mappings, conversions, package yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

The reviewed sources do not define a universal paste specification or establish equivalence to tamarind water, juice, blocks, extract, or concentrate; no measurement or substitution is inferred.

sources.title: Translation Bureau, TERMIUM Plus: TAMBAQUI
sources.locator: Fish record; universal entry Colossoma macropomum; English and French tambaqui; French noun marked correct masculine.
sources.supports: Associates the English and French display tambaqui with Colossoma macropomum. Also lists blackfin pacu and cachama, which are not adopted as aliases.

sources.title: Amapá State Institute for Scientific and Technological Research (IEPA), Guia do pescado do Amapá — feiras de Macapá
sources.locator: Tambaqui entry and Tambaqui Assado na Brasa (ou no Forno) recipe, printed p. 45.
sources.supports: Identifies Tambaqui as Colossoma macropomum and documents a regional whole-fish food recipe. The approximately 2 kg ingredient and cook time are source-specific, not a standard measure or yield.

sources.locator: Species identity and Vulnerable listing for wild populations.
sources.supports: Identifies Colossoma macropomum and explains the Brazilian Vulnerable listing for wild populations. Retain as dated listing context, not as the current operational fishery-status statement.

sources.title: Brazil Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture, Pesca do tambaqui segue permitida pelo Governo Federal
sources.locator: Federal fishing status, current rules, October–February defeso, licensed aquaculture, and recovery-plan status.
sources.supports: States that federal fishing remains permitted under current management rules, including the October–February defeso; no restrictions apply to tambaqui produced in licensed aquaculture; the recovery plan remains in development. Brazilian status context only, not product-specific compliance or Canadian sourcing evidence.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only tambaqui / tambaqui for Colossoma macropomum with no aliases. The proposed species name is supported by the federal bilingual terminology record and a regional government food guide. Do not add blackfin pacu, cachama, or broader pacu terms because they can widen a species-specific picker identity. The guide’s whole-fish recipe quantity is source-specific; no reusable measure, form, density, mapping, yield, recipe link, conversion, or substitution is supported. Record Brazilian vulnerable-listing and current fishery-rule context in the ledger only; do not encode origin, harvest method, sourcing, or compliance behavior in the catalog.

sources.title: OQLF, tapenade
sources.locator: Definition, preferred term, English translation, and note on green variants
sources.supports: Pairs French tapenade with English tapenade and documents green-olive variants. It does not make every olive spread a tapenade.

sources.title: Maison Fayard, Green Olive Tapenade
