decisions.reason: Add tapenade / tapenade as a distinct olive-based condiment identity. OQLF supplies the French/English name and documents green variants; the Canadian product is one composition example. Do not alias generic olive paste or infer that capers or anchovy paste are tapenade synonyms. Leave forms, measurements, conversions, yields, substitutions, and recipe links unset.

sources.title: OQLF, tapioca
sources.locator: Definition and notes on the product family and its forms.
sources.supports: Defines tapioca as manioc-derived food starch and notes that it can appear as powder, flakes, small balls, or pearls. Supports the product family only; does not make all tapioca a pearl product.

sources.title: OQLF, perle de tapioca
sources.locator: Definition, preferred French term, and English terms.
sources.supports: Defines a tapioca pearl as a food product made from tapioca starch; gives the preferred French term perle de tapioca and English terms tapioca pearl and tapioca ball. Explicitly discourages bulle de tapioca and French boba.

decisions.reason: Accept tapioca pearls as a separate identity from extracted tapioca starch, with the OQLF-supported French singular search term and English tapioca ball alias. Leave broad tapioca, French boba, forms, measures, substitutions, and recipe links unset.

sources.title: OQLF, fécule de manioc
sources.locator: Definition and English terms
sources.supports: Defines wet-extracted manioc starch and lists manioc starch, cassava starch, and tapioca starch as English terms; tapioca flour is marked obsolete. The record distinguishes extracted starch from whole-root flour.

sources.title: Bob's Red Mill, 5 Tapioca Flour Substitutes to Test Out
sources.locator: Cornstarch section, especially the thickening-liquids substitution guidance and cooking-stage/appearance comparison.
sources.supports: Says tapioca flour/starch and cornstarch both thicken liquids and that cornstarch can replace tapioca starch in a recipe when used as a thickener. It advises adding cornstarch at the beginning rather than the later stage recommended for tapioca, and describes tapioca as glossy versus cornstarch as matte. It gives no replacement amount or tested recipe-specific ratio.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach, AnswerLine: Tapioca
sources.locator: Tapioca entry: product forms, interchangeability warning, and cornstarch comparison.
sources.supports: Defines tapioca as cassava-root starch and distinguishes pearls, flakes/powders, and instant/minute granules, cautioning that the forms are not interchangeable. Its 2 tablespoons tapioca powder per 1 tablespoon cornstarch statement is the opposite substitution direction; its separate 1:1 statement concerns instant tapioca. Neither ratio is reversed or transferred to tapioca starch replacing cornstarch.

sources.title: King Arthur Baking, Pie Thickener
sources.locator: Quick-cooking tapioca and cornstarch notes and fruit-specific thickener tables.
sources.supports: Lists quick-cooking tapioca alongside cornstarch as a fruit-pie thickener, gives fruit-specific quantities, and describes quick tapioca’s bright, clear, stippled/sticky result. The source does not test a tapioca-starch substitution or state a shared ratio; quick-cooking tapioca is not treated as the catalog’s extracted-starch identity.

sources.title: King Arthur Baking, Ingredient Weight Chart
sources.locator: “Tapioca starch or flour” row: 1 cup = 4 oz = 113 g; separate quick-cooking-tapioca row excluded.
sources.supports: Publishes 1 cup = 4 oz = 113 g for its unqualified tapioca starch or flour entry. The chart does not state cup capacity, identify a product, or specify a row-specific filling method; retain as a source-specific portion only.

sources.title: Bob's Red Mill, Flour Weight Chart
sources.locator: Tapioca Flour/Starch row: 30 g per 1/4 cup and 120 g per 1 cup; 1-cup entry recorded.
sources.supports: Lists its Tapioca Flour/Starch chart row at 30 g per 1/4 cup and 120 g per 1 cup. Record only the 1-cup value; the quarter-cup figure is the same chart row rather than an independent method. The product/SKU, cup capacity, and tapioca-row filling method are not specified.

decisions.reason: Accepted extracted manioc starch as tapioca starch. Did not alias it to cassava flour or deprecated tapioca flour.

Add manioc starch as an English alias for the existing extracted-starch identity because OQLF lists it as an English term. Keep cassava starch unassigned because the exact phrase overlaps the two active Brazilian polvilho displays; keep tapioca flour inactive as obsolete. Add no other aliases or numeric/runtime data.

Record one directional, qualitative tapioca-starch-to-cornstarch alternative for liquid thickening only. Bob’s Red Mill supports the functional substitution and notes a different addition stage and matte-versus-glossy result, but supplies no ratio. Preserve the different directions and forms in the Iowa State source; keep quick-cooking tapioca pie quantities out of this finding. Add no active rule, recipe-line link, measurement, unit mapping, or identity alias. The bundled recipe corpus has no tapioca demand.

Record the King Arthur and Bob’s Red Mill tapioca starch/flour chart values as separate source-specific portions. They differ by 7 g per nominal cup; neither page supplies a common cup capacity or a tapioca-row-specific fill method. Keep measurementState blocked_pending_evidence, defaultDensity null, and unitMappings empty. Add no form, active conversion, recipe link, yield, or change to the existing directional qualitative substitution finding.

substitutionFindings.context: A cooked liquid recipe in which tapioca starch/flour serves only as the thickener.
substitutionFindings.basis: Bob’s Red Mill says cornstarch can work in place of tapioca starch when thickening liquids. It recommends changing the addition stage: cornstarch can be added at the beginning, while tapioca is commonly added later. The source provides no replacement quantity or recipe-tested ratio.
adjustments: Add cornstarch at the beginning rather than at the later stage used for tapioca, following the source’s general method guidance.
expectedEffects: Cornstarch gives a more matte finish; tapioca often gives a glossy result.
limitations: This is one manufacturer’s qualitative guidance for liquid thickening, not a tested recipe-specific equivalence or quantity ratio.
Do not reverse the direction or transfer Iowa State Extension’s cornstarch-to-tapioca powder ratio to this finding.
Do not extend to tapioca pearls, flakes, quick-cooking/instant granules, gluten-free baking/binding, pie-thickener quantities, or other uses without evidence for those forms and contexts.
Do not activate as an automatic substitution rule or attach it to a recipe line; no bundled recipe uses tapioca starch.

sources.supports: The primary-study abstract reports triplicate cakes, cookies, biscuits, and breads made with 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 100% teff flour blends, with different physical outcomes among product types. It does not establish a general home substitution ratio or state the percentages' mass/volume basis.

decisions.reason: Accept teff flour / farine de teff as a distinct FLOUR_AND_STARCH milling identity, supported by a manufacturer product name and Québec French-market product wording. Keep bare teff and tef out of aliases because they refer to grain naming and the OQLF spelling note requires reviewer judgment. This identity decision does not establish density, unit mappings, or reusable measurement guidance; see the later R725 decision for a bounded source-specific substitution finding.

Record Westpoint's 10–20% flour-reduction/equal-weight teff instruction as product- and recipe-context-specific evidence. Bob's Red Mill's product page and guide give different percentages, while the study reports product-dependent outcomes; none supports one transferable teff-flour replacement rule. Keep measurement research open and add no active rule or recipe link.

Record Bob's Red Mill's 1/4 cup (35 g) manufacturer-label serving as product-specific portion evidence. Because the label specifies neither cup capacity nor flour fill/weigh method, keep reusable generic measurement unsupported and add no density, unit mapping, conversion, or active recipe guidance. Preserve R725 substitution research and finding.

replacements.roleInCompound: Westpoint Teff Flour replacing part of the recipe's all-purpose flour; the manufacturer directs an equal-weight replacement for the amount removed.

substitutionFindings.context: Westpoint Naturals' unqualified Teff Flour product, made from 100% South African teff, in chocolate cookies, cakes, or brownies involving cocoa, chocolate, brown butter, or brown sugar.
substitutionFindings.basis: Westpoint directs reducing recipe flour by 10–20% and replacing the removed amount with an equal weight of teff. Although equal-weight replacement is explicit, the page does not state whether the 10–20% reduction itself is based on mass or volume. Preserve the source wording and range; do not derive a numeric replacement amount or an active ratio.
expectedEffects: Westpoint says this product enhances earthy flavor in these baked goods; the page does not report a controlled comparison.
limitations: One manufacturer's product and chocolate-oriented recipe contexts only; do not generalize to all teff flour, including color-qualified rows.
The source gives no named formula or test result; the percentage basis is unspecified even though the replacement is described by equal weight.
The source's separate pancake suggestion and 50/50 banana-bread example are not part of this finding.
No global or contextual runtime substitution rule or recipe-line link is supported by this finding alone.

decisions.reason: Accept whole teff grain / teff d'Abyssinie as a GRAIN_AND_CEREAL identity distinct from teff flour. Use CFIA's French crop label; keep OQLF's recommended but non-current spelling tef inactive pending Québec review. Do not add aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions.

Add tef as a French search alias on the existing teff-grain reference only. The OQLF-hosted GDT entry lists tef for the cereal and calls its orthography recommended while noting it is non-current; TERMIUM Plus lists tef as correct and teff / teff d'Abyssinie as correct normalized French terms. CFIA's French cereal list supports the existing display teff d'Abyssinie, and a Montreal-based company's French whole-seed product page uses graines de teff. The exact alias improves lookup without merging teff grain with teff flour: tef will select only teff grain, while teff and farine de teff retain their current boundaries. Keep the current French display pending any separate human Québec sign-off; add no tef alias to flour, no measures, forms, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

Add the source-attested French search alias graines de teff to the existing whole-grain reference. Retain the normalized display teff d'Abyssinie, the current tef alias, the English display teff, the GRAIN_AND_CEREAL category, and the separate teff flour identity. The exact phrase matches the current Montréal retailer's French whole-seed title and ingredient statement. Keep density, unit mappings, forms, recipe links, conversions, yields, and substitutions unchanged; the retailer's 1/8 tasse (30 g) nutrition portion is SKU-specific, not a generic measure.

Use graines de teff as the French display for the existing edible whole-teff grain identity because current Montréal/Québec and Canadian product sources use that exact French product wording. Preserve teff d'Abyssinie as a French alias because CFIA and TERMIUM support it as a formal/correct normalized term, and preserve the existing tef alias with its OQLF non-current spelling note. Keep English teff, the separate teff-flour identities, forms, numeric data, recipe links, conversions, yields, and substitutions unchanged.

sources.title: Institut de Technologie Alimentaire du Sénégal, Formations à la carte
sources.locator: Techniques de transformation: lines 163–172
sources.supports: Lists production of Sankhal, thiacry or couscous, and Arraw separately. Supports product boundaries, not a formula or measure.

sources.title: Maad MTL, Thiakry (Dégué), 600 g
sources.locator: Product description and preparation instructions

sources.supports: Uses THIACRI as the product label, describes fine millet granules cooked by steam and used with yogurt, and separately lists Arraw, Sankhal, millet flour, and thiéré. The attached 200 g line says grains de mil and is not assigned to thiacri.

sources.title: FAO/Senegal traditional foods and recipes, Thiacry Mil
sources.locator: Page 13, ingredients and preparation
sources.supports: Lists 200 g ready-to-cook millet thiacry granules and preparation for one recipe with no serving count. Supports one source-scoped whole-recipe amount only.

sources.title: OQLF, millet (GDT)
sources.locator: French terms and generic-grain note
sources.supports: Lists millet, mil, and petit mil and notes that millet can cover several species. It does not define thiakry or approve a product-specific display.

sources.title: OQLF, gruau (GDT)
sources.locator: Québec/Canada definition and extended cereal-porridge usage
sources.supports: Defines gruau as a cooked oatmeal dish and notes extension to other cereal porridges. Supports excluding the prepared-food term from the dry-granule identity.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2026 open data record
sources.locator: Food Name and Measure Weight Conversion CSV downloads; browser tool returned 403
sources.supports: Identifies the current relational CSV dataset for measurement review. The download failure does not establish whether a thiakry record or usable measures exist.

sources.title: Afritibi, Thiakry
sources.locator: Product copy and replacement claim
sources.supports: Suggests thiakry can replace rice or pasta but gives no amount, dish context, or preparation crosswalk. It does not support an active substitution rule.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: FAO/Senegal Thiacry Mil recipe: 200 g granulés de thiacry de mil prêts à cuire.
measurementObservations.foodState: Ready-to-cook granules as stated by the recipe; source-specific preparation later moistens and steams them.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Published recipe ingredient amount.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Complete recipe amount; the source gives no serving count.

substitutionFindings.context: General replacement of rice or pasta with millet-based thiakry in recipes.
substitutionFindings.basis: Afritibi makes a broad product-use claim without a quantity, dish scope, or preparation crosswalk. The evidence does not support a global or contextual rule.
limitations: Do not transfer the claim to non-millet thiakry products or prepared dairy desserts.
Do not infer a replacement ratio, cooking method, water amount, or serving conversion.
Keep millet couscous (thiéré), Arraw, Sankhal, and prepared thiakry dishes distinct.

rejectedCandidates.candidate: Use thiakry in place of rice or pasta based on general product copy.
rejectedCandidates.reason: No dish context, quantity, preparation crosswalk, or validated replacement ratio is supplied.

decisions.reason: Add the millet-scoped pre-cooked thiakry granule identity with source-attested French spelling aliases. Keep non-millet uses, thiéré, Arraw, Sankhal, prepared dishes, and product-specific measures separate. Add no forms, defaults, mappings, recipe links, conversions, yields, or active substitutions.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File 2015: Spices, thyme, fresh (Food Code 215)
sources.versionOrDate: Online CNF 2015 serving-portion surface; page details modified 2019-03-01.
sources.locator: Available serving sizes and refuse.
sources.supports: The listing reports 5 ml = 0.8 g and 15 ml = 2.4 g for fresh thyme. It also displays 1 leaf = 4.0 g and 32% stems/refuse; the leaf figure is unexplained and is not recorded as a count observation.

sources.title: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Standard Reference Release 28: Food Group 02, Spices and Herbs
sources.locator: NDB 02049 and 02042, common-measure tables.
sources.supports: Reports fresh thyme at 1 tsp = 0.8 g and 1/2 tsp = 0.4 g. For dried thyme it reports leaves at 1 tsp = 1.0 g and 1 tbsp = 2.7 g, and ground thyme at 1 tsp = 1.4 g. The measure table gives no brand or filling method.

sources.title: Health Canada, Canadian Nutrient File
sources.locator: Data in the Canadian Nutrient File; 2026 download and interim online 2015 notes.
sources.supports: Identifies CNF 2026 as the current downloadable relational dataset and says the 2015 online CNF remains available as an interim measure. The exact 2026 thyme food and serving-measure rows were not verified in this review.

sources.title: Health Canada, Best uses for fresh and dried herbs
sources.locator: How much to use; Dried herbs; Fresh herbs.
sources.supports: Gives general guidance that one-third of a fresh amount can be used when replacing fresh herbs with dried herbs, plus general use and timing advice. It does not name thyme; it is not used to activate or widen a thyme-specific substitution.

sources.title: University of Pennsylvania Human Resources, Healthier Holiday Recipes: Traditional Herbed Roast Turkey
sources.versionOrDate: PDF copyright 2020 Association of Diabetes Care & Education Specialists; recipe credits Diabetic Living (2007).
sources.locator: Traditional Herbed Roast Turkey, PDF page 2, ingredients and steps 1–2.
sources.supports: For a 12–14 lb turkey the formula lists 1 tablespoon snipped fresh thyme or 1 teaspoon dried thyme, crushed, used inside the cavity and on the exterior before roasting. One formula only; it does not report a side-by-side test, sensory result, or general conversion.

decisions.reason: Preserve the historical CNF 2015 and USDA SR28 fresh-thyme portions as separate source-specific observations. Keep measurement blocked until the exact current CNF 2026 thyme row and measures are verified. Record only the turkey-formula fresh-to-dried option; do not create an active form conversion, density, mapping, recipe link, or generic substitution rule.

measurementObservations.foodState: Fresh; the listed preparation is not further specified.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Historical CNF volume portion; chopping, packing, and filling method are unstated.

measurementObservations.foodState: Fresh; the listed preparation is not further specified.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Historical CNF volume portion; chopping, packing, and filling method are unstated.

measurementObservations.quantityBasis: USDA SR28 common-measure entry; spoon filling and leveling method are unstated.

measurementObservations.foodState: Fresh; SR28 reports 32% stems.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: USDA SR28 common-measure entry; spoon filling and leveling method are unstated.

substitutionFindings.context: Traditional Herbed Roast Turkey formula for a 12–14 lb turkey; the herb seasoning is placed inside the cavity and on the exterior before roasting.
substitutionFindings.basis: The recipe lists 1 tablespoon snipped fresh thyme or 1 teaspoon dried thyme, crushed.
limitations: One recipe formula and turkey-roasting process; this is not a controlled comparison or a general herb conversion.
The source does not state a flavour or performance outcome for choosing either option.
The recipe says dried thyme, crushed; it does not establish a link to the separate dried-thyme-leaves catalog identity.

sources.title: Tianjin Library, 舌尖上的二十四节气 小寒寻味 天津冬菜
sources.locator: Food identity, preparation description, and Tianjin seasoning-use examples.
sources.supports: Identifies Tianjin winter vegetable as a Chinese-cabbage preserve made by pickling and fermentation and gives regional culinary-use examples. Incidental brand history, exact process, nutrition, health, and sensory claims are not catalog defaults.

sources.title: Jiang, Fu, Li, and Wang, Characterization of Functional Microorganisms in Representative Traditional Fermented Dongcai from Different Regions of China
sources.locator: Introduction; regional identity and substrate distinction.
sources.supports: Peer-reviewed study distinguishes regional Dongcai and describes Tianjin Dongcai as Chinese-cabbage based, separately from Sichuan mustard-based Dongcai. Microbiology, composition, study samples, garlic proportions, and process findings remain study-specific; no correction-specific finding is used.

sources.title: Pauline D. Loh, China Daily, Preserving flavors
sources.locator: Tianjin pickled-vegetable wording, name, and culinary-use description.
sources.supports: Supports the English wording Tianjin pickled vegetable and the regional dongcai name. Its stated vegetable combination and salt description are one account and do not define a universal formulation.

sources.title: The Woks of Life, Dried, Cured & Pickled Ingredients
sources.locator: Section Tianjin Preserved Vegetables (冬菜, Dōngcài).
sources.supports: Secondary culinary glossary corroborates the English wording Tianjin preserved vegetables and qualitative uses. Its process and ingredient details do not establish a universal formula, measure, or form.

sources.title: OQLF, chou de Chine
sources.locator: Raw Chinese-cabbage group terms only; does not name the preserve.
sources.supports: Supports raw-vegetable terms chou de Chine and chou chinois only. It does not standardize a French term for Tianjin dongcai; preserve this source on its existing owners.

substitutionFindings.context: Replacing Tianjin dongcai in a defined soup, noodle, braise, or stir-fry role and amount.
substitutionFindings.basis: The reviewed sources describe Tianjin dongcai and its culinary uses but do not recommend another ingredient as a replacement for it. Regional and substrate similarity is not evidence of interchangeability.
limitations: Do not infer a replacement from Napa cabbage, mustard greens, shared pickling methods, or another preserved vegetable.
Search results describing Tianjin dongcai as a substitute for Yibin ya cai establish the opposite direction only and do not support replacing Tianjin dongcai.
No defined recipe role, replacement amount, method, or adjustment supports an active rule.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Tianjin dongcai as a geographically qualified regional preserved-food identity. Keep it distinct from other foods called dongcai and neighboring fermented or pickled vegetables. Use the provisional descriptive fr-CA display and only the two source-supported English aliases; add no forms, recipe links, reusable measures, conversions, yields, or active substitutions.
No transferable household measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, or finished-food yield is supported. The sources’ formulations and fermentation descriptions remain regional or study-specific.
No reviewed source recommends a replacement for Tianjin dongcai in a defined dish role and quantity. Similarity to other cabbage or preserved-food identities does not establish substitution.

sources.title: TERMIUM Plus, TIGER NUT
sources.locator: Record 1; subject field Fruits and Vegetables (Types and Processing - Food Ind.); English and French terms and definitions.
sources.supports: Defines tiger nut as the edible tuber of Cyperus esculentus and supplies the paired French term souchet comestible plus French synonym names. The recorded terminology variants support search aliases only; the entry does not establish measurements or prepared-product equivalence.

sources.title: PROSEA, Plants yielding non-seed carbohydrates, Cyperus
sources.locator: Taxon and uses sections, lines for Cyperus esculentus and Cyperus rotundus.
sources.supports: Identifies chufa/tiger nut and French amande de terre for Cyperus esculentus, cultivated for edible tubers eaten raw, cooked, or roasted. It separately describes C. rotundus tubers, which are not cultivated as food in the same way; the catalog identity therefore stays scoped to C. esculentus.

sources.title: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Cyperus esculentus
sources.locator: Common names, Uses (Ethnobotany), and Edibility sections.
sources.supports: Confirms tiger nut, chufa, and earth almond common names and edible C. esculentus tubers. Culinary preparation examples include raw/cooked consumption, drying and grinding, beverage use, oil, and roasted use; those details remain source-scoped and do not define catalog forms or measurements.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic tiger nut / souchet comestible for the edible tuber of Cyperus esculentus. Keep it separate from the existing tigernut-flour and defatted-tigernut-flour identities, from oil or beverage products, and from the related C. rotundus. Use only source-attested terminology; do not generalize source preparation examples. Add no form, measurement, density, unit mapping, recipe link, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: Tigernuts Traders, defatted tigernut flour
sources.locator: Product and processing descriptions
sources.supports: Identifies a separate defatted product made after oil extraction and further processing; keep it outside whole-tuber flour.

sources.title: Government of Canada, TERMIUM Plus, TIGER NUT
sources.locator: Definition and French common names
sources.supports: Defines tiger nut as the edible tuber of Cyperus esculentus and lists French common names including souchet; it does not define flour terminology.

sources.title: Tigernuts Traders, farine de souchet fine
sources.locator: French product heading and product-family listing
sources.supports: Uses farine de souchet for a ground-tuber flour and lists fine, extra-fine, and defatted products separately; supports the display without making grades aliases.

sources.title: Government of Canada, TERMIUM Plus, TIGER NUT
sources.locator: Terminology record dated 2022-08-12.
sources.supports: Defines edible Cyperus esculentus tuber and lists French common terms including souchet and noix tigrée; it does not define flour wording.

sources.title: Tigernuts Traders, farine de souchet fine
sources.locator: French manufacturer product catalog.
sources.supports: Uses farine de souchet for its flour product family; manufacturer usage outside Québec, not evidence that grades are aliases.

sources.title: La Moisson, Farine de noix tigrées
sources.locator: Product body and ingredient statement.
sources.supports: Québec retailer calls the product farine de souchet and lists organic tiger nuts/tubers as the sole ingredient; title wording is not adopted as an alias.

decisions.reason: Accept a whole-tuber flour identity for Cyperus esculentus. Keep defatted flour, grind grades, tubers, oil, and butter separate; add no aliases, forms, numeric data, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions. No bundled recipe line matched.

Retain `tigernut flour / farine de souchet`. Québec retail and manufacturer wording support the display; keep farine de noix tigrées out as an alias because it is a product title and the source explains that this is tuber flour. Keep defatted flour separate and add no numeric or substitution behavior.

sources.supports: Supports external recipe use of fresh tilapia fillets; its eight-fillet amount for four servings has no mass and is not a standard portion or bundled recipe link.

sources.title: CFIA, Guidance on determining the common names for fish sold or processed in Canada

measurementObservations.foodState: Fresh, raw product listing.

substitutionFindings.context: A Kidney Community Kitchen Jamaican steamed fish recipe changed from snapper to tilapia in a diet-specific potassium context. This single adaptation does not establish a general tilapia-for-snapper rule or a reusable ratio; no global or contextual replacement is accepted for snapper, cod, sole, pollock, or other fish.
substitutionFindings.basis: The cited adaptation is recipe-specific and differs from general culinary substitution guidance.
limitations: Do not generalize the diet-specific recipe change to other dishes or nutritional contexts.
Do not infer interchangeability from shared fish category.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only, species-neutral tilapia fillets / filets de tilapia as a Canadian/Québec market group for unseasoned fillets sold fresh or frozen. Keep the singular French retailer phrase filet de tilapia as the sole alias so it matches the current local product wording; retain species names, whole fish, and prepared/seasoned products outside this identity. The Nile tilapia species candidate remains unallocated.

Keep the fresh/frozen package amounts, CNF food-guide serving, and recipe quantities only as source-specific observations. Add no active measure, default density, unit mapping, fillet count conversion, package conversion, cooking/edible yield, or reusable substitution.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List search results for tilapia
sources.locator: Official indexed result rows for Oreochromis urolepis hornorum and Sarotherodon melanotheron, among other taxa.
sources.supports: The indexed official result table shows the exact English/French pair Tilapia / Tilapia on more than one species row. It also shows narrower or differently paired names for other taxa. Supports only a qualified shared-name group, not a taxon, complete membership list, product form, or culinary equivalence.

sources.title: CFIA Fish List, Canadian fish common names
sources.locator: Fish List overview; common names paired with scientific names and Taxonomic Serial Numbers for Canadian fish labelling.
sources.supports: Defines the scope of the Canadian fish-labelling common-name resource. Species-specific rows support exact common-name and species associations; the list does not establish culinary equivalence.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: tilapia
sources.locator: Definition and preferred French term tilapia; English and Latin entries also include Nile-specific terms.
sources.supports: Supports the generic French term tilapia and definition as an edible freshwater fish. Nile tilapia and Oreochromis niloticus wording are not transferred to this name group; perche d’Afrique is not added as an alias.

sources.title: CFIA, Guidance on determining the common names for fish sold or processed in Canada
sources.locator: Sections 4 and 5.2.2: Fish List scope and consideration of group names for multiple species.
sources.supports: Describes the CFIA Fish List role and says group names covering multiple species may be considered. It does not approve this catalog-authored display or establish culinary equivalence.

decisions.reason: Add a separate visibly qualified tilapia / tilapia shared-name group for the exact bilingual common name used across multiple fish species. This is a catalog search identity, not a taxon, species membership list, preparation state, fish-label authorization for the qualified display, or culinary-equivalence claim. Preserve the existing tilapia fillet and whole-fish references and held Nile-tilapia candidate unchanged; do not transfer their product or species evidence.

decisions.reason: Add timur as a Nepalese pepper identity bounded to the source-supported Zanthoxylum armatum product. Keep it distinct from Sichuan pepper and generic peppercorn; do not add Nepal pepper as a global alias pending Québec wording review, or numeric/substitution data.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only toasted corn germ / germe de maïs grillé for the human-food ingredient class supported by a current Canadian English product declaration and Québec French retail label wording. The French display is market-attested, not OQLF-preferred. Keep raw corn germ, oil-milling germ meal/cake, corn germ oil, and composite foods distinct. The finished Tostitos serving is not a measure for its germ ingredient. Keep aliases and forms empty, default density null, unit mappings empty, and add no measurements, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions. No bundled recipe demand was found.

sources.supports: Describes soy sauce combined with fresh calamansi at the table; editorial food-culture evidence, not a formal product definition.

decisions.reason: Add a bottled, ready-to-use Filipino soy-sauce product with calamansi as a separate condiment identity. Use toyomansi soy sauce with calamansi / sauce soya toyomansi. Keep it distinct from generic soy sauce, calamansi, and fresh, variable table-mixed toyomansi dipping sauce; add no aliases. No recipe links, forms, measurements, conversions, yields, or substitutions are supported.

sources.title: MASAF, DOP/IGP product-specification index, section 1.8
sources.locator: Section 1.8, three balsamic product-specification links
sources.supports: The Italian Ministry index lists separate specifications for Aceto Balsamico di Modena, Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena DOP, and Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Reggio Emilia DOP.

sources.title: MASAF, production specification for Aceto balsamico tradizionale di Modena
sources.locator: Articles 1–8 of the production specification currently listed by MASAF
sources.supports: Defines the Modena PDO name, province and grape-origin boundary, cooked-must process, fermentation and cask aging, minimum 12-year aging, analytical requirements, bottling, package sizes, and label rules. Density is a minimum analytical threshold; containers are protected-product packaging, not kitchen measures.

sources.title: Consorzio Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena, English product specifications
sources.locator: Articles 2–8 of the English product-specification page
sources.supports: Confirms the English product name, Modena production and bottling boundary, minimum 12-year process, permitted Extravecchio label wording, analytical threshold, and package rules. The national specification remains primary legal evidence.

sources.title: European Commission, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/512
sources.locator: Recital 14, distinction between Aceto Balsamico di Modena PGI and Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena PDO
sources.supports: States that the Modena PGI and Modena PDO use different raw materials and production methods and remain distinct products.

sources.title: Costco Canada, French product page — Andrea Milano Vinaigre balsamique traditionnel de Modène DOP, 25 ans, 100 ml
sources.locator: French title and product details for item 2000414
sources.supports: Current Canadian French product title uses DOP and product details also call this certified product AOP. Its 25-year age and 100 mL package are SKU-specific and not general measures or package yield.

sources.title: Costco Canada, English product page — Andrea Milano Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena DOP, 25 years, 100 ml
sources.locator: English title and product details for item 2000414
sources.supports: Confirms the English Canadian title, protected designation and 100 mL SKU from the French page; not an independent product or general measurement source.

sources.title: OQLF, Grand dictionnaire terminologique — Vinaigre balsamique
sources.locator: Term record and English equivalent.
sources.supports: Supports the Québec French/English pair vinaigre balsamique / balsamic vinegar and a distinct grape-must product identity.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena PDO / vinaigre balsamique traditionnel de Modène AOP as a SAUCE_AND_CONDIMENT reference. Use the exact Italian PDO designation as the only English alias and the Canadian French DOP title as a qualified French alias for the AOP display. Keep generic balsamic vinegar, Modena PGI, Reggio Emilia PDO, glazes, reductions, creams, and flavored products separate. Do not convert the specification analytical density minimum or protected package sizes into kitchen measures. No bundled recipe demand or tested substitution was found; add no forms, numeric mappings, observations, package yields, conversions, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: Cooking with Ria, Caribbean Green Seasoning Recipe (Authentic Trinidad-Style)
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp05-caribbean-condiments-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: First-person Trinidad culinary source describes island/household variation, no single correct formula, and explicitly distinguishes green seasoning from Haitian epis, sofrito/recaito, and Jamaican jerk seasoning. Supports a Trinidad-specific candidate and rejection of a universal Caribbean alias. Recipe amounts and substitutions are not promoted.

sources.title: Foodie Nation, Trini Green Seasoning Recipe
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp05-caribbean-condiments-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Trinidadian food source attests the local name Trini Green Seasoning and the use of chadon beni in its version. Its recipe is one local example only.

sources.title: Marchés publics de Montréal, Callaloo with pan-fried cod
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp05-caribbean-condiments-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Montréal public-market recipe by chef Marie J. Modeste names green seasoning and uses it in a Trinidadian-inspired callaloo. Supports Québec/Canadian recipe use, not a universal regional formula.

sources.title: Walmart Canada, Assaisonnement vert frais Karibbean Flavors
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp05-caribbean-condiments-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: French-language Canadian retail listing uses assaisonnement vert frais and describes Trinidadian flavors. Marketplace text is product-specific and not independently verified by Walmart; used only to report a fr-CA wording example, not as a terminology standard.

sources.title: Walkerswood, Green Seasoning
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp05-caribbean-condiments-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Jamaican manufacturer describes its all-purpose green seasoning as made from fresh Jamaican produce. This is an adjacent Jamaica-branded product; it is not treated as an alias or proof of identity with Trinidadian green seasoning.

decisions.reason: Accept Trinidadian green seasoning as a regional compound seasoning distinct from Jamaican green seasoning, Haitian epis, sofrito, and recaito. Keep the French descriptive display provisional and do not add generic assaisonnement vert as an alias.
The fr-CA display assaisonnement vert trinidadien is a transparent provisional translation requiring independent Québec review.

sources.title: Jiang et al., The content and distribution pattern of chemicals and bioactive compounds of triticale grains
sources.versionOrDate: 2024; International Journal of Food Science & Technology 59(8):5502–5511
sources.locator: Abstract and milling-fraction description.
sources.supports: Distinguishes coarse and fine bran from flour and whole-grain fractions obtained by milling triticale in a laboratory mill. The fractions and composition are specific to the study cultivars and procedure, not universal commercial grades, nutritional values, or measures.

sources.title: Agil and Hosseinian, Dual functionality of triticale as a novel dietary source of prebiotics with antioxidant activity in fermented dairy products
sources.versionOrDate: 2012; Plant Foods for Human Nutrition 67(1):88–93; DOI 10.1007/s11130-012-0276-2
sources.locator: Abstract; study use of triticale bran in yogurt.
sources.supports: Documents human-food use of triticale bran in a yogurt study. The study-specific 4% inclusion ceiling, formula behavior, and reported antioxidant results are not generic measures, health claims, or substitution rules.

sources.title: Kaszuba et al., Content of Phenolic Acids in the Grain of Selected Polish Triticale Cultivars and Its Products
sources.locator: Materials and Methods, grain-milling process and bread-baking procedure.
sources.supports: Describes bran obtained from milling selected triticale cultivars and its use in one bran-enriched bread formula. The cultivar, milling procedure, 10% formula inclusion, analytical findings, and outcomes remain study-specific and are not generic nutrition or recipe guidance.

sources.title: OQLF, triticale (GDT)
sources.locator: GDT triticale entry; preferred French base name.
sources.supports: Supports the French base name triticale and its English equivalent. It does not define triticale bran or establish son de triticale as a preferred compound.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT: son
sources.locator: GDT son entry, alimentation / céréale traitée; definition and note.
sources.supports: Defines son as the peripheral cereal portion separated during milling. The entry does not decide the specific triticale compound, and its note also discusses other milling by-products and animal feed.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Labelling and composition requirements for grain and bakery products
sources.locator: Common name — Bran.
sources.supports: States that unqualified bran is understood as wheat bran and that the grain must be stated for bran from another grain. Supports explicit triticale qualification in English naming, not human-food use or French terminology.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only generic triticale bran / son de triticale as the edible bran fraction separated from triticale grain during milling. Primary milling and food studies establish the distinct fraction and human-food use; OQLF supports only the base French terms triticale and son, so the compound display remains provisional pending Québec review. CFIA supports naming the source grain in English. Keep feed/distilling fractions, shorts, mill-feed, bran-containing blends, and triticale meal/flour/grain/flakes separate. Study-specific fractions, compositions, amounts, formulations, and performance findings are not generalized. Add no aliases, forms, measures, recipe links, conversions, yields, or substitutions.

sources.title: Arva Flour Mill, Triticale Flakes
sources.locator: Current standalone Ontario product page, product title and cart listing
sources.supports: An Ontario flour mill offers a standalone retail product titled Triticale Flakes. Supports the English identity name only; the page does not establish a flaking method, French display, recipe direction, or transferable measure.

sources.title: Metro, Country Harvest 14 Grains Sliced Bread
sources.locator: Current Canadian listing, product number 063400138711, ingredient declaration
sources.supports: The Canadian product ingredient declaration names triticale flakes in a formulated whole-grain and seed mix. Supports Canadian ingredient wording, not a standalone product specification or household measure.

sources.title: Super C, Pain tranché aux 14 grains Country Harvest
sources.locator: Current French Canadian listing, product number 063400138711, ingredient declaration
sources.supports: The matching Canadian product number lists flocons de triticale in a formulated grain mix. Supports current French product-ingredient wording, not a standalone product specification or flaking process.

sources.title: OQLF, triticale (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred Québec French term, grammatical gender, and English equivalent
sources.supports: Supports the base French noun triticale and its English equivalent; the entry does not define a flake compound or processing behavior.

sources.title: Québec Food Directory, Boulangerie Grissol Melba Toast Grain Entier
sources.locator: Current product sheet, ingredient declaration
sources.supports: A Québec food-directory product sheet lists flocons de triticale in a multigrain ingredient mix. Corroborates current Québec French wording; it does not define a standalone product or general flaking method.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only triticale flakes / flocons de triticale as a processed cereal product distinct from whole triticale grain, flour or meal, other cereal flakes, and composite grain mixes. Add no aliases, forms, density, unit mapping, measurements, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, farine de triticale (GDT)
sources.locator: Preferred term and English translation
sources.supports: Lists farine de triticale as the preferred Québec French term and triticale flour as its English translation. Supports the display pair only; it does not define milling specifications or a grade.

sources.title: Usito, triticale
sources.locator: Definition and metonymic sense for the grains and flour
sources.supports: Defines triticale as a cereal hybrid of wheat and rye and includes its grains and extracted flour in the metonymic sense. Supports keeping triticale flour distinct from wheat and rye flour; it does not define a flour grade.

sources.title: Government of Saskatchewan, Triticale: Production and Use
sources.locator: Milling and Baking section
sources.supports: Describes triticale flour ground as whole grain and used in health-food products, and says the food market is poorly developed. Supports the existence of a narrow food-flour identity; it provides no flour grade, household measure, or generic substitution ratio.

sources.title: Statistics Canada, Monthly Millers Survey, 2024
sources.locator: Question 8, human-consumption products; Triticale cereal flour production and stocks
sources.supports: The mill survey asks respondents reporting human-consumption products to record triticale flour output and stocks as a named product category. This is recognition in an archived industry survey, not evidence of current production volumes, retail availability, or kitchen measures.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only triticale flour / farine de triticale as a FLOUR_AND_STARCH product distinct from triticale grain, triticale flakes, wheat flour, rye flour, and unresolved triticale meal. Use the direct OQLF bilingual term pair. Keep aliases empty, default density null, unit mappings and forms empty, and do not generalize the Saskatchewan whole-grain description, derive grain-to-flour yields, or add measurements, conversions, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: P. J. Barnes, Composition of cereal germ preparations
sources.locator: Abstract; triticale germ preparation and food-ingredient potential.
sources.supports: The primary study names triticale among the cereals whose germ fractions were prepared by impact milling and evaluated for potential food-ingredient use. The study also notes high linolenic-acid content in its rye and triticale germ samples, which could lead to oxidation problems. Supports a research-prepared triticale germ fraction only; its preparation and sample-specific findings do not establish retail prevalence, a standardized milling or purity specification, a kitchen measure, storage guidance, or substitution.

sources.title: OQLF, triticale (GDT)
sources.locator: GDT triticale entry; preferred French base name.
sources.supports: Supports only the French base name triticale and its English equivalent. It does not attest the descriptive compound germe de triticale or define this cereal-germ fraction.

decisions.reason: Accept identity-only triticale germ as a generic cereal fraction explicitly prepared and evaluated for potential food use in the primary study. Keep it distinct from triticale grain, bran, flakes, flour, sprouted grain, and other cereal germs. The French compound germe de triticale is a provisional descriptive display; OQLF supports the base cereal term only. Keep the study preparation and oxidation observations tied to its samples. Add no aliases, form, recipe link, measure, density, unit mapping, conversion, yield, or substitution.

sources.title: CFIA, List of Grains and Field Crops
sources.locator: Cereals list, entries for Triticosecale spp. / Triticale and Eragrostis (= Poa) abyssinica / Teff
sources.supports: Lists triticale and teff as cereal crops and supplies their English common names. Supports cereal-category placement and names only; this is a crop list, not an edible-product specification.

sources.title: ACIA, Liste de grains et grandes cultures
sources.locator: Section Céréales, entries Triticosecale spp. / Triticale and Eragrostis (= Poa) abyssinica / Teff d’Abyssinie
sources.supports: Lists the same cereal species under the French names triticale and teff d’Abyssinie. Supports French display wording and category placement; the list does not define consumer product forms.

sources.title: Government of Saskatchewan, Triticale: Production and Use
sources.locator: Utilization and Milling and Baking sections
sources.supports: Identifies triticale as a small-grain cereal, states that grain has a growing human-food market, and describes whole-grain triticale flour used in food products. The page also describes feed, silage, and forage; those uses are excluded from the ingredient identity.

sources.title: Usito, triticale
sources.locator: Definition and metonymic sense for the grains and flour
sources.supports: Current Québec French dictionary defines triticale as a cereal grass from wheat and rye and uses the same term for its grains and flour. Supports the French name and that it is distinct from wheat and rye.

sources.title: Santé Canada, Blé et triticale - Allergènes alimentaires prioritaires
sources.locator: Sections identifying triticale as a priority food allergen and defining it as a wheat-rye hybrid
sources.supports: Confirms triticale is recognized in Canadian food labeling as a food ingredient and defines the crop boundary. Notes it is not usually offered on the market; this limits prevalence claims but does not make the food identity a feed identity.

decisions.reason: Accept food triticale grain / triticale as a GRAIN_AND_CEREAL identity distinct from wheat, rye, flour, feed grain, silage, and forage. Use the current Québec French spelling supported by Usito and CFIA; add no aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, yields, conversions, or substitutions.

sources.title: General Mills Canada, Trix
sources.locator: Current Canadian English product page, product name, description, and product image
sources.supports: Identifies Trix as a finished cereal and describes six shapes of crispy puffs with fruit flavours. The 14 g whole-grain statement is not the total serving mass or volume.

sources.title: General Mills Canada, Trix (French-Canadian page)
sources.locator: French-Canadian product page, product name and description
sources.supports: Calls Trix “la céréale” and describes its crispy fruit-shaped puffs. This supports a descriptive French display but is not an OQLF terminology ruling or an exact retailer product heading.

sources.title: Metro Québec, Céréales en forme de fruits, Trix
sources.locator: Product title, 303 g package, product number 065633150836, and ingredient declaration
sources.supports: Lists the named Trix cereal as Céréales en forme de fruits, Trix, 303 g, product number 065633150836, and declares a formulated ingredient list. Retailer wording supports the product-specific French name; package mass is not a kitchen measure and the formula may change.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only Trix cereal / Céréales Trix for the named Canadian finished cereal. Keep it separate from fruit, corn, rice flour, puffed grains, and other cereal identities. Use descriptive French product wording without claiming an OQLF ruling. Do not add brand or fruit-shape aliases, component links, a measure, form, density, mapping, conversion, recipe link, yield, or substitution. Metro’s 303 g package and General Mills’ 14 g whole-grain statement are not total serving measures.

sources.title: CaviarHub, Oeufs de truite - caviar rouge
sources.locator: Product title, qualified alternate name, serving guide, and product-specific description.
sources.supports: Supports œufs de truite and caviar de truite wording; lists 50 g and 100 g formats and a seller guide of 50 g for 1–2 people and 100 g for 2–4. Species, origin, processing, and guide remain SKU-specific.

sources.title: CaviarHub, Trout Roe
sources.locator: Product title and alternate term.
sources.supports: Supports trout roe and trout caviar wording on the English page for the same seller product; its flavor comparison to salmon roe gives no recipe role or replacement ratio.

sources.title: CaviarHub, Caviar & fish roe delivery in Québec City
sources.locator: Québec City delivery product listing.
sources.supports: Lists the trout-roe product for delivery to Québec City; retailer offer does not guarantee province-wide or continuing availability.

sources.title: Oysters & Caviar Montréal, Trout Roe
sources.locator: Product description, origin, species, package options, and availability.
sources.supports: Identifies a separate retailer SKU as Oncorhynchus mykiss with Germany origin and 50 g/100 g options; page was sold out at access. Facts are not generalized to the identity.

sources.title: SAIL, Œufs de truite — Pautzke
sources.locator: Product category and use description.
sources.supports: Identifies a trout-eggs item under fishing lures and use in spawn netting; this is bait and is excluded as human-food identity evidence.

sources.title: OQLF, GDT: truite arc-en-ciel
sources.locator: Species entry and Québec commercial context.
sources.supports: Identifies rainbow trout as Oncorhynchus mykiss and describes the Québec commercial context; it does not identify the species of generic trout-roe listings.

sources.title: OQLF, GDT: caviar
sources.locator: Definition and note on caviar made from non-sturgeon fish eggs.
sources.supports: Supports qualifying caviar by the fish name when the eggs are not from sturgeon; supports caviar de truite as a qualified expression, not bare caviar.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: CaviarHub trout roe, seller guide for 1–2 people
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Seller-specific guide suggests 50 g for 1–2 people; not a general serving standard.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Retailer-published serving guide.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: CaviarHub trout roe, seller guide for 2–4 people
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: Seller-specific guide suggests 100 g for 2–4 people; not a general serving standard.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Retailer-published serving guide.

substitutionFindings.context: Reviewed CaviarHub’s description of salmon roe as a more intense alternative to its trout roe product.
substitutionFindings.basis: The retailer gives a flavor comparison but no dish context, quantity ratio, adjustment, or outcome for replacing trout roe in a recipe.

Do not infer reciprocal substitution or interchangeability among trout roe, salmon roe, tobiko, masago, lumpfish roe, bottarga, milt, sturgeon caviar, or uni.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only trout roe / œufs de truite with the qualified aliases trout caviar and caviar de truite. Keep the identity species-neutral and exclude bait, seller-specific processing, package sizes, and generic roe/caviar terms. Record only the CaviarHub serving suggestions as source-specific portion observations; add no reusable measure, density, unit mapping, form, conversion, yield, recipe link, or active substitution.

sources.title: Brazil Ministry of Health, Alimentos regionais brasileiros, 2nd ed.
sources.locator: North-region, TUCUPI, p. 96
sources.supports: Describes tucupi as a partially fermented sauce made from manipueira, the liquid separated during cassava-flour production, after starch settles and is removed; seasonings are added later. It documents culinary use in tacacá and with meat. The source also names tucupi-doce for one white-cassava product, whose alias/product boundary remains unresolved. No measurement or food-safety instruction is activated.

sources.title: Brazil Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture, Aprenda como fazer o tradicional Tacacá
sources.locator: Tacacá description and ingredient/component sections
sources.supports: Describes tucupi as seasoned bitter-cassava broth used in North-Brazil tacacá and lists it separately from goma de mandioca, jambu, and dried shrimp. This recipe supports the ingredient identity and culinary role, not a universal formulation or product standard.

decisions.reason: Add tucupi / tucupi as a distinct SAUCE_AND_CONDIMENT identity. Keep it separate from raw manipueira, cassava flour, tapioca starch, cassava gum, and Guyanese cassareep. Do not add manipueira or tucupi-doce as aliases; add no form, measurement, density, conversion, substitution, or recipe link.

The French display remains provisional pending independent Québec terminology review, and the source term tucupi-doce needs a product-boundary review before it can be treated as an alias or separate identity.

sources.title: Anova Culinary, Sous Vide Tuna
sources.locator: Ingredients for 4, tuna-steak line
sources.supports: States two tuna steaks, about 1 1/2 to 2 inches thick, at 10-12oz. / 280-320g each. Does not identify species, trim, skin/bone status, or edible-versus-as-purchased basis.

decisions.reason: Record the Anova recipe's two printed per-steak ranges as separate source-reported mass intervals. Preserve the stated thickness and one-steak basis, printed units and precision, and unknown endpoint semantics. Species, trim, skin/bone state, and edible-versus-as-purchased basis are unstated. Do not derive a midpoint, convert between the co-reported ranges, or activate a mapping, density, package yield, recipe edit, or substitution.

valueIntervals.unitConvention: avoirdupois mass ounce; not fluid ounce

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Tuna steaks, about 1 1/2 to 2 inches thick
measurementObservations.foodState: Listed as an ingredient before sous-vide cooking and searing; species, trim, skin/bone state, and edible-versus-as-purchased basis are not stated.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: Recipe ingredient list for four; its one line assigns each of two steaks the printed ranges.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One steak, as stated by "each"; not scaled from the four-serving yield and not a cooking-yield measure.

sources.title: Bolivia, Ministerio de Desarrollo Productivo y Economía Plural, Industria Papa El Alto
sources.locator: 2024, presentation pp. 21–23 and chapter I, printed p. 27
sources.supports: Describes chuño and tunta as naturally dehydrated potato products; calls chuño negro “normal,” distinguishes it from whitish chuño tunta, and describes a culinary use. Government overview, not a full production standard or recipe.

sources.title: De Haan et al., Traditional processing of black and white chuño in the Peruvian Andes
sources.locator: Economic Botany 64(3), 2010, repository abstract and citation
sources.supports: Research abstract distinguishes black chuño processing from the more complex white chuño process involving water and notes regional variants. Abstract is not a universal process specification.

sources.title: Arcos and Holguín, Variedades de papas nativas con aptitud para procesamiento en tunta
sources.locator: INIA / EEA-Illpa, 2010, pp. 65–66, section BG3
sources.supports: Names chuño negro, chuño blanco (tunta), and moraya; reports one Puno field process for white chuño/tunta. Its variable wording does not settle moraya’s cross-regional synonym status.

sources.title: INACAL, Inacal aprobó norma técnica para impulsar buenas prácticas de procesamiento artesanal de la tunta
sources.supports: Summarizes the Peruvian artisanal-processing standard and describes tunta as a white potato product with successive freezing, river-water immersion, and sun drying. The summary is not a Québec naming authority.

sources.title: INACAL, Inacal: conoce los requisitos de calidad en el procesamiento de la papa y sus derivados
sources.locator: 2022-05-30, section on NTP 011.802:2017 and papa seca
sources.supports: Summarizes a Peru-specific papa seca route that selects, washes, peels, cooks, cuts, and dries potato; supports product-boundary comparison, not a universal definition.

sources.title: Peru Compras, Resolución Jefatural N.° 063-2019, El Peruano
sources.locator: 2019-06-27, p. 34, technical sheet title “Tunta o Chuño Blanco”
sources.supports: Approves a technical sheet under the commodity name Tunta o Chuño Blanco. Supports this source-specific name pairing, not universal regional use.

sources.title: Programa Nacional Cuna Más, Directiva de Adquisición de Alimentos
sources.locator: RDE 002229-2024-DE, 2024-11, non-perishable foods list
sources.supports: Lists papa seca separately from Papa Deshidratada (tunta o moraya o chuño). This procurement grouping is not proof of universal equivalence among the grouped products.

sources.title: Instituto Nacional de Salud del Perú, Tablas Peruanas de Alimentos
sources.supports: Separately lists papa chuño negro, moraya, papa seca, potato flour, black-chuño flour, and moraya flour; entries establish product labels but not processing equivalence or recipe instructions.

sources.title: FAO, Racines, tubercules, plantains et bananes dans l’alimentation humaine
sources.locator: 1990, French chapter on potato processing
sources.supports: French technical text distinguishes chuño blanco, chuño negro, and papa seca by process and gives culinary contexts. Supports retaining source-language product names in French, not a Québec-specific term.

sources.title: FAO, International Cookbook for Quinoa: Tradition and innovation
sources.locator: 2014, p. 49, quinoa and lamb broth recipe
sources.supports: English ingredient list names white chuño (tunta) for one Peruvian recipe. Supports the English gloss and a specific use, not a claim that all chuño is white chuño.

sources.title: Office québécois de la langue française, GDT entries pomme de terre and amidon
sources.locator: Entries for pomme de terre and amidon; targeted lookups for chuño/chuno/tunta
sources.supports: Confirms Québec French terms for potato and starch; targeted chuño/chuno/tunta lookups did not surface an entry. Limited negative search result, not proof no accepted term exists.

sources.title: Perú Travel, La Carapulcra
sources.locator: Ingredient list and preparation steps for papa seca
sources.supports: Names papa seca as a distinct recipe ingredient and instructs to toast, cool, wash, soak, and drain it before cooking in carapulcra. This is one official tourism recipe, not a product standard; its quantities and preparation sequence are not adopted as universal data.

decisions.reason: Add tunta (white chuño) / tunta (chuño blanco) as a distinct VEGETABLE_AND_AROMATIC whole-tuber product identity. The source evidence supports tunta paired with chuño blanco but not a global alias for plain chuño or moraya. Keep it separate from black chuño, papa seca, generic potato, flour, and starch. Add no aliases, forms, density, unit mappings, measurements, conversions, substitutions, or recipe links.

sources.title: OQLF, sucre turbinado
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp02-cane-sweeteners-boundary-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.
sources.supports: Gives preferred French terms sucre turbinado and sucre demerara in one entry and describes crystal-size variants. This conflicts with distinct trade/product naming; ambiguity is retained.

sources.title: Canadian Sugar Institute, Les types de sucre au Canada
sources.locator: Source-to-claim map in docs/catalog/proposals/wp02-cane-sweeteners-boundary-review-20261009.md; evidence scope retained in supports.

Keep the wider CFIA Gluten Flour class distinct as an unresolved equivalence question; do not create another reference or broaden the existing specific aliases. CFIA defines the class by partial starch removal and sets moisture and starch limits without a protein minimum or vitality test. Codex distinguishes vital, devitalized, and solubilized wheat-protein products by hydrated function and composition, while OQLF defines farine de gluten without specifying vital properties. The Canadian Bob's Red Mill product links the name Gluten Flour to vital wheat gluten on that SKU only; the separate Québec Artisan Tradition listing gives no composition. Add no new alias, form, reusable measure, density, mapping, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

sources.supports: Accepts T. fruticosum, lists T. triangulare as a synonym, records water leaf among English common-name data under the synonym, and gives the native range as tropical and subtropical America. Taxonomic evidence only; not African food-use or Québec naming evidence.

sources.title: FAO, Food Composition Table for Use in Africa, Talinum entry

sources.title: Kwenin, Wolli, and Dzomeku, Assessing the nutritional value of some African indigenous green leafy vegetables in Ghana, Journal of Animal & Plant Sciences 10(2), 2011

sources.supports: Identifies water leaf (Bokoboko) as T. triangulare and as a food leaf sampled in Ghana’s Ashanti Region, separately from cocoyam leaves, amaranth, and moringa. The paper’s indigenous wording is not used as a botanical-origin claim; its nutritional values do not support recipe conversions.

sources.supports: Uses waterleaf / water-leaf for Hydrophyllum and French hydrophylle. This is a Canadian botanical homonym boundary, not an identity or French translation for edible Talinum.

sources.title: Green Focus Farms / Les Fermes Fondi, Water leaf Frais

sources.supports: Metadata/search title includes Waterleaf (Gbure / Feuilles d’eau); rendered French title and copy use Water leaf / water leaf and identify T. triangulare with Nigerian and Cameroonian cooking contexts. Supports direct Canadian food naming, not a Québec terminology ruling. The metadata phrase Feuilles d’eau remains retailer-specific; package choices and sold-out status do not support conversions or current general availability.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only waterleaf / water leaf for edible leaves of Talinum fruticosum, using the accepted Kew name and keeping T. triangulare as a synonym alias. Regional food sources and current Canadian African-food retail support the bounded identity. Keep Feuilles d’eau and other regional names as evidence only; the French display is a provisional borrowed retail name pending Québec terminology review. Add no forms, measures, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

sources.title: Cereals & Grains Association, Aleurone
sources.locator: Approved definition (2010): cereal aleurone tissue location and separation boundary.
sources.supports: Supports the outer-endosperm tissue boundary and general milling separation of cereal aleurone from germ and starchy endosperm. The definition is not a wheat-specific retail grade, purity threshold, kitchen measure, or health claim.

sources.title: Fenech et al., Aleurone flour is a rich source of bioavailable folate in humans
sources.locator: Abstract: human cereal study using cereal made from isolated wheat aleurone flour.
sources.supports: Identifies wheat aleurone flour prepared from isolated wheat aleurone cells and used to make cereal in a human-food study. The 100 g amount is cereal, not aleurone flour; trial servings and outcomes remain study-specific.

sources.title: Fenech et al., Aleurone flour increases red-cell folate and lowers plasma homocyst(e)ine substantially in man
sources.locator: Abstract: controlled intervention using bread made with aleurone flour.
sources.supports: Documents aleurone flour in bread consumed in a human-food study. The 175 g bread portion, study ingredients, and clinical outcomes stay scoped to that trial; they establish no flour measure or general use level.

sources.locator: Abstract: distinguishes minimally processed wheat bran and wheat aleurone fractions and reports an aleurone-bread study.
sources.supports: Supports distinction between the wheat bran and aleurone fractions and the food use of aleurone in bread. Trial preparations, servings, and results remain source-specific and provide no generic measure or substitution.

decisions.reason: Add identity-only wheat aleurone flour / farine d’aleurone de blé for the isolated wheat aleurone fraction used in human-food studies. Keep it distinct from wheat bran, wheat bran flour, wheat germ, and other cereal aleurone fractions. The French display is descriptive and provisional.
Human-food study servings and bread formulas are not reusable flour measures; no household volume, density, mapping, conversion, or yield is supported.
Food-use trials do not establish a general replacement for wheat flour, bran, germ, or other ingredients.

decisions.reason: Canadian sources distinguish wheat meal from ordinary wheat flour and durum semolina, but the evidence does not establish a sufficiently precise consumer ingredient boundary or a Québec French name for wheat meal alone. The current tariff groups wheat meal with groats and semolina under `gruaux et semoules de froment (blé)`; generic `semoule de blé` would overlap the existing durum-semolina identities. Keep this as a research candidate and do not add an active reference or alias until a specific product/process definition and independently supportable bilingual name are established. No measurement or substitution evidence is inferred.

Add whole wheat meal / farine de blé entier brute as a narrowly scoped FLOUR_AND_STARCH identity. A live manufacturer defines its whole-kernel milling boundary, while OQLF independently supports the Québec French name and English translation. Keep bare wheat meal, groats, cracked wheat, wheat bran, whole-wheat flour, and durum semolina distinctions intact. Do not activate the coarse whole wheat flour alias because it overlaps the existing whole wheat flour picker query; do not add whole grain wheat meal without independent terminology support. No density, unit mapping, form, measurement, conversion, yield, or substitution data is inferred.

Recheck current Canadian and Québec product evidence. Current listings and ingredient labels use the explicitly qualified whole wheat meal name; a historical Québec package is described as cracked-wheat cereal/meal. These examples reinforce the narrow whole-wheat-meal scope but do not establish one generic wheat-meal consumer product or a standalone Québec French name. Keep the existing whole-wheat-meal identity scoped, keep unqualified wheat meal out of the active catalog and aliases, and add no measurements, forms, conversions, yields, recipe links, or substitutions.

Keep Backschrot 1700 as a distinct unresolved wheat-grind candidate. German sources list it separately from ordinary wheat-flour types and wholegrain, and distinguish Schrot as coarser than Mehl. The evidence does not establish a Québec French consumer name or equivalence to the active whole-wheat-meal identity. Do not add it as an active reference or alias and infer no measurement or substitution.

R22 rechecked current Canadian product, terminology, regulatory, and trade evidence. The manufacturer and retailer examples remain explicitly whole wheat meal; OQLF names the whole-wheat product; CFIA and the Canadian Importers Database use unqualified wheat meal in broad bread-ingredient or trade classifications without defining a standalone consumer milling boundary or a Québec French name. Keep the existing whole-wheat-meal reference narrowly scoped and keep bare wheat meal unresolved, inactive, and out of its aliases. Add no form, measurement, conversion, yield, recipe link, or substitution.

R104 rechecked the bare wheat meal and closed wheatmeal spellings against current Canadian food standards, tariff classifications, and human-food statistics. These sources recognize the terms but do not establish one consumer milling boundary or Québec French name; the tariff's 1.25-mm rule groups groats and meal and is not a kitchen grind specification. OQLF and current product evidence support only the narrower whole-wheat-meal identity. Keep both generic spellings unresolved, do not add aliases, and leave the verified identity state scoped to the active whole-wheat row.

R674 reviewed a current source lead with a published amount and formula-specific all-purpose-flour alternative, but the recipe calls its ingredient “whole wheat/meal flour” without specifying a coarse meal grade. Keep the source as a scoped research lead on the existing whole-wheat-meal record, set measurement and substitution research to blocked pending a grade match, and add no observation or active replacement rule.

sources.title: Alvarez et al., Sugar reduction and replacement of wheat flour with quinoa flour in shortcrust cookies: effects on nutritional, physical, and sensory properties
sources.versionOrDate: Food Production, Processing and Nutrition 7, article 72 (2025); DOI 10.1186/s43014-025-00323-2
sources.locator: Abstract and Materials and Methods, Raw Materials and Manufacture of Cookies; Tables 1 and 6.
sources.supports: Primary study tests 15% and 30% wheat-flour replacement with a named Blanca de Juli quinoa flour from RENACER S.A.C. in shortcrust cookies with separately varied sugar reduction. It does not identify the flour as Tootsi product 31501 or support a general replacement rule.

decisions.reason: Accepted white quinoa flour as a distinct color-qualified milling identity. The Québec and Canadian product labels support farine de quinoa blanc; keep it separate from generic quinoa flour and add no aliases or numeric behavior.

Record Tootsi's 1/4 cup (40 g) Nutrition Facts portion as product-specific evidence for code 31501. It does not establish a reusable measurement for the existing white-quinoa-flour reference, so keep active density and unit mappings empty and make no substitution or package-yield change.

Complete the deferred substitution review by recording Tootsi's up-to-25% product guidance as a blocked, source-scoped finding. The named base flour, ratio basis, and recipe scope are not established, and studies of other quinoa flours are formulation-specific. Keep active substitution behavior and all catalog data unchanged.

measurementObservations.foodDescription: Tootsi organic white quinoa flour, supplier product code 31501, described as finely ground white quinoa seeds.
measurementObservations.foodState: Flour as sold in the named product listing.
measurementObservations.measurementMethod: The supplier's Nutrition Facts panel reports 1/4 cup (40 g); neither language page gives a cup capacity, filling/compaction method, or independent weighing procedure.
measurementObservations.quantityBasis: One product-specific Nutrition Facts portion for Tootsi code 31501 only. Do not transfer it to generic, roasted, red, or black quinoa flour, and do not derive an active density or unit mapping.

sourceQuantity.unitConvention: Source-stated 1/4 cup; cup capacity and filling method are unspecified.

substitutionFindings.context: Tootsi product 31501 states that its white quinoa flour can replace up to 25% of flour in recipes; determine whether this can be represented as a reusable replacement for the catalog reference.
substitutionFindings.basis: The Tootsi English and French product pages identify the same product and repeat the same manufacturer advice. They name no source flour, do not define the percentage denominator or mass/volume basis, and give no recipe-type, method, or adjustment limits. Wang et al. test multiple quinoa-to-wheat ratios across cookies, bread, and Chinese steamed bread and report product-type-dependent effects. Alvarez et al. test a separate RENACER Blanca de Juli flour in shortcrust cookies at 15% and 30% wheat-flour replacement, with outcomes also depending on sugar reduction. Neither study matches Tootsi 31501.
limitations: Retain the up-to-25% statement as Tootsi product 31501 guidance only; it does not name the flour to replace or define an enforceable replacement pair.
Do not assume the percentage is by mass or volume or derive a recipe amount from the separate R734 nutrition portion.
The studies use other quinoa-flour materials and specified formulations; do not transfer their ratios or outcomes to Tootsi 31501 or to unqualified home recipes.
No matching bundled recipe line exists, and the current rule model cannot express the unnamed product-specific base flour and broad recipe scope.

sources.title: Švec and Hrušková, Characteristics of Bread and Biscuit Made With Wheat and Rice Flour Composites
sources.versionOrDate: Journal of Food Technology Research 1(2), 2014, 156–163; DOI 10.18488/journal.58/2014.1.2/58.2.156.163
sources.locator: Abstract and reported wheat/rice composite bread and biscuit results.
sources.supports: The study examines 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30% white-rice-flour replacement in wheat-flour composite products. decisions.reason: Accepted white rice flour as a distinct source-grade flour identity. Manufacturer product names and the milled-without-bran source grain distinguish it from brown rice flour and the unqualified rice-flour family entry. Complete bounded measurement and wheat-replacement research for the existing white-rice-flour identity. Record Bob’s Red Mill’s 1/4 cup (40 g) product label and the manufacturer chart’s 1 cup (160 g) row only as named-product observations; do not infer an identity-wide measure, density, or mapping. Study outcomes are formula-specific and do not support an active substitution. Keep brown, glutinous, generic rice flour, and white rice grain distinct; add no aliases, forms, conversions, yields, or recipe links.

substitutionFindings.basis: The study reports formula-specific bread changes, including bread volume falling from 319 to 154 ml/100 g at 30% and lower crumb acceptability above 20%; biscuit effects were smaller and varied by level. limitations: Do not encode the tested percentages, water adjustments, loaf effects, or biscuit outcomes as general substitution guidance.

Complete the still-open substitution-evidence review for white whole-wheat flour with King Arthur Baking's direct, partial replacement guidance. Complete the measurement and general wheat-flour replacement research for the existing whole-barley-flour identity. The Whole Grain Stamp's 40 g figure is whole-grain content per serving, GoBarley's 37 g flour portion is for pearled barley, and its whole-barley pancake recipe gives no mass equivalent. substitutionFindings.context: Unscoped replacement of wheat flour with whole barley flour in home recipes.

limitations: The 20% and 40% biscuit formulas and the 80% wholegrain-barley / 20% wheat bread formula are study-specific, not general replacement ratios.
